#1. The Sustainable Traveler Is More Mainstream Than the Industry Thinks

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: A trio of travelers during a hike.  Unsplash / NEOM

There's a widespread misconception about travelers looking for sustainable options. Rather than being vanishingly rare earnest eco-seekers, there are part of the mainstream and often pragmatic in their choices.

Travel often pictures the sustainable traveler as part of an earnest tribe that books the eco-lodge and pays a green surcharge. Our evidence strongly suggests this is a misconception. Skift’s research with 74,000 travel consumers in the top 40 outbound markets shows 77% believe travel should benefit communities and the environment, and 24% go further, actively seeking sustainable options and accepting trade-offs to get them.

First, let’s rewind. A 2021 Skift/EarthCheck study found 62% of travelers across 11 surveyed markets were actively seeking out responsible operators, and a third were ready to pay 10% or more for green certification. Saudi and Chinese travelers led this responsible movement with close to 80% taking that approach. Five years on the signal is, if anything, stronger. Today,70% of trave

Skift's research with 74,000 travel consumers across the top 40 outbound markets finds that sustainable travel is not confined to a small, earnest niche: 77% say travel should benefit communities and the environment, 70% say they prioritize destinations and businesses committed to sustainability, and 24% actively seek sustainable options and accept trade-offs to get them. The data also complicates the familiar say-do gap. Across Skift's seven traveler segments, Culture Seekers rate themselves below average on feeling responsible — 68% against a 73% average — yet 57% get around by public transport, the highest of any segment. Connoisseurs say more and ride less: 88% feel responsible, 44% will pay for premium, and only 38% use public transport, while 25% want a business-class seat. As Skift reads it, one segment lowers what tourism costs a place and the other raises what it earns. Together the two account for roughly 169 million outbound leisure trips a year, about one in four. The guidance for operators is to match the archetype to the destination's problem — Culture Seekers for crowded gateways and peak seasons, Connoisseurs for fragile assets and limited capacity — with DMOs, hotels, and investors in a place backing the same archetype.

#2. United, Air Canada Add Transborder Routes After Renewing Partnership

United and Air Canada will strengthen connectivity between their home countries next year with six new routes and more flights on some existing city-pairs.

Air Canada said Friday that it has renewed its Transborder Joint Business Agreement with United, which currently supports more than 1,200 connecting itineraries. Since 2022, the pact has added 20 routes between the U.S. and Canada; the new connections would also operate under that agreement.

Air Canada said it will launch service between Toronto and Louisville, Kentucky; between Montreal and Indianapolis; and between Edmonton and Newark, New Jersey.

The carrier does not currently serve Louisville. The connection to Toronto will be Louisville’s only international service.

Toronto-Louisville will run from April to October, Montreal-Indianapolis from June to September, and Edmonton-Newark from June to October.

The airline will also increase capacity between Edmonton and San Francisco by deploying the larger Airbus A220 on the route.

United will launch new seasonal service to St. John’s, Newfoundland, from Newark, and add connections from Denver to Ottawa and Quebec City. It will also increase flights between Washington, D.C., and Quebec City, and increase daily seats between Denver and Winnipeg by 65%.

Start dates for the United routes were not immediately available.

“Canada is an incredibly important part of United’s international network, and our partnership with Air Canada has made it easier for families and friends to stay connected, supported economic growth, and created new opportunities to explore unique destinations,” United Senior Vice President of Global Network Planning and Alliances Patrick Quayle said in a news release. “Our schedule has grown every year since our transborder agreement was signed in 2022, and the new routes and flights we’re announcing today further underscore our commitment to investing in Canada and making travel between our two countries easier.”

Delta Air Lines now has Wi-Fi service available throughout nearly every flight — including its longest service to Asia, Australia and the South Pacific.

The Atlanta-based carrier on Tuesday announced it had closed its “last coverage gap” over the Pacific Ocean, thanks to a new satellite that just came online in the last week.

Delta also said it had equipped more than 95% of its planes with the tech to support free Wi-Fi for every customer — a rollout that’s expected to wrap up in the next few months.

In a lot of ways, it’s a milestone that’s years in the making.

Back in early 2023, Delta kickstarted an industry trend when it announced plans to make Wi-Fi service free to all members of its loyalty program.

Most major U.S. airlines have done the same since then.

Yet, despite upgrading Wi-Fi tech across its fleet — and outfitting nearly 1,300 planes with the complimentary service — Delta’s on-board internet has drawn plenty of scrutiny, of late.

Over the past few weeks, headlines have swirled about Delta’s decision not to upgrade its fleet with Starlink service, which today is generally viewed as the fastest Wi-Fi in the sky.

All of Delta’s biggest competitors have either begun moving over to Starlink — or plan to.

That includes top rival United Airlines, which has talked up its Wi-Fi in a pointed status match offer meant to tempt longtime Delta flyers to switch their loyalties.

It’s probably not the backdrop Delta envisioned in January 2020, when it first laid out its vision of free web-browsing for all.

But the carrier insists it’s not falling behind in the increasingly competitive race by airlines to win customers with the promise of home-like internet at 35,000 feet.

“Global full coverage at scale — whether you’re on a regional jet or an [Airbus] A350 going to Sydney or Melbourne or Auckland — and having that on almost 1,300 airplanes? That is something that is very unique in today’s world,” Ranjan Goswami, Delta’s chief marketing and product officer, told TPG.

“That’s a milestone we have,” Goswami added, “that will take others some time to get there.”

Delta also argues its existing Wi-Fi is getting faster.

The carrier is in the process of moving planes over to Wi-Fi service powered by a new satellite from its top provider, Viasat, which is expected to significantly boost on-board bandwidth — and reduce slowdowns reported by customers earlier this year.

That switchover — which so far has drawn “very positive” reviews, Delta says — is expected to be complete on North and South America flights by Thanksgiving.

Delta is also wrapping up Wi-Fi upgrades on its fleet of regional jets and smaller Boeing 717s.

Together, Goswami says, these changes should offer a noticeably better experience for passengers in the near future.

“You’re going to see a demonstrable improvement on overall bandwidth to the airplane,” he said. “Those are improvements literally happening right now.”

Beyond that, Delta also has long-term plans to upgrade its Wi-Fi tech further.

Earlier this year, the carrier became the largest in the world to sign on to new service from Amazon, which is designed to offer a web-surfing experience similar to what Starlink users find today.

The other? It won’t begin appearing on Delta planes until 2028.

In the meantime, United has already installed Starlink on 43% of its jets, according to a real-time tracker the carrier published last week — itself a sign of how competitive the airline industry’s “Wi-Fi race” has gotten.

Alaska Airlines is also about 40% of the way complete with Starlink installations.

And Southwest Airlines last week said it expects to have its whole fleet outfitted with the tech before either of those two carriers.

Each of those airlines plans to offer the service free to members of their loyalty programs, matching the policy Delta once made the industry standard — but with connectivity that will arguably be better than what Delta has today.

Goswami, for his part, says he’s “not worried,” pointing to Delta’s global coverage that virtually guarantees connectivity whether you’re flying from Los Angeles to Sydney— or from Atlanta to Dayton.

Of course, United soon will be able to offer the same breadth of connectivity. American, too.

Still, Goswami expressed confidence — not only in Delta’s future plans with Amazon — but also in the Wi-Fi network the airline has nearly finished installing.

“It’s like repainting the Golden Gate Bridge,” he said. “When you finish repainting, you start painting again because you have to start over. But the beauty here is, this is based off of a really solid foundation.”

#4. American Airlines Could Order Up To 70 Long Haul Jets This Week—Making A Bigger Bet On Business Class And Asia

American Airlines could announce its next widebody aircraft order as soon as this week – after close of business Wednesday, but most likely early Thursday morning before markets open alongside their quarterly earnings release. The airline has been shopping for new long haul planes for months. Now the question is whether they’ll buy aircraft that fit the network they’ve been running, or commit to something more ambitious. I’ve argued that the Airbus A330-900 makes the most sense because of their routes, availability of the planes, and cost. But I wouldn’t dismiss an A350 order, including the much larger A350-1000, if American gets the right price and intends to fill the plane with a lot more premium seats. Aviation watchdog JonNYC has discussed an announcement around earnings or the employee meeting afterward. Chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Cranky Flier that he expects a deal within the next couple of months, describing another 50, 60 or 70 aircraft arriving from 2030 onward. Up to 65 planes was reported in September. And that could be split between firm orders and options. I’m also hearing that American has been looking at the Boeing 787-9 and 787-10, along with the Airbus A350-900 and A350-1000 – and not the A330-900. This comes from someone who’s shared accurate information with me before, but I don’t vouch for this specifically. Pieper Wants A Different Long Haul Network My case for the A330-900 has been that much of its flying is across the Atlantic or down to South America. They don’t need the largest aircraft or the most range, and Airbus could make the economics attractive enough to overcome the cost of adding another fleet. Pieper himself just called the A330 family the “perfect Atlantic airplane.” So there’s still a case for buying those planes, putting them on suitable Europe and South America routes, and freeing up 787s for longer flying. But Pieper also wants Los Angeles to become American’s Pacific gateway again. The 787-9 can do much of this already. How I’d Think About The Aircraft Much of the published analysis has favored the 787 or A330. I’d look at the candidates this way: Airbus A330-900: Still a sensible workhorse for much of American’s existing network. A lower purchase price or better delivery positions would be the reasons to choose the plane, while leaving the longest Pacific missions to the 787s. Boeing 787-9: The easiest choice since American already has the pilots and maintenance operation. It can add routes without committing to the largest aircraft on each departure. Boeing 787-10: I’ve been skeptical of buying too much capacity. It offers more space while retaining much of the existing 787 operation’s commonality. That’s attractive on substantial Atlantic and South America routes, even if it isn’t as flexible as the -9 for the longest missions. Airbus A350-900: The less aggressive Airbus choice if American wants more premium cabin space and long haul flexibility. A family order could give American smaller and larger versions for different routes. Airbus A350-1000: The hardest to justify as a blanket replacement for 777-200s. I can see it much more readily as part of a mixed fleet, serving selected routes with substantial premium demand and giving American room to expand its Pacific operation. The 777-300ERs move to Heathrow completely. The Boeing alternatives have also improved. Higher takeoff weights for the 787-9 and 787-10 were certified in March, giving airlines more payload or range. The 777X is tougher. It adds both a very large aircraft and the uncertainty of a new program. Pieper’s preference for letting other airlines work through a new type’s early problems would argue against it. The A350-1000 Case Depends On The Cabin And The Deal Japan Airlines puts just 239 passengers on its A350-1000: six in first class, 54 in business class, 24 in premium economy and 155 in coach. American’s newest premium 787-9s carry 244. American could use the extra floor space for more premium seats, rather than a huge increase in coach passengers. It would still be paying to fly a larger airplane. American would need enough additional premium revenue to justify it, including outside peak travel periods, and potentially without using the plane to Heathrow, if they concentrated their 777-300ER fleet there. A350s then go to Tokyo, Sydney and additional Pacific flying from Los Angeles. The 777-300ER refurbishment brings 70 business class suites and 44 premium economy seats. Meanwhile, putting newer, more fuel-efficient aircraft on longer Pacific flights would give American more flying hours over which to earn back their higher ownership cost if scheduled efficiently. It still doesn’t tell us what plane eventually replaces the 777-200s, though those will be around the fleet for a while since they’re getting new cabin interiors. American’s current widebody fleet is all-Boeing. Airbus could make a really aggressive offer to get back in, and Pieper has said Boeing’s commonality advantage can be overcome economically. Boeing and Airbus have huge order backlogs. It’ll be interesting to see when the new planes they order arrive. Robert Isom has said that backlogs don’t matter, because American Airlines is an important enough customer that airframe manufacturers will find the planes to sell to them. Much of the published analysis has favored the 787 or A330. I’d look at the candidates this way:

Boeing 787-9: The easiest choice since American already has the pilots and maintenance operation. It can add routes without committing to the largest aircraft on each departure.

Airbus A350-900: The less aggressive Airbus choice if American wants more premium cabin space and long haul flexibility. A family order could give American smaller and larger versions for different routes.

Airbus A350-1000: The hardest to justify as a blanket replacement for 777-200s. I can see it much more readily as part of a mixed fleet, serving selected routes with substantial premium demand and giving American room to expand its Pacific operation. The 777-300ERs move to Heathrow completely.

The Boeing alternatives have also improved. Higher takeoff weights for the 787-9 and 787-10 were certified in March, giving airlines more payload or range.

The 777X is tougher. It adds both a very large aircraft and the uncertainty of a new program. Pieper’s preference for letting other airlines work through a new type’s early problems would argue against it.

It would still be paying to fly a larger airplane. American would need enough additional premium revenue to justify it, including outside peak travel periods, and potentially without using the plane to Heathrow, if they concentrated their 777-300ER fleet there. A350s then go to Tokyo, Sydney and additional Pacific flying from Los Angeles. The 777-300ER refurbishment brings 70 business class suites and 44 premium economy seats.

Meanwhile, putting newer, more fuel-efficient aircraft on longer Pacific flights would give American more flying hours over which to earn back their higher ownership cost if scheduled efficiently. It still doesn’t tell us what plane eventually replaces the 777-200s, though those will be around the fleet for a while since they’re getting new cabin interiors.

American’s current widebody fleet is all-Boeing. Airbus could make a really aggressive offer to get back in, and Pieper has said Boeing’s commonality advantage can be overcome economically.

Boeing and Airbus have huge order backlogs. It’ll be interesting to see when the new planes they order arrive. Robert Isom has said that backlogs don’t matter, because American Airlines is an important enough customer that airframe manufacturers will find the planes to sell to them.

New planes wont help with Asian route till service improves

Logic would suggest a mix of new 787s, but since we don’t know the purchase prices and delivery dates, it’s hard to guess. Since their equipment would “work,” Airbus might make AA an offer they can’t refuse.

Will be interesting to see what they officially go with. I’d expect it’ll be all-Boeing, and that the Airbus mention has just been a bargaining chip. That said, I’d be pleasantly surprised if they add a350s.

I’d be glad to see increased capacity to Asia, though I certainly won’t be flying with AA. Give me my miles back, Toby.

#5. Delta’s Free Wi-Fi Rollout Is 95% Complete, But Its Edge Over United Won’t Last Long

In early 2023, Delta Air Lines started introducing free inflight Wi-Fi for SkyMiles members, in partnership with T-Mobile. While the airline was a decade behind JetBlue, this was pretty revolutionary among the “big three” US carriers. Unfortunately the actual rollout of free Wi-Fi didn’t go as fast as planned, and kept getting delayed.

There’s now a positive update, as Delta has shared that the rollout of free Wi-Fi is almost complete, and this latest update is particularly good for long haul travelers.

In February 2023, Delta started slowly rolling out free Wi-Fi for SkyMiles members. This came as part of a project where Delta began installing Viasat Wi-Fi on a vast majority of aircraft, but obviously that doesn’t happen overnight.

So while Delta did a pretty good job of getting free Wi-Fi live on domestic flights, the rollout on long haul flights has been excruciatingly slow. That has left many Delta travelers frustrated, since some long haul flights have had huge coverage gaps.

That brings us to the positive news — Delta has now announced that free Wi-Fi is available on nearly 1,300 aircraft, operating roughly 95% of flights. The latest progress here is that free Wi-Fi is now available on Asia-Pacific routes, possible thanks to Viasat’s new satellites, which should boost coverage and bandwidth.

Delta is now promising full fleet connectivity by early 2027, as coverage extends to remaining Boeing 717s and Delta Connection Embraer regional jets, which are the only fleet types not consistently offering free Wi-Fi.

Delta claims that it now offers free connectivity across its full international network, and calls itself the only global carrier to offer that. I don’t understand how the airline can make those claims, because:

Here’s how Ranjan Goswami, Delta’s Chief Marketing and Product Officer, described this latest development:

“We know how important connectivity is for travelers who want to stay connected wherever they fly, whether you’re traveling for business, reconnecting with family or setting out on a long-awaited trip. Bringing free global Wi-Fi across our international network is an important milestone in making the Delta experience more consistent and connected, especially on some of our longest journeys.”

It’s great to see Delta getting close to wrapping up its free Wi-Fi rollout project. A four year rollout for free Wi-Fi sure is a long timeline. That’s especially true when you consider we were promised free Wi-Fi on all long haul flights by the end of 2024, when the real timeline ended up being nearly two years later. Admittedly these delays have largely been outside of Delta’s control, given that they’re reliant on upgraded technology.

In early 2027, there’s perhaps a brief period where Delta can do a victory lap, and point out how it’s the only one of the “big three” US carriers to offer free Wi-Fi on all flights. However, that will go from a major advantage to a major disadvantage pretty quickly, as Delta and United essentially trade spots on connectivity.

United is in the process of rolling out Starlink Wi-Fi. So far nearly half of planes have Starlink, and the plan is for the project to be completed by the end of 2027. The same is true for Southwest, but I understand Delta wants to compare itself to “global” carriers (just not those outside the US).

Say what you will about Elon Musk (and I have a lot to say, trust me!), but Starlink is in a different league than Viasat when it comes to speeds. While Delta plans to introduce Amazon Leo, which should compete with Starlink, that will only be available in 2028 at the earliest, and Delta has only committed to installing this on 500 aircraft, well under half of its fleet. As many will be aware, this has obviously caused quite the controversy in recent times, especially with comments reportedly made by Delta CEO Ed Bastian.

Here’s what I actually find to be most interesting about Delta’s latest announcement. Historically, we’ve heard airlines offering Viasat Wi-Fi describe it as “fast.” I get how that was maybe accurate back in 2013, when the alternative was systems like OnAir, offering speed that made dial up look lightning fast by comparison.

But nowadays there’s no denying that the average Viasat connection on a plane is anything but high speed. I think it’s noteworthy how Delta’s 2023 announcement about rolling out free Wi-Fi used the word “fast” seven times, while it’s barely mentioned in this announcement. At the very bottom, there is mention of how this “Wi-Fi provides SkyMiles Members with fast, free connectivity,” but that’s it. So I commend Delta for its (increasing?) honesty here.

Delta has announced that its free Wi-Fi rollout is now 95% complete, as the airline has free connectivity on nearly 1,300 aircraft. The expectation is that the remaining planes (Boeing 717s and select Delta Connection Embraer jets) will have free connectivity by early 2027.

The latest update is that Delta now has free Wi-Fi on Asia-Pacific routes, which was without a doubt the biggest gap the carrier had when it came to connectivity. That’s great news, and Delta now claims to have free Wi-Fi on all international flights.

What do you make of Delta’s Wi-Fi rollout progress?

#6. Europe Wants Tourists Beyond Big Cities. AI Search Stands in the Way.

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Left: Dylan Ratigan, Journalist, Author, and Entrepreneur, Reservations.AI; Center: Eduardo Santander, CEO, European Travel Commission; Right: Moderator: Rafat Ali, CEO/Founder, Skift. They spoke at the Skift Transatlantic Summit 2026 in Dublin, Ireland, on October 15, 2026. Skift / Bryan Brophy

Europe’s overtourism fix depends on two systems it doesn’t control: AI search that favors the obvious, and overly complicated transport that discourages the curious from visiting less familiar places.

France wants international visitors to spend €100 billion a year by 2030, up 29% from last year’s level, without adding to the crowds in Paris and its other best-known cities. The plan relies on longer stays, higher spending per night, and more off-peak travel.

France isn't alone. Ireland's tourism policy, published in December, targets a 15% rise in revenue from overseas visitors by 2031. The Netherlands, Spain, and Croatia have also written visitor dispersal into their national strategies.

One obstacle stands in the way. Travelers increasingly pick destinations by asking an AI chatbot, and tourism boards haven't figured out how to get their lesser-known places into the answer.

Another problem: Once a visitor lands at a hub airport, moving on by train, connecting flight, or rental car remains complicated, costly, and largely unprotected if anything goes wrong.

Artificial intelligence could help with both issues. But only if the industry

European destinations are writing visitor dispersal into national tourism policy — France wants international visitor spending to reach €100 billion a year by 2030, a 29% rise on last year, without adding to crowds in Paris, while Ireland targets a 15% increase in overseas visitor revenue by 2031, and the Netherlands, Spain, and Croatia have similar strategies. Speakers at the Skift Transatlantic Summit in Dublin described two obstacles. First, distribution: Google referrals to tourism board sites are falling — Atout France reported a roughly 20% drop in searches ending on its websites — while AI chatbots tend to repeat the same recommendations. Skift Research found that in 29% of persona-destination pairs the models themselves rated a strong fit, the destination was never recommended. Second, logistics: once travelers land at a hub, onward travel by train, connecting flight, or rental car remains complicated, expensive, and largely unprotected when a leg fails. Atout France, Tourism Ireland, and Madrid's tourism board are rebuilding content for AI crawlers and tracking chatbot visibility, and the European Commission's Passenger Package and sustainable tourism strategy aim to address through-ticketing and cross-border car rental. Aer Lingus interim CFO Reid Moody said the vast majority of European demand will still go to big cities in 2030, with change arriving at the margins.

#7. Alaska Airlines Adds Osaka And Tahiti Routes From Seattle, Putting Hawaiian’s A330 Fleet To Work Far From Home

Alaska Airlines is adding nonstop flights from Seattle to Osaka and Tahiti next year, using Hawaiian Airlines Airbus A330s. I welcome both additions, though there is something rather interesting about flying “Hawaiian” between Washington State and Japan or French Polynesia without going anywhere near Hawaii.

Alaska’s Seattle international expansion will include two more routes in 2027:

Both routes are scheduled to use Hawaiian Airlines Airbus A330-200 aircraft.

Credit to Ishrion Aviation for flagging the new routes ahead of any formal announcement by Alaska:

Alaska Airlines to commence 2 new routes:

• Seattle (SEA) to Osaka (KIX) 4 weekly from May 14• Seattle (SEA) to Papeete (PPT) 3 weekly from June 11

Operated with Hawaiian A330. pic.twitter.com/vaqQqXAA6e

— Ishrion Aviation (@IshrionA) October 20, 2026

The Osaka service is scheduled as follows:

All times are local. Scheduled flight time is 11 hours and 50 minutes westbound and 10 hours and 20 minutes eastbound.

Osaka is useful not only for visiting the city itself, but also for reaching Kyoto and the broader Kansai region, a region I hope to finally visit next year. Alaska’s Seattle network should provide connecting traffic beyond the local market, which is one advantage of operating this flight from its largest hub.

The Tahiti service is scheduled as follows:

Scheduled flight time is 10 hours and 25 minutes southbound and 10 hours northbound.

The morning arrival in Tahiti should be useful for travelers continuing to another island, subject to the connecting schedule. For passengers heading to Bora Bora, getting to Papeete is only part of the journey, though Alaska has teased a new partnership Air Tahiti, which just took delivery of brand new all-business class ATR 72-600.

Air Tahiti Nui tried but failed its own Seattle – Papeete route, but did not have the connecting traffic that Alaska Airlines will theoretically be able to offer.

Both new longhaul flights will be operated the A330, which has a 2-2-2 configuration is business class and was originally intended for more leisure routes to Hawaii. Alaska will retrofit these planes starting in 2028, but you can expect a seat like this for now:

> Read More: Hawaiian Airlines A330-200 First Class (LAX-HNL)

One Mile At A Time points out the interesting branding exercise underway at Alaska Air Group.

You will be able to fly from Seattle to Osaka or Tahiti on a Hawaiian aircraft without touching Hawaii. There is nothing inherently wrong with that (Alaska has spent years flying routes that never come close to Alaska).

Still, Hawaiian’s identity is particularly tied to its home. The name, livery, hospitality, and destination have long complemented one another. Seeing that brand deployed between Seattle and Japan is a reminder that these aircraft now serve the priorities of a much larger network.

Commercially, I understand it. Alaska has a substantial connecting hub in Seattle, and Hawaiian brought the widebody aircraft that make this expansion possible.

But it does complicate the explanation of what each brand represents. If Hawaiian is the Hawaii brand and Alaska is the broader international brand, these flights do not fit neatly into that distinction. Passengers will probably care far more about the schedule, fare, seat, and service, but I do have to question the longterm viability of many of the nonstops from Honolulu.

Indeed, the other question is what happens to the existing Honolulu service.

Both Honolulu–Osaka and Honolulu–Tahiti remain on sale. These Seattle additions should therefore be described as additions, not announced replacements…at least for now.

But I do wonder whether both Honolulu routes will remain in their current form over the long term as Alaska works to improve the economics of the Hawaiian operation.

The markets are different. A Japanese traveler visiting Hawaii is not interchangeable with one visiting Seattle. Nor does a Seattle–Tahiti flight replace what is currently the only nonstop between Hawaii and French Polynesia.

There can certainly be a case for serving both hubs. Nevertheless, aircraft time is finite. Alaska will be comparing what an A330 can earn from Honolulu with what it can earn from Seattle, including the connections available at each airport.

A nonstop Seattle flight may also remove some reason for mainland passengers to connect through Honolulu, further depressing yields. Even so, I would not predict that either route is about to disappear. Hawaiian is also planning substantial investment in its Honolulu-based A330 fleet, including new interiors beginning in 2028.

But the overlap does seems a bit redundant so I would not necessarily expect both routes to last indefinitely.

Alaska is adding four weekly Seattle–Osaka flights beginning May 14, 2027, and three weekly Seattle–Tahiti flights beginning June 11, using Hawaiian A330s. Travelers will certainly welcome more options from Seattle and I am interested in how these routes perform. But I will also be watching Honolulu. Alaska can preserve the Hawaiian name while substantially changing where its aircraft fly…and these additions are another example of that evolution.

#8. Lufthansa Adds Munich To Phoenix Flights, The First Lufthansa Group Route To Arizona

Lufthansa has announced plans to add another new destination in the United States. Just yesterday we learned how the airline will add a new route to Columbus, Ohio (CMH), but that’s not the only new market being added. Lufthansa Group will also operate its first-ever route to Arizona!

Lufthansa has announced that as of August 3, 2027, it’ll launch 3x weekly flights between Munich (MUC) and Phoenix (PHX). The 5,823-mile flight will operate in both directions on Tuesdays, Fridays, and Sundays, using an Airbus A350-900. There’s no mention of the plane featuring Allegris cabins, so I’d assume this will be one of the carrier’s older A350s, without first class, and without the new business class (though that could change).

This will be the first time that any Lufthansa Group airline operates nonstop, regularly scheduled flights to Arizona. Lufthansa Group long haul low cost carrier Discover Airlines (at the time branded as Eurowings Discover) was going to launch a route from Frankfurt (FRA) to Phoenix in the spring of 2020, but the pandemic got in the way of that ever launching, and it never ended up happening.

Lufthansa notes how “the state capital of Arizona is one of the fastest-growing regions in the USA.” The timing of this route launching is noteworthy, since it comes after the peak summer travel season. If you’re looking at this from a European point of sale perspective, that makes sense, since people don’t generally want to visit Phoenix in summer. Then again, most transatlantic service in recent years has been motivated by a US point of sale, so…

Phoenix is of course a huge hub for American. In terms of long haul service, we’ve seen nonstop flights to London (LHR) on both American and British Airways for years. That’s perfectly logical, when you combine the local demand with the endless connection possibilities on American.

When it comes to service to Europe from Phoenix, in 2024 we saw Air France launch flights to Phoenix out of Paris (CDG), so that’s the only SkyTeam service to Europe out of the airport. Now we’re also seeing a Star Alliance service to Europe out of the airport.

This isn’t the first link between Germany and Phoenix, though. It’s a route that German leisure carrier Condor operated for quite some time, but it was ultimately cut in 2025, and hasn’t returned since.

Perhaps the biggest aviation story out of Phoenix has been the airport’s new Asia route within the past year, served not by one, but by two, Taiwanese carriers. There’s now service between Taipei (TPE) and Phoenix on two airlines — China Airlines launched flights in December 2025, and Starlux Airlines launched flights in January 2026.

As of August 2027, Lufthansa will launch a new 3x weekly flight between Munich and Phoenix. With this, Phoenix will have transatlantic flights from all three of the transatlantic joint ventures. That’s fair enough in terms of the overall competitive position of joint ventures, though obviously the airline is at a significant frequency disadvantage for overall service compared to American and British Airways.

What do you make of Lufthansa adding Munich to Phoenix flights?

#9. Lufthansa Adds New U.S. Destination

Lufthansa will launch the only nonstop connection between Germany and Ohio next year.

Starting May 5, 2027, the German flag carrier will link Frankfurt and Columbus, Ohio. Service will operate three times weekly using Boeing 787-9 aircraft with 287 passenger seats.

The flight will be the first and so far only service between Columbus and Europe; the only intercontinental service at Columbus; and the only service between the state of Ohio and Germany.

“The new service will provide both business and leisure travelers with a convenient nonstop connection to Germany, as well as onward destinations across our Lufthansa Group network,” Dirk Janzen, Lufthansa Group’s vice president of passenger sales for the Americas, said in a news release. “The launch of this route is an important step in our continued expansion in the United States, our most important market outside the Lufthansa Group’s home markets.”

Columbus and Ohio officials said Lufthansa’s new route will benefit the 38 German companies operating in the Columbus area and promote investment and job creation. Germany is the third-largest source of international investment in Ohio, behind only Japan and Canada, and more than 750 German-owned business establishments operate in the state.

Lufthansa said its Columbus-Frankfurt flights will have 28 lie-flat business class seats, 28 premium economy seats, and 231 economy seats.

The airline will serve 27 destinations in the U.S. next year.

#10. Alaska Airlines Adds Osaka And Revives Failed Tahiti Route—Seattle Long Haul Doesn’t Look Good

Alaska Airlines is adding Seattle flights to Osaka and Tahiti using Hawaiian Airlines Airbus A330s. One brings back a route that Air Tahiti Nui abandoned after losing millions of dollars. The other serves a Japanese gateway that’s long been a fallback for me when business class awards to Asia haven’t been available – because it simply doesn’t sell as well. I’m more surprised that they’re the next places Alaska wants to send its widebodies as it builds a global hub in Seattle. Osaka has a better story than Tahiti, especially with Alaska planning to join American Airlines and Japan Airlines in their transpacific joint venture. Ishrion Aviation flagged the new routes, and AeroRoutes has the filed schedules: Seattle – Osaka Kansai starts May 14, 2027, four times weekly. Flights leave Seattle at 12:10 p.m. and arrive at 4 p.m. the next day. The return leaves Osaka at 6 p.m. and arrives in Seattle at 12:20 p.m. the same day. Seattle – Papeete starts June 11, 2027, three times weekly. Flights leave Seattle at 11:55 p.m. and arrive at 7:20 a.m. the next day. The return leaves Tahiti at 5 p.m. and arrives in Seattle at 6 a.m. the following morning. Air Tahiti Nui Already Tried Seattle With Alaska’s Help I covered Air Tahiti Nui’s Seattle launch and Alaska partnership in March 2022. The flight started that October. A week after the announcement, I was writing about business class awards being widely available. By September 2025, I was covering the airline’s financial problems and a study recommending that Seattle be dropped. Its Seattle flying generated a roughly $16 million loss in 2024, which is significant for how little flying was involved at the small airline. Air Tahiti Nui then announced it would suspend the twice-weekly route effective January 31, 2026. So Alaska is returning to a market where its partner couldn’t make the numbers work. And that partner already had Alaska connections. Saying that Alaska can feed the flight with connections doesn’t alone suggest why the route will work. However, Alaska controls the connecting schedules, fares and seat inventory. They keep the combined itinerary’s revenue rather than splitting it with an independent long haul airline, although the connecting flights have costs and seats they could sell to somebody else. They can market the flight directly to their frequent flyers, sell upgrades and make the destination part of the reason customers keep using an Atmos Rewards credit card. Three flights a week offer more choices than two. That can help sell trips, although it also means more seats to fill. Hawaiian already serves Tahiti. Alaska isn’t starting from scratch with a destination it’s never operated to. It’s a good schedule, though. An early arrival gives passengers time to connect to Bora Bora or continue to Moorea, rather than having to spend a night on Tahiti. A late night Seattle departure also leaves plenty of time for arriving domestic connections, and the 6 a.m. return supports onward flights. It’s less attractive for fleet utilization – 9 hours and 40 minutes on the ground in Papeete. Osaka Has A Better Case—Especially With Japan Airlines I’ve been sending readers toward Osaka when Asia awards weren’t available for a long time. Here’s my March 2016 post identifying Los Angeles–Osaka as the route to try for business class seats when other transpacific options were difficult. I’m skeptical of treating Osaka as an obvious premium revenue opportunity. Delta flew Seattle–Osaka before the pandemic. Alaska also gets to add a destination missing from Seattle’s current nonstop network, rather than one with direct competition, but also one that no one is flying now for a reason. The opportunity comes from Alaska’s planned entry into the American Airlines–Japan Airlines joint venture. That would let the airlines share revenue, coordinate pricing, schedules and sales. Japan Airlines would have a financial reason to sell Alaska’s Osaka flight, instead of primarily keeping passengers on its own aircraft through Tokyo or Los Angeles. Japan Airlines brings Japanese customers, corporate relationships and distribution that Alaska can’t recreate on its own, and they could sell more useful itineraries, including trips arriving in Tokyo and returning from Osaka, without caring as much which airline operates the route. Osaka Kansai doesn’t offer Tokyo’s connecting network. Much of Japan Airlines’ domestic Osaka operation is at Osaka Itami. This will be largely about selling trips to and from the Kansai region, with Alaska distributing passengers across its network in Seattle. Where Do The Aircraft Come From? Alaska has scheduled Tokyo Narita to return to a 787 this month, replacing the A330. And Hawaiian has already cut routes, including its seasonal Auckland service. So it’s not clear to me what aircraft is being used here, and whether it’s already been freed up. The bigger product problem is that they’re launching in 2027 with the old cabins. Hawaiian’s A330s have 278 seats, just 18 of them in business class. The seats are fully flat, arranged 2-2-2. I’ve flown and reviewed them. They’re fine for couples, but window passengers don’t have direct aisle access. The small business class cabin limits how many expensive seats Alaska has to sell, which may suit leisure markets but also limits the revenue upside. Hawaiian’s A330s already have free Starlink internet. Where Should Alaska Be Focusing Long Haul Growth? Going for Osaka and Tahiti so early makes me worry for Alaska’s long haul prospects from Seattle – that ‘this is the best they can do’ may mean they’re already scraping the bottom of the barrel. However, it strikes me that there may at least be some better alternatives. Nadi. Another South Pacific vacation destination, but Fiji Airways connections would let Alaska sell onward trips to Australia, New Zealand and other islands as well. On the other hand it could also mean undercutting Alaska’s own ambitions to those destinations. For now, though, many will be destinations without non-stop competition from Seattle (though often itineraries that could be flown one-stop, e.g. via San Francisco or Los Angeles). Manila. There’s a broader market for visiting friends and relatives, plus onward Philippine connections, though Philippine Airlines already flies nonstop from Seattle. It’s also a substantially longer flight than Osaka, and a large passenger market doesn’t guarantee high fares on that route in particular. Sydney. That’s certainly a stronger business premium route and a broader market. It would need a 787 and there aren’t any announced plans or Alaska to join American’s joint venture with Qantas. Madrid. For the European expansion, this would connect Alaska’s hub with Iberia’s hub and provide access beyond Spain. Alaska’s planned entry into the Atlantic joint venture would strengthen this. It would also mean choosing where to deploy its 787s. More flying on existing routes. For instance, moving Seoul from five weekly flights to daily, and keeping a widebody on a profitable Hawaii route could be stronger than a money-losing long haul destination. Taipei, Hong Kong and Singapore are easy cities to put on a wish list, but they already have competition. Meanwhile, Hawaiian already operates to both Papeete and Osaka, and both work with A330s making them ‘easy’ next routes to launch rather than the best opportunities Alaska would choose given the option to fly 787s. Still, Alaska has raised its ambition to at least 15 intercontinental destinations from Seattle by 2030. If Tahiti is already near the front of the queue, I’m less confident about the depth of opportunity there. I covered Air Tahiti Nui’s Seattle launch and Alaska partnership in March 2022. The flight started that October. A week after the announcement, I was writing about business class awards being widely available.

By September 2025, I was covering the airline’s financial problems and a study recommending that Seattle be dropped. Its Seattle flying generated a roughly $16 million loss in 2024, which is significant for how little flying was involved at the small airline. Air Tahiti Nui then announced it would suspend the twice-weekly route effective January 31, 2026.

So Alaska is returning to a market where its partner couldn’t make the numbers work. And that partner already had Alaska connections. Saying that Alaska can feed the flight with connections doesn’t alone suggest why the route will work. However,

It’s a good schedule, though. An early arrival gives passengers time to connect to Bora Bora or continue to Moorea, rather than having to spend a night on Tahiti. A late night Seattle departure also leaves plenty of time for arriving domestic connections, and the 6 a.m. return supports onward flights. It’s less attractive for fleet utilization – 9 hours and 40 minutes on the ground in Papeete.

Going for Osaka and Tahiti so early makes me worry for Alaska’s long haul prospects from Seattle – that ‘this is the best they can do’ may mean they’re already scraping the bottom of the barrel. However, it strikes me that there may at least be some better alternatives.

Manila. There’s a broader market for visiting friends and relatives, plus onward Philippine connections, though Philippine Airlines already flies nonstop from Seattle. It’s also a substantially longer flight than Osaka, and a large passenger market doesn’t guarantee high fares on that route in particular.

Sydney. That’s certainly a stronger business premium route and a broader market. It would need a 787 and there aren’t any announced plans or Alaska to join American’s joint venture with Qantas.

Madrid. For the European expansion, this would connect Alaska’s hub with Iberia’s hub and provide access beyond Spain. Alaska’s planned entry into the Atlantic joint venture would strengthen this. It would also mean choosing where to deploy its 787s.

More flying on existing routes. For instance, moving Seoul from five weekly flights to daily, and keeping a widebody on a profitable Hawaii route could be stronger than a money-losing long haul destination.

Taipei, Hong Kong and Singapore are easy cities to put on a wish list, but they already have competition.

Meanwhile, Hawaiian already operates to both Papeete and Osaka, and both work with A330s making them ‘easy’ next routes to launch rather than the best opportunities Alaska would choose given the option to fly 787s.

Still, Alaska has raised its ambition to at least 15 intercontinental destinations from Seattle by 2030. If Tahiti is already near the front of the queue, I’m less confident about the depth of opportunity there.

Yikes. So negative, Gary. Pissing on Tahiti and Japan as “scraping the bottom of the barrel”… psh.

Tim will appreciate your support. After all, AS is DL’s biggest competitor in SEA. He’s gonna advise AS to ‘just stay home’ because of ‘fuel.’ Yeah, wouldn’t it be nice if your opponents just quit. (And, no, crews based in Hawaii aren’t that much of an impediment here either; they’ll work it out.)

Sure, everybody wants those brand-new 787s suites-with-doors (I do, too). But, until those delivery slots open up, deploying paid-off A330s onto unserved markets out of a fortress hub is smart. 2-2-2 lie-flat is still better than no-lie-flat. (Tim, remind us how ‘great’ Delta’s ancient 763s are.)

There are also nuances between Air Tahiti Nui and what Alaska is doing here. Alaska actually owns the Seattle schedule, controls the domestic feed, keeps all the ticket revenue, and integrates it directly into Atmos Rewards.

Same goes for Osaka. More nuance. Once Alaska formally plugs into the AA/JAL transpacific joint venture, JAL has a direct commercial incentive to sell and feed that KIX flight instead of forcing everyone over Tokyo or Los Angeles.

Cheer up, everyone. These may actually be good redemptions someday soon.

Tahiti seems like a poor business choice, but I’m personally happy about it because I’m overdue for a return visit. I’m pretty sure the excess capacity will cause Atmos to offer an attractive award sale on the route. It will probably be in coach — there seems to be an plethora of free-spending vacationing elites these days, so the front cabin may be occupied — but that’s OK with me.

#11. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#12. These 28 credit cards can get you free checked bags on your next flight

Checked bag fees can add up quickly, especially if you travel frequently or with companions.

Fortunately, many airline credit cards offer a free checked bag for the primary cardholder and, in some cases, several travelers on the same reservation.

Here's a look at the cards that can help you avoid checked bag fees, how their benefits work and what to know before booking your next flight.

*The information for the Frontier Airlines World Mastercard, the Hawaiian Airlines World Elite Mastercard, the JetBlue Plus Card, the JetBlue Premier Card, the JetBlue Business Card, the Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier Credit Card and the United Club Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuers.

Alaska Airlines' first checked bag fee starts at $45. A second checked bag costs $55.

But if you have the Atmos Rewards Summit Visa Infinite credit card ($395 annual fee), Atmos Rewards Ascent Visa Signature credit card ($95 annual fee) or the Atmos Rewards Visa Signature Business Card ($70 for the company and $25 per card in annual fees), you're in luck. You can check the first bag for free for yourself and up to six additional passengers (seven people total) on the same reservation on flights marketed by Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

Note, however, that you must purchase your Alaska or Hawaiian flight with your Atmos card in order to receive this benefit.

American Airlines charges $45 for a first checked bag when purchased online ($50 at the airport) on domestic itineraries and flights to neighboring countries like Canada and Mexico. The second checked bag is $55 if purchased online ($60 at the airport).

There are four cobranded options that offer a first free checked bag on domestic American Airlines itineraries:

The Platinum Select and Business cards extend this free checked baggage benefit to you and up to four traveling companions on your reservation.

Meanwhile, the Globe and Executive World Legend cards offer the same free checked bag benefit, but it extends to up to eight traveling companions on the same reservation.

Keep in mind that there are route restrictions on these baggage benefits.

Related: Best credit cards for American Airlines flyers

Delta charges $45 each way for a first checked bag on flights within the U.S. A second checked bag costs $55.

However, most of the carrier's consumer and business credit cards offer two free checked bags on eligible flights.

Eligible Delta cardholders receive a free first checked bag for themselves and up to eight companions on the same reservation.

On domestic U.S. flights, primary cardholders also receive a free second checked bag. However, companions only receive this benefit if they hold their own eligible Delta credit card as a primary cardholder.

To receive these benefits, make sure your Delta SkyMiles number is included in your reservation.

Here are the six Delta cards that offer this perk:

Frontier Airlines charges varying prices for checked bags depending on how and when you buy them. It is generally cheapest to prepay for checked baggage at the time of booking.

Here is an example of Frontier checked bag fees on a flight from Denver International Airport (DEN) to Washington National Airport (DCA) in mid-January, starting at $69 each:

Luckily, if you hold the Frontier Airlines World Mastercard ($99 annual fee), you'll receive two free checked bags on all Frontier Airlines-operated flights when you pay with your card. Checking a bag on just one round-trip itinerary can cover the card's annual fee.

Related: Why the Frontier Airlines Mastercard became the newest credit card in my wallet

Hawaiian charges $45 for the first checked bag and $55 for the second checked bag on flights between the U.S. mainland and Hawaii. For interisland travel, the first checked bag is $30 and the second checked bag is $40.

Hawaiian Airlines World Elite Mastercard holders receive two free checked bags (when they use the card to purchase tickets directly from Hawaiian Airlines or Alaska Airlines); however, travel companions aren't included in this benefit. The card comes with a $99 annual fee.

Note that the business version of this card does not come with free checked bags.

Eligible Atmos Rewards cardholders may also receive a free first checked bag on Hawaiian Airlines flights, as outlined above.

First checked bags on JetBlue start at $39 for the first bag and $59 for the second bag on domestic flights. For transatlantic flights, first checked bags start at $64 and second checked bags start at $109. These prices can vary depending on whether the flight is during off-peak or peak season.

Thankfully, you get a free first checked bag with the JetBlue Plus or JetBlue Business (both with a $99 annual fee) when flying on JetBlue-operated flights. You can also receive this benefit with the JetBlue Premier, which charges an annual fee of $499.

The free first-checked-bag benefit extends to you and up to three travel companions on your reservation. Keep in mind, the flight must be booked on your eligible JetBlue card to receive this benefit.

Related: The best credit cards for JetBlue flyers

Southwest, once famously known for its "bags fly free" policy, now charges $35 for the first checked bag. A second bag will cost $45.

A-List elite status members receive one complimentary checked bag, and A-List Preferred members, Business Select passengers and those traveling on Choice Extra fares receive two complimentary checked bags.

If you hold any of the following five cards, you and up to eight traveling companions on the same reservation will receive one free checked bag each:

Related: Southwest announces major loyalty shake-up, new elite tiers

United charges at least $50 for the first checked bag on all domestic flights and $60 ($55 if prepaid) for the second checked bag.

However, you can apply for one of five Chase cards to avoid checked bag fees:

However, there's a big caveat here: For the perk to apply, you must have your MileagePlus number on your reservation and purchase your ticket with the applicable card. So, if you use a different card with a better earning rate on airfare, you may miss out on the free checked bags.

Related: Best United Airlines credit cards

While opening any of the airline credit cards above is a great way to save on checked bag fees, what happens if you fly with multiple carriers throughout the year?

If you prioritize price or convenience over sticking with one particular airline, it may not be worth applying for a cobranded credit card that offers perks solely on that one carrier.

An alternative is to apply for a credit card that comes with more general travel benefits and can offset your checked bag charges:

A common misconception is that your credit card will offer an additional free checked bag because of elite status, your ticket class or an international itinerary. Unfortunately, these cards' fee waivers don't usually apply if you already get a free checked bag due to your elite status, class of service or travel to an overseas destination.

Therefore, you will not receive an additional free checked bag beyond your existing allowance just for holding a credit card that offers this benefit. Some airlines make exceptions, but check your airline's policy before assuming an additional bag will be covered.

Some credit cards offer free checked bags for multiple companions. This sounds great, but there's a potential downside.

When you search for flights, airlines usually show one fare class for the entire reservation, not a mix of cheaper and more expensive seats. That means if only three seats are available at $300 and the next fare is $400, booking four people on one reservation will price all four tickets at $400.

In that scenario, paying an extra $100 per person just to save $70 per round-trip checked bag clearly isn't worth it.

Before booking group travel, compare prices by searching individually or in smaller groups and weigh the savings against any baggage benefits.

Flights can be costly on their own, not to mention when checked bag fees are added.

Thankfully, there are several ways to avoid these costs. In fact, some of the cards on this list that offer a free checked bag carry annual fees under $100.

Even if you fly with a specific airline just a few times a year, it can be easy to justify paying the ongoing annual fee, and that's not even factoring in any welcome bonuses or other perks the cards offer.

#13. Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them

A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

From a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real company.

You think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

You may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

That does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

Do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

If the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

We call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the company, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

Open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car company, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

First, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

If you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car company, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

At a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

No. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

The goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:

Inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

Scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

Inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official company, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

Before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.

Agoda is pushing into luxury accommodation, with supply vice president Andrew Smith telling Skift that the Booking Holdings-owned OTA has "doubled" its premium supply over the past four years. The clearest evidence is in new signings: a September partnership with Singapore-based Capella Hotel Group covering 12 Capella and Patina properties across eight markets, including Capella Singapore for the first time, and a flagship store for Marina Bay Sands that sells Paiza and Sands Collection rooms plus experiences. Agoda said searches for five-star accommodation rose in 2025 versus 2024 in three of its top luxury destinations — up 15% in Kuala Lumpur, 10% in Bangkok, and 2% in Bali. The economics remain the open question for hotels: Accor and H World have estimated direct booking costs at about 4% to 5% of revenue against OTA commissions of 10% to 15%, and Agoda did not answer Skift's questions on whether the Capella deal includes joint marketing, preferred placement, exclusive rates, or loyalty benefits. Agoda has not disclosed booking figures for the segment, so its luxury case currently rests on supply counts and search growth rather than evidence that travelers are paying five-star rates on the platform.

#17. Etihad 787 Enters Runway At Boston Without Clearance, Causes Go Around

The pilots of an Etihad Boeing 787 seemingly didn’t process the instructions they read back to air traffic control, and that caused a go around for another aircraft. Kudos to the air traffic controller, and you’ve also gotta love the golden retriever-esque Republic Airways pilot…

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the air traffic control audio and a visualization of an event that happened at Boston Logan Airport (BOS) on Thursday, October 15, 2026. Etihad flight EY7 was operated by a Boeing 787-9, and had just landed from Abu Dhabi (AUH). The pilots were instructed to taxi via R and N, and to hold short of runway 4L. Those instructions were correctly read back.

However, when the plane actually approached runway 22R/4L (which was the runway being used for landings), it just continued across it, rather than stopping. The air traffic controller immediately caught this, and told the Etihad pilots to stop, while he told the Republic Airways (“Brickyard”) plane to go around.

This didn’t at all escalate, and the Etihad pilots were given instructions to continue their taxi after that. It was only when the plane approached the ramp that the ground controller gave the Etihad pilots a number to call for a possible pilot deviation.

Kudos to the air traffic controller for catching this situation, and taking swift action. Now, I’m not sure why the air traffic controller told the Etihad plane to stop and hold position while on a runway they weren’t supposed to be on, but that’s besides the point (presumably he just saw something wrong, and the instinct was to say “stop”).

Two things stand out to me here. First of all, this Brickyard pilot really likes talking on the radio, doesn’t he? He just probably hasn’t been doing this long enough to be jaded.

Second of all, I’m curious what exactly the Etihad pilots were thinking. I know it had been a long trip for them, but you have four pilots in the cockpit, and no one realized they were taxiing onto an active runway? My only theory is that they were over on the 22R side of the runway (rather than the 4L side), and somehow they didn’t connect the dots that this was the runway they weren’t cleared to cross. That still doesn’t make sense, but then again, what does?

Credit to the air traffic controllers for not making a huge deal of this, and prioritizing essential communication, and then giving the pilots a number to call for a possible pilot deviation. Could you imagine the fit that dude at JFK would’ve had if someone did this? It would’ve been a five minute lecture, with a healthy dose of taunting.

I can’t tell for sure if the Etihad pilots immediately realized their mistake (because the guy working the radio seemed to be on his best behavior going forward), or if they were truly unaware of what happened.

An Etihad Boeing 787 entered a runway it was instructed to hold short of at Boston Logan Airport. There’s no real good explanation for this, because the pilots read back instructions correctly. Well done to the air traffic controller for catching this.

There was likely no imminent danger here (the regional jet hadn’t yet landed, and unless it was going to overrun the runway, odds are it wouldn’t have even made it as far down the runway as where the 787 was crossing). But still, a heavy jet entering a runway without permission is pretty bad…

What do you make of this Etihad Boeing 787 runway incursion in Boston?

#18. PayRewards Can Turn A $10,000 Business Bill Into 40,000 Points—Even If The Vendor Doesn’t Accept Credit Cards

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

A $10,000 business bill can generate 20,000 credit card rewards points plus another 20,000 points transferable to Singapore Airlines or Cathay Pacific, even when the vendor doesn’t accept credit cards.

That’s the interesting proposition behind PayRewards. Using a card that earns 2 points per dollar and their highest earning option, you’d pay $615 in fees to generate those 40,000 combined points. There’s no charge to open an account and no monthly platform fee. It’s a bill payment service like Plastiq, but on steroids.

For a business with substantial expenses that otherwise earn nothing, this creates a potentially valuable way to accumulate miles for premium cabin travel. Qualifying business payment expenses may also receive deductible expense treatment, which significantly improves the economics. (Deductibility of the optional charge for additional points needs to be considered separately, I think.)

PayRewards is the new U.S. arm of Australia’s pay.com.au. The company announced its U.S. launch and $28 million in new funding on August 24. I saw its U.S. chief commercial officer explain the service in this Geobreeze interview.

You fund a business payment with an eligible American Express, Visa or Mastercard, or from your bank account. PayRewards then pays the recipient by bank transfer, wire or check. Your supplier doesn’t have to start accepting cards for you to put the expense on yours. There are two separate charges when you use a credit card: the cost of processing the card payment, and an optional charge to earn PayRewards points. Payment Option    Total Percentage Fee    PayRewards Points Per $1 Card, without additional PayRewards points    2.9%    0 Card + Core    4.65%    1 Card + Plus    6.15%    2 Bank account + Core    1.75%    1 Bank account + Plus    3.25%    2 Credit card rewards are additional to the PayRewards points shown in the table. With bank funding, there’s no credit card earning and no extra 2.9% card processing charge. Wire delivery costs $16, and paper checks cost $5. Here’s the $10,000 example using a card that earns 2 transferable points per dollar: $290 to process the card payment. $325 for the Plus option, earning 20,000 PayRewards points. 20,000 points from the credit card, assuming the payment qualifies for its normal 2 point earning rate. $615 total fees for 40,000 combined points. That’s about <1.54 cents per point. They’re separate currencies, with their own transfer options. This calculation counts rewards on the $10,000 bill itself and doesn’t count additional card points you'd earn on the fees. The optional PayRewards points cost 1.75 cents each with Core, or 1.625 cents each with Plus. Moving from Core to Plus costs another $150 on a $10,000 bill and produces another 10,000 points — 1.5 cents apiece for that additional tranche. Plus earns the most PayRewards points and has the lower average acquisition cost. You can also choose it with bank funding: $325 generates 20,000 PayRewards points, without involving a credit card. This is most interesting for bills that otherwise earn nothing, particularly when the card spending also helps complete an initial bonus offer. Competitors include Melio and BILL, which has 2.9% card payment fees, and Plastiq at 2.99%. PayRewards’ additional attraction is the option to earn its own transferable currency on top of card rewards. Deductible business processing expenses can lower the effective cost further. For example, a $290 expense that qualifies for a deduction costs $188.50 at a 35% marginal tax rate. However, business expenses must be ordinary and necessary. An optional payment to acquire points for personal travel doesn’t obviously qualify. In its 2025 American Express settlement, the Justice Department specifically rejected the claim that inflated wire fees incurred to generate personal rewards were fully deductible. #19. JetBlue Launches New International Route

JetBlue on Thursday started nonstop service between Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and Cali, Colombia.

The connection, announced earlier this year, operates daily using Airbus A320 aircraft. Cali is JetBlue’s fourth destination in Colombia, after Cartagena, Medellín, and Barranquilla. Service to Barranquilla launched earlier this month, on Oct. 1.

The carrier said Cali service will strengthen connectivity in Latin America and the Caribbean and give more travelers from Colombia access to its North American network.

Cali is the most populous city in southwest Colombia.
