#20. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#21. She Refused To Trade Her Aisle Seat For A Middle, Then Says The Other Passenger Cried For Three Hours

A traveler says the woman beside her cried for three hours after she refused to trade her aisle seat for a middle seat so the woman could sit with her husband. I would have declined too, though I think there is room to defend your seat without turning someone else’s tears into a public spectacle.

Travel blogger Tomiko Harvey says she was flying from Istanbul to Washington, D.C., when the woman in the middle seat beside her asked her to switch with her husband.

The proposed trade would have put Harvey in a middle seat two rows ahead for the roughly ten-hour journey. She declined.

According to Harvey’s account, the woman then cried for three hours, explaining that she missed her husband and wanted to rest her head on his shoulder.

Meanwhile, Harvey described the husband as:

“two rows up in a middle seat with his headphones on, sleeping in heavenly peace the entire flight.”

Apparently, he was managing the separation rather well.

Harvey shared footage online, and the story has attracted considerable attention. We have her account of the conversation and the duration of the crying, not an independently established explanation from the other passenger.

I would not have given up my aisle seat for a middle seat on a ten-hour flight either.

There is nothing wrong with wanting to sit beside your spouse nor is there anything wrong with politely asking whether someone will switch. I disagree with the idea that merely making the request is offensive.

But an aisle for a middle is a substantial downgrade for many travelers, particularly on a longhaul flight. You are asking someone to give up the ability to get up without disturbing anyone and spend hours wedged between two other people.

The person declining does not owe you an explanation.

It does not matter whether Harvey paid extra for her aisle seat, selected it through a status benefit, or simply received it at check-in. It was her assigned seat, and she was entitled to keep it.

If sitting together is important, arrange it before boarding. Sometimes aircraft changes, cancellations, or rebooking separate people who did everything right, so I would not automatically assume this couple was too cheap to select seats.

Even then, the solution cannot depend on a stranger accepting a worse seat. If sitting together is so important, ask to be rebooked on another flight.

Offer something comparable or better. If all you have is a middle seat, recognize that the answer may be no and accept it graciously.

Harvey also says she congratulated the woman after landing for getting through the flight without sitting beside her husband.

I understand being annoyed after sitting beside someone crying for hours (which itself sounds like an exaggeration). But keeping your seat is enough…there is no need to add a little humiliation on the way out.

Nor do we really know what else was going on with this woman. Her explanation may sound absurd to someone who flies frequently, but people can be anxious or overwhelmed for reasons that are not apparent to the stranger beside them.

That does not obligate Harvey to move, but she also need not assume the tears were a calculated attempt to manipulate her. No means no.

I would have politely declined, put on my headphones, and left it there. Compassion does not require ten hours in a middle seat, and holding your ground does not require a victory speech.

But on the other hand, why does this scene from Airplane! keep coming to mind?

A traveler says her seatmate cried for three hours after she refused to give up an aisle seat so the woman could sit with her husband.

Harvey was entitled to decline. An aisle-to-middle swap on a longhaul flight is a favor, and a rather large one. Ask politely, accept the answer, and remember that wanting someone else’s seat does not make it yours.

I would have kept the aisle too…but skipped the gratuitous “congratulations” after landing.

#22. Nomad Citizen: A New Social Safety Net for Entrepreneurs

If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

The travel insurance company Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just launched what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single plan. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

Nomad Citizen covers people under 56 and earning at least $4,000 USD per month. You sign up online, choose your start date, declare that you’re in good health, and confirm you’ll be outside your passport country for more than half the year. You can also add your partner and any children under 18.

But who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really quickly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

For those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the plan can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

Income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

If you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

Health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

For health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This new Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

#23. Best Day Trips from Toronto: Easy Escapes for 2026

Looking for the best day trips from Toronto? Whether you’re craving waterfalls, wineries, beaches, or small towns, Ontario is packed with incredible places to explore just a short drive from the city. The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls, Elora, Blue Mountain, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours from the city.

We’ve lived in Toronto and traveled all around the province—and trust us, you don’t need to go far to find adventure. From hiking trails along the Niagara Escarpment to paddling the Grand River or sipping wine in Prince Edward County, there’s a day trip here for everyone.

Most of these destinations are within a 2-hour drive from Toronto, so you can head out in the morning and be back home in time for dinner. If you’re short on time but big on wanderlust, these are the top 25 Toronto day trips to add to your weekend plans in Ontario.

The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls for first-time visitors, Hamilton for waterfalls and food, Elora for small-town charm and the gorge, Stratford for theatre, Blue Mountain for outdoor adventure, Prince Edward County for wineries and beaches, and the Toronto Islands for an easy car-free escape. Most are within 1 to 2.5 hours of the city, but places like Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are better as long day trips or overnight getaways.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

The best day trips from Toronto include popular destinations like Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Elora, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours of the city.Toronto Islands and Canada’s Wonderland offer easy escapes under an hour, perfect for families and low-stress outings.Elora and Stratford are ideal for those seeking small-town charm combined with nature and culture.Longer trips such as Muskoka and Algonquin Provincial Park provide stunning wilderness experiences but require more travel time.

Best for: skyline views, beaches, biking, picnics, and car-free exploringTravel time from Toronto: 10–15 minute ferry from downtownSuggested day: Take the ferry in the morning, explore Ward’s Island or Centre Island, rent bikes, have a picnic, and return near sunset for skyline views.

The Toronto Islands are the easiest day trip from Toronto because you don’t even need to leave the city. Once you step off the ferry, it feels like a completely different world, with beaches, bike paths, picnic areas, and one of the best views of the Toronto skyline.

This is a great option if you want a low-stress day trip without a long drive. You can spend the day walking, cycling, swimming in summer, or simply relaxing by the water.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go late afternoon if you want the best skyline photos. The view of downtown Toronto from the islands is one of the classic shots of the city.

Best for: families, thrill rides, water park fun, and summer day tripsDrive from Toronto: about 30–45 minutesSuggested day: Arrive early, hit the big roller coasters first, cool off at Splash Works in the afternoon, and stay into the evening if the park has special events.

Canada’s Wonderland is one of the easiest family day trips from Toronto. It has roller coasters, kids’ areas, live entertainment, water rides, and Splash Works, which is perfect on a hot summer day.

This is a full-day outing, especially if you are visiting with kids or trying to ride the major coasters. It’s busy in summer, but that is part of the experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Buy tickets online and arrive before opening if you want to make the most of the day. The biggest rides get long lines quickly.

Best for: hiking, conservation areas, mountain biking, skiing, and quick nature escapesDrive from Toronto: about 40–60 minutesSuggested day: Start with a hike at Rattlesnake Point or Kelso, have lunch in town, then add Mount Nemo or Crawford Lake if you want a second outdoor stop.

Milton is one of the best quick nature escapes from Toronto. It sits along the Niagara Escarpment and gives you access to hiking trails, lookout points, conservation areas, and outdoor activities without committing to a long drive.

Kelso Conservation Area is great year-round, with hiking and mountain biking in warm weather and skiing or snowboarding in winter. Rattlesnake Point and Mount Nemo are also excellent for escarpment views.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Milton is ideal when you want a real outdoor day but don’t want to spend half the day in the car.

Best for: waterfalls, hiking, food, art, museums, and waterfront trailsDrive from Toronto: about 1 hourSuggested day: Visit a waterfall in the morning, explore Dundurn Castle or the waterfront in the afternoon, then head to James Street North for dinner or Art Crawl if it’s the second Friday of the month.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines nature and city energy in one easy trip. You can hike to waterfalls, visit museums, walk the waterfront, eat downtown, and still be back in Toronto by evening.

The waterfalls are the main draw, but Hamilton has become much more than an outdoor stop. James Street North, King William Street, the waterfront, and the city’s food scene make it worth a full day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the full city-and-nature experience, see our guide to the best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario.

Best for: scenic drives, hiking, fall colours, cider, and countryside escapesDrive from Toronto: about 45–60 minutesSuggested day: Visit the Cheltenham Badlands, go for a hike, stop at a cidery or café, and enjoy a relaxed countryside drive.

Caledon is a great day trip when you want fresh air, rolling hills, and a slower pace. It’s close to Toronto but feels rural, making it perfect for a scenic drive or a low-key outdoor day.

The Cheltenham Badlands are the most famous stop, but Caledon also has trails, conservation areas, farm shops, and cideries that make it easy to turn a short drive into a full afternoon.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Caledon is especially beautiful in fall. Go early if you are visiting popular spots during peak colour season.

Best for: first-time visitors, waterfalls, wineries, romance, and classic Ontario sightseeingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit Niagara Falls in the morning, then drive 20 minutes to Niagara-on-the-Lake for wineries, heritage streets, boutique shopping, or dinner.

Niagara Falls is one of the most famous day trips from Toronto, and it still delivers every time. Start with Horseshoe Falls, then add Journey Behind the Falls, the Niagara SkyWheel, Clifton Hill, or the Hornblower boat cruise if you want the full experience.

After the falls, slow the pace down in Niagara-on-the-Lake. The town is known for wineries, pretty streets, historic buildings, theatres, and one of the most charming main streets in Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If it is your first visit, do the falls first while you still have energy, then end the day with wine country and dinner in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

Things to do in Niagara Falls Where to Stay in Niagara FallsNiagara on the Lake Day Tours Niagara Day Tours from TorontoNiagara on the Lake

Best for: small-town charm, gorge views, tubing, kayaking, boutiques, and river adventuresDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Walk the town in the morning, hike along the Elora Gorge, have lunch downtown, then go tubing or kayaking if you are visiting in summer.

Elora is one of Ontario’s prettiest small towns and one of the best day trips from Toronto for people who want both nature and charm. The town has boutiques, bakeries, cafés, stone buildings, and a relaxed weekend feel.

The Elora Gorge is the highlight. The cliffs rise above the Grand River, and the trails offer beautiful views. In summer, tubing and kayaking add a little adventure to the day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Elora gets busy on summer weekends, so arrive early if you want parking, lunch, and time on the river.

Best for: theatre, food, culture, gardens, romantic day trips, and small-town charmDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Explore downtown, walk along the Avon River, have lunch, browse the shops, and see a Stratford Festival performance if one fits your schedule.

Stratford is one of the best cultural day trips from Toronto. It’s known for the Stratford Festival, but even without a show, the town is worth visiting for its riverfront, restaurants, gardens, heritage buildings, and independent shops.

This is a slower, more polished day trip. It’s ideal for couples, theatre lovers, and anyone who wants a break from the city without heading into the wilderness.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are seeing a show, build extra time into the day. Stratford is made for wandering before or after the theatre.

Best for: small towns, paddling, biking, river views, history, and easy food stopsDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Start in Paris for river views, shops, and lunch, then continue to Brantford for the Bell Homestead, Grand River trails, or a bike ride.

Paris is one of the prettiest small towns in Ontario, with the Grand River running through town, a compact downtown, cafés, bakeries, and great views from the riverfront. It’s a perfect low-key day trip when you want somewhere pretty but not overcomplicated.

Nearby Brantford adds history and trails to the day. The Bell Homestead tells the story of Alexander Graham Bell and the first long-distance telephone call, while the Grand River trails are excellent for walking, biking, and paddling.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pairing Paris and Brantford makes the day feel more complete. Do Paris for the charm and Brantford for the history and trails.

Best for: markets, food, Mennonite culture, tech-meets-tradition, families, and easy wanderingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market in the morning, explore the village, then head into Kitchener-Waterloo or Cambridge for food, history, or the Butterfly Conservatory.

Kitchener-Waterloo and St. Jacobs make a great day trip because they offer such a mix of experiences. You can visit one of the best-known markets in Ontario, see Mennonite farms and horse-drawn buggies, then head into a modern university and tech region.

St. Jacobs is the classic stop, especially if you love markets, bakeries, crafts, and small-town shopping. Nearby Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge, and Galt add more food, history, and riverside exploring.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a market day if you can. St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market is the anchor of this day trip.

Best for: beach-town nostalgia, Lake Erie, fish and chips, pier walks, and casual summer daysDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Walk the pier, have lunch at The Arbor or a local fish-and-chips spot, relax by the beach, then continue along Lake Erie if you want a mini road trip.

Port Dover is a classic Ontario beach town. It has a sandy beach, a pier, casual restaurants, shops, and that old-school summer feeling that makes you want to slow down.

This is not a polished luxury escape, and that is exactly the point. Port Dover is relaxed, nostalgic, and easy. It’s the kind of place where a hot dog, a walk by the water, and a sunset can be the whole plan.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Use Port Dover as the starting point for a Lake Erie mini road trip to Turkey Point, Port Rowan, or local wineries and breweries.

Best for: paddling, cottage-country scenery, lift locks, museums, Indigenous art, and relaxed exploringDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit the Peterborough Lift Lock, explore the Canadian Canoe Museum, paddle or walk along the water, then stop for food or local shopping before heading home.

Peterborough sits at the gateway to the Kawarthas and gives you a taste of cottage country without driving too far. It’s a good choice if you want water, history, culture, and a relaxed pace.

The Peterborough Lift Lock is the classic stop, and the Canadian Canoe Museum adds a meaningful look at paddling history and Indigenous craftsmanship. The area also has riverside trails, breweries, and access to the Trent-Severn Waterway.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t treat Peterborough as just a place to pass through on the way to cottage country. It has enough to fill a full day.

Best for: skiing, hiking, biking, spa days, village atmosphere, and four-season adventureDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Spend the morning hiking, skiing, or visiting Scenic Caves, then explore Blue Mountain Village and finish with Scandinave Spa if you want a slower end to the day.

Blue Mountain and Collingwood are technically a longer day trip, but they are worth it if you start early. In winter, Blue Mountain is one of the most popular ski and snowboard areas near Toronto. In summer, it becomes a hub for hiking, biking, patios, and outdoor activities.

Scenic Caves, Blue Mountain Village, the waterfront in Collingwood, and Scandinave Spa all make this area easy to customize depending on your travel style.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the day to feel less rushed, pick one main activity. Don’t try to ski, spa, hike, shop, and eat your way through the whole region in one day.

Best for: beach days, families, swimming, paddleboarding, summer energy, and easy sand-and-sun escapesDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Arrive early, set up on the beach, swim or paddleboard, grab lunch nearby, and stay for sunset if traffic is manageable.

Wasaga Beach is one of Ontario’s classic summer day trips. It is known for its long sandy shoreline, shallow water, and big beach-day energy.

This is a good choice when you want a simple day: cooler, towels, sunscreen, water, snacks, and sand. It can get very busy in summer, but that is part of the Wasaga experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go early on hot weekends. Parking and prime beach spots fill up fast. Book ahead with Ontario Parks or you can pay at parking lots.

Best for: lakes, paddling, fall colours, cottage-country scenery, breweries, and small townsDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Pick one town as your base, such as Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, or Huntsville, then add a lake stop, short hike, brewery, or boat cruise.

Muskoka is one of Ontario’s most famous cottage-country regions, with lakes, forests, docks, small towns, and that unmistakable smell of pine trees and campfires.

It is a bit of a long day trip from Toronto, but it works if you choose one area instead of trying to see the entire region. Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, Huntsville, and Port Carling all make good anchors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Muskoka is better when you slow down. Choose one town, one lake, and one great food stop instead of racing between too many places.

Best for: wineries, beaches, food, art, romantic getaways, and summer road tripsDrive from Toronto: about 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit a winery or two, explore Picton or Wellington, stop at Sandbanks or a beach, and have dinner before heading back.

Prince Edward County is one of the best food-and-wine day trips from Toronto, though it also works beautifully as an overnight getaway. It has boutique wineries, cideries, beaches, farm stands, restaurants, art galleries, and small towns.

Sandbanks Provincial Park is the major beach draw, but the whole county is made for slow exploring. It’s ideal for couples, food lovers, and anyone who wants a countryside escape.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: For a true day trip, don’t overbook tastings. Pick one area of the county and enjoy it properly.

Best for: wilderness, paddling, hiking, fall colours, wildlife, and big nature daysDrive from Toronto: about 3 hoursSuggested day: Leave before sunrise, choose one hiking trail or guided paddling experience, stop at a lookout or visitor centre, and head home before you are too tired.

Algonquin is a stretch as a day trip, but it can be done if you start early and keep the plan simple. This is one of Ontario’s most iconic wilderness areas, with forests, lakes, hiking trails, canoe routes, and wildlife.

You won’t see all of Algonquin in a day, and you shouldn’t try. But a single hike, paddle, or scenic drive can still give you a taste of why the park is so special.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Algonquin is much better as an overnight, but if you only have one day, choose one trail or activity and make that the focus. Algonquin Outfitters offers excellent one-day guided tours .

No car? Book this Toronto to Algonquin Provincial Park private Tour.

Best for: The Grotto, Georgian Bay, hiking, turquoise water, cliffs, shipwrecks, and big adventure daysDrive from Toronto: about 3.5 to 4 hoursSuggested day: Leave very early, visit the Grotto or hike a section of the Bruce Trail, stop in Tobermory if time allows, and expect a long drive home.

Bruce Peninsula National Park is one of the most spectacular places in Ontario, but it is a very long day trip from Toronto. The Grotto, Georgian Bay cliffs, turquoise water, and Bruce Trail scenery make it unforgettable.

This is best for travellers who do not mind a long drive and a full day outdoors. For most people, it works better as an overnight getaway, but it can be done in a single ambitious day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Reservations and parking rules matter here. Plan ahead, start early, and don’t wing it on a summer weekend.

Hamilton, Elora, and Niagara Falls are the best day trips from Toronto for waterfalls. Niagara Falls is the most famous, Hamilton has the greatest variety, and Elora gives you dramatic gorge scenery along the Grand River.

Wasaga Beach, Port Dover, Sandbanks in Prince Edward County, and the Toronto Islands are the best beach day trips from Toronto. Wasaga is best for a classic summer beach day, while Sandbanks is better if you want dunes and a longer road trip.

Niagara-on-the-Lake and Prince Edward County are the best wine-focused day trips from Toronto. Niagara-on-the-Lake is easier for a one-day trip, while Prince Edward County feels more relaxed if you can stay overnight.

Canada’s Wonderland, Toronto Islands, Niagara Falls, the Toronto Zoo, and Wasaga Beach are some of the best family-friendly day trips from Toronto. They offer easy activities, food options, and enough to fill a full day without complicated planning.

Milton, Hamilton, Elora, Algonquin Provincial Park, and Bruce Peninsula National Park are the best hiking day trips from Toronto. For an easy hike close to the city, choose Milton or Hamilton. For a bigger adventure, choose Algonquin or Bruce Peninsula.

Stratford, Elora, Paris, and Niagara-on-the-Lake are the best small-town day trips from Toronto. Each has a walkable centre, good food, independent shops, and enough charm to fill a relaxed day.

The best day trips from Toronto under 2 hours include Hamilton, Niagara Falls, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Elora, Stratford, Paris, Caledon, Milton, Kitchener-Waterloo, and Wasaga Beach. These are the easiest options if you want to leave in the morning and be back home by dinner.

Yes, Niagara Falls is one of the easiest and most popular day trips from Toronto. It takes about 90 minutes by car, and you can visit the falls, Journey Behind the Falls, Clifton Hill, the Niagara SkyWheel, and the Hornblower boat cruise in a single day if you start early.

For nature close to the city, Hamilton’s waterfalls, Milton’s conservation areas, Elora Gorge, and Caledon are some of the best choices. For bigger wilderness, Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are spectacular, but they work better as long day trips or overnight escapes.

Yes, but your options are more limited. Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Toronto Islands, and some towns along GO Transit or VIA Rail routes are possible without a car. For waterfalls, conservation areas, beaches, and rural towns, driving is usually much easier.

One way to ensure your vacation goes smoothly is to be prepared for anything — including illnesses, weather and hotel evacuations. Minor injuries and ailments are another risk. That’s why we recommend taking a portable first-aid everywhere you go.

If you get sick or hurt while abroad, having the right remedies on hand can save you the hassle of searching for a drugstore in a foreign place — and, in some cases, even save your life.

Here are some basic items to pack in your travel first-aid kit so you’ll never be caught off-guard.

Travelers with severe allergies are probably accustomed to packing prescription antihistamines or an Epi-Pen wherever they go. But even if this isn’t you, you never know when you may encounter a new type of pollen or get a bad reaction to an insect bite while traveling. Or, like me, you might learn the hard way that you’re allergic to a new brand of sunscreen on the first day of your beach vacation (yikes).

Ever since that experience, I always bring a supply of over-the-counter allergy pills and antihistamine eye drops, plus anti-itch cream for heat rashes, bug bites and the like.

Band-Aids, Steri-Strips, butterfly bandages and hydrocolloid plasters can come in handy for minor cuts and scrapes. I keep an emergency supply in my carry-on, and rarely a trip goes by that I don’t break into it, whether for a passport paper cut or hiking-induced blisters.

Not only will the right bandage make you a lot more comfortable (so you can actually enjoy your trip), it can also help prevent infection (so you won’t end up spending your vacation in an emergency room).

Before applying any bandage, be sure to clean the wound first. Liquids like rubbing alcohol antiseptic sprays could be tricky to get through airport security, so go for antiseptic wipes instead.

If you or a traveling companion suffer a more severe injury and are bleeding significantly — especially if you’re out in the wilderness — one of these could buy you time while help arrives.

Hemostatic gauze is treated with chemicals that encourage blood coagulation, or clotting. Instead of placing it over a wound, pack it tightly inside the wound and apply firm pressure.

Meanwhile, an emergency trauma dressing, also known as an Israeli bandage, has a locking bar to apply 40 pounds of pressure. Just make sure you read the instructions and understand how to use it properly before adding it to your first-aid kit.

Dehydration can strike anywhere, whether you’re sightseeing during a heat wave or suffering through a long-distance flight in economy.

Many TPGers swear by electrolyte powders to combat dehydration. Simply pour one into a water bottle and shake thoroughly, and it will go a long way in keeping you feeling your best.

Tweezers are essential if you get a splinter. In more serious scenarios, a pair of trauma shears or a multitool can come in clutch when you need to remove clothing fast. And it’s never a bad idea to carry an emergency glass-breaking tool.

These shears have a built-in strap cutter, glass breaker and oxygen tank wrench, and this multi-tool offers everything from tweezers to scissors to a magnifying glass.

Not only can a good flashlight help you assess and treat after-dark injuries, it can also light your path to help you avoid tripping and hurting yourself in the first place. Plus, a bright, long-distance light will make you easier to locate when you’re calling for help, and you can even use it to signal SOS in Morse code.

This pocket-sized option is under four inches long with a beam that can reach over 200 feet, and it’s USB rechargeable.

Sunscreen isn’t just for long beach days and high-altitude hikes. Sometimes, the worst burns happen to travelers who didn’t apply sunscreen because they thought they weren’t at risk while, say, casually strolling around a city.

It’s always a good idea to pack some aloe vera gel to soothe any burns — but your best bet is to stop the burns before they start, so pack sun protection wherever you go. I keep a small Cadence capsule of sunscreen in my travel purse so I can easily reapply it to my face and shoulders while I’m out sightseeing.

Ice packs are handy for everyday aches and pains, sports injuries and burns. The single-use chemical variety is activated by pressing or squeezing, which sets off an endothermic reaction to provide you with instant cooling relief — no freezer required.

Many instant ice packs contain TSA-regulated ammonium nitrate. You can still pack them in your carry-on or checked bag, as long as the capacity of each container and overall quantity you’re bringing do not exceed TSA limits.

Some everyday ailments are even more common when we travel — like viruses caught on airplanes, motion sickness from boat rides or upset stomachs caused by overindulging in a new destination. Plus, some countries regulate common remedies, making it impossible to get your hands on them without a prescription.

I always pack a travel-sized quantity of over-the-counter painkillers, stomach settlers and sleep aids in case the need arises. I use a pill container to keep them all in one place and avoid the chaos of half a dozen bottles or plastic baggies rattling around in my suitcase.

Before zipping up your first-aid kit, check out our guide to traveling with medicine to make sure you aren’t packing something that isn’t allowed in your destination.

If you or a travel companion has heart issues, it could be worth investing in St. John Ambulance’s Pocket AED, which is roughly the size and weight of a can of soda. This device doesn’t come cheap at around $1,400, but considering the 90% mortality rate for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest victims, it could be a true lifesaver.

Ready to pack your own travel first-aid kit? You can purchase travel-size portions of common remedies, or get a pill container and refill it from your larger bottles at home (this one comes with pre-printed labels).

Alternatively, you can purchase a pre-packed first-aid kit designed for travel; consider a waterproof option if you’ll be spending lots of time at the beach.

#25. Vrbo Exempts Some Properties From Losing Subscription Plans: Scoop

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Brown by the Beach vacation rental, Beachball Properties, Orange Beach, Alabama. Beachball Properties

With some hosts and property managers upset about being unable to renew or convert to subscriptions, Vrbo should be more transparent about why some listings qualify for an exemption while others don't.

Some Vrbo listings will be allowed to keep their annual subscriptions even as Vrbo ends its legacy subscription model on October 29, Skift has learned. They include some users of Vrbo’s in-house Escapia property management system, as well as others not on Escapia.

Most listings on annual plans will be required to move to a 12% commission on each booking when their plans expire. The subscription can cost less than that for some hosts, and some hosts and homeowners have expressed concern about the change.

"A very small number of listings that met multiple criteria were grandfathered into the retired subscription model," Vrbo said in a statement. "Because the subscription model is a legacy offering, partners can’t add new listings to it, regardless of their current model."

Vrbo didn't specify the number of listings involved.

Vrbo will retire its legacy annual subscription model on October 29, moving most hosts to a 12% commission per booking that includes payment processing, up from the current 5% host commission. Skift has learned that a limited set of listings — including some, but not all, users of Vrbo's in-house Escapia property management system, plus some listings not on Escapia — were grandfathered into the subscription. Vrbo said only "a very small number of listings that met multiple criteria" kept the plan, and it has not disclosed the criteria or the number of listings involved. About 12% of U.S. Vrbo listings and 6% globally pay roughly $699 a year regardless of booking volume, a holdover from HomeAway. Property manager Ginger Harrelson calculated that a listing now needs only about $5,825 in annual Vrbo bookings before the subscription beats 12%, down from a roughly $14,000 breakeven under the 5% model. Some hosts said subscription purchases were blocked before the October 29 deadline; one host's $19,500 renewal for 28 listings didn't go through and the listings were suspended. Other managers welcomed the change: Mary Beth Miles of Vacation Rental Collective said a flat 12% is consistent with OTA practice and brings Vrbo roughly in line with Booking.com and Airbnb, which she said charge around 15% and 15.5%.

#26. Alaska Launching Seattle To Osaka & Tahiti Flights, Using Hawaiian A330s

We know that Alaska Airlines is currently trying to build up a global hub out of Seattle Tacoma International Airport (SEA), following its acquisition of Hawaiian Airlines. While the initial goal was to launch 12 long haul routes out of the airport by 2030, that number has since been increased by 25%, to 15 routes. Along those lines, the two latest long haul routes for the airline have just been revealed, with a twist.

In the spring of 2027, Alaska plans to launch two new routes from Seattle — the oneworld airline will fly to Osaka, Japan (KIX), and Papeete, French Polynesia (PPT).

As of May 14, 2027, Alaska will begin operating 4x weekly between Seattle and Osaka, with the following schedule:

AS867 Seattle to Osaka departing 12:10PM arriving 4:00PMAS868 Osaka to Seattle departing 6:00PM arriving 12:20PM

The 5,040-mile flight is blocked at 11hr50min westbound and 10hr20min eastbound. The service will operate westbound on Sundays, Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, and eastbound on Mondays, Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays.

As of June 11, 2027, Alaska will begin operating 3x weekly between Seattle and Papeete, with the following schedule:

AS987 Seattle to Papeete departing 11:55PM arriving 7:20AM (+1 day)AS988 Papeete to Seattle departing 5:00PM arriving 6:00AM

The 4,782-mile is blocked at 10hr25min southbound and 10hr northbound. The service will operate southbound on Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays, and northbound on Sundays, Thursdays, and Saturdays.

Alaska Airlines to commence 2 new routes:• Seattle (SEA) to Osaka (KIX) 4 weekly from May 14• Seattle (SEA) to Papeete (PPT) 3 weekly from June 11Operated with Hawaiian A330. pic.twitter.com/vaqQqXAA6e

Alaska Airlines will use Hawaiian Airlines Airbus A330s for both of these routes, featuring 278 seats, including 18 business class seats and 260 economy seats. While these planes have Starlink, they otherwise have pretty outdated interiors. The planes are expected to get tip-to-tail overhauls starting in 2028, but that’s still quite a ways out.

These both strike me as cool route additions.

In the case of Osaka, it’s a market that’s from the mainland United States only otherwise served by United out of San Francisco (SFO) and Japan Airlines out of Los Angeles (LAX). Alaska seems well positioned here, in terms of having a good West Coast gateway, plus the general demand for travel to the region (it’s the closest long haul airport to Kyoto).

In the case of French Polynesia, it’s a market that’s from the mainland United States otherwise served by French Bee and United out of San Francisco, and by Air France and Air Tahiti Nui out of Los Angeles. Air Tahiti Nui had tried the route between Seattle and Tahiti, but ultimately failed.

I suspect Alaska’s logic is that the carrier has more ability to create demand, thanks to the incredible loyalty it has in Seattle, the Atmos Rewards program, etc. After all, it’s not that people don’t travel to French Polynesia, they just weren’t inclined to travel on Air Tahiti Nui out of Seattle.

Now, there are two additional interesting things here. First, Osaka and Papeete are served by Hawaiian out of Honolulu as well, so I can’t help but be curious if these destinations get pulled out of Hawaii. One of the issues we’ve seen is that much of Alaska’s long haul growth has come by pulling comparable routes out of Hawaii (simply because it wasn’t profitable). As of now the destinations are on sale out of both hubs, so we’ll see.

Second, I can’t help but find this whole Alaska and Hawaiian branding situation to be a bit of a mess. It’s perfectly logical that Alaska would want to fly an A330 from Seattle to Papeete, but keep in mind this plane will have Hawaiian branding. Alaska Air Group’s plan was to have the A330s based in Honolulu with Hawaiian branding, and have the 787s based in Seattle with Alaska branding. Now we’re going to see these A330s once again flying without touching Hawaii.

I imagine Atmos Rewards and Alaska Air Group frequent flyers will get used to these branding quirks, but it’s definitely an unconventional approach…

Alaska Airlines is launching two new routes out of Seattle, as the airline will fly to both Osaka, Japan, and Papeete, French Polynesia, with both services kicking off in the spring of 2027. The catch is that both routes will be operated by Hawaiian Airbus A330s. That’s not illogical in terms of the planes you’d think would be allocated to this service, but it sure creates some branding confusion, since these planes are supposed to operate flights to and from Hawaii.

Either way, it’s cool to see Alaska adding long haul destinations from the mainland that aren’t served by American or Delta!

What do you make of Alaska’s two new long haul routes?

#27. Airlines Can Now Lose Airport Slots They’ve Held For Years—Europe’s Top Court Says They Aren’t Property

Europe’s top court has just said airlines can lose historic airport slots, and that those slots aren’t protected property under the EU Charter. That started as a fight over Dublin Airport, but it has much wider ranging implications. Slots are the right to take off and land at a particular time at an airport. They determine which airlines can compete. The carriers already holding them have received a government subsidy that lets them keep out competition. I’ve argued that we should replace grandfathered slot controls with congestion pricing. What The European Court Decided The October 15 ruling in Case C-857/24 is over Dublin’s 32 million annual passenger limit, imposed through terminal permissions in 2007 and 2008. Historic slots are temporary and these permissions aren’t protected property under the EU Charter. The court says they were always conditional. At airports where demand exceeds the number of flights the government deterimines can be accommodated, that permission can be enormously valuable. The allocation usually starts with the airlines already there and they keep to keep access. For a new competitor to enter (or an existing airline to grow service) they can lease from another airline. That airline makes money by not flying, but giving the right to someone else. They received something valuable from the government And they rent it to another airline, profiting I covered the U.S. version in June, when Spirit’s creditors valued its 22 LaGuardia slots at $87 million. The FAA was threatening to retire them if they didn’t go to a low-fare carrier. That created a fight between creditors seeking the most money and government officials seeking their preferred buyer. Use-It-Or-Lose-It Creates Problems Once an airline has valuable access, regulators want it used. Otherwise the airline could prevent competitors from flying while offering passengers nothing. So we get minimum use requirements. These can encourage a carrier to operate a flight to preserve future access, even when the flight itself wouldn’t otherwise justify operating. Then capacity falls because of controller shortages, for instance, and regulators don’t want carriers flying merely to protect their slots. So they waive the requirements. As I covered in June, the FAA extended staffing-related relief at JFK and LaGuardia through October 30, 2027. Under the waiver, carriers can return up to 10% of their slots and have those treated as used. (They won’t fly, but neither can anybody else.) Charge For The Congestion A Flight Creates An additional flight at a crowded airport imposes costs on other flights: longer queues, missed connections, wasted crew and aircraft time. Airlines bear some of those costs themselves, especially when they operate a large share of the airport. A better approach is to charge for scarce capacity, with higher prices at congested times and lower prices when the airport has room. Publish charges far enough in advance that airlines can build schedules and sell tickets around them. That gives carriers choices: Pay for the busiest time if passengers value it enough to pay for it. Move a flight to a less congested period. Use a larger aircraft where that makes sense, spreading the capacity charge across more passengers. Reduce frequencies that don’t justify their costs. Aircraft don’t all consume identical runway capacity, so a sensible system would account for that too. And paying a charge wouldn’t override safe operating limits. Air traffic control still has to manage weather, separation and disruptions. This would also require usable gates and terminal access. Selling access to a runway while letting incumbents exclude competitors from the gates would accomplish very little. The objection is that large airlines can afford peak charges. Of course they can. But under grandfathering, they already control much of the peak access. A new entrant may have to persuade the very airline it wants to compete against to sell or lease it permission. With congestion pricing, access wouldn’t depend on that competitor’s agreement. How Congestion Pricing Solves Airport Capacity And Delays Think of a runway like a heavily used road approaching its capacity. As use approaches 100% of capacity, planes have to queue. Each additional flight imposes delay costs on everyone else, but the airline only internalizes its own delay cost. So airlines are incentivized to overschedule. Slots try to deal with this by capping the number of flights in a period. Congestion pricing says: “You can operate whenever you like, but you must pay the actual total cost of the delay you impose on others.” Slots are a crude cap: “X movements per hour.” They’re allocated via grandfather rights and use it or lose it. They’re adjusted infrequently and administratively. Once you have the slot, the flight becomes ‘free’ regardless of the delay it causes. Charging per flight movement that approximates the marginal delay cost to others works better. When the system is uncongested, the price is low or zero. As demand approaches or exceeds capacity, prices rise sharply. Airlines operate a flight in that time slice if they are willing to pay – if the value of the flight to passengers and the airline is greater than the congestion charge. That way, you get the flights that generate the highest value relative to the delay they cause. You also get natural spreading of flights to shoulders or off-peak times, reducing congestion, to lower costs. It can encourage use of larger aircraft to spread the cost out across more passengers, and also de-banking of hubs. A slot freezes peak delay – a “19 slots per hour” rule means you get 19 flights per hour, regardless of delay and irrespective of whether those are 19 regional jets or widebodies. There’s no incentive to move those any of those flights 20 minutes to spread out peak loads. Slots are also bad at handling weather events and air traffic control issues. Those might reduce an airport’s capacity from (say) 60 to 35 flights per hour. That’s when we get ground delay programs and ad hoc rationing. Congestion pricing can do the work for you, and prioritize the most valuable flights. Instead of stressing the system, airlines contribute towards paying for a better one. (If you want to make it revenue-neutral, cut landing fees or passenger charges to offset and just use congestion pricing for the incentives.) Ultimately, the same price applies to everyone – incumbent airline or new entrant in the market. Aircraft don’t all consume identical runway capacity, so a sensible system would account for that too. And paying a charge wouldn’t override safe operating limits. Air traffic control still has to manage weather, separation and disruptions. This would also require usable gates and terminal access. Selling access to a runway while letting incumbents exclude competitors from the gates would accomplish very little. The objection is that large airlines can afford peak charges. Of course they can. But under grandfathering, they already control much of the peak access. A new entrant may have to persuade the very airline it wants to compete against to sell or lease it permission. With congestion pricing, access wouldn’t depend on that competitor’s agreement. How Congestion Pricing Solves Airport Capacity And Delays Think of a runway like a heavily used road approaching its capacity. As use approaches 100% of capacity, planes have to queue. Each additional flight imposes delay costs on everyone else, but the airline only internalizes its own delay cost. So airlines are incentivized to overschedule. Slots try to deal with this by capping the number of flights in a period. Congestion pricing says: “You can operate whenever you like, but you must pay the actual total cost of the delay you impose on others.” Slots are a crude cap: “X movements per hour.” They’re allocated via grandfather rights and use it or lose it. They’re adjusted infrequently and administratively. Once you have the slot, the flight becomes ‘free’ regardless of the delay it causes. Charging per flight movement that approximates the marginal delay cost to others works better. When the system is uncongested, the price is low or zero. As demand approaches or exceeds capacity, prices rise sharply. Airlines operate a flight in that time slice if they are willing to pay – if the value of the flight to passengers and the airline is greater than the congestion charge. That way, you get the flights that generate the highest value relative to the delay they cause. You also get natural spreading of flights to shoulders or off-peak times, reducing congestion, to lower costs. It can encourage use of larger aircraft to spread the cost out across more passengers, and also de-banking of hubs. A slot freezes peak delay – a “19 slots per hour” rule means you get 19 flights per hour, regardless of delay and irrespective of whether those are 19 regional jets or widebodies. There’s no incentive to move those any of those flights 20 minutes to spread out peak loads. Slots are also bad at handling weather events and air traffic control issues. Those might reduce an airport’s capacity from (say) 60 to 35 flights per hour. That’s when we get ground delay programs and ad hoc rationing. Congestion pricing can do the work for you, and prioritize the most valuable flights. Instead of stressing the system, airlines contribute towards paying for a better one. (If you want to make it revenue-neutral, cut landing fees or passenger charges to offset and just use congestion pricing for the incentives.) Ultimately, the same price applies to everyone – incumbent airline or new entrant in the market. Think of a runway like a heavily used road approaching its capacity. As use approaches 100% of capacity, planes have to queue. Each additional flight imposes delay costs on everyone else, but the airline only internalizes its own delay cost. So airlines are incentivized to overschedule.

Slots try to deal with this by capping the number of flights in a period. Congestion pricing says: “You can operate whenever you like, but you must pay the actual total cost of the delay you impose on others.”

Slots are a crude cap: “X movements per hour.” They’re allocated via grandfather rights and use it or lose it. They’re adjusted infrequently and administratively. Once you have the slot, the flight becomes ‘free’ regardless of the delay it causes.

Charging per flight movement that approximates the marginal delay cost to others works better. When the system is uncongested, the price is low or zero. As demand approaches or exceeds capacity, prices rise sharply.

Airlines operate a flight in that time slice if they are willing to pay – if the value of the flight to passengers and the airline is greater than the congestion charge.

That way, you get the flights that generate the highest value relative to the delay they cause. You also get natural spreading of flights to shoulders or off-peak times, reducing congestion, to lower costs. It can encourage use of larger aircraft to spread the cost out across more passengers, and also de-banking of hubs.

A slot freezes peak delay – a “19 slots per hour” rule means you get 19 flights per hour, regardless of delay and irrespective of whether those are 19 regional jets or widebodies. There’s no incentive to move those any of those flights 20 minutes to spread out peak loads.

Slots are also bad at handling weather events and air traffic control issues. Those might reduce an airport’s capacity from (say) 60 to 35 flights per hour. That’s when we get ground delay programs and ad hoc rationing. Congestion pricing can do the work for you, and prioritize the most valuable flights. Instead of stressing the system, airlines contribute towards paying for a better one. (If you want to make it revenue-neutral, cut landing fees or passenger charges to offset and just use congestion pricing for the incentives.)

Ultimately, the same price applies to everyone – incumbent airline or new entrant in the market.

Good- close all European airports to Russia and their allies like Iran, N Korea and the US.

Good – This is a good fulcrum to cut the number of flights , by halving the number of slots . Too many flights . Airspace is too crowded with flights to nowhere . For example , Frankfurt to Ohio .

I agree that we can come up with better ways to use free-market models to solve issues like slots. Very intelligent people (often economists) build upon the work of previous brilliant minds to tackle issues like this. You need the incentives right. And, yes, these are problems that need to take in mind that blind laissez faire adherence won’t get good results when the problem involves the commons. You can’t let anybody broadcast on any frequency they want. But, you also need to design auction systems that allocate the product in an efficient way (e.g., getting those who value it more—and can pay that—to pay more) while maximizing the return to the public on the commons.

I don’t really believe that congestion pricing alone will work. What happens if more flights are willing to pay high congestion -based fees at particularly desirable times of day than can be accommodated? Queueing can only handle a certain amount of overflow. And, if everyone paid a big premium to fly at that time, there are going to be a lot of very unhappy campers. You still need slots, even if you change what they cost based on time of day and have a system for reallocating them.

This explains why Frontier’s s schedule is so heavily tilted to off-peak times.

@Gary, Did you mean this as it was printed? “Aircraft don’t all consume identical runway capacity” because it’s wrong. A CRJ consumes the same runway capacity as a 777. The runway is allocated to one plane at a time, and it’s perishable. Doesn’t matter the type of aircraft. Unless you’re going to nitpick over a few seconds.

Perhaps I’m nitpicking over one line in an otherwise good article. 🙂

Gary, I knew you’d go full-libertarian on this, like usual. It’s so fun to debate market theory, but you’re ignoring why this case actually happened. Dublin Airport hit a hard cap of 32 million passengers a year, set back in 2007. No amount of “congestion pricing” fixes that cap. That pricing just decides which rich airline pays to fly; it doesn’t change the law. The court ruled that old airport slots don’t usurp local planning laws built to control noise, traffic, and pollution. If you want more flights, you don’t need free-market theory. You’d need local legislators to change the cap. Seems unlikely.

@Pilot93434 — Please nitpick away, since this is your area!

@Pilot93434 – yes I’m talking about spacing between the aircraft, and second add up over the course of an entire day, right?

#28. Lufthansa Retires A340-600

Lufthansa this week retired the Airbus A340-600 after 23 years of operation.

The carrier’s final A340-600 departed Washington Dulles on Sunday and landed at Frankfurt on Monday. There were 267 passengers and 15 crew on board; many purchased tickets specifically to be a part of the final flight, the airline said.

“We will never forget this last flight with the A340-600,” said Lufthansa Frankfurt hub manager Francesco Sciortino, who also served as captain of the flight. “I am grateful that this aircraft has safely carried more than 40 million guests across the globe in 23 years.”

Lufthansa took delivery of its first A340-600 in 2003. At about 247 feet, it was the longest passenger aircraft in the world at the time. Its first destinations in Lufthansa’s network were Buenos Aires and Santiago de Chile.

The airline operated a total of 24 A340-600s over the years.

Lufthansa will replace the A340-600 with the A350-1000, Boeing 787 Dreamliner, and 777-9.

The carrier still operates the A340-300; that aircraft will be retired in 2027.

#29. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

That’s highly competitive in any hotel market for two rooms and the x-factor comes in the form of privacy, full on kitchens, gym facilities, often and a pool or entertainment area and laundry too.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#30. Review: Air India A350-900 Business Class, An Outstanding Product

Air India’s A350-900 business class offered a fabulous experience on my short flight from Delhi to Mumbai, with a comfortable suite, excellent service, a delicious Indian lunch, and complimentary Wi-Fi. I voluntarily gave up first class to take this flight and was very glad I did.

My flight from Delhi to Mumbai was only about two hours, but it gave me an opportunity to try Air India’s new A350 business class. This was a flight I had been looking forward to, even though it was not the flight I originally booked.

A comfortable bed is hardly necessary on a journey this short. Nevertheless, I appreciated the chance to stretch out after lunch, and the food and service were excellent. In terms of a two-hour domestic flight, it really does not get much better than this.

I originally booked this journey in first class on an Air India Boeing 777-300ER using 25,000 Air Canada Aeroplan points.

Part of the attraction was the opportunity to visit Air India’s new first class lounge in Delhi. But that lounge is on the international side of the airport, and my domestic first class ticket would not get me inside (I certainly tired but was not going to engage in any ticketing shenanigans).

With that settled, I noticed an earlier flight to Mumbai operated by an Airbus A350-900. Business class was available for 12,500 Aeroplan points, and switching would get me into Mumbai about two hours earlier. I made the change, paying a C$100 change fee but using half as many points. I have explained that decision in more detail here.

I still want to try Air India First Class on an international flight. But for this journey, I thought the A350 would make for a more useful review.

After picking up my boarding pass, I headed to the Air India domestic lounge, though changing to the earlier flight left me with only about 15 minutes in the lounge.

I arrived at the gate about 2:35p and we began boarding at 2:45p, precisely 45 minutes prior to departure.

Stepping onboard through door 1L, I turned right and made my way to my seat toward the rear of the cabin.

Air India’s A350-900 has 28 business class suites arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration, with direct aisle access and a sliding door at every seat. Behind business class are 24 premium economy seats and 264 economy seats.

These aircraft were originally intended for Aeroflot, and the business class seat is the same design found on some Turkish Airlines A350s, the Collins Aerospace Horizon product. It is among my favorite business class seats.

All seats have direct aisle access and privacy doors, a personal wardrobe (barely big enough for a single garment), a vanity, and a storage cabinet. Each seat converts into a fully flat bed, 6 feet, 6 inches long. All seats also have a universal A/C and USB-A socket. The cabin feels open and spacious, particularly without overhead bins over the center seats and as an added bonus, each seat has an individual air vent.

The seat was very comfortable, and I particularly appreciated the tray table. Unlike the Collins Aerospace Super Diamond seats, the table did not brush against my knees. That may seem like a small detail, but it makes a difference when sitting or trying to find a comfortable position.

Another thing I noticed was how clean everything was. Every little crevice around the seat looked clean. That should be a basic expectation, but it was still something I appreciated because sadly is it rare.

There was a pillow and blanket waiting at the seat. This was not the full longhaul bedding setup, but the small blanket and pillow was the nevertheless appreciated. After lunch, I reclined the seat into a bed, closed the sliding door, and took a nap. The bed was comfortable, and with the door shut, the suite felt fairly private.

I was tired and very happy to have a bed, even if I could not enjoy it for very long.

Window had nice shades, like first class on British Airways or Lufthansa.

I also liked the elegant lamp in each suite.

This is certainly a seat I would be happy to spend a longhaul flight in…I’d gladly fly this from Newark to Delhi.

The seat was excellent, but the food and service also impressed me on this flight.

Pre-departure beverages were offered, and there were two hot towels during the journey. A printed menu was also distributed, with four meal choices.

The high protein superseed bowl sounded good, but I chose the Indian option, Amritsari Choley Tikki.

I was very pleased with both the meal and its presentation. This was a hearty lunch, and I enjoyed it very much.

Alcohol is not served on Air India’s domestic flights, but I was fine with sparkling water and later mint tea.

I used the lavatory toward the end of the flight and found it spotless. There was mouthwash and air freshener in addition to soap.

The cleanliness throughout the aircraft stood out. My seat area was clean when I boarded, and the lavatory remained clean after the meal service.

The full inflight entertainment library was available, including hundreds of movies, television shows, audio selections, and games. Instead, I put on the tailcam, switching to the nosecam when we landed in BOM. I love the tailcam on the A350 and was pleased to find it activated on this flight.

As an aside, I really enjoyed the Air India safety video:

Disposable headphones were provided (Air India offers nicer noise-cancelling headphones on longhaul flights).

Weather wasn’t great outside both in Delhi and Mumbai:

Wi-Fi was also complimentary and worked well during my flight. Air India uses a service provider called Nelco.

Finally, Air India still publishes an in-flight magazine, which seems so quaint in 2026.

The flight attendants were attentive and courteous, and they took excellent care of me throughout the flight. The welcome beverage, printed menu, hot towels, and nicely presented lunch made the service feel quite complete despite the short flight time.

I appreciated that the kindness was led by Sonal, the purser, who took care of my side of the aisle. This entire crew complemented the seat with warm and attentive service and I left very impressed.

We arrived in a very wet Mumbai. It was monsoon season, and  it had been raining for five days straight (and would rain almost nonstop for the three days I was there too). Looking outside, that was not difficult to believe.

My Air India A350-900 flight from Delhi to Mumbai greatly exceeded my expectations.

The seat was comfortable, which I expected having flown on it before with Turkish Airlines, but the aircraft was clean, the Indian lunch was delicious, and the flight attendants provided excellent service. Complimentary Wi-Fi and the tailcam were welcome additions, and I even managed a nap after lunch.

I gave up first class to take this flight, but it did not feel like a downgrade. Now I am even more interested in trying Air India on a longhaul journey. This was a fabulous domestic flight.
