#43. Sea to Sky Highway Named One of the Best EV Road Trips in the World

Most people know the Sea to Sky Highway as one of Canada’s most beautiful drives. It winds from the edge of Vancouver along Howe Sound, climbs past waterfalls and mountain viewpoints, and continues toward Whistler and Pemberton.

Now, it has another reason to be on your road trip list: it has been named one of the best EV road trips in the world.

According to a study by iSelect, British Columbia’s Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally among the world’s most EV-friendly road trips. The study analyzed 48 iconic road trips across six continents and scored each route based on factors such as charging infrastructure, distance, estimated charging cost, and traveller reviews.

For Canadian travellers, that is a big deal. EV road trips are no longer just about whether you can make it from one charger to the next. The best routes now combine scenery, reliable charging access, reasonable costs, and places you actually want to stop along the way.

Yes. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of the best EV road trips in Canada because it is relatively short, scenic, well-travelled, and supported by charging options along the route. iSelect ranked it seventh in the world for EV road trips, with 49 chargers available across its 121-mile route and a road trip score of 88.15 out of 100.

The route is ideal for electric vehicle drivers because it connects major destinations like Vancouver, Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton without requiring a long, remote drive through charging gaps.

Electric vehicles are becoming a bigger part of travel planning. The International Energy Agency expects global electric car sales to reach 23 million in 2026, representing 28% of total car sales. That means more travellers are thinking about charging stops the same way they used to think about gas stations, rest areas, and coffee breaks.

Charging infrastructure is also expanding. The IEA reported that the worldwide stock of public charging points reached more than 7 million at the end of 2025, with nearly 1.8 million public chargers added in 2025 alone.

That shift matters for road trips. A few years ago, EV travel could feel like a math problem with scenery attached. Now, on the right routes, it can feel much closer to a normal road trip — as long as you plan ahead.

The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally in iSelect’s study. The route stretches from Horseshoe Bay toward Pemberton, passing through some of British Columbia’s most famous scenery, including Howe Sound, Squamish, Whistler, and the Coast Mountains.

Chart idea: create a simple horizontal bar chart titled Top 10 EV Road Trips in the World, using the Road Trip Score column. This would work well just below the table.

One of the most interesting parts of the ranking is that Canada appears twice in the global top 10.

The Kootenay Highway ranked second in the world, with a score of 99.24 out of 100. The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh, with a score of 88.15. That gives Canada two of the highest-rated EV road trip routes in the world according to iSelect’s index.

That should not be surprising to anyone who has road-tripped through British Columbia. Canada’s western mountain routes already offer some of the best scenery in the world. The difference now is that EV infrastructure is starting to make those drives more accessible for electric vehicle owners.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not a long cross-country endurance test. That is part of what makes it such a good EV route.

The drive from Vancouver to Whistler is short enough for many modern EVs to handle comfortably, but scenic enough that you will want to stop anyway. Instead of treating charging as an inconvenience, you can build it into the trip.

Stops like Squamish, Shannon Falls, Brandywine Falls, Whistler Village, and Pemberton give travellers natural breaks along the way. For EV drivers, that means charging can happen while you eat, hike, shop, or take photos instead of sitting around watching a battery percentage crawl upward.

Horseshoe Bay is a great place to start if you are coming from Vancouver. It has waterfront views, ferry traffic, cafes, and a relaxed village feel before the highway begins climbing toward Squamish.

Shannon Falls is one of the easiest scenic stops on the Sea to Sky Highway. The short walk to the waterfall makes it a perfect break on the way to Squamish or Whistler.

Squamish is one of the best stops on the route. It has food, coffee, outdoor shops, hiking access, and views of the Stawamus Chief. It is also a practical place to stop, stretch your legs, and check your charge before continuing north.

The Sea to Sky Gondola is one of the most popular attractions along the route. It offers sweeping views over Howe Sound and the surrounding mountains, making it an easy way to turn the drive into a full day trip.

Brandywine Falls is another easy stop between Squamish and Whistler. The walk is short, the waterfall is impressive, and it is a good reminder that the Sea to Sky Highway is not just about getting to Whistler.

Whistler is the main destination for many Sea to Sky road trips. In summer, it is great for hiking, biking, patios, lakes, and mountain views. In winter, it becomes one of North America’s most famous ski destinations.

Pemberton is a quieter extension of the trip beyond Whistler. It offers mountain scenery, farmland, and a slower pace for travellers who want to continue past the busiest part of the route.

Even on EV-friendly routes, it is still smart to plan your charging stops ahead of time. Check charger locations, charging speeds, plug types, and whether stations are available or out of service before you start driving.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not the place to play battery roulette. Mountain roads, weather, traffic, and detours can all affect range. Keep a buffer so you are not stressed if a charger is busy or unavailable.

EV range can drop in cold weather, heavy rain, strong winds, or mountain driving. The Sea to Sky Highway includes elevation changes, so it is better to plan conservatively.

The best EV road trips are the ones where charging fits naturally into the route. Stop for lunch in Squamish, explore Whistler Village, or take a scenic break while the car charges.

Do not wait until you are in a parking lot with weak signal to download a charging app. Set up your accounts, payment methods, and route planning tools before you leave home.

For an EV road trip, we would use a mix of navigation, charging, and general travel apps.

For more trip-planning tools, see our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

Absolutely. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of Canada’s great scenic drives whether you are driving an electric vehicle, hybrid, or gas-powered car.

The EV ranking simply shows that the route is becoming more accessible for modern travellers. The scenery was already there. The charging infrastructure is what makes it easier for EV drivers to enjoy the route with more confidence.

The Sea to Sky Highway’s global ranking is part of a bigger shift in travel. Sustainable travel is no longer just about choosing trains over planes or staying in eco-lodges. For many travellers, it now includes how they drive, where they charge, and whether road trips can be done with lower emissions.

Canada has the scenery. The challenge has always been distance. As charging infrastructure improves, more Canadian road trips will become realistic for EV drivers.

That is good news for travellers, but it is also good news for smaller communities along the way. EV road trips encourage people to stop longer, spend locally, and build their route around towns, restaurants, viewpoints, parks, and overnight stays.

Before driving the Sea to Sky Highway in an electric vehicle, make sure to:

The Sea to Sky Highway has always been one of Canada’s most spectacular drives. Now it is also being recognized as one of the best EV road trips in the world.

That combination makes sense. The route is scenic, manageable, practical, and packed with places worth stopping. For EV drivers, that is exactly what makes a great road trip. You do not want to plan your entire day around charging. You want charging to fit into a journey you already wanted to take.

From Vancouver to Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton, the Sea to Sky Highway proves that EV travel does not have to mean giving up adventure. It just means planning the route a little smarter.

And honestly, if your charging stop comes with mountain views and a coffee in Squamish, that is not exactly a hardship.

#44. Which Credit Card Should You Use For Hotel Spending? Here’s The Math

As a savvy consumer, you should always do what you can to maximize your return on spending, and tailor that to particular categories. In this post, I’d like to take a look at the best credit cards to use for hotel spending — no, I’m not talking about the best hotel credit cards, necessarily, but instead, which cards offer the best return on hotel spending.

Typically recommending which credit card is best for a particular bonus category (like dining, grocery stores, gas stations, everyday spending, etc.) is easy. That’s not really the case when recommending which credit card to use at hotels, since you don’t just have to consider which credit cards broadly offer the best bonus categories for travel, but you also have to consider whether the hotel brand you’re staying at has a co-branded credit card that offers bonus points for stays at that specific brand. Then there’s the whole topic of booking through credit card hotel portals.

So let’s take a look at the most rewarding credit cards for hotel spending in general (regardless of the brand you’re staying at), and then compare that to the bonuses offered by specific co-branded hotel credit cards.

Broadly speaking, what are the most rewarding credit cards for hotel spending? For this section, I’m excluding co-branded hotel credit cards. That’s because I’m looking at the cards that offer the best bonuses on hotel spending in general, rather than the best bonuses for a particular brand of hotel.

The below rewards for spending are based on my latest miles & points valuations of transferable points currencies, and I’m only including cards that are still open to new applicants. Below is a chart summarizing this, and then I’ll have a more detailed explanation.

As you can see above, there are cards that offer anywhere from 2-5x points per dollar spent on hotels, with a return that I value at anywhere from 3.4% to 6.8%.

Can you get a better or worse return when using a co-branded hotel credit card? To be comprehensive, let’s look at the co-branded credit cards issued by Choice Privileges, Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt, and Wyndham Rewards. First let me share how much I value a point in each of these currencies (and of course let me emphasize that everyone should use their own valuation of points):

To keep things fairly simple, let’s look at the co-branded credit card(s) from each of the hotel groups that offers the highest return on hotel spending (keep in mind the main reason to get hotel credit cards could be for the elite status and free night certificates that they offer). Below is a chart summarizing this, and then I’ll have a more detailed explanation.

The Choice Privileges Select Mastercard offers 10x points on Choice spending, which I value at a return of 6%. This is quite good — it’s not quite as good as the rewards offered on the Chase Sapphire Reserve (personal or business), by my valuation, but is otherwise very competitive.

The Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card (learn more) offers 14x points on eligible purchases made directly with hotels and resorts in the Hilton portfolio, which I value at a return of 7%. This is excellent, and beats the return on spending offered by all transferable points cards, though only by a narrow margin.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) offers 12x points on IHG hotel spending, which I value at a return of 6%. This isn’t quite as good as the return on spending offered by some transferable points cards, though others may feel differently based on their valuation of points.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more), Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card (learn more), and Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more), offer 6x points on Marriott hotel spending, which I value at a return of 4.2%. This isn’t as good as the return on spending offered by some transferable points cards.

That being said, some may wish to still use a Marriott co-branded credit card, since there aren’t many other ways to efficiently earn Bonvoy points. Furthermore, keep in mind that the Bonvoy Bevy Card offers 1,000 bonus points per eligible Marriott stay for cardmembers, beyond the 6x points.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more) offer 4x points on Hyatt hotel spending, which I value at a return of 5.6%. While not quite as good as the return on spending offered by the Chase Sapphire Reserve, some may still wish to use one of these cards, due to the additional rewards and sweet spots on spending.

The Wyndham Earner Business Card (learn more) offers 8x points on Wyndham hotel spending, which I value at a return of 4.8%. This is decent, but not quite as good as the return offered by some other cards.

Everyone will value points differently, and those with different points valuations may also come up with different conclusions. As you can see, based on my valuation:

What’s surprising is that co-branded hotel credit cards largely don’t offer a better return for stays at their “own” hotels than some of these cards do.

Based on my valuation of hotel points, I’d argue that Hilton Honors is the only program where it generally makes sense to use a co-branded credit card rather than a transferable points card. I can also see merit to doing this with World of Hyatt, given the additional perks for spending, but it’s not some slam dunk.

While I wouldn’t consider it to be a core part of the analysis, one other thing that has to be mentioned is that some credit card portals nowadays offer bonus points when you book hotels through them. Here are the most popular ones, ranked by their return on spending: :

I value all of those points at 1.7 cents each, so to me that’s like a return of 8.5% to 20.4%, depending on the card. That of course sounds amazing, but just keep in mind there’s often an opportunity cost to booking through these portals.

You’ll often find better prices or a better overall value elsewhere. Furthermore, unless you’re booking specifically through the luxury hotel programs, you typically won’t earn points or receive elite credits on these stays, so there’s a tradeoff. Lastly, hotels often prioritize third party guests last for things like room assignments, upgrades, etc., so don’t be surprised if you don’t get treatment that’s quite as good as booking direct.

It’s always worth trying to maximize your return on hotel spending. It’s interesting how the return on spending at hotels varies, and often you’ll find the best return on transferable points credit cards, rather than the credit cards actually associated with the hotel group.

In general, the Chase Sapphire Reserve and Sapphire Reserve Business are going to offer the best return on hotel spending, as you earn 4x points, which I value at a 6.8% return. However, some people may still prefer to use a co-branded hotel credit card, especially if those points are otherwise hard to earn, or if there are some threshold spending bonuses that make it worthwhile.

What’s your go-to credit card for hotel spending?

#46. American Adds New Route to South America

American Airlines will add a new nonstop connection to Latin America early next year.

Starting Jan. 15, 2027, the carrier will connect Miami and Barcelona, Venezuela. Service will operate three times weekly, on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, using Embraer E175 aircraft.

Barcelona will be American’s third destination in Venezuela, after Caracas and Maracaibo. The airline has not served Barcelona before.

“American is proud of the robust service we’re providing to Venezuela and prouder still that we are the only U.S. airline serving Venezuela,” American Senior Vice President and Chief Government Affairs Officer Stephen Neuman said in a news release. “The addition of Barcelona further strengthens our long-standing commitment to the country.”

American resumed service to Venezuela in April after a roughly seven-year pause.

Barcelona and nearby Puerto La Cruz are major commercial and industrial centers in eastern Venezuela, the carrier said, and the new route should help foster new business ties between the two countries.

American is the only U.S. airline currently flying to Venezuela, though both United and JetBlue have announced plans to serve Caracas in the near future.

#47. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#48. Carnival Spirit Down to Single Port Call on 15-Night Repositioning Cruise

Carnival Cruise Line adjusted the itinerary of the Carnival Spirit due to adverse weather conditions on the West Coast.

According to a statement sent to guests, a visit to Puntarenas, Costa Rica, that was scheduled for Saturday, October 17, 2026, had to be cancelled.

The Carnival Spirit is currently offering a repositioning voyage to Mobile that departed from Seattle earlier this year.

In addition to a transit of the Panama Canal, the 16-night cruise originally included visits to Cabo San Lucas, Mexico; Puntarenas, Costa Rica; and Cartagena de Indias, Colombia.

With the most recent change, the ship is only scheduled to visit the Colombian port before heading to its homeport in Alabama.

“We made every effort to reach Puntarenas, but after sailing a wider route to avoid the most severe weather from Hurricane Trudy, strong opposite currents reduced our speed,” Captain Lorenzo Calogero said in a statement issued onboard.

“Unfortunately, we will not be able to arrive within the required entry window to call on the destination,” he added.

With a planned visit to Cabo San Lucas cancelled due to delays in the ship’s departure from Seattle, which was postponed by one day, the visit to Costa Rica was set to be the cruise’s first.

“We will spend the day at sea as we make our way to Panama. We are truly sorry the weather is interfering with our plans,” Calogero added.

He noted that the safety of guests and crew is the company’s priority, while thanking guests for their understanding.

Shore excursions booked through Carnival for Puntarenas were automatically cancelled, with fares refunded to passengers’ onboard accounts.

“My team and I remain committed to making sure the rest of your voyage is safe, fun and memorable,” Calogero added.

After transiting the Panama Canal on Monday, October 19, 2026, the Carnival Spirit is scheduled to visit Cartagena de Indias on Tuesday, October 20, 2026.

The vessel will then spend four days cruising the Caribbean before concluding the repositioning voyage in Mobile.

#49. Austrian Airlines Flight From Tel Aviv Gets MiG-29 Escort After Bomb Threat Forces Diversion

An Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna diverted to Sofia under a Bulgarian MiG-29 fighter escort after a bomb threat on Sunday. Searches found no danger, and passengers eventually continued to Vienna, but a telephone call was enough to turn an ordinary flight into a frantic military and police operation.

Austrian Airlines flight OS82 was operating from Tel Aviv (TLV) to Vienna (VIE) on October 18, 2026, when a security threat prompted a diversion to Sofia, Bulgaria (SOF). The Airbus A320 was carrying 51 passengers and six crew members.

According to Reuters, Bulgarian MiG-29 fighters were scrambled as the aircraft approached the Romanian border. A fighter escorted the passenger jet to Sofia. Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner subsequently confirmed that the threat had been made by telephone to Vienna Airport. Authorities are investigating, but he declined to provide further details.

Passengers disembarked in Sofia while authorities searched the aircraft and screened those onboard. Austrian Airlines confirmed:

“During the search of the affected aircraft, the passengers, and the crew, no danger was identified.”

All passengers subsequently reboarded, and the flight continued to Vienna, arriving earlier this morning.

I am thankful nothing dangerous was found, but this was hardly a harmless practical joke.

Imagine looking out your window and seeing a fighter escort, then landing in a country you had no intention of visiting and waiting while authorities determine whether your aircraft is safe. Even when a threat proves empty, passengers lose time, crews face an unexpected diversion, and police and military resources are drawn into the response.

I would not fault Austrian for taking it seriously. Once a threat is received, the crew has to deal with the information available at that moment. Discovering afterward that nothing dangerous was onboard does not make the precaution unreasonable. But identifying whoever made the threat should be a priority. If investigators establish that someone knowingly fabricated it, I hope there are serious consequences…

Austrian Airlines passengers reached Vienna after a bomb threat diverted their flight to Sofia under a MiG-29 escort. Searches found no danger, and everyone was able to continue. While it is positive news that there was no actual threat to the aircraft, nevertheless, an empty threat can still cause substantial disruption, and whoever was responsible should be held accountable.

Bomb threats should be ignored. Diverting was foolish.

If there’s a bomb, there wouldn’t be a threat. If there’s a threat, there wouldn’t be a bomb.

And what it there actually was a bomb? They should have checked the plane before take off. And they did. The threat doesn’t increase the likelihood of a bomb the least bit.

I’ve always wondered the purpose of a military plane escort. It doesn’t change the situation.

Saudi carriers have restored service, but they can’t restore the confidence that international airlines and event organizers need. The longer foreign carriers stay out, the more Riyadh’s events-led Q4 turns into a lost quarter for hotels and for business, sporting and leisure events.

More than a third of all flights from Saudi Arabia were canceled or did not fly on Monday amid continued attacks by Iran-aligned Houthi rebels, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.

Around 322 out of 941 (or 34%) scheduled flights from the kingdom were canceled or did not fly on Monday, said Cirium. This marked an improvement from Sunday when more than half of all scheduled flights in Saudi Arabia were canceled or did not fly, the data showed.

Riyadh airport reported the most canceled flights (66%) on Monday, followed by Abha (48%), Dammam (31%), and Jeddah (15%), Cirium data showed.

#51. DOT delays rule change on airline maintenance delays

A new federal rule that could change what passengers are owed after certain flight delays will be on hold for a couple more months.

The new regulation could leave airlines off the hook to pay for passengers' expenses like meals and hotels due to some maintenance disruptions.

The measure, which was part of a sweeping aviation bill passed by Congress in 2024, had been slated to take effect this week.

But the U.S. Department of Transportation now plans to wait until the 2027 to implement the change.

Once in place, passengers stranded because of a mechanical delay or cancellation could have less luck getting the airline to pay for expenses that pile up.

Today, some airlines reimburse passenger expenses when a maintenance-related cancellation or long delay pops up. Those disruptions have historically been deemed "within the airline's control."

Under the changes greenlit by Congress in 2024, certain unscheduled maintenance incidents would no longer be considered "controllable" by the airline.

Among them: Unscheduled maintenance issues that can't wait until after the flight to be addressed.

In those situations, airlines may no longer be on the hook to fulfill consumer guarantees, like paying for meals, hotel stays or ground transportation.

"The number of delays and cancellations for which air carriers provide amenities and compensation to consumers is expected to be reduced," the DOT wrote in its final rule implementing the changes.

Several other types of flight disruptions would also no longer be counted as within the airline's control, including:

Airlines would still be on the hook for other "controllable" delays and cancellations like crew scheduling.

And not all maintenance issues will be exempt, so passengers should err on the side of requesting reimbursement if they get stranded — as the saying goes, "You can always ask." You can find the full list of promises carriers have made at FlightRights.gov.

Flight trouble due to bad weather or air traffic control issues have historically counted as "uncontrollable," and passengers must typically pay for their own expenses if they get stuck.

However, some credit cards have built-in travel insurance that can help offset those expenses.

This rule change does not affect federal refund rules. Passengers are owed a refund if their flight is canceled or significantly delayed — regardless of the reason — if they ultimately choose not to fly.

The DOT had expected to implement the maintenance-related changes on Oct. 19.

However, the agency now plans to go live with the new regulation to start the new year, beginning with flights departing on Jan. 1.

You can read more about what these changes mean for consumers and the best way for travelers to protect themselves in our full breakdown of this issue.

#52. Air Canada Thinks Outside The Box, With Unique Winter-Only Europe Route

In recent times, we’ve seen airlines add all kinds of new destinations in Europe, made possible by both booming premium leisure travel demand, as well as aircraft that can economically serve these missions, like the Airbus 321XLR.

However, virtually all of these route additions are either year-round or summer seasonal, since that’s typically where the demand is. Well, Air Canada deserves credit for adding something that we don’t often see from a legacy carrier based in North America — I’m talking a route to Europe that only operates in winter, and not summer.

Air Canada is aggressively taking delivery of Airbus A321XLRs, which the airline is primarily using to add new destinations in Europe. The thing is, we’re largely seeing the airline operate these routes in summer seasonal markets, so where are the planes supposed to fly in winter? The latest idea seems to be Spain!

Air Canada has announced that it will launch winter-only flights between Montreal (YUL) and Seville (SVQ) as of the fall of 2027. Specifically, the route will operate with the following schedule:

AC958 Montreal to Seville departing 8:30PM arriving 9:30AM (+1 day)AC959 Seville to Montreal departing 12:45PM arriving 2:40PM

Air Canada intends to operate this route up to 4x weekly, with an interesting gap — it’ll operate between September 8, 2027, and January 8, 2028, and again between February 18 and June 3, 2028. In other words, the route is operating except in the dead of winter, and it’s not operating in the peak of summer.

The 3,461-mile route is blocked at 7hr eastbound and 7hr55min westbound. It’ll be operated by one of Air Canada’s new A321XLRs, featuring 182 seats, including 14 business class seats and 168 economy class seats.

Air Canada and United without a doubt have the most creative network planners of any airlines in North America. Air Canada Chief Commercial Officer and general network whiz Mark Galardo had the following to say about this new route:

“The addition of Seville further bolsters Air Canada’s growing global network and cements Air Canada as the largest airline by seats offered between Canada and Spain. As the only non-stop service between the city and North America, Air Canada’s new service will unlock more of Andalusia and the world for our customers and Aeroplan Members while delivering a step-change in global connectivity for Seville. Enabled by the next-generation capabilities of our expanding Airbus A321XLR fleet, Seville builds upon recent additions to Palma de Mallorca and Tenerife and marks another unique Air Canada destination in Southern Europe.”

Seville is known for being beautiful, but the reality is that it gets incredibly hot in summer, with highs in the mid-90s.

So while it’s unconventional, it’s very cool to see Air Canada essentially skipping the destination in the peak of summer, and presumably using the A321XLR for a route that has high demand but a short tourist season.

I do find it interesting that the route doesn’t operate for around six weeks between early January and the middle of February. I’m curious if that’s motivated by the rather cold weather in Seville, or just no one traveling that time of year, because everyone is working… or both?

Speaking of weather in Europe in general, I understand many people travel to Europe in summer because that’s when families have time off school. But there is something that cracks me up about the annual exodus to Europe in July, only to then be around endless Americans complaining about how hot it is, and how poorly the air conditioning works. This route shouldn’t have that issue, at least not too much. 😉

In late 2027, Air Canada will launch a new route between Montreal and Seville, which will operate up to 4x weekly, using an Airbus A321XLR. What makes this unique (other than it being the only transatlantic route to Seville) is that it only operates in winter, so it’s essentially a counter-seasonal route.

That’s some very cool creativity to see, given that airlines have all kinds of summer seasonal routes, but then struggle to figure out where to send their planes in winter. I hope this proves to be a success, and that we see more routes like this.

What do you make of Air Canada’s winter service to Seville?

#53. Airfares Dropped After Passengers Booked On 26% Of Trips—Don’t Let The Airline Keep The Money

I wrote a couple of months ago about AI services like pAIback which track the flights you’ve already booked, identify when the price drops, and get the difference back for you as a travel credit. Another one I mentioned at the time was Junova. I’ve been testing several of these sites and Junova has done a nice job identifying these drops and acting quickly on them. And they have a lot of airfare data from their customers. They’ve released it and it’s some interesting stuff. Junova found lower fares in the final week before departure on 155 of 5,000 summer airline bookings. For 119 of those, it was the first price drop they’d recorded. Airlines have been lowering fares and doing it close to departure. In fact, nine bookings produced a price drop in the last 24 hours before departure. That’s lower than when a ticket was originally booked. That’s a reason to keep checking the price of a ticket you’ve already bought. If your fare lets you recover the difference (which is usually the case, excluding basic economy), you can grab a good price when you find it and still benefit when it falls later. Junova looked at a random sample of 5,000 bookings departing from June 1 through August 31, 2026 on American, United, Delta, Southwest and Alaska Airlines. They report at least one successful price drop on 1,310 bookings (26.2%). I’ve been telling readers to keep checking prices after booking for years. The disappearance of change fees on many tickets made this really valuable. A $40 fare drop wasn’t helpful when changing the ticket cost $150. Now that most tickets reprice without a fee, you can capture the $40. Most Of The Final Week’s Winners Hadn’t Saved Earlier Here’s what Junova found, using all 5,000 bookings as the denominator: Result   Bookings   Share Of All Bookings At least one successful price drop   1,310   26.2% A price drop in the final week   155   3.1% First recorded drop in the final week   119   2.38% A price drop in the final 24 hours   9   0.18% More than one successful price drop   546   10.92% Five or more successful price drops   57   1.14% These categories overlap. A booking can have several price drops, including one in the final week and another on the last day. Even among the nine bookings that saved in the last 24 hours, six were getting their first recorded reduction. More than 500 bookings saved at least twice. Fifty seven had at least five successful reductions. Airlines forecast what they can sell and what customers will pay. If bookings don’t develop as expected, cheaper seats can become available again. However, these numbers don’t tell you whether waiting to buy would have been a good gamble. The report doesn’t show how much fares rose on other bookings, though ~60% of the successful bookings had their first recorded drop at least 30 days before departure. How To Get A Credit When The Price Of Your Ticket Drops My advice for buying a ticket remains: learn what your trip usually costs, buy an attractive fare when your plans are firm, and keep watching afterward. Track the flights and fare you actually bought. A cheaper basic economy ticket, different departure time or connection isn’t necessarily a lower price for the same trip. Match the passenger count, too. Claim the difference. A price alert doesn’t issue a credit. Use the airline’s change process or ask an agent to reprice your ticket. Keep checking after the first reduction. This report found hundreds of bookings with additional savings. Know whether you’ll use the credit. Check its expiration and who can spend it. A credit on an airline you won’t fly again before it expires isn’t worth its face value. This can influence your choice of airline. You can do this yourself, or pay someone to handle it. pAIback and Junova are two services that will do it for you, for a percentage of the savings, both charge 20%. Airlines are pushing back a little bit – Alaska just started requiring customers to cancel and rebook to capture a lower fare, with potential complications for seats and companion discounts. Hopefully others don’t follow. Last year we had booked United Polaris class from LAX to Melbourne. 200k per person was not an unreasonable amount. About a week before the flight I checked in and found it had dropped to 100k per person. I was able to cancel and rebook the exact same seats. My biggest win so far.

Can you do the same with a mileage ticket? Just as an example: I booked an int’l business class ticket at 175k. on AA. Per chance, I noticed it went down to 129.5k and was still available. I called AA and had rep. cancel and rebook saving me 45.5k miles. Only because I chanced upon it. Is there also a service that watches this for a mileage ticket?

Another tool that watches and captures refunds is AutoPilot. It worked for me! https://fly.withautopilot.com/login

@joshua chopp I was wondering the same thing…

Google Flights is free, doesn’t charge a commission, set the reminder, get an email, easy peasy.

SkyKey is the only service that works also on award tickets.

Airlines should be all for these services because it increases the likelihood you’ll fly with them again sooner when you have credit that is expiring. You’re motivated to use the credit even if there are better deals.

#54. Livery of the Week: Aegean Airlines

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Aegean Airlines’ standard livery combines two shades of blue with a predominantly white fuselage, reflecting the colors closely associated with Greece. Introduced in 2020, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in roughly two decades and coincided with the arrival of its first Airbus A320neo aircraft.

The new livery was officially unveiled in February 2020, during a ceremony in Athens attended by Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis. Three newly delivered A320neos were presented in the updated colors, marking the beginning of a broader fleet modernization program.

Developed by London-based design firm PriestmanGoode, the redesign replaced Aegean’s previous white, blue, and red scheme with a more streamlined appearance. The new color palette incorporates Aegean Blue, Silver Blue, and white, drawing inspiration from the Aegean Sea and the Greek sky.

The most prominent change appears on the aircraft’s vertical stabilizer. A deep blue tail features sweeping white and lighter-blue elements that extend toward the rear fuselage. The design creates a continuous appearance between the tail and the rest of the aircraft.

Large dark-blue “AEGEAN” titles appear above the forward cabin windows, while the engines are also painted blue. The remainder of the fuselage is primarily white, eliminating the red cheatline and gray lower fuselage found on the airline’s previous livery.

The redesign also updated Aegean’s longtime twin-seagull logo. The birds had been part of the carrier’s earlier branding, but the new version introduced more geometric shapes and a symmetrical arrangement. According to PriestmanGoode, the updated emblem draws inspiration from classical Greek architecture while retaining a connection to the airline’s original identity.

Aegean’s previous livery had featured two seagulls flying in front of a yellow sun on a dark-blue tail. That scheme appeared on several generations of aircraft, including Boeing 737s operated during the carrier’s early years and the Airbus A320-family aircraft that later became the backbone of its fleet.

The 2020 redesign was introduced alongside Aegean’s investment in new-generation Airbus aircraft. The airline initially ordered 30 A320neo-family jets in 2018 before expanding its commitments, with the updated livery appearing on both A320neos and A321neos.

The new branding extended beyond the aircraft exterior. Aegean also introduced redesigned cabin interiors, uniforms, and other customer-facing elements incorporating the same colors and geometric patterns.

#55. Can You Pack Power Banks in Checked Luggage? 2026 Airline Battery Rules Travellers Need to Know

Most travellers now fly with several battery-powered items: a phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones, smartwatch, portable charger or vape. But packing one of them in the wrong bag can cause real problems at the airport.

In 2026, aviation safety authorities are warning travellers to pay closer attention to lithium batteries after reports that millions of batteries are still being packed incorrectly. The biggest mistake is simple: power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not go in checked luggage.

They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat, smoke or catch fire. This matters even more when your carry-on gets taken away at the gate and sent underneath the plane.

No. Power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not be packed in checked luggage. They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat.The same goes for loose camera batteries, spare laptop batteries, rechargeable battery packs, vape devices and phone battery charging cases. If your carry-on bag is taken away at the gate and checked underneath the plane, remove all power banks and spare batteries before handing it over.Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras with batteries installed are treated differently from spare batteries, but the safest habit is still to keep valuable battery-powered electronics in the cabin whenever possible. If an airline allows a device to be checked, it should be completely powered off, protected from damage and prevented from turning on accidentally.

The safest habit is simple: power banks, spare batteries and removable batteries stay with you. Valuable electronics are usually better in the cabin too.

Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage because they contain lithium batteries that can overheat if damaged, poorly packed, overcharged, exposed to heat or affected by a defect.

In rare cases, lithium batteries can enter thermal runaway. That means the battery heats faster than it can cool itself down. It may swell, smoke, burn or ignite.

If that happens in the cabin, passengers and crew can spot the problem quickly. Cabin crews are trained to respond to battery incidents. If the battery is hidden inside a suitcase in the cargo hold, it is much harder to access.

That is why this rule is not just airport red tape. A small charger in the wrong bag can become a serious safety issue.

Before you check a suitcase, look for anything with a loose, spare or removable lithium battery.

These items should stay in your carry-on or personal item:

You should also think carefully before checking valuable electronics with installed batteries, including:

Some airlines may allow certain devices with batteries installed in checked luggage if they are completely powered off and protected from damage. But for most travellers, the smarter choice is to keep electronics in the cabin.

Checked bags get dropped, delayed, searched and occasionally sent on their own little vacation. Your laptop does not need that character-building experience.

This is where the rules confuse a lot of travellers.

A spare battery is any battery that is not installed inside the device it powers. A power bank also counts because it is an external battery used to charge other devices.

A battery installed in a device is different. This includes the battery built into your phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones or smartwatch.

If the battery is loose, removable or used to charge something else, do not check it. The FAA’s lithium battery guidance says power banks and spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage.

Gate-checking is one of the easiest ways to accidentally break the battery rule.

You may pack your power bank correctly in your carry-on at home. Then you reach the gate, the overhead bins are full and the agent tags your carry-on to go underneath the plane.

At that moment, your carry-on has become checked luggage.

The easiest system is to keep all power banks and spare batteries in one small pouch inside your personal item. If your roller bag gets gate-checked, you can remove the pouch in seconds instead of digging through your suitcase while the boarding line gives you the collective death stare.

Airlines measure lithium-ion battery size in watt-hours, written as Wh.

Most standard phone power banks are under 100 Wh and are usually allowed in carry-on baggage. Larger batteries may require airline approval, and very large batteries are generally not allowed in normal passenger baggage.

The 100 Wh rule matters most for large laptop power banks, professional camera gear, video equipment and drone batteries.

A typical 10,000 mAh power bank is often around 37 Wh. A 20,000 mAh power bank is often around 74 Wh. Larger power banks can get close to the limit, so check before you pack.

According to CATSA’s battery packing guidelines, travellers should keep batteries and electronic devices containing batteries in their carry-on baggage, avoid damaged or recalled batteries, and protect spare batteries from short-circuiting.

Look for the Wh rating printed on the back, bottom or side of the power bank. Newer batteries often show this number clearly.

If the label only shows mAh and volts, you can calculate watt-hours with this formula:

Since 1,000 mAh equals 1 Ah, a 20,000 mAh power bank is 20 Ah.

That would usually fall under the 100 Wh carry-on limit.

If the label has rubbed off and the airline cannot confirm the battery rating, the item may be refused. Do not rely on guessing at the airport.

Laptops, phones and tablets have batteries installed inside the device, so they are not treated the same way as loose spare batteries or power banks.

However, airline rules vary. If an airline allows these devices in checked luggage, they should be completely powered off, protected from damage and packed so they cannot accidentally turn on.

That means fully powered off, not sleeping, hibernating or sitting there quietly planning to wake up mid-flight.

In practice, keep phones, laptops and tablets in the cabin whenever possible. They are valuable, easy to damage and often essential if your checked bag is delayed.

No. Vapes and e-cigarettes should not be packed in checked luggage because they contain batteries. They should travel in the cabin and must not be used or charged during the flight.

Rules for vaping products also vary by destination, and some countries restrict or ban them. If an adult is legally travelling with one, it still needs to follow airline battery rules.

If you are packing for someone else, check for these before closing a checked suitcase. A vape tossed into checked luggage can create the same battery issue as other lithium-powered devices.

Smart luggage can usually be checked only if the battery can be removed.

A smart bag is luggage with built-in charging, tracking or other battery-powered features. If the bag is going into the cabin and meets carry-on size limits, it may be accepted as a carry-on. If it has to be checked, the battery must usually be removed and brought into the cabin.

If the battery cannot be removed, the airline may refuse to accept the bag as checked luggage.

Before travelling with smart luggage, find the battery compartment at home. Do not wait until the check-in counter to discover that the “removable” battery requires a tiny screwdriver, a prayer and the patience of a saint.

The drone or camera body may be allowed in checked luggage by some airlines, but spare lithium batteries should be removed and carried in the cabin.

Spare camera batteries and drone batteries should be individually protected so the terminals cannot touch metal or each other. Use the original packaging, a battery case, a protective pouch or tape over exposed terminals.

If you travel with several batteries for photography or video work, check your airline’s quantity limits before you fly. Battery rules can be stricter for professional video gear and larger drone batteries.

Loose batteries should never be thrown into a bag with coins, keys, jewellery, cables or other metal objects. Battery terminals can short-circuit if they touch metal.

This is especially important for camera batteries, drone batteries and loose rechargeable cells.

Do not travel with a battery that is swollen, cracked, leaking, unusually hot, damaged or recalled.

A swollen power bank is not “probably fine.” It is a damaged battery and should be taken to an appropriate recycling or disposal location.

Before flying with an older power bank, check the model number and look for current recall notices from the manufacturer or your government recall site. Some recalled power banks may be prohibited onboard entirely.

If a battery looks questionable, leave it at home. Replacing a charger is cheaper than dealing with a safety incident at the airport.

If a battery or device becomes hot, starts swelling, smokes, sparks or smells strange during a flight, tell the cabin crew immediately.

Do not put it in the overhead bin. Do not hide it in a bag. Do not take it to the washroom. Cabin crew are trained to respond to battery incidents, but they need to know right away.

The goal is not to handle the problem yourself. The goal is to alert the people trained to deal with it.

Before leaving for the airport, do this quick check:

This takes less than two minutes and can prevent a pulled bag, confiscated item or airport delay.

Before you check a suitcase or hand over a carry-on at the gate, make sure:

Before you check any bag, open it and look for batteries.

Power banks, portable chargers, spare batteries and removable lithium batteries stay with you in the cabin. Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras are usually safer in your carry-on. If your carry-on gets taken at the gate, remove your battery pouch before the bag goes underneath the plane.

The goal is not to stop travelling with electronics. The goal is to stop packing them on autopilot.

A two-minute battery check before every flight can save your bag, your gear and possibly your travel day.

#56. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#57. Capital One Venture Business Card Review

If you’re a traveler like me, chances are you’re always on the lookout for ways to make your trips more affordable. That’s why I collect points and miles: they help me lower my travel costs so I can spend my money on what’s actually important…which is usually booking more trips!

One card that can help you earn more points and miles — which translates to more free flights and free hotel stays — is the Capital One Venture Business card. It’s an easy-to-use card perfect for travels who want to simplify their points and miles collecting. Here’s everything you need to know about the card to help decide if it’s for you. It’s a solid business card for those who don’t want a high annaul fee card but want some added perks besides just getting miles when you spend money.

Table of ContentsWhat Is It?Rental Car PerksTravel PartnersWho Is This Card For?

The Capital One Venture Business card is the new rebranded version of Capital One’s Spark Miles. But it has some noteworthy improvements that I think make it worth adding to your wallet. Here’s a look at the card’s main perks:

The annual fee for the card is just $95, which means it’s effectively free once you factor in the two statement credits. With a default 2x miles for every dollar spent, that makes this card a solid choice for everyday spending. And without a ton of differing spending categories, the card is very easy to use, making it perfect for travelers new to the points and miles game.

In addition to giving you Hertz Five Star status, which lets you skip the counter at select locations while also offering a wider selection of cars, the card also offers rental car coverage when renting a car for business reasons. You’ll need to charge the full fee to your card and also decline the company’s collision damage waiver, but once you do that, you’ll be covered for damage due to both collisions and theft.

While I don’t often rent cars for work, I appreciate the free collision coverage and being able to skip the line (especially at busier rental locations).

With this card, you’ll earn Capital One miles. You can use them like you would any other rewards program: to get cash back, book travel directly, or transfer them to travel partners.

The easiest option is to redeem your miles for travel in the Capital One travel portal, which works like booking through Expedia or any other online travel agency. Doing so is very straightforward. You simply search for and book your flight, hotel, or rental car and choose “miles” as your payment method. It’s basically like using your miles as cash, at a value of one cent per mile.

Both options are super easy to implement, which is why this is a great card for newbies. And if this is the only way that you’ll use your miles, go for it! Using them is better than letting them sit around.

However, you can usually get more for your miles when you transfer them to Capital One’s transfer partners.

The ability to transfer to travel partners is what makes Capital One miles valuable. While the actual value varies based on what you book, you can usually find airline and hotel redemptions worth much more than the aforementioned 1 cent per mile.

Transferring to travel partners is a bit more work than using the portal, but there are more tools than ever to help you maximize your miles (such as point.me for finding flights and Awayz for finding award hotel stays).

Here are their current hotel and airline transfer partners:

This card is best for business travelers who are looking for an easy-to-use card to help them earn points and miles. While I personally think the Capital One Venture X Business card is a better card, it comes with a higher annual fee so, if you want a solid travel card for your business and don’t need the upgraded perks of the Capital One Venture X Business card, this is the Capital One card for you. And since the credits cover the annual fee, the card is essentially free!

The new Capital One Venture Business card has an amazing welcome offer, a respectable 2x on every purchase, and some solid perks for regular travelers. And with its low annual fee, this card is a no brainer for travelers looking for a new business card. I just wouldn’t wait too long — this huge welcome offer isn’t gonna last forever!

#58. United Airlines Expands Economy Meal Preorders To Shorter Flights

United Airlines is expanding fresh meal preorders in economy to shorter flights, a welcome shift that unlocks more meal options on hundreds of daily flights.

United announced today that it is lowering the distance threshold for fresh food preorders in economy from flights over 1,190 miles to flights over 900 miles across North America and the Caribbean.

The airline says the expansion covers approximately 420 additional flights per day, giving up to 65,000 more passengers daily access to the option.

These are paid Bistro on Board meals, not complimentary meals being added to economy. Nevertheless, being able to select something in advance is welcome, particularly on flights that overlap with a meal.

Passengers can select eligible food and retail items through the United app or united.com beginning five days before departure and until 24 hours before departure.

On the website, look under “Trips.” The app will also notify passengers when preordering opens for their flight.

The rotating fresh food selection currently includes:

Snackboxes and other eligible snacks can also be ordered in advance, but these are also available for purchase onboard.

United also cautions that preordered meals may not be available under certain circumstances. Choosing in advance improves the process (as does requiring pre-payment), but it is not an absolute guarantee that your meal will make it onboard.

As United has improved its technology and limited Bistro On Board to pre-order only, this expansion makes a lot of sense.

For tight connections, having a fresh option onboard can be quite useful and the food is often just as good, if not better, than overpriced airport options (Tortas Frontera exempted). Preordering also gives United a better indication of what passengers actually want. Loading food that people have already selected strikes me as a more sensible approach than guessing how many burgers or breakfast sandwiches might sell, though I still wish United would load at least a few extra each flight for those who may have booked last minuted or been re-accomodated due to irregular operations.

Of course, the food still needs to be worth buying.

I recently tried Jeff Mauro’s Chicago patty melt. The beef was great, but the rye bread was dried out, there was hardly any giardiniera, and I could not find the caramelized onions. I am a big fan of Jeff Mauro and think the sandwich has potential, but it needs some work before I would order it again (which, by the way, he indicated to me after my post that he is looking into). His Chicago bagel breakfast melt was much better.

That is the practical limit of this announcement: making a meal easier to order does not make it a better meal. Still, expanding access to the existing menu is a sensible improvement, and I appreciate United offering more than a snackbox on these flights. Separately, United says its Tapas, Takeoff, and Recline snackboxes will receive refreshed contents beginning November 1. We will see what changes inside.

United is expanding fresh economy meal preorders to flights over 900 miles across North America and the Caribbean, adding approximately 420 eligible flights per day.

Passengers can order between five days and 24 hours before departure through the app or website. The meals still cost extra, but having more opportunities to choose something before boarding is welcome. I’m hoping that over time United will be able to expand the menu, offering more sandwiches, salads, and entrees that can be specifically catered in order to reduce waste onboard. But this is a good first step.

Not to suggest that UA change the current policy, but there may be some ways they could add meals to shorter flights without substantially increasing catering costs. Hear me out, but I have to wonder how much the uptake is for full meals on redeyes? I’ll still order something if its offered just for the heck of it, but on a midcon redeye departing at 2330 and arriving at 0430, I’ve observed the majority of the passengers in F sleeping, so not taking into account pre-orders, all the other meals basically get thrown out. Granted UA at least offers food on redeyes whereas DL and AA just do the snackbasket regardless of flight length (exception seems to be West Coast-NYC), but I wouldn’t mind UA switching back to the CO coldplate (cold cuts, cheese, veggies, etc) on <3.5hr redeyes if it meant offering meals in F on the shorter flights like DENSAN or EWRSTL for example.

One other thought though….while I'd rather have a proper meal on those short flights, if they are going to let Y pax order hot BoB items, maybe the solution is offer the option to F paxs as well, or at least offer the Express bistro boxes?

Im a big fan of this move… is it effective immediately?

Yes. In fact, I flew IAH-ORD over the weekend and it was already available.

The biggest winner is almost everything IAH/EWR-Florida.

And ORD. I think only MIA was just barely over the old threshold

Funny how we gush over (for purchase) inflight meals being ordered in advance. I guess the airlines have us trained well…

It’s not ideal, but it’s better than nothing and better than what DL and AA offer as BOB options.

It’s funny…IAH-DCA/BWI had hot meals for purchase (as they were over the previous threshold) but IAH-IAD did not.

However, they kind of just watered down their recently improved Y service on international flights. The salad course on the tray is now much smaller and the “appetizer” service (hummus, cheese, nuts/olives) has now been eliminated in favor of pretzels.

#60. Hotels Could Become One of Ixigo’s Two Biggest Businesses

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Ixigo CEO Aloke Bajpai (left) and Co-CEO Rajnish Kumar. Ixigo

Ixigo has the product and a steady stream of customers. What remains is the hard part of convincing budget travelers that the room they book online is the room they’ll get.

Ixigo expects hotels to become one of its largest businesses within four to five years, co-founder and group co-CEO Aloke Bajpai said on the company’s earnings call Monday. He said the category could be “if not the largest, maybe the second largest” in its mix by gross transaction value (GTV).

Hotels are still small, accounting for 2.1% of GTV. The company’s stated ambition is “to become the largest player serving this part of the hotel market,” and Bajpai said growth is not optional. “There is no choice, we have to grow,” he said.

Ixigo’s logic for hotels starts with who its customers are. Around 94% of its transactions involve travel to or from Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, and nine in 10 trips it sells are by train or bus. “Many travelers looking for an affordable room are already booking their journey with us,” Bajpai said. That gives it a ready audience and keeps acquisition costs lo

Ixigo, India's online travel company built on train and bus bookings, told investors it expects hotels to become one of its two largest businesses by gross transaction value within four to five years. Hotels currently account for 2.1% of GTV. Co-founder and group co-CEO Aloke Bajpai said the company is targeting the budget end of the market — roughly 60% of Indian hotel room nights sell for under INR 2,000 ($21), much of it independent properties with low online penetration — and that its existing customer base supplies the demand, with more than 86% of hotel bookings in the quarter coming from people already on its platforms. Ixigo is contracting with more than 12,000 properties across about 1,100 towns, up from 10,000 last quarter, and spent around INR 110 million ($1.2 million) on hotels in the quarter, mostly on people and technology. Bajpai said the investment phase should last two to three years. The shift comes as trains mature — the category has fallen from more than half of GTV to the low 40s, and Bajpai said he does not expect that share to improve — and as the Indian flight market shrank in volume with fares up around 30% on several routes. Second-quarter GTV rose 22% to INR 53 billion ($559 million), revenue grew 13% to INR 3.2 billion ($34 million), and profit after tax hit an all-time high of INR 634 million ($6.7 million).
