#61. Key Cruise Ship Drydocks in October

Cruise Industry News looks into key drydock projects taking place across the industry in October.

Margaritaville at Sea Beachcomber Cruise Line: Margaritaville at Sea Capacity: 2,720 guests Tonnage: 103,000 Year built: 2003 Drydock Period: September 26, 2026 to TBD Shipyard: Harland & Wolff (Belfast, Northern Ireland)

The former Costa Fortuna arrived at the Harland & Wolff shipyard in late September to be transformed into the Margaritaville at Sea Beachcomber.

Handed over to Margaritaville at Sea earlier this year, the 2003-built ship is undergoing a major refurbishment, which will see the debut of new public areas and venues onboard.

The vessel is also expected to undergo technical maintenance and upgrades before welcoming guests for its maiden season in Miami on January 9, 2027.

Oceania Marina Cruise Line: Oceania Cruises Capacity: 1,260 guests Tonnage: 65,000 Year built: 2011 Drydock Period: October 11 to November 5, 2026 Shipyard: Chantier Naval de Marseille (Marseille, France)

The Oceania Marina is undergoing an extensive refurbishment as part of the OceaniaNEXT program, having arrived at the Chantier Naval de Marseille earlier this month.

Every stateroom will be redesigned with new layouts, furnishings and bathrooms, while public areas will feature updated furnishings, new carpeting and refined lighting. The 2011-built ship will also introduce new venues, such as the Founders Bar and the Chef’s Studio.

The vessel will resume service in early November, offering itineraries in the Mediterranean before repositioning to the Caribbean for the winter.

World Voyager Cruise Line: Mystic Cruises Capacity: 200 guests Tonnage: 9,300 Year built: 2020 Drydock Period: October 10 to October 20, 2026 Shipyard: Lisnave (Setúbal, Portugal)

The World Voyager entered drydock at the Lisnave shipyard in Portugal earlier this month for a repair project.

As previously reported by Cruise Industry News, the Mystic Cruises vessel is having one of its stabilizers replaced ahead of its upcoming season in Antarctica.

The 200-passenger expedition ship will resume service in early November, kicking off its first season under charter to Quark Expeditions.

MSC Opera Cruise Line: MSC Cruises Capacity: 2,160 guests Tonnage: 65,591 Year built: 2004 Drydock Period: October 10 to October 29, 2026 Shipyard: Palumbo (Valletta, Malta)

The MSC Opera entered drydock at the Palumbo shipyard in Malta earlier this month for routine maintenance and class work.

While further details of the project were not announced, the vessel is expected to undergo technical overhauls, in addition to statutory inspections and hotel upkeep.

The 2004-built ship will welcome guests back in late October, kicking off a trans-Atlantic crossing to the Dominican Republic ahead of its year-round operations in the Southern Caribbean.

Norwegian Escape Cruise Line: Norwegian Cruise Line Capacity: 4,200 guests Tonnage: 163,000 Year built: 2015 Drydock Period: October 12 to October 28, 2026 Shipyard: Chantier Naval de Marseille (Marseille, France)

After pausing its regular operations in North America, the Norwegian Escape arrived in France for drydock earlier this month.

The 163,000-ton vessel is undergoing technical maintenance and class work before welcoming guests back for a trans-Atlantic crossing in late October.

Starting in mid-November, the Norwegian Escape will offer weeklong cruises to the Caribbean from Port Canaveral.

#62. Lufthansa Will Fly To Columbus, Ohio, Thanks To $46.9 Million Revenue Guarantee Program

It’s always fun to see an airport get long haul service for the first time, so here’s a really cool example of that, as Columbus, Ohio, will be getting its first-ever transatlantic link! While that’s a pretty exciting route for the community, this seems pretty risk free for the airline, given the insanely generous incentives being offered by the airport (thanks to Jay for flagging this).

As of May 5, 2027, Lufthansa intends to commence 3x weekly nonstop flights between Frankfurt (FRA) and Columbus (CMH). The route is expected to be operated on Wednesdays, Fridays, and Sundays, in both directions, with the following schedule:

LH406 Frankfurt to Columbus departing 11:15AM arriving 2:00PMLH407 Columbus to Frankfurt departing 4:20PM arriving 6:15AM (+1 day)

The 4,248-mile route is blocked at 8hr45min westbound and 7hr55min eastbound. It will be operated using a 287-seat Boeing 787-9, featuring new Allegris cabins. This includes 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats, and 231 economy seats. Tickets will go on sale as of tomorrow, Tuesday, October 20, 2026.

Suffice it to say that this is a very cool addition to Columbus’ network. The only international service the airport otherwise gets is on Air Canada from Toronto (YYZ) and Montreal (YUL), and on American, Southwest, and Viva from Cancun (CUN), with most of that service being seasonal.

Here’s what Dirk Janzen, VP of Lufthansa Passenger Sales for the Americas, had to say:

“We are very pleased to connect Columbus and the state of Ohio directly with our Frankfurt hub, the first intercontinental flight from this great city. The new service will provide both business and leisure travelers with a convenient nonstop connection to Germany, as well as onward destinations across our Lufthansa Group network. The launch of this route is an important step in our continued expansion in the United States, our most important market outside the Lufthansa Group’s home markets. We look forward to strengthening the connections between Ohio and Europe, and to welcoming travelers from Columbus and the surrounding region.”

Here’s how Daren Griffin, President of the Columbus Regional Airport Authority, describes this:

“Today’s announcement is a tremendous milestone for the Columbus Region and Ohio. Lufthansa’s new nonstop service to Frankfurt provides our passengers with a direct link to one of the world’s strongest global networks, enhancing connectivity, competitiveness and continued growth. At a time of extraordinary transformation for our airports and our region, this new service establishes Ohio’s gateway to continental Europe. It strengthens our state’s connections to the global economy and creates new opportunities for communities across Ohio. We couldn’t be more excited about what it means for our businesses, travelers and the future of Ohio”

So, what’s Lufthansa’s motive for launching service to Columbus, an airport that doesn’t otherwise have any long haul flights?

The argument of course is that hundreds of people travel every day from Ohio to Europe, and this service will help serve that demand. Admittedly unless you’re specifically traveling between Columbus and Frankfurt, there are probably other one stop routings available as well (to a US gateway, and then nonstop to any of dozens of different markets in Europe).

It’s also specifically pointed out how there are 38 German-based companies operating in the Columbus region, and I think that’s a reason it makes sense for Lufthansa to be the European carrier to be first to add service to Columbus.

Now, if we’re being honest, there’s a very simple reason that this service is launching, and it’s not purely about demand. Just read the press release:

The new route builds on the success of JobsOhio’s Air Service Restoration program, which works with airports, regional partners and airlines to establish routes that are important to economic development. JobsOhio created the program after businesses and stakeholders said during a 2019 statewide listening tour that air service at Ohio airports had declined more sharply than in competitor states. Through the program, JobsOhio and regional partners share revenue guarantees that reduce the risk for airlines launching new service.

Since 2020, it has helped bring 32 new routes and 15 route expansions with six airlines to five Ohio airports, adding more than 590,000 new seats and more than 187,000 additional seats each year and generating an estimated $230 million in annual economic impact. JobsOhio has committed $36.8 million in revenue guarantees, alongside $10.1 million from local partners.

As you can see, the community has provided a staggering $46.9 million in revenue guarantees to airlines since 2020, to add service. While it’s normal for airports to provide economic incentives for new service, that is a massive amount of money. This money is indirectly taxpayer funded, in the sense that the JobsOhio money comes from liquor sales.

So while not all of that is going to Lufthansa, the airline is basically launching a route here on which it presumably can’t lose money, and in this environment, that’s a pretty good deal. It’s not entirely clear how much of that $46.9 million has been spent on those incremental 590K seats that have reportedly been added, but if you do simply divide it out, we’re talking about $80 per passenger.

Let me be clear — none of this is intended to rag on Columbus, as it’s totally normal to see airports offer incentives for new service. However, Columbus is spending an especially large sum, and there’s absolutely no way a route like this would launch without incentives (which is fair enough). The real sign of success is if the route continues once the incentives dry up.

As of May 2027, Lufthansa will launch 3x weekly nonstop flights between Frankfurt and Columbus using a Boeing 787. What a cool new route for an airport that doesn’t currently have any long haul service. If an airline were to launch transatlantic flights from Columbus, it makes sense that it would be Lufthansa, given the German connection in the region.

However, this route is really possible thanks to the massive revenue guarantee program that’s in place for airlines, and I imagine this will be the most rewarded new route yet, given its implications. Congrats to the Columbus region, and here’s to hoping the route lasts even after the revenue guarantee runs out.

#64. Delta Revives Short-Lived Transatlantic Route

Delta is bringing back a transatlantic route next spring, adding to the carrier’s international schedule for summer 2027.

The Atlanta-based airline announced Friday that flights between Boston and Reykjavik, Iceland, will begin April 12, 2027. Service will operate through Oct. 30, with tickets going on sale this weekend.

The daily service will be operated by a Boeing 757-200. Delta briefly served the market in 2021, according to Cirium Diio schedule data.

According to the airline, Reykjavik will become its 14th unique long-haul destination and 16th international destination from Boston during the peak summer season.

The move follows Delta’s recently announced Boston–Venice service, which begins May 7, 2027. That route will operate four times weekly through Oct. 29 using Airbus A330-300s. The carrier is also increasing Boston–Milan flights to daily in 2027

#65. 12 Airline Booking Traps That Could Cost You Money in 2026

Airline websites are not necessarily badly designed, even though they often feel that way. In many cases, the booking process is doing exactly what it was designed to do: get you focused on the lowest advertised fare before revealing the cost of everything else.

You start with a flight that looks like it costs $400. By the time you add a carry-on bag, choose a seat, and work through the final checkout screens, the total is suddenly $650.

After more than 18 years of travel to over 130 countries, we still catch ourselves slowing down to double-check airline bookings. The difference now is that we know where the expensive mistakes are usually hiding. We also use flight-search and tracking tools to compare routes and monitor changes. See our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

The lowest price on the first screen is rarely enough information to tell you which flight is actually cheapest. You need to compare the complete journey, including baggage, seats, fare restrictions, connections, operating airlines, and the risk involved if something goes wrong.

To avoid costly airline booking mistakes, compare the total price of the journey rather than the advertised base fare. Check the conditions of the exact fare, baggage allowances, operating airline, cabin on every segment, connection times, and whether the flights are issued on one protected ticket.Before paying, compare the flight as a round trip, two one-way tickets, and a multi-city itinerary. Before leaving home, verify your passport, visas or travel authorizations, transit requirements, check-in deadline, and gate-closing time.

These airline booking traps—also common flight-booking mistakes—can turn an apparently cheap ticket into the most expensive option.

One of the first mistakes travellers make is comparing flights by airline logo.

You see the airline you normally use, remember the points sitting in your account, and stop comparing. But loyalty should not convince you to pay hundreds of dollars more for a worse schedule, a more restrictive ticket, or a fare that excludes everything you need.

Airline points can still be valuable, especially when you are close to earning useful status or have benefits such as complimentary baggage. But loyalty should be one part of the calculation, not the starting point.

The days of automatically paying more because “this is our airline” are over. Loyalty should follow value, not the other way around.

Basic Economy can be a perfectly reasonable fare. The trap is buying it without understanding what has been removed.

It may work well when you are taking a short flight, travelling with only a small personal item, do not care where you sit, and are confident your plans will not change.

The problem is that airline websites normally display the lowest available fare first. Once you are in booking mode, it is easy to select that number and move forward without reading the restrictions.

You may save $40 on the ticket and then spend $85 adding the carry-on bag you needed from the beginning.

Before booking Basic Economy, price the next fare category. A Standard Economy ticket may cost more initially but include a carry-on bag, checked luggage, seat selection, or greater flexibility.

Also consider whether seat selection genuinely matters. Travellers with children, mobility considerations, medical needs, or a strong need for an aisle or window seat should include that cost when comparing fares.

Do not buy the lowest number. Buy the fare that includes what you actually need.

Airlines do not necessarily sell every Economy Class seat at the same price. Seats are divided into fare classes or pricing tiers, often called fare buckets.

When the cheapest tier sells out, the price can jump even when the aircraft still has many empty seats.

That is one reason a flight might appear at $480 in the morning and $620 later that day. It does not always mean the plane suddenly filled up. It may mean the least expensive fare class is no longer available.

When you see a noticeable price increase, do not assume you must either pay it immediately or lose the trip.

A competitor may now be cheaper. In other cases, the next fare level may include baggage, seat selection, or flexibility that makes it better value than the stripped-down ticket you were originally considering. A fare jump is a signal to widen the search, not automatically accept the new price.

For the tools we use to compare dates, airports, and fare changes, see our guide to the best travel apps for finding flights.

The standard airline search box encourages travellers to enter a departure city, destination, outbound date, and return date.

That does not mean a traditional round trip is always the cheapest or most efficient way to book.

Before purchasing an expensive international itinerary, compare it three ways:

An open-jaw ticket means flying into one city and returning home from another.

For example, if you are travelling through Europe, you might fly into Paris and return from Rome. Even if the airfare is similar to a return ticket from Paris, you could avoid paying for a train or flight back to your starting point. You may also save a hotel night and an entire day of backtracking.

Different airlines can also be used in each direction. One carrier may offer the best outbound flight, while another has a much better return schedule.

When comparing separate tickets, check baggage fees, fare restrictions, connection risks, and cancellation policies. The goal is not to find the cleverest itinerary. It is to determine which option gives you the best total trip.

With a codeshare flight, the airline selling the ticket may not be the airline flying the plane.

You might purchase the journey through one airline’s website and then arrive at the airport to discover that a partner carrier operates the flight.

Before buying, look for the words “operated by” in the flight details.

Then check the itinerary on both airline websites. Confirm the aircraft, seat map, baggage allowance, terminal, and check-in instructions.

After booking, make sure you have the operating carrier’s reservation number. The confirmation number issued by the airline selling the ticket may not work on the partner airline’s website.

Codeshares are not automatically bad. They can provide more destinations and useful connections. The problem is that they create a handoff between companies, and that handoff can become confusing when you need assistance.

As we have learned, one of the most expensive sentences in travel can be: “You need to contact the other airline.”

Mixed-cabin fares are one of the easiest airline traps to miss.

The search result may display a large Premium Economy or Business Class label, making it appear that the entire journey is in the upgraded cabin.

Then you expand the flight details and discover that the 40-minute connection is in Premium Economy while the eight-hour overnight flight is in regular Economy.

We have come close to booking this type of itinerary several times.

Before paying, check the cabin listed beside every individual segment. Make sure the premium seat is on the flight where you will actually benefit from it.

Do not assume one premium segment provides premium benefits throughout the trip.

Screenshot the cabin shown for each flight and confirm that it appears correctly in the final reservation. A mixed-cabin fare is only a deal when the upgraded cabin is on the part of the journey that matters.

There is rarely one simple baggage policy that applies to every passenger flying with an airline.

Do not check only the airline’s general baggage page. Open the conditions attached to the specific fare and route you are considering.

This is especially important when connecting from a transatlantic flight to a smaller airline or low-cost carrier within Europe. A bag accepted on the first flight may be too large, too heavy, or not included on the next one.

A bag fitting inside the overhead compartment does not automatically mean it meets the airline’s rules. Wheels, handles, and outside pockets are normally included when the bag is measured.

Price your luggage before buying the flight. A ticket that appears $30 cheaper can quickly become more expensive once the necessary baggage is added.

Paying for bags online in advance is also frequently less expensive than waiting until the airport, although the difference varies by airline.

Finally, weigh your suitcase at home using a real scale. Picking it up and declaring that it “feels about 20 kilos” is not a reliable baggage strategy.

Once you know your allowance, follow our two-minute checked-bag routine before handing your suitcase over at the airport.

A self-transfer may be the most expensive mistake in this guide.

Some search and booking sites combine two separate tickets and display them as one journey. Look for warnings such as:

The critical detail is that the airlines may not recognize the flights as one protected itinerary.

If the first flight is delayed and you miss the second one, the second airline may consider you a no-show. You could lose the remaining flights on that reservation and be forced to purchase a new last-minute ticket.

The first airline may not be responsible for helping because it transported you to the destination shown on its ticket.

Leaving the international transit area can also trigger entry or transit requirements that would not apply during a normal airside connection.

Self-transfers can work when you have a long buffer, carry-on luggage, an airport you understand, and enough flexibility to absorb a disruption.

We would not use one when connecting to a cruise, wedding, organized tour, or once-daily long-haul flight.

Always compare the self-transfer price with a protected itinerary. The higher fare may not simply be buying convenience. It may be buying the airline’s responsibility to get you to your final destination.

Airlines can sell a connection that technically meets the airport’s minimum requirements.

That does not necessarily mean it is comfortable, sensible, or suitable for you.

A 45-minute connection at a large international airport might involve:

If a connection makes you nervous while sitting at home, it will not feel better when you are waiting for the aircraft door to open. Choose connection time based on the consequences of missing the next flight.

A long layover can be inconvenient. A missed connection can cost a full day or derail the entire trip.

We use third-party flight sites for research. They are useful for comparing airlines, dates, and routing options.

Buying through one is a separate decision.

A third-party fare may be genuinely cheaper, but make sure you are comparing the same product. It could involve:

The biggest issue normally appears when the schedule changes or the flight is cancelled.

The airline may tell you to contact the company that issued the ticket. The booking company may then tell you that only the airline can resolve the flight.

Before buying, find the itinerary through the search site and compare it directly with the airline. When the price difference is small, booking with the airline may be worth it for easier communication during disruptions.

Also check the payment currency. Some booking sites offer to convert the total into your home currency. This feels convenient but may include a less favourable exchange rate.

When your credit card does not charge a foreign transaction fee, paying in the original currency may be less expensive. Compare the final converted amount and check your card’s fees rather than choosing a currency based on familiarity.

Some of the most expensive travel problems do not happen during booking. They happen at the airport after your hotel, tour, rental car, or cruise has already been paid for.

A valid passport may not be enough to enter your destination or transit through a connecting country.

Depending on your nationality, route, and destination, you may need:

A passport can be valid on your departure date and still fail to meet the destination’s entry requirements. Complicated connections are also a good reason to review our international travel safety tips before departure.

Names matter too. The name on your airline ticket should match your passport and any visa or travel authorization. Do not assume that a nickname or commonly used name will be accepted.

Before an international trip, take five minutes to verify:

Canadian travellers should verify current destination-specific requirements using official government travel advisories and the relevant embassy or immigration authority, since entry and transit rules can change.

Five minutes at home can save the entire trip at the airport. For our complete pre-departure routine, read our travel safety checklist for 2026.

Departure time is when the aircraft is scheduled to leave. It is not the time you should arrive at the gate.

Boarding begins earlier, and the gate closes before departure. The exact cutoff depends on the airport, airline, route, and destination.

Once the gate is closed, seeing the aircraft through the terminal window will not save your seat.

If you miss the flight, the cost may extend far beyond a replacement ticket. You might also lose:

Build your airport schedule backward from the airline’s check-in, baggage-drop, boarding, and gate-closing deadlines.

Check current security conditions using the airport’s official app or website, but do not treat an estimated wait time as a guarantee. Add time for airport parking, shuttle transportation, baggage drop, security, passport control, terminal changes, and finding the gate.

It is better to have extra time near the gate than to spend the start of your trip running through an airport while your name is being called over the loudspeaker. Arriving early does not help much if your carry-on slows you down at screening. Read our airport security tips and common mistakes before packing.

Before confirming a flight, we recommend checking the entire itinerary one final time.

The best defence against airline booking traps is not a secret search setting or complicated flight hack. It is slowing down long enough to compare the complete journey.

All 12 of these traps work best when travellers are rushing.

We see a low fare, get excited about the trip, and want to finish before the number changes. The booking process then reveals the bags, seats, restrictions, connections, and other costs after we have already become emotionally committed to the flight.

The cheapest flight is not necessarily the one with the lowest number on the first screen. It is the flight that gets you to your destination without surprise charges, unrealistic connections, or an expensive problem at the airport.

After more than 18 years of travelling, experience has not made us immune to booking mistakes. It has simply taught us when to stop, reopen the details, and check everything one more time.

Take five minutes before pressing confirm. Those five minutes could save hundreds of dollars—or save the entire trip.

#66. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…

#67. American Airlines Passengers Evacuate Onto Wing After Emergency Landing In St. Louis

Passengers aboard an American Eagle flight to Philadelphia found themselves evacuating onto a wing in St. Louis after an emergency return to the airport. For one mother onboard, this was also her children’s first flight…quite an introduction to flying.

American Eagle flight AA5089, operated by PSA Airlines CRJ-900 (N574NN), returned to St. Louis Lambert International Airport (STL) on October 17, 2026, shortly after departing for Philadelphia (PHL).

According to local NBC affiliate KSDK, passengers described a frightening experience that ended with an evacuation. Olivia Clancy was traveling with her two children, both flying for the first time. Reports describe an unusual smell, haze in the cabin, and oxygen masks dropping. After the aircraft returned, passengers used an overwing exit to get out.

“It felt like that plane was going to go down because of the smoke and the way that the flight crew was behaving.”

American has confirmed a reported odor prompted the return. The aircraft was removed from service for a maintenance inspection, and the airline said it arranged later flights for affected travelers. The cause has not been publicly established and there is no indication that there was a fire onboard.

I am thankful the aircraft returned safely. But imagine taking your children on their first flight and finding yourself helping them out of an emergency exit instead of arriving in Philadelphia.

I fly so often that I can recite United’s safety demonstration from memory…well, almost. An incident like this is a reminder that knowing where the exits are and listening to the crew is worth a few moments of attention, even on a short regional flight.

And I also wouldn’t read too much into Clancy’s rather dramatic recounting of the incident. A passenger can quite sincerely believe she narrowly escaped death without knowing whether the aircraft was ever close to crashing…and that does not make her fear any less real.

Nor would I conclude that the crew overreacted because the aircraft landed safely. The maintenance findings should help explain what happened but I cannot say the over-wing evacuation was unnecessary, especially if the smoke was coming from the flight deck or front galley.

But I do question how the post-evacuation was handled. It seems that flight attendants just yelled and screamed for people to get off the aircraft…and told them to run away from the aircraft as fast as possible:

“We got out, and they just told us to run. So, we were just running … You don’t know if this plane is going to blow up!”

It does appear that emergency crews were outside the aircraft, so I hope that they didn’t run too far, though I realize that sort of evacuation made an already traumatic experience even more traumatic…

An American Eagle flight returned to St. Louis after a reported cabin odor, with passengers evacuating after landing. American removed the aircraft from service for inspection and arranged alternative flights. The aircraft was ferried to Knoxville (TYS) yesterday afternoon, a major maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) base for the CRJ-900 fleet, where it currently sits.

I hope the children whose first flight ended this way have a much more ordinary experience next time. Flying is usually wonderfully uneventful, which is something we tend to take for granted.

#68. Amtrak Guest Rewards guide: How to earn and redeem points

Whether you take Amtrak for a quick trip along the Northeast Corridor or a cross-country train journey, it's worth joining Amtrak Guest Rewards. This free loyalty program lets you earn points on paid train tickets and redeem them for future travel, upgrades, lounge access and more.

But there's more to Amtrak Guest Rewards than earning points on train tickets. You can also earn points through cobranded credit cards and partners, while frequent riders can unlock additional perks through elite status.

Here's what you need to know about earning and redeeming Amtrak points and getting the most from the Guest Rewards program.

You can earn Amtrak Guest Rewards points in many different ways, ranging from traveling on Amtrak to spending on Amtrak credit cards and even completing online surveys.

Members earn 2 points per dollar spent on Amtrak travel. Plus, you'll get a 25% point bonus when traveling in business class and a 50% point bonus when traveling in Acela first class.

That means you'll earn 2.5 points per dollar spent on business-class tickets and 3 points per dollar spent on Acela first-class tickets.

Related: Amtrak enters a 'whole new era' with Airo trains for the Cascades, Northeast Regional

U.S. residents can earn Amtrak points with two cobranded credit cards as follows:

Both cards offer a 5% rebate on points when you redeem them for Amtrak travel and have no foreign transaction fees. Plus, your points won't expire as long as your card account remains open.

You may want to get the Amtrak Guest Rewards Mastercard if you ride frequently enough to benefit from the onboard food-and-beverage rebate but don't want to pay an annual fee. Meanwhile, the Amtrak Guest Rewards Preferred Mastercard is a better option for frequent Amtrak riders who want extra perks and the ability to earn tier qualifying points with their card.

The information for the Amtrak Guest Rewards Mastercard and the Amtrak Guest Rewards Preferred Mastercard has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

You can transfer Bilt Points to Amtrak Guest Rewards at a 2:1 ratio in increments of 1,000. This means that for every 2,000 Bilt points that you transfer to Amtrak, you'll get 1,000 Amtrak points.

Bilt Blue members must transfer at least 2,000 points, while other Bilt members can transfer as few as 1,000 points. However, you'll want to consider whether the value you'd get when transferring Bilt points to Amtrak is better than what you'd otherwise get when redeeming Bilt points.

Once you earn Amtrak points, you have several options for redeeming them.

Amtrak doesn't have a fixed award chart, and redemption rates generally vary with paid fares. Amtrak says redemptions start at just 400 points, but I found this ticket for the 16-minute ride from New York to Newark for just 188 points.

In general, the number of Amtrak points you'll need to redeem scales directly with the ticket's current cash price. So, you can generally expect to get around 2.6 cents per Amtrak point when redeeming for train travel. For example, I found a train from New York to Washington, D.C., for 750 points or $20 per ticket.

As such, you'd get 2.67 cents per point on this redemption.

You can also book Points & Cash rates. You'll see this option on the final payment screen when booking a train ticket with points. For example, here are the Points & Cash options Amtrak gave me for a ticket that would otherwise cost 2,175 points or $58.

I could use my entire Amtrak balance (1,568 points) on a Points & Cash booking, which is appealing since I don't travel on Amtrak all that frequently. However, I'd only get 1.54 cents per point while doing so, which is much less than the 2.66 cents per point you'd get when redeeming the full 2,175 points for the $58 ticket. As such, you'll usually want to avoid Points & Cash tickets unless you can get close to 2.6 cents per point or have no other way to use the points.

You can redeem 2,500 Amtrak points for a one-class space-available upgrade on a one-way paid ticket. This means you could upgrade from coach to business, or business to first class on Acela, using an upgrade coupon.

You can redeem for an upgrade coupon on the Amtrak website or in the Amtrak app. Then, you can apply the coupon to an eligible one-way ticket within 12 hours of departure, subject to availability. Each upgrade coupon can only be used once and expires 12 months after you redeem points for it.

You can also redeem 1,500 Amtrak points on the website or in the app for a single-visit lounge pass valid at participating Amtrak lounges at eligible stations.

Lounge passes are generally accepted at Metropolitan Lounges in New York (Moynihan Train Hall), Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles, Philadelphia, Portland and Washington, D.C.

You can buy a single-visit lounge pass for $35 ($50 in New York), so you'd get 2.33 cents per point (3.33 cents per point in New York). You can only use a lounge pass at your departure station or scheduled layover station up to three hours prior to your scheduled departure time. Lounge passes expire 12 months after you redeem points for them.

You can also redeem Amtrak points for various gift cards, including Amazon, Chipotle and Grubhub. Redemptions are usually 2,500 points for a $25 gift card or 5,000 points for a $50 gift card.

Unfortunately, you'll only get 1 cent per point when redeeming Amtrak points for gift cards.

Related: What credit cards should you use to purchase gift cards?

You can pay $10 per 1,000 points to transfer your points to another member's account. This is a poor-value way to redeem your points, especially since you can skip the sharing fees and book awards for other travelers directly from your account.

Related: 14 of the most scenic train rides on Earth

Amtrak Guest Rewards has its entry-level member tier as well as three elite tiers that you can reach based on the tier qualifying points you earn each calendar year. Here's an overview of the four tiers and some of the perks members at these tiers get each membership year:

Once you earn a status, you'll keep that status for the remainder of the calendar year you earned it in, all of the next calendar year and through the end of February of the following year.

If you want to secure Amtrak elite status, you'll need to earn tier qualifying points each calendar year. Elite points-earning bonuses don't affect the amount of tier qualifying points you'll earn on train tickets. But here's how you can earn tier qualifying points:

So, you could earn Select status by spending $2,500 on nonpremium Amtrak travel, $2,000 on business-class fares or $1,667 on Acela first-class fares. You can also earn up to 4,000 tier qualifying points per year through spending on the Amtrak Guest Rewards Preferred Mastercard at a rate of 1,000 tier qualifying points per $5,000 in qualifying purchases.

Amtrak Guest Rewards is worth joining, even if you only travel by train occasionally. You can earn points on paid Amtrak tickets and redeem them for future travel, often getting about 2.6 cents per point.

Frequent Amtrak travelers may also find value in one of the cobranded credit cards or through elite status. But regardless of how often you ride, you'll generally get the most value from your Amtrak points by redeeming them for train tickets rather than gift cards or Points & Cash bookings.

Amtrak Guest Rewards is free to join for U.S. and Canadian residents. Members can earn at least 2 points per dollar spent on eligible Amtrak travel and redeem their points for train tickets and other rewards.

Amtrak Guest Rewards points are generally worth around 2.6 cents each when redeemed for train tickets. Other redemption options, such as gift cards and Points & Cash bookings, often provide less value.

Amtrak Guest Rewards points expire after 24 months without qualifying earning or redemption activity. However, your points won't expire as long as you have an open Amtrak Guest Rewards Mastercard or Preferred Mastercard account.

Bilt members can transfer points to Amtrak Guest Rewards at a 2:1 ratio. However, Amtrak isn't a direct transfer partner of other popular programs like Chase Ultimate Rewards or American Express Membership Rewards.

Amtrak Guest Rewards awards points to the person traveling, regardless of who purchases the ticket. Make sure your Amtrak Guest Rewards membership number is attached to your reservation to earn points.

If your Amtrak points haven't posted within seven days of travel, you can submit a missing points request within 120 days of your trip. New members can also claim points for eligible travel taken up to 21 days before joining the program.

You can redeem Amtrak Guest Rewards points to book train tickets for another traveler, even if you aren't traveling with them. This lets you avoid the fees associated with transferring points directly to another member's account.

#69. The Quiet Rise of Loveholidays on a 20-Year-Old Business Idea

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

UK’s Loveholidays didn’t invent dynamic packaging — it built its muscle through scale. The big test ahead is whether it can replicate it in Europe.

Loveholidays is one of the biggest travel companies most people outside Britain have never heard of. The privately held company sold £3.4 billion ($4.5 billion) of holidays in the year to October 2025, largely by doing something that has been around since the early days of online travel: combining flights and hotels dynamically at the moment a customer searches.

That model has become a major part of the British package-holiday market, where travelers have long been comfortable buying flights and accommodations together. Loveholidays did not invent dynamic packaging, but it has scaled it much further than its closest rival. Revenue rose 25% last year to £344.5 million ($456 million), adjusted EBITDA rose 39% to £112.7 million ($149 million), and more than half of bookings came from repeat customers, according to the private company’s financials I analyzed from the UK’s Companies House and from answers the company gave to my detailed questions.

Loveholidays, a privately held British online package-holiday seller, sold £3.4 billion ($4.5 billion) of holidays in the year to October 2025 using dynamic packaging — combining third-party flights and hotels in real time at the moment a customer searches. Revenue rose 25% to £344.5 million ($456 million) and adjusted EBITDA rose 39% to £112.7 million ($149 million), with the adjusted EBITDA margin climbing from 29% to 33%, according to Companies House filings analyzed by Skift and answers the company provided. Profit grew faster than bookings, which rose 15%, and transaction value, which rose 17%. Marketing spending increased to £143 million ($189 million) but fell as a share of revenue from about 45% to 42%, while roughly 55% of bookings came from repeat customers and about a third came through an app with more than six million downloads. The filings also show £16.6 million ($22 million) of supplier rebates tied to tourist board and hotel incentives and virtual-card payment volumes, plus £12.1 million ($16 million) of technology investment. Loveholidays launched in 2012, eight years after rival On the Beach, and is now roughly 2.7 times larger by transaction value and 2.8 times larger by revenue and adjusted EBITDA at almost identical margins.

#70. Outsite Review: The Best Place to Stay for Digital Nomads

Balancing travel and remote work will always be one of the biggest challenges on the road. When you’re a digital nomad, it’s always a struggle to balance sightseeing and also get your work done in a nice, quiet environment. No one wants to spend hours searching for a coffee shop or be in one that is uncomfortable. It is something I’ve struggled with a lot in the past.

Working from the road used to mean hunching over a tiny hostel common room table or arguing with an Airbnb host who swore their internet was “super fast” (only to find out it couldn’t even load a basic email).

But, as remote work has expanded post-pandemic, a ton of coliving spaces have popped up that combine the benefits of a coworking space with the social atmosphere of a hostel (but without the dorm-style basic amenities). They are meant for those digital nomads who want a nice place to stay where they can not only get work done but also meet other travelers (as remote work can be isolating since you’re doing it alone)!

The biggest and most popular platform for remote workers doing this is Outsite, which has a lot of beautiful locations around the world.

And, in this post, I’ll go over everything you need to know about them and my experience staying with them on a recent trip to Bordeaux.

Founded in 2015, Outsite is a global network of coliving and coworking spaces designed specifically for remote workers, location-independent entrepreneurs, and digital nomads.

They started with a single house in Santa Cruz, California, aimed at people who wanted to surf and work. Today, they have over 5,000 members and 50 locations you can choose from.

Currently, anyone can book a stay at Outsite but if you’re a member, you get access to more perks and better rates. You can pay a yearly membership of $199 or pay once for a lifetime membership at $499. Perks include access to members-only locations, 1 week free in new destinations, 50% off in flash sales, 40% off extended stays, new member mixers, a job & sublets board, and some lifestyle perks.

It’s easy to use, too. You just browse their website, filter by destination or the type of vibe you want (beach, city, mountains), and book your private room.

Outsite operates like a boutique hotel meets a coworking space. When you book an Outsite, you are booking a private bedroom. Most rooms have their own private en-suite bathrooms, though some budget-friendly rooms share a bathroom with one other person.

Every location features massive, beautifully furnished communal areas. You get to enjoy fully-equipped chef’s kitchens that you could never afford in a solo Airbnb. Plus, you get spacious living rooms, outdoor patios, and often roof decks or pools (location depending).

Every single location has a dedicated coworking space built right into the house. I’m talking ergonomic chairs, plenty of outlets, monitors you can plug into, and blazing-fast, enterprise-grade Wi-Fi. You can wake up, make your coffee, and be at a proper desk in a state of deep focus within five minutes.

Plus, there’s a social aspect to all Outside locations. Every location has a dedicated Community Manager. Before you even arrive, you are added to a local WhatsApp group and locations organize weekly events like family-style dinners, group weekend trips, Friday night tapas crawls, and morning yoga sessions. You really get a lot of chances to meet people.

And the community manager is a great resource. During my stay at their Bordeaux location, they were available to share tips, suggest places to eat, and just be there to answer any questions I had. It was really helpful.

First, the properties are really nice. Their place in Bordeaux had modern furniture, comfy chairs to work from, laundry facilities, and even a small gym. The rooms were really nice too. I had a private desk, a comfy bed, and a really lovely bathroom (the water had GREAT shower pressure!).

The shared kitchen was super clean (cleaners come daily) and the counter space was huge. It was the kind of kitchen I wish my house had. You could cook some really good meals here. (Coffee and tea are always provided for free!)

Plus, I love the design. The spaces are designed with natural light, plants, and local art. It feels incredibly far removed from the sterile environment of a corporate hotel. It feels like you are staying at your very wealthy, very cool friend’s house.

However, for me, the main draw for using Outsite is the community aspect. Being a remote worker means you’re often working alone. Whether in a hotel or a coffee shop, it’s just you and your community. It’s hard to meet people.

At Outsite, you are surrounded by your fellow digital nomads who can relate to your life experience. They aren’t backpackers on a trip wondering why you are sitting on your computer all day when you should be exploring. Because everyone is there to work and live, there’s a shared bond. You’re there to work and have fun. Most people at the Bordeaux location were there for at least two weeks. Our community manager organized a bunch of weekend events to help people get to know each other, too.

First, Outsite is not a budget backpacker option. If you are used to spending $15 a night in a dorm room in Southeast Asia, Outsite is not for you. You are paying a premium for the private room, the guaranteed workspace, and the community curation. That said, when you factor in the cost of renting an Airbnb plus buying a monthly pass to a local coworking space, Outsite likely comes out cheaper.

Second, the popular locations book up fast. If you want to spend July in their Lisbon house or January in their Costa Rica location, you need to book months in advance. You can’t always be spontaneous with their most sought-after properties.

Do I have to be a member to book a stay? No! Anyone can book a stay at Outsite. However, if you plan on staying for more than a few days, the $199 annual Membership pays for itself almost immediately through the discounted nightly rates.

Is there an age limit? There is no official age limit, but you must be at least 18 (and in some locations, 21) to book. The vast majority of guests are working professionals in their late 20s, 30s, and 40s. It definitely skews a bit older and more professional than your average backpacker hostel.

Is there a minimum number of nights required? For most locations, the minimum stay is just 2 nights, making it easy to pop in for a weekend. However, some specific locations (especially in major cities with strict local housing laws like New York) may require a 30-day minimum stay.

Can I bring my pet? Generally, no. Because it is a shared living environment with communal kitchens and living spaces, most Outsite locations do not allow pets to ensure the comfort of all guests (and to prevent allergy issues).

Living the digital nomad life shouldn’t mean sacrificing your career progression, your comfort, or your social life. You shouldn’t have to choose between traveling the world and having a comfortable desk chair, or seeing new cities and having a consistent group of friends. I met some cool people while I stayed with them in Bordeaux.

Outsite is a great platform for people who want the perks and comforts of a private home, the productivity of an office, and the social life of a hostel. I think sharing a home creates a sense of intimacy, and you will absolutely make some friends out of it.

Be sure to check them out on your next trip and go find your tribe!

#71. Newark Airport Shops Invented Their Own Water Brands—Exclusive Bottles, Captive Customers

A passenger at Newark airport found a refrigerator full of bottled water with names like Echo, Habitas, tbH and Tydal Hydro. He wanted to know why he’d never encountered these brands anywhere else. There’s a simple answer: the concessions company owns the brands. They were developed for the airport. That makes it harder to check whether you’re getting the “street pricing” that airports promise. You might have some idea what Poland Spring costs outside the terminal, but what’s the going rate for Habitas? What kind of mob situation is happening with the bottled water at EWR? These brands don’t exist anywhere else on the face of the earth — @joncoffey October 18, 2026 A designer’s portfolio identifies airport concessionaire OTG Management as the client for a 2023 water branding project. The CIBO airport concessions shops commissioned separate identities for alkaline and spring waters to replace familiar national brands. Those designs match the bottles in the photo. I looked for the trademarks and OTG applied for the name BOUGIE BRANDS. Applications for tbH, Habitas and Tydal Hydro waters name Bougie Brands, LLC. Now, the small bottles at bottom right are True Clear, which is a Staples brand so it’s actually sold outside airports. I can’t read a water price in this photo so the reply in the twitter thread “And they’re probably $13” is not the actual price but it almost seems plausible. My favorite explanation was, “They are rare, that’s why they are so expensive.” A New Label Doesn’t Eliminate The Street Pricing Rule Many airports limit what concessionaires can charge relative to comparable businesses outside the terminal. The details vary by airport. The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey’s current manual allows street price plus up to 15%, along with a separately authorized employee benefit and retention surcharge of up to 3%. A $10 street item can be sold at $11.85++. Controlling the water brands offers better margins and makes it harder for customers to recognize the markup. But the airport regulation expressly covers the same or similar items. It provides for comparisons with other retailers when the concessionaire doesn’t have an off-airport business. So they’re not just supposed to charge whatever they want even for white label water. There’s also supposed to be a cheaper option available. The Port Authority’s Value for Money guidance calls for a 16–20 ounce spring water bottle at $2 or less where bottled water is sold, or another affordable water option approved by the agency. The program also requires customers to be able to identify its value offerings. It’s not clear in the photo what the value brand is here. New York Has Promised To Fix Airport Prices Before I’ve been writing about OTG’s version of airport retail since CBGB became a Newark airport restaurant. A legendary punk club’s name, licensed for a place where you ordered using an iPad. Now there’s a collection of water brands developed for the airport shops, too. In 2021, there was the $27.85 Sam Adams at LaGuardia, plus a 10% COVID recovery fee. OTG called the price a ‘mistake.’ A subsequent investigation found 25 customers had paid $23–$27 for a seasonal beer. The Port Authority promised proactive enforcement. In 2023, a passenger reported paying $7.66 for a one liter Smartwater at JFK. The payment tablet asked for a tip, too. Airports have even encouraged surcharges as a way around their own price caps. Philadelphia authorized a separate 3% surcharge while retaining its street pricing limit. New York’s rules now permit surcharges to circumvent their own street pricing rules as well. Calling part of the price an employee benefit charge doesn’t make it any less part of the price. (Nor does the money actually mean they’re spending more on employee benefits, which are a cost of running the business.) The surcharge goes to the business. Airport operating costs are higher. Employees face badging requirements, inconvenient parking and security checks so it takes higher wages to recruit them. Deliveries through security are harder. Rents can be extraordinary, and airports often take a percentage of sales on top. Several differently named stores may be run by the same concessions company, so walking to the next shop doesn’t mean they’re competitors. The airport has helped create those costs and restrictions, and it shares in the revenue. Passengers aren’t the airport’s customers, they’re the mark. TSA Makes Avoiding Costly Water Harder The TSA’s War on Water liquid restrictions give the shops an advantage. You can buy an inexpensive bottle on the way to the airport, but generally can’t bring that full bottle through the checkpoint. We certainly don’t need the restrictions with new, slower screening machines. And it eliminates competition for monopoly retailers airside inside the terminal. You can bring an empty bottle through security and refill it. But it’s often unclear how often those refill station spouts are sanitized, particularly when people press the mouths of their bottles against them. They should display cleaning and filter change records, not how many plastic bottles have been saved. And if you do buy a bottle, there’s the checkout. Newark self-checkout terminals absurdly ask for tips. At Austin, I even encountered one that wouldn’t accept $0.00. The tip should default to zero for self-serve. Self checkout terminals that refuse to allow zero for a tip are the bane of my traveling existence.

I avoid purchasing anything from the concessions inside airports and can’t remember when I last bought something with my own $$. . If everyone, or even most everyone, would boycott the concessions, even for a short period of time, there would be a dramatic reduction in prices. Everything is obscenely overpriced and the airport managers love it as they can continue to charge high tenancy fees.

Seems like a lot of trouble to avoid a rule that we and everyone knows is always ignored by the authorities anyway.

It’s okay that not everyone is able to afford this carefully-sourced, crafted water.

Don’t buy this crap. Corporate crooks take advantage of the consumer’s so badly it’s getting out of hand.

I know you’re a germaphobe, but I always bring an empty water bottle with me through security and then fill it up (either at an airport lounge or a water fountain) and I’ve been doing this for probably 20 years. I’m still alive and have never caught any germ that I’m aware of. I recommend this simple, obvious and free. Better to stress about real problems that are harder to solve.

The haws water station is completely sanitary and it take enough that nothing touches the tap. It’s like a water fountain which is sanitary but was ragged upon to sell bottled water.

Stop this insanity of bottled water. Just refill your own post security. You don’t Even need filtrées water ; just use tap water. It’s just fine. Sheesh.

It’s okay that not everyone is able to afford this carefully-sourced, crafted water.

For a Premium Hydration Experience ™, please consider an artisan brand with the finest processed Newark municipal tap water.

I know some of you will think it’s literally COMMUNISM, but, we can avoid this nonsense with actual enforcement of sensible consumer protections… like, if you don’t like being forced to tip, or to have to purchase water, or whatever other late-stage capitalist atrocity is gettin’ ya… just vote better representation that actually cares about you and your fellow travelers, not Airlines for America.

#72. Osaka Station Hotel, Marriott Autograph Collection Review: Come For The Specialty Salon & Breakfast

For the hotel portion my first class quest to Japan, I had the chance to spend a night at the 418-key Osaka Station Hotel, Marriott Autograph Collection, which opened in July 2024. This followed a stay at the Bulgari Tokyo, Waldorf Astoria Osaka, and Patina Osaka, so this was my final stay of the trip.

Osaka Station Hotel is utterly fascinating. The hotel is owned by the rail company West Japan Railway Company (JR West), so it has a bit of a train theme, and for that matter, it’s located on top of Osaka Station (as you might expect based on the name).

Osaka Station Hotel is huge, given its room count, and it was also the cheapest of the hotels I visited in Osaka. While I found aspects of the public facilities of the property to be a bit uninspiring, there are things I really loved — the breakfast buffet is easily one of the best I’ve seen anywhere in the world, the Specialty Salon (which I had access to on account of my Bonvoy status) is one of the best club lounges I’ve seen anywhere, and this hotel has a proper bathhouse (for better or worse), which is always quite the experience.

Here’s the kicker — you’d expect that a Marriott Autograph Collection property would likely be the least “authentic” Japanese of the hotels I stayed at on this trip, but the opposite was the case. I’d estimate the guests here were 90%+ domestic, and every single staff member was Japanese (to the point that communicating was sometimes a challenge). I absolutely loved my stay here, though I’d say that the breakfast and the Specialty Salon are really what set this place apart, and without either of those, I’d feel a bit different.

The Osaka Station Hotel belongs to Autograph Collection, and therefore is also part of Marriott Bonvoy.

If paying cash, rates here tend to start at around $300-400 per night, including taxes & fees, and they do vary a bit seasonally. The hotel belongs to the Marriott Luminous program, so for booking through that, you receive complimentary breakfast, a room upgrade subject to availability, a $100 property credit, a welcome amenity, and more. That’s how I booked, and I paid around $350 for my one-night stay.

When it comes to redeeming Bonvoy points, pricing is dynamic, and currently rates start at 55,000 Bonvoy points per night. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, those points are worth 0.7 cents each, so paying cash was the better value. That’s especially true when you consider the outsized value of a Luminous booking on a one-night stay.

Osaka Station Hotel is located in the JP Tower Osaka, and takes up floors 29 through 38, which are the top floors of the building. JP Tower Osaka offers a direct connection to the West Gate of the JR Osaka Station, so you have easy access to public transit.

Let me emphasize that Osaka Station is different than Shin-Osaka Station, as the latter is where the bullet train service is from (though there are frequent rail connections between the two stations).

Osaka Station Hotel has a ground floor entrance (which looks rather cool), and then there’s a long hallway leading to the elevators, which will take you to the lobby, located on the 29th floor.

Once on the 29th floor, I found the spacious lobby. Given the huge size of this hotel plus the (presumably) fairly short average length of stay, the lobby can get really busy with check-ins and check-outs.

The good news is that the reception area is very well staffed, so there’s rarely a wait. Due to my Marriott Bonvoy Ambassador status, I was immediately escorted up to the Specialty Salon, where my check-in would take place.

The lobby also has plenty of seating. On the one hand, the whole area feels a bit generic. On the other hand, there are some cute touches, like the use of brick, plus the cool lighting.

I also love the digital clock, where the time changes based on people sweeping up trash on the dial. How fun!

A central part of the lobby is the water station, which is more than just your typical water fountain, as it’s inspired by the station’s former public water fountain.

Guests can not only refill water here, but it also features capsule toy machines that can be purchased.

As mentioned above, check-in took place in the Specialty Salon (which I’ll talk more about in a bit), but first I’ll cover the details of the room. Guest rooms at the hotel are located on levels 30 through 38. I had used a Marriott Bonvoy Nightly Upgrade Award to confirm an upgrade to a scenic corner king room, and specifically, I was assigned room 3349.

Given that the hotel’s 400+ guest rooms are spread across just nine floors, each floor is rather big, so I got a good number of steps just getting to and from my room.

The scenic corner king rooms at Osaka Station Hotel are 613 square feet (57 square meters), so they’re a good size, most comparable to a junior suite. I found the room’s interior to be modern, inviting, upscale, and well-maintained, but I can’t say that it felt particularly luxurious or unique.

The room had the living area right by the entrance, and then the bedroom area at the back of the room, with no real separation between the two areas.

The living area was spacious, with a table with one chair, and a sitting area with a chair and a daybed, along with a wall-mounted TV. Given the amount of space, I found it odd that there wasn’t a table with at least two chairs, and/or a proper couch. Of course traveling alone that didn’t bother me, but I’m talking more big picture…

The bed was back in the corner of the room, and there was another TV there. The bed was definitely on the firmer side (not surprising, given that this hotel primarily targets Japanese guests), but not uncomfortably so.

Perhaps the coolest aspect of the design was the wood paneling on the ceiling.

There was a counter with the minibar setup in the main part of the room, which had a coffee machine, a kettle, and a variety of drinks and snacks. Osaka Station Hotel offers a complimentary minibar, though it’s only filled once per stay (perfect for a one-night stay, hah). It had water, juice, beer, and sake, along with some candy.

I also had a lovely welcome amenity, including some delicious grapes and sweets, along with a personalized message and gift from “my” Ambassador on the bed. He’s one-of-a-kind!

The bathroom spanned the entire length of the room, and could be accessed either from between the living room area and bed, or from the hallway right by the entrance. The bathroom had double sinks, a tub, a walk-in shower with excellent water pressure, and a bidet-style toilet in a separate room.

Toiletries were in reusable containers from Hahonico, and there was also a nice selection of dry amenities.

There was also a decently sized closet space next to the bathroom.

When it comes to views, the room looked out over surrounding buildings, with the river in the distance. If you’re a train enthusiast, you may also appreciate the views of the rail. Personally I preferred the view from the Waldorf Astoria Osaka, though I greatly preferred this to the view from Patina Osaka.

For what it’s worth, I’ve seen some people complain of noise issues here from the train, but that’s not something I experienced.

Osaka Station Hotel has a gym on the 30th floor, which can be accessed by guests 24/7. The gym is fairly large, with a good selection of Life Fitness equipment. The gym was solid, and I appreciated the views. Despite the hotel’s 400+ rooms, the gym didn’t actually ever seem to have more than a few people in it.

Osaka Station Hotel has the Ofuro bathhouse, located on the 30th floor, right next to the gym. This is open daily from 7AM until 10PM, and complimentary access is only permitted for those staying in Specialty Salon rooms, those staying in suites on any floor, as well as Bonvoy Ambassador and Titanium members.

As I understand it, there’s not even a way to purchase access to this if you’re not eligible otherwise, so it’s really intended to be a perk for those who are eligible. Just to be thorough, let me mention that the hotel doesn’t otherwise have any sort of spa or pool facilities.

This place is as authentic as bathhouses get. It’s a situation where you’re welcomed at reception, immediately have to put on slippers, then have to take those slippers off and put on different slippers when you get to the actual bathhouse area, etc. And of course nudity is required, so it’s always fun to have someone standing there, saying “please take your clothes off now.” Alrighty then…

Anyway, I know it’s a huge faux pas, but I try to give OMAAT readers a sense of every aspect of a hotel experience, so I did manage to get some pictures (after ensuring there was no one else in the facility, so I wasn’t violating anyone’s privacy, since that’s something that’s of course of utmost importance to me).

The bathhouse has the typical changing areas, as well as shower facilities, which you need to use before getting into the baths.

Then there’s the actual area with baths, along with a cold plunge, sauna, steam room, etc.

Then there’s a relaxation area within the bathhouse, and then a larger relaxation room for hanging out, which even has complimentary drinks.

Without a doubt, one of the highlights of the Osaka Station Hotel is the Specialty Salon, which is located on the 38th floor. Honestly, this Specialty Salon is the reason I specifically sought out this hotel, as I had heard amazing things about it.

There are two ways to get access to the Specialty Salon, as this isn’t a standard club lounge that all Marriott Bonvoy Platinum members and above get access to. The first method is to outright pay for a Specialty Salon room (any room in the “Specialty” category). At current rates, these seem to go for around $250 per night more than a standard room. The other method is to have Bonvoy Ambassador status — let me emphasize that Platinum and Titanium members don’t get access.

This is honestly one of the best club lounges I’ve ever seen to — we’re talking Laurent-Perrier champagne throughout the day, and caviar and cooked to order beef tenderloin in the evening. Incredible. The Specialty Salon is huge, and wasn’t at all crowded during my stay. Even during the happy hour, at most half of the tables were ever occupied.

The lounge has several seating options, most of which include dining tables, and the entire space has views looking out over the city.

In terms of the hours, the Specialty Salon is open daily from 7AM until 10PM, with the following services:

The first thing worth noting is that the lounge has alcohol all day, and a very impressive selection no less. We’re talking everything from Laurent-Perrier champagne, to cocktails prepared by a bartender. There’s also a decent coffee machine, though no barista prepared coffee.

Let’s start with breakfast, which was excellent, but paled in comparison to what was available in the restaurant (which I could also enjoy, thanks to my Marriott Luminous booking). The breakfast selection was extensive and high quality, with really good pastries and croissants (like, really, really good), cold cuts, cheese, fruit, yogurt, cereal, along with several hot dishes.

There was also a small breakfast menu you could order off of, so I had the Japanese breakfast, of course.

The afternoon tea then consisted of finger sandwiches, along with all kinds of sweets, ranging from chocolates, to tarts, to croissants and pastries (the daytime snacks were essentially a subset of this).

My favorite thing was the fruit parfaits. The idea is that they had little glasses with fruit, and then they have a frozen yogurt machine to fill up the rest of the glass. Honestly, I shouldn’t be allowed near this, because it was just too tasty.

The evening selection was very high quality, and had cold cuts, cheese, and all kinds of individually portioned items… including caviar!

Beyond the buffet, there’s also a menu off of which you can order one item. I opted for the roast beef with onion sauce.

Suffice it to say that this is not your typical Marriott club lounge spread!

Then the night caps consisted of a nice dessert selection.

All-in-all, this was easily one of the best club lounges I’ve ever visited, perhaps along with the Rosewood Hong Kong. As a Bonvoy Ambassador member, it’s of course incredible to get free access to this.

However, I have to note the obvious dilemma that such a lounge presents. Osaka is an incredible food city, and in order to justify the cost of paying for access to this lounge, you also have to actually enjoy some of the services. You could easily just eat here and never leave, so that makes it tough to justify…

When it comes to restaurants & bars at Osaka Station Hotel, there are several options:

Let’s start with The Moment Grill & Dining, the hotel’s main restaurant. There’s a breakfast buffet from 6:30AM until 10:30AM, a lunch buffet from 11:30AM until 3PM, and a dinner buffet from 5:30PM until 10PM. The restaurant is large, and has a pretty cool design.

This is where I had breakfast, and to my surprise, it was truly one of the highest quality breakfast buffets I’ve ever seen. It’s funny, because the restaurant was super crowded (even though I got there the second it opened), and there was no a la carte selection to go along with the buffet, or even servers to bring you coffee. But my goodness, the quality was truly next level.

There was everything from a beef carving station, to an on-demand sushi station, to the same delicious fruit parfaits as in the Specialty Salon, to the freshest melon imaginable. I’ll let the pictures speak mostly for themselves. Without the Specialty Salon and/or the breakfast, I think this is a totally okay hotel, but these two things make the property memorable.

Next, there’s Teppanyaki Mizuki, open nightly from 5PM until 10PM. After my previous three hotels in Japan all had their Japanese restaurants closed the night I was staying, I figured I had to eat here, even though I wasn’t exactly hungry due to the club lounge. For that matter, I had a credit to spend, so…!

The restaurant was beautifully appointed, and had both a lounge area, and then the main dining area.

Given the exchange rate between the USD and JPY, most Japanese dining experiences are a bargain nowadays, compared to what we’re used to paying in the US. However, my gosh, this place was expensive. I ended up ordering the 140g (around five ounces) beef from the Mie Prefecture, and that cost 29,500 JPY (186 USD). Fortunately I had a credit, but yikes!

In fairness, the beef was exceptional, among the best I’ve had in my life, so it was certainly high quality.

When it comes to additional outlets, there’s The Lobby Lounge, open daily from 11AM until 7PM. I didn’t have anything here, but it has a typical menu of drinks, light bites, afternoon tea, etc.

Lastly, there’s the generically named Main Bar, which is anything but generic, and it’s open nightly from 5PM until 12AM. This is actually a hidden speakeasy — it’s located down a hallway from the lobby, with a door simply labeled “Station Master’s Office” (in Japanese… or so they claim).

This is such a fun space with all kinds of train themed art, and there’s also an original cocktail list. However, I couldn’t possibly consume more this stay, so I just had a look.

Osaka Station Hotel is a huge hotel, and it’s heavily targeted at domestic guests. So service is very authentic, which I love. This was definitely the hotel this trip where staff spoke the least English, which is fair enough, given the target demographic.

As you’d expect for a hotel of this size, service wasn’t terribly personalized, except in the Specialty Salon, where service was very attentive.

Osaka Station Hotel, part of Marriott Autograph Collection, has been on my list to stay at since it first opened, and I’m so happy I had the chance to check it out. This is a large, (mildly) train themed hotel on top of Osaka Station.

I have mixed feelings about this property. If I were just booking a standard room, I probably wouldn’t select this hotel, since the property isn’t that charming, there’s no pool, etc. As I see it, this hotel is all about the Specialty Salon and the amazing breakfast. If you get access to either of those, then that certainly moves the needle in favor of staying here.

I’m absolutely delighted I stayed here, but I probably wouldn’t return for the simple reason that if I had access to the Specialty Salon again, I would have a hard time leaving the hotel to eat, and that’s kind of sad in Japan! Hah, but consider that an endorsement of the property…

#73. Lufthansa Names First Destination for A350-1000

Lufthansa’s first Airbus A350-1000 is expected to arrive next month, airline officials said Thursday.

The aircraft will be flown from Airbus’ facility in Toulouse, France, to Munich some time in mid-November. It is expected to enter service on Dec. 3, with a nonstop flight from Munich to Tokyo-Haneda.

In the following weeks, the A350-1000 will also serve Shanghai and Singapore, Lufthansa said.

“The introduction of the new A350-1000 is part of the largest fleet modernization in the history of the Lufthansa Group and a key driver on the path to more sustainability,” Heiko Reitz, Lufthansa’s Munich hub manager, said in a news release. “Our new flagship features 40 percent more Business and Premium Economy seats. To put it simply: the A350-1000 strengthens our premium hub in Munich.”

Lufthansa’s first A350-1000 is nicknamed “Deutschland” and has already been painted in the carrier’s special 100th anniversary livery. The same design was applied to several other aircraft this year to mark the centennial of Deutsche Luft Hansa.

Lufthansa has ordered 15 -1000s. The first 10 will join Lufthansa’s mainline fleet and be based at Munich.

#74. Increase in Cruise Ship Calls Reported for Valparaíso

The Corporacion de Puertos del Conosur has announced the start of the 2026-27 cruise season at the Port of Valparaíso, which includes 30 scheduled calls through April 2027.

The organization views the 25 percent increase over the previous season as good news for Chile.

The corporation said in a press release that the season began on Saturday, October 17, with the arrival of the Fridtjof Nansen, operated by HX Expeditions, at the Valparaíso Port Terminal (TPV).

The vessel arrived from the Port of Callao, Peru, and continued to Niebla in the Los Rios Region.

During its stay, the cruise ship welcomed visits from the mayors of Valparaiso and Vina del Mar, Camila Nieto and Macarena Ripamonti, respectively; Puerto Valparaíso Board Chair Gonzalo Le Dantec; the regional minister for Economy, Cristian Mella; and Sernatur Director Carolina Carrasco.

Juan Marcos Mancilla, the corporation’s vice president and Puerto Valparaíso’s logistics manager, said the increase in calls is very good news for the city and the country’s cruise industry.

“This season, we will go from 24 ships recorded in the previous cycle to 30 calls scheduled to date, a 25 percent increase,” Mancilla said.

The season will end on April 15, 2027, when the Roald Amundsen departs.

Mancilla added that the result reflects Puerto Valparaiso’s commitment to the cruise sector and the corporation’s efforts to promote the industry nationwide.

“We are working with the various stakeholders across the port and tourism sectors to ensure this activity contributes to the development of the communities that receive cruise ships and of the country as a whole,” he said.

The organization’s Executive Secretary, Eric Petri, welcomed that Valparaiso will receive more cruise calls than the previous season.
