#75. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

#76. 25 Best Travel Apps for 2026: The Apps We Actually Use

We reviewed every recommendation and added new apps for AI trip planning, eSIMs, flight tracking, budgeting, and travel safety.

After travelling to more than 130 countries, we have used travel apps for everything from finding a last-minute room and navigating a city offline to translating menus, tracking flights and staying connected without paying ridiculous roaming charges. Some apps have earned a permanent place on our phones. Others have become outdated, overpriced or unnecessary.

For this 2026 guide, we cut through the clutter and chose the travel apps that solve real problems before and during a trip. You do not need to download every app on this list. Choose the ones that match your destination, travel style and the problems you are most likely to face.

The best travel apps for 2026 are Google Maps for navigation, Google Translate for language help, WhatsApp for communication, TripIt for organizing reservations, Google Flights for comparing airfare, Booking.com for hotels, Airalo or another destination-appropriate eSIM for mobile data, Uber for rides and AllTrails for hiking. Most travellers need only one or two apps from each category.

The Best Travel Apps for 2026 at a Glance

Our picks are based on usefulness, ease of use, geographic coverage and whether the app solves a genuine travel problem. We have also included alternatives where the best choice depends on your destination.

Before getting into specialized apps, these are the five we would start with. They cover navigation, translation, communication, flight updates and trip organization.

Google Maps is still the app we use most often while travelling. It handles driving, walking and public-transit directions, lets us save hotels and restaurants, and shows opening hours, recent reviews and nearby services.

Before leaving reliable Wi-Fi, download the map for your destination. Offline maps are especially useful when you land without mobile data or drive through an area with poor reception. Keep in mind that live traffic, some transit information and certain search features may not work offline.

What we like: It combines navigation, trip planning and local research in one place.

What to know: Directions, opening hours and business listings are not always accurate. Double-check important information directly with the business.

Our verdict: Download it before almost any trip.

Google Translate has helped us order food, read signs and have simple conversations in places where we did not speak the language. You can type a phrase, speak into the phone or point the camera at text for an instant translation.

Download the languages you expect to use before your trip. That gives you a useful backup when you do not have data, although online translations can be more complete.

What we like: The camera function is incredibly useful for menus, ticket machines and signs.

What to know: Translations can be awkward or wrong, especially with slang, regional phrases and complicated instructions.

Our verdict: It is one of the most useful free international travel apps.

WhatsApp is the default communication tool in many parts of the world. Hotels, tour companies, drivers and local contacts often use it instead of standard text messages.

It supports individual and group chats, voice calls, video calls, photos, documents and live-location sharing over an internet connection. That makes it useful for keeping a travel group together or confirming a pickup without paying international texting charges.

What we like: It is widely used and keeps trip communication in one place.

What to know: It needs mobile data or Wi-Fi. Check the phone number carefully before sharing personal information or sending money.

Our verdict: Install it before leaving home and verify your number while you can still receive regular text messages.

This may not be the most exciting recommendation, but it is one of the most practical. Download your airline’s official app before departure and sign in to your booking.

Airline apps can provide mobile check-in, boarding passes, gate notifications, delay information and rebooking options. During a disruption, the app may update before airport screens or email notifications do.

What we like: It gives you a direct line to the airline’s current information about your flight.

What to know: Push notifications are useful, but do not rely on them alone. Keep checking the departure board and listen for airport announcements.

Our verdict: Download it for every flight, even if you delete it after the trip.

TripIt turns confirmation emails into one organized itinerary. Forward your flight, hotel, rental-car and activity confirmations, and the app puts the details in chronological order.

This is particularly useful on complicated trips with several flights, hotel changes or train journeys. Instead of searching through your inbox at a check-in desk, you can pull up the reservation in one place.

What we like: It reduces the chaos of juggling confirmation emails.

What to know: Review imported details because automatic parsing is not infallible. Real-time alerts are generally part of the paid plan.

Our verdict: Best for multi-stop trips, business travel and anyone who likes everything organized.

AI can be helpful for brainstorming routes, comparing neighbourhoods, creating packing lists and turning scattered ideas into a first-draft itinerary. It should not be treated as the final authority on visa rules, border requirements, prices, opening hours, transit schedules or safety alerts. Verify anything that could cost you money or prevent you from entering a country.

ChatGPT is most useful when you give it real constraints: your travel dates, budget, interests, pace, mobility needs and where you are staying. It can then help turn those details into a practical first draft rather than a generic list of attractions.

We also use AI to compare neighbourhoods, create checklists and identify questions we still need to research. The trick is to treat the result as a planning assistant, not a booking engine or government authority.

What we like: It is flexible and can quickly reorganize a complicated trip.

What to know: AI can produce outdated or invented information. Always confirm bookings, travel rules, prices and operating hours through official sources.

Our verdict: Excellent for planning and editing; unreliable as the sole source of truth.

Wanderlog combines itinerary planning, maps, reservations, notes and collaboration. It is useful for road trips and group travel because several people can add places and adjust the plan.

The visual map helps reveal when an itinerary makes no geographic sense. That sounds obvious, but it is remarkably easy to plan breakfast on one side of a city, lunch on the other and dinner back where you started.

What we like: The shared planning and map view make group trips easier.

What to know: A detailed itinerary can become cluttered. Keep some flexibility rather than scheduling every hour.

Our verdict: A strong choice for collaborative planning and road trips.

Finding a cheap flight is only part of the job. These apps help us compare dates, monitor prices and track disruptions once the trip begins.

Google Flights is not a conventional downloadable app, but it remains one of the fastest ways to compare airfare. The calendar and price graph make it easy to see whether leaving a day earlier or using a nearby airport could reduce the fare.

Set a price alert when you are not ready to book. Google Flights sends updates when fares change, but you will usually complete the purchase with the airline or another booking provider.

What we like: It is fast, flexible and excellent for comparing dates.

What to know: It does not show every airline or every possible fare. Compare the final price, baggage allowance and change rules before booking.

Our verdict: Our first stop for airfare research. Before pressing confirm, read our guide to airline booking traps that can make a cheap flight cost more

Skyscanner is useful when you know you want to travel but have not settled on a destination. Its flexible search tools can surface options by month, country or broad destination.

It also compares hotels and rental cars, although we mainly use it for flight discovery. Once you find a fare, pay close attention to whether the booking is through the airline or an online travel agency.

What we like: Flexible searches are ideal for travellers who can follow the deal.

What to know: The cheapest result is not automatically the best one. Customer service and change policies vary by booking provider.

Our verdict: Best for inspiration and flexible travel dates.

Available on: iOS and supported Apple devices

Flighty turns a flight number into a detailed timeline with schedule changes, aircraft information and disruption updates. Frequent flyers appreciate how quickly it presents complicated flight information.

It is most useful on travel days, especially when weather or airport congestion starts knocking schedules sideways. The free version is enough for occasional travellers, while frequent flyers may value the paid alerts.

What we like: It presents flight changes clearly and can reduce airport uncertainty.

What to know: Some of its best features require a subscription, and platform availability may not suit every traveller.

Our verdict: A specialist app worth considering if you fly often.

Finding the right place to stay is about more than price. We look at location, recent reviews, cancellation policies, hidden fees, and whether the property actually suits the way we travel. These accommodation apps make it easier to compare hotels, apartments, hostels, and vacation rentals without bouncing between a dozen websites.

Booking.com remains one of the easiest places to compare a wide range of accommodation, from simple guesthouses to luxury hotels. The filters are especially useful when we need parking, a specific neighbourhood, breakfast, air conditioning or a refundable rate.

Read recent reviews rather than relying only on the overall score. We pay particular attention to comments about noise, cleanliness, construction and whether the room matches the photos.

What we like: Huge inventory and practical search filters.

What to know: Cancellation and payment rules vary by property. Confirm whether taxes and resort fees are included before booking.

Our verdict: Our top general-purpose hotel app.

Airbnb is most useful when we want a kitchen, laundry, a living area or enough bedrooms for a group. It can also provide options in neighbourhoods with few conventional hotels.

Compare the total price rather than the nightly rate. Cleaning charges, service fees and local taxes can change the value quickly. Read the house rules and cancellation policy before paying, and check whether the host has a substantial history of recent reviews.

What we like: It can provide more space and practical amenities than a hotel.

What to know: Quality is inconsistent, and fees can make a seemingly cheap stay expensive.

Our verdict: Best for longer stays and groups, not automatically the cheapest option.

Best for: Hostels, dorms, private rooms and social accommodation

Price: Free to search; booking deposit or fees may apply

Hostelworld makes it easy to compare hostels by location, room type, atmosphere and recent guest reviews. It is particularly useful for solo travellers who care about communal spaces and meeting other people.

Do not assume every hostel is a party hostel—or that every quiet-looking property will actually be quiet. Read recent reviews for comments about security, lockers, bathrooms, noise and the surrounding area.

What we like: It provides hostel-specific details that general hotel sites often miss.

What to know: A low bed price can rise after taxes, linen fees or deposits. Check whether lockers require your own padlock.

Our verdict: The most useful specialist app for hostel travellers.

There is no single eSIM provider that is cheapest or fastest in every country. Compare the local network, amount of high-speed data, hotspot rules, validity period and whether the plan is data-only before buying.

Airalo makes it straightforward to buy and install an eSIM before a trip. You choose the destination, select a data package and follow the installation instructions on a compatible phone.

We like that it removes the need to find a physical SIM card immediately after landing. Regional plans can also be convenient on multi-country trips, although a country-specific plan may offer better value.

What we like: Easy setup and broad destination coverage.

What to know: Most plans are data-only, and the local network or speed can vary. Check phone compatibility before purchasing.

Our verdict: A convenient starting point for travellers new to eSIMs.

Ubigi is worth comparing with Airalo because eSIM value changes by country. In some destinations, one provider may offer a better local carrier, more data or a longer validity period.

Install the app and eSIM before departure whenever possible. Take screenshots of the setup instructions in case your connection disappears halfway through activation.

What we like: It gives travellers another established option instead of assuming one provider always wins.

What to know: Coverage and value depend on the specific plan. Read the plan details rather than buying based only on the headline price.

Our verdict: Compare it destination by destination.

Getting around an unfamiliar city can be one of the most confusing parts of travel. These apps help us compare public transit, plan longer connections, and arrange rides when trains or buses are not practical.

Citymapper can be easier to understand than a standard map when a city has several transit systems layered on top of one another. It compares routes, shows transfers and often gives useful instructions about which station exit to use.

We find it particularly useful in large cities where choosing the wrong train direction or exit can add a surprising amount of time.

What we like: Clear transit directions and route comparisons.

What to know: Coverage is limited to supported cities, and live information depends on local transit data.

Our verdict: Excellent in cities where it is available.

Rome2Rio is useful during the early planning stage when you know where you want to go but not how to get there. Enter two places and it outlines possible combinations of flights, trains, buses, ferries and driving routes.

We use it as a starting point rather than the final booking authority. Once we understand the route, we verify schedules and buy tickets directly from the transport operator whenever practical.

What we like: It makes complicated overland connections easier to visualize.

What to know: Estimated times and prices can change. Confirm every important connection with the operator.

Our verdict: One of the best tools for answering, ‘How do we actually get there?’

Uber can remove the uncertainty of explaining a destination, handling cash and negotiating a fare in an unfamiliar city. The app shows the route, vehicle and driver details before the ride begins.

Availability and regulations vary widely. In some destinations, another local app is more common, and airports may require pickup from a designated ride-hailing area.

What we like: Upfront trip details and cashless payment are convenient.

What to know: Surge pricing can be expensive. Always confirm the licence plate and driver before getting into a vehicle.

Our verdict: Useful where it operates, but check the dominant local alternative.

Managing money abroad can get complicated quickly. Exchange rates, foreign transaction fees, ATM charges, and shared expenses all add up, especially on longer trips or when travelling with other people. These apps help us understand what things really cost, manage different currencies, and keep track of who paid for what without turning dinner into an accounting meeting.

Wise lets eligible customers hold and exchange several currencies and spend with a linked card. It can be useful for frequent travellers, remote workers and anyone receiving money in more than one currency.

Always compare the total conversion cost with your regular bank or credit card. The best option depends on your country, card benefits and the type of transaction.

What we like: Transparent conversion information and multi-currency tools.

What to know: Availability, card features and fees vary by country. It is a financial service, so protect the account with strong security.

Our verdict: A useful tool for frequent international travellers.

XE is the app we open when a price full of unfamiliar zeros makes our brains quietly leave the room. It converts currencies quickly and helps you understand what a meal, taxi or hotel actually costs in your home currency.

Remember that the rate shown in a converter is not necessarily the rate your bank, ATM or exchange desk will give you after fees.

What to know: It shows a reference rate, not a guaranteed retail exchange rate.

Our verdict: Keep it on your phone for quick price checks.

Splitwise prevents the end-of-trip ritual where everyone stares at a pile of receipts and suddenly forgets who paid for the rental car. Add shared expenses as you go, assign who owes what and let the app calculate the running balance.

It is particularly helpful for groups using different payment methods or taking turns covering major expenses.

What we like: It reduces awkward money conversations and messy arithmetic.

What to know: It records debts but does not automatically settle every balance. Agree on currencies and exchange rates at the beginning of the trip.

Booking tours and activities in advance can save time, especially when popular attractions have timed entry or limited availability. We use these apps to compare tours, skip-the-line tickets, day trips, and local experiences, but we always check the operator, recent reviews, cancellation policy, and exactly what is included before booking.

GetYourGuide is useful when timed-entry tickets sell out or when a guided visit adds real context. It covers major attractions, walking tours, food tours, day trips and airport transfers in many popular destinations.

Read the cancellation policy and identify the actual tour operator before booking. A marketplace can list several versions of what looks like the same experience.

What we like: Strong inventory in major tourism destinations.

What to know: Quality depends on the local operator, not only the booking platform.

Our verdict: A good place to compare organized experiences.

Viator has a broad inventory of tours and activities around the world. We use it to see what is available, compare departure times and identify experiences that may be difficult to organize independently.

As with any marketplace, read the newest reviews and check exactly what is included. A low starting price may refer to a basic option without transport, admission or the advertised upgrade.

What we like: It covers an enormous range of destinations and activities.

What to know: Listings from different operators can look very similar. Check inclusions, pickup details and cancellation terms.

Our verdict: Best for comparing a wide range of tours.

Finding the right trail or campsite takes more than choosing the prettiest photo. We look at distance, difficulty, recent trail conditions, offline map access, weather, and whether the route matches our experience level. These hiking, camping, and outdoor apps help us plan more confidently, but they should always be used alongside proper preparation and local safety information.

AllTrails is an easy starting point for finding hikes by location, distance, difficulty and user rating. Recent reviews can reveal muddy sections, closures, parking problems and trail conditions that a static guidebook cannot.

Download the route before leaving reception and carry a backup. A phone app is useful, but it does not replace proper preparation, weather awareness or a dedicated navigation tool in remote terrain.

What we like: It makes trail discovery accessible and provides recent user feedback.

What to know: Crowdsourced routes can be inaccurate. Do not rely on a single phone app for serious backcountry navigation.

Our verdict: Best for day hikes and casual outdoor planning.

Gaia GPS is aimed at travellers who need more detail than a simple trail list. It supports topographic maps, route planning and map layers useful for hiking, camping and remote travel.

Learn how to use it before heading into the backcountry. Download the required maps, carry power and tell someone your route. Technology is helpful right up until the battery dies.

What we like: Detailed mapping and route-planning tools.

What to know: It has a learning curve, and important map features may require a subscription.

Our verdict: Better suited to experienced outdoor travellers than casual city walkers.

The following apps can be excellent, but they are more specialized or depend heavily on your destination:

Hidden-city ticketing involves booking a connecting itinerary and intentionally leaving at the connection instead of taking the final flight. It can violate airline conditions, makes checked baggage impractical and can cause the rest of an itinerary to be cancelled. We would not build a trip around it.

Price forecasts can be useful signals, but airfare and hotel prices remain unpredictable. Treat predictions as estimates, not promises. Book when the price, schedule and cancellation terms work for your trip.

Use apps to organize information, not to replace official immigration sources. Entry requirements can depend on nationality, residency, passport type, trip purpose and even transit airports.

Google Maps can provide offline driving navigation for downloaded areas, and Google Translate supports downloaded language packs. Outdoor apps such as AllTrails and Gaia GPS can offer offline maps depending on the plan. Save boarding passes, hotel addresses and reservation numbers before leaving Wi-Fi.

AI can build a useful first draft, but it should not be allowed to quietly invent your holiday. Use it to organize ideas, compare possible routes and identify questions. Then verify flights, hotels, opening hours, ticket rules, visa requirements and safety information through official or first-party sources.

An eSIM can be useful when your regular carrier charges high roaming fees. Compare the local network, data allowance, hotspot rules and validity period before purchasing.

Google Maps and Google Translate support downloaded offline content. Some hiking apps provide offline maps through paid plans. Download everything before leaving reliable Wi-Fi.

The best travel app is not the one with the longest feature list. It is the one that solves a problem at the moment you need it. For us, Google Maps, Google Translate, WhatsApp, an airline app and an itinerary organizer cover the basics. From there, we add an eSIM, flight tracker, budgeting app or hiking map depending on the trip.

Download your essentials before leaving home, test that you can sign in and save critical information offline. Then put the phone away once in a while. The app is supposed to help you experience the trip—not become the trip.

#77. American Reports Thursday With Fuel And Debt Looming

American Airlines reports Q3 2026 results before the market opens on Thursday, October 22. Isom’s management team in Fort Worth has given investors a preview of what to expect. In July, it guided to an adjusted loss of $0.10 to $0.70 per share on revenue growth of 16-19%, with capacity growth of 3-5%, and fuel at about $3.75 per gallon (which seems ambitious, in my view), a $1.7bn increase over last year. Analysts are sitting near the middle of that range, with MarketBeat’s consensus at a loss of about $0.33 per share on roughly $16.2bn of revenue.

The second quarter of 2026 set the stage. Revenue hit a record $16.7bn, up 16.3%, and American still earned just $71MM (GAAP)/$99MM adjusted. Fuel expense rose more than $2.2 billion, or 83%, and higher fares offset nearly half of it. Matthew covered the numbers in his Q2 post, and I argued in July that American is growing itself into a hole.

Every airline is paying more for jet fuel, and Delta shed some light on what this looks like in practice. Delta’s adjusted operating margin fell to 9.4% from 11.1%, its fuel bill rose 62%, and it cut full-year EPS guidance to $5.10 to $5.60 from $6.50 to $7.50, as Matthew laid out. Delta still earned $1.5bn of adjusted pre-tax profit while it did that. United reports on Tuesday, October 20 after the close, and said in July it expected to recover 80% to 90% of its third-quarter fuel increase through higher revenue. If United gets close to that, the argument that fuel alone explains American’s results is a tough story to sell.

American’s adjusted operating income in Q2 was $453MM on $16.7bn of revenue, a margin of about 2.7%. The quarters are not identical, so the comparison is not perfect, but the gap is wide enough that fuel cannot be the whole explanation – as it never is. Investors mostly agree. American’s shares closed near $11.87 on Friday, October 16, down from the mid-$13 range in late September, and analysts have cut targets from BMO ($19 to $15.50), Bank of America ($17 to $15), and Goldman Sachs ($13 to $11, with a sell rating). Morgan Stanley now forecasts deeper losses for American and JetBlue, noting that jet fuel is running at roughly double what had been expected.

American ended June with about $28.9bn of long-term debt and finance leases, made up of $3.1bn due within a year and $25.8 billion beyond that, per its second-quarter balance sheet. Operating income was $446MM for the quarter and just $405MM for the first half on a GAAP basis. Total available liquidity was $11.3bn, and management says it is committed to reducing debt. However, as we sw earlier this year, American paid off a chunk of debt only to issue almost the same amount of future debt. That’s not paying it down, that’s kicking the can further down the street instead of picking it up.

There are a bunch of changes that might be a sign that the carrier is taking change seriously. American ended service to Doha, Santa Maria, California, and Tijuana, according to Benzinga, and announced (6) New York-area route exits in October. CEO Robert Isom has also sent a memo to employees, that American plans to order widebody aircraft before the end of the year. Adding long-haul metal while pulling routes, with debt this high and margins this thin justifies my prior concerns that the carrier is trying to grow its way out without fixing its fundamental problems. Matthew argued this week that American’s push to become a premier global airline should start with working seats and on-time departures, and the same logic applies to the balance sheet. It’s saying “we’re premium now” while failing to fix the basics.

If there was one number to provide helpful guidance, it will be the Q4 2026 estimates. In September, CFO Devon May, said fourth-quarter fuel was running about $1 per gallon above the July assumption, roughly $1 billion in added cost, and American promised a fuller outlook with this report. That affirms my suggestion above that $3.75/gallon is woefully unrepresentative of the world American flies in. It’s less a question of how much guidance drops, but what’s the overall trajectory at that point and are the numbers reasonably achievable? Capacity also plays a factor. Guidance calld for growth of 3-5% in the third quarter, and Isom has already said Q4 could be trimmed if fuel stays high (which it has and there’s no signs of stopping.) How deep that trim goes will tell us how much pressure management feels. The third indicator will be the new orders. A widebody announcement alongside a weak quarter would reinforce hwo the company approaches forward debt, future growth, and the current state of affairs with regard to equipment.

There is a possibility of a surprise, all be it small. American beat consensus in Q2 with adjusted EPS of $0.15 against $0.03 expected, and most of the bad news for the quarter might already be baked into that price. It’s possible the company surprises us, or more specifically, me.

American heads into Thursday’s call with a guided loss, a stock under $12/share, and about $28.9bn of debt. Fuel is a large part of the story for every carrier. Delta found a way to earn $1.5bn through it, though, and American’s margin was thin before the price spike arrived. If management’s Q4 outlook is cautious and the capacity plan is trimmed, it could demonstrate either caution (welcome news) or failure to perform (also likely.) If the plan stays as it is and a widebody order follows, investors will be asked for patience by the management whose strategy produced the low margin. American Airlines earnings are already in doubt before Thursday morning arrives, but honestly, how many more quarters will investors see Delta, United, Southwest, Alaska, and even Allegiant finding a way while American blames the same factors they all share?

#78. Airbnb Joins Vrbo and Marriott In Paying Guests When It Rains Too Much

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Krzysztof Kowalik / Unsplash

The idea is that paying travelers when rain passes a certain threshold can help increase conversions among those worried about weather spoiling their plans. The question is whether guarantees will spread to other types of weather — like the extreme heat seen in Europe this summer.

Airbnb has become the latest company to offer a weather guarantee, joining Vrbo and Marriott in giving travelers the option to protect their trips against substantial rainfall.

Airbnb is now selling an insurance product underwritten by insurer Chubb, which can be added on to a booking at checkout.

Travelers are given between €50 and €1,000 per day if it rains at least 1.5mm in an hour between 8am and 8pm local time for a specific amount of time at the specific location of the Airbnb, per Airbnb’s FAQs.

Chubb automatically measures rain using third-party data — from radar, satellites and forecasts from NOAA, European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts and NASA — and issues payment so travelers do not have to make a claim themselves.

Airbnb has started selling a weather guarantee underwritten by insurer Chubb, joining Vrbo, JetBlue Vacations, and Marriott's Homes & Villas by Marriott Bonvoy in offering travelers rain protection at checkout. Airbnb's product pays between €50 and €1,000 per day when rainfall hits at least 1.5mm in an hour between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. at the property's location, with Chubb using radar, satellite, and model data from NOAA, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, and NASA to trigger automatic payouts without a claim. It is available only to residents of 10 EU countries and excludes snow, hail, sleet, ice, and wind. Vrbo, owned by Expedia, uses WeatherPromise, which is a guarantee rather than an insurance product and pays up to the full cost of the stay when rainfall exceeds a threshold set per trip. WeatherPromise CEO Daniel Price said the product is priced and structured individually for each traveler and said his user research indicates offering it signals to guests that the weather will be good, which he said can lift conversion for partners. Neither Airbnb nor WeatherPromise disclosed the commercial terms with partners, and both products measure rain — not the extreme heat that disrupted European tourism this summer.

#79. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

Drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

The sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

The Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most users will likely never switch back.

The marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

The color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

The Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

#80. Air France & Air Côte d’Ivoire Add Codeshare, Loyalty Reciprocity: Am I In Luck?!

Air France and Air Côte d’Ivoire have just announced plans to launch a codeshare agreement and loyalty reciprocity, and regular OMAAT readers will know why I’m excited about this, at least in theory. 😉

Air France and Air Côte d’Ivoire have signed a reciprocal codeshare agreement for the route between Paris (CDG) and Abidjan (ABJ). Starting October 25, 2026, Air France will place its code on flights operated by Air Côte d’Ivoire, and Air Côte d’Ivoire will place its code on flights operated by Air France, giving customers wide choice of departure times between France and the Ivory Coast.

Let me emphasize that a codeshare agreement is not the same as a joint venture. The airlines can’t actually coordinate fares or schedules, so expect to still see different prices for flights on the two airlines. This is simply about each airline being able to market flights of the other airline.

On top of that, Air France and Air Côte d’Ivoire are also aligning their loyalty programs, Flying Blue and sMiles. The launch is planned for the end of 2026. With this, Flying Blue members will be able to earn and redeem miles on Air Côte d’Ivoire operated flights between Paris and Abidjan. Meanwhile sMiles members will be able to earn miles on Air France operated flights between Abidjan and Paris, and redeem miles across the entire Air France network.

Many people don’t realize this, but Air France actually owns a stake in Air Côte d’Ivoire. This is clearly less about Air France thinking it’s a good investment, and more about historical ties between the countries, and government pressure. So I suppose it’s not surprising to see the two airlines partnering.

Here’s how Air France CEO Anne Rigail describes this:

“This codeshare agreement marks a new milestone in our cooperation. By combining our offering on the Paris–Abidjan route, we are giving our French, Ivorian and international customers greater choice and flexibility, while helping to strengthen the economic and cultural ties between France and Côte d’Ivoire.”

Here’s how Air Côte d’Ivoire CEO Laurent Loukou describes this:

“Introducing codesharing with Air France on the Abidjan–Paris route is the first step in a partnership that will be extended to other destinations across the Air France network before the end of the first half of 2027. Implementing all phases of this agreement will enable us to expand the range of services between Abidjan and Paris, and beyond. Most importantly, from the launch of this agreement, our flights will be marketed through Air France’s global network to and from Côte d’Ivoire.”

I certainly don’t want to rag on aviation in Africa broadly, as you have some very well run carriers, like Ethiopian Airlines, which actually operate in a way that makes sense, reflecting demand, unserved markets, etc. But then you also have so many national airlines that are simply vanity projects that are about prestige — we’re talking Air Côte d’Ivoire, Air Senegal, Air Tanzania, etc.

Air Senegal has already failed, Air Tanzania is a mess, and not much about Air Côte d’Ivoire makes sense either. I mean, the airline acquired two Airbus A330-900neos, which it exclusively flies between Paris and Abidjan. Based on published data, load factors have been pretty abysmal, and that shouldn’t come as a surprise:

So we’ll see how this all plays out in the long run, but there’s simply no economic reality where Air Côte d’Ivoire’s service makes sense, Air France partnership or not.

Now, OMAAT readers will know why I’m excited about this partnership, which is that we’re being promised Flying Blue award redemptions on Air Côte d’Ivoire. This is the last airline in the world that I haven’t flown in first class, and I’ve committed to doing so ASAP, just in the interest of my completionist tendencies. The thing is, Air Côte d’Ivoire’s first class fares are high, the product doesn’t look like anything special, and no one actually seems to book it.

So I am crossing my fingers (hi, friends at Flying Blue!) that we see redemptions in first class. After all, Flying Blue has rolled out some other first class redemptions on partners, so I’d sure love to see this. Unfortunately I imagine that’s highly unlikely, though. Using the redemption calculator on Air Côte d’Ivoire’s own website, it indicates that “no matching redemption rule” is found for first class awards through its own program. Bleh! Maybe you need some sort of government status to unlock these awards? 😉

Please don’t make me pay full price for Air Côte d’Ivoire first class, only to be disappointed! Then again, who knows… maybe it’s actually the world’s best kept secret, with a caviar and champagne bar onboard, plus inflight massages. There has to be more to the experience than just being able to carry-on 80 pounds worth of bags… right?

Air France and Air Côte d’Ivoire are strengthening their partnership, with a new codeshare agreement on the route between Paris and Abidjan, along with loyalty reciprocity. Air France actually owns a stake in Air Côte d’Ivoire, but that seems to be more for political reasons rather than in order to turn a profit on that investment.

There’s not much merit to Air Côte d’Ivoire operating two A330neos inefficiently in a market where Air France dominates in every way, but then again, that’s not surprising. I’m just hoping that we get some good award options out of this (Flying Blue, please, please, please, convince them to do first class awards!).

What do you make of this new partnership between Paris and Abidjan?

#81. TSA Pauses ‘Gateside’ Expansion

A program that lets specially screened visitors pass through airport security to see off loved ones at the gate is apparently being scaled back.

TSA’s “Gateside,” announced in September, was initially available at 13 U.S. airports. It expanded to hundreds more in recent weeks, according to TSA news releases.

But as of this week, the program has apparently been scaled back to the original 13 airports. TSA has not yet commented on the reversal, but some affected airports have.

“TSA recently returned Gateside by TSA PreCheck operations to the original 13 participating airports, at least for the time being,” Denver International Airport, one of the expansion airports, told CNN on Thursday.

Officials at Norfolk International Airport in Virginia, another expansion airport, told the outlet that they learned of the change through complaints and messages from customers, not from TSA directly.

Gateside allows TSA PreCheck members and those with Known Traveler Numbers to clear security without a ticket for a departing flight. This enables members of the public to greet or say goodbye to family and friends at the gate, visit a traveler during a layover, or access airport shops and restaurants.

Such visits have generally not been permitted since the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001.

The original 13 airports, where Gateside remains in effect, are Dallas/Fort Worth, Detroit, Las Vegas, Mesa Gateway in Arizona, Los Angeles, San Diego, Salt Lake City, Oklahoma City, Little Rock, Arkansas, Indianapolis, Omaha, Nebraska, Wichita, Kansas, and Columbus, Ohio.

Adding an authorized user to your credit card allows someone else, such as a family member or trusted friend, to make purchases on your account. Their spending can also help you earn rewards faster and meet spending requirements for welcome bonuses or other benefits.

Dependin on the card, authorized users may also benefit from the account's positive credit history and receive valuable card perks, such as lounge access and statement credits for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck applications.

Here's a look at the best rewards cards for authorized users, the benefits they offer and what to consider before adding someone to your account.

Here are some credit cards that offer valuable benefits to authorized users:

The Capital One Venture X offers premium travel benefits for a $395 annual fee, with the option to extend select perks to authorized users.

Venture X authorized users can receive complimentary Hertz President's Circle status* upon enrollment, along with eligible travel and purchase protections. They can also receive access to Capital One lounges and Priority Pass lounges for an additional $125 annual fee per authorized user.

*Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

You can add up to four authorized users at no additional cost. If you want an authorized user to receive eligible lounge access, you'll pay $125 annually for that card.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X.

The annual fee for the primary account is $795 and Chase Sapphire Reserve primary cardholders can expect plenty of perks. Authorized users, however, can only rely on a few in their own right.

Authorized users receive access to Maple Leaf Lounges and Air Canada Cafés when departing on a Star Alliance member airline flight, and their own Priority Pass Select membership, which offers access to over 1,700 airport lounges worldwide. They also receive unlimited access to Chase Sapphire Lounges.

In addition to lounge access, authorized users can also enjoy at least 12 months of complimentary DoorDash DashPass (must be activated by Dec. 31, 2029). Authorized users are also covered by Chase’s extensive travel protections.

Each additional Sapphire Reserve card costs $195 annually.

To learn more, see our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

The Amex Platinum has an $895 annual fee and offers two types of additional cards: a paid additional Platinum Card and a no-annual-fee Companion Platinum Card. The paid version provides a broader range of premium travel benefits.

Paid authorized users are entitled to their own Global Entry ($120 every four years) or TSA PreCheck (up to $85 every four years) application fee reimbursement and can register for hotel and rental car elite status. They also receive access to the American Express Global Lounge Collection, including Delta Sky Club*, Centurion and Priority Pass™ lounges with the same entry privileges as the primary cardmember.

*When traveling on same-day Delta flights; eligible Platinum cardmembers will receive 10 visits per eligible Platinum Card per year to the Delta Sky Club or to Grab and Go when traveling on a same-day Delta-operated flight.

Authorized users also have access to booking through Fine Hotels + Resorts, along with all the extra benefits that it confers.

(Enrollment is required for select benefits)

Additional Platinum Cards cost $195 each annually. You can also add Companion Platinum Cards at no additional annual fee.

Companion cards earn 5 points per dollar spent on flights booked through Amex Travel or directly with airlines (on up to $500,000 of these purchases per year, then 1 point per dollar spent) and on prepaid hotels on Amex Travel and 1 point per dollar spent on all other spending.

However, Companion cardmembers are not eligible for Priority Pass membership or access to Centurion Lounges. Furthermore, they do not qualify for other perks such as annual Uber Cash and elite status at certain hotels and rental car agencies.

To learn more, see our full review of the Amex Platinum.

Like the personal Platinum card, the Amex Business Platinum offers premium travel benefits to eligible additional cardmembers, although the cost is higher.

Business Platinum authorized users are eligible for Global Entry/TSA PreCheck statement credits ($120 every four years for Global Entry and up to $85 every four years for TSA PreCheck) and receive access to Centurion, Priority Pass and Delta Sky Club lounges* — among other benefits.

*When traveling on same-day Delta flights; eligible cardmembers will receive 10 visits per eligible card per year to the Delta Sky Club or to Grab and Go when traveling on a same-day Delta-operated flight.

Authorized users also get access to the Amex Business Platinum’s suite of travel and purchase protections.

Enrollment is required for select benefits.

Business Platinum cardmembers can tack on additional cards for $400 each, so it’s not nearly as good a deal as with the personal card. That said, it’s still worth considering if you have an employee who travels frequently.

To learn more, see our full review of the Amex Business Platinum.

The benefits offered by the Delta SkyMiles Reserve and the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business are very similar, so let’s consider them together. Both of these cards carry annual fees of $650.

Authorized users of both cards get access to Delta Sky Clubs* and Amex Centurion Lounges when they travel on flights marketed and operated by Delta and present a same-day Delta boarding pass.

*Reserve cardmembers will receive 15 Visits per year to the Delta Sky Club; to earn an unlimited number of Visits each year, the total eligible purchases on the Card must equal $75,000 or more per calendar year.

Additional cards cost $175 per year each for both the Reserve and Reserve Business. Since these cards offer the same perks for their authorized users, the choice comes down to which card makes more sense for your wallet long-term.

To learn more, see our full reviews of the Delta SkyMiles Reserve and Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business.

Citi’s top-tier American Airlines cobranded card has an annual fee of $695 per year. While authorized users don't receive all the primary cardholder's benefits, they can still access eligible Admirals Club locations.

Additional cardholders can access eligible American Airlines Admirals Clubs and bring immediate family members or up to two guests at no additional charge, subject to the lounge's entry requirements. However, they don't receive access to partner lounges through this benefit.

Additionally, spending by authorized users counts toward earning bonus Loyalty Points each year — these are credited to the primary cardholder's account.

You can add up to three authorized users for $175 annually. Each additional authorized user beyond those three costs another $175 per year.

To learn more, see our full review of the Citi AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard.

Beyond the perks offered by individual cards, there are other reasons you might consider adding someone to your account.

Adding an authorized user can help you earn rewards faster, since their purchases count toward your account's spending activity. This can be especially useful when working toward a welcome bonus or spending-based benefits, such as elite status. Some issuers also offer targeted bonuses for adding authorized users.

Authorized users may also benefit from the primary cardholder's positive credit history, potentially helping them build or improve their own credit. Depending on the issuer, adding an authorized user may also provide additional options for sharing or transferring rewards.

Related: Should my partner get their own card or be added as an authorized user?

Of course, there are also a few potential downsides to consider before adding someone to your account.

The biggest consideration is that the primary cardholder is responsible for all purchases, even those made by authorized users. Authorized users generally aren't responsible for repaying the account balance, although issuer policies and individual circumstances may vary.

Additional cards may also come with annual fees, and authorized users don't always receive the same benefits as primary cardholders.

Before adding someone to your account, make sure you understand the costs, benefits and available spending controls.

Related: Everything you need to know about authorized credit card users

There are many reasons to add an authorized user to your credit card account. It can help someone build their credit and improve their score, net you extra spending toward a welcome bonus and extend the use of your points to friends or family members.

Certain high-end credit cards also bestow value-added benefits on authorized users, such as lounge access, Global Entry reimbursements and inflight purchase discounts.

As always, when considering a credit card, consider your spending habits and needs and then determine whether adding authorized users will provide enough value to justify any annual fees you might incur.

And remember that as the primary cardholder, you're responsible for purchases made by authorized users.

Related: Is it worth becoming a Citi / AAdvantage Executive authorized user for Admirals Club access?

#85. Tauck Adds Two More Riverboats in 2027, Boosting River Capacity

Tauck is in the middle of its most ambitious river cruise expansion yet, with four new riverboats in two years adding 30 percent more river capacity since 2025.

The Lumière on the Rhône and the Serene on the Seine launched in the spring of 2026, and two more ships are coming in 2027, CEO Jennifer Tombaugh told Cruise Industry News in an interview for the 2027 European River Market Report. The Saudade will join the Andorinha on Portugal’s Douro River, while the Reverie will sail the Seine as a sister to the Serene.

France capacity is growing 50 percent and the Douro is nearly doubling. A third Rhône riverboat is planned for 2028.

In all, Tauck will offer 37 European river cruises in 2027, including six Tauck Bridges family itineraries and a new six-day format on the Douro, Seine and Danube for guests with tighter schedules.

“River cruising continues to be one of the most popular ways to experience Tauck for the first time, and with these new shorter itineraries, we can now offer that exceptional entry point to all our guests with limited time,” Tombaugh said.

Despite the growth, the company is not changing its scale. Tauck’s fleet averages just 110 guests per vessel, with no ship carrying more than 130.

“That smaller scale is fundamental to the Tauck experience, not something we’re willing to compromise on at all,” Tombaugh said. “Every Tauck riverboat is custom-built to our specifications, and one of our guiding principles is intentionally carrying fewer guests than similarly sized vessels.”

Guest surveys have shaped the new ships, Tombaugh said, driving more Tauck Suites and larger staterooms. Around 80 percent of cabins on the two 2027 ships measure 225 square feet or more.

The company also launched Roam by Tauck this year, its first new brand in 17 years. Targeting travelers in their 40s and 50s with groups of just 16 guests, it will debut with at least two river itineraries.

“Roam reflects an opportunity to serve a different traveler at a different stage of life, but it doesn’t replace or redefine the Tauck river experience,” Tombaugh said.

On sustainability, the Lumière and the Serene are designed to run on hydrogenated vegetable oil (HVO) wherever supply allows, and Tombaugh said the plan was to eventually transition the entire fleet to HVO or retire older vessels.

“The technology is ready today, but availability varies by region and waterway,” she said.

#86. Buying Top-Tier Status With a Credit Card: The 2027 Math

Update: Corrected United, Delta, IHG and American Platinum Pro figures based on reader feedback. Thank you to everyone who weighed in.

There are still a band of super flyers out there that live and breathe the concourses of Dallas/Fort Worth, and know the barista at the Soho lounge at JFK. They qualify for elite status the old fashioned way (or by status match, at least this week.) I was once among them, I am no longer. I still travel a great deal, just not the consultants special out on Sunday night, back on Thursday afternoon. My role has shifted now to a business owner and my travel has changed accordingly with a mix of nearfield international destinations, and long haul scattered by conference and product launches. With the changing of my travel patterns has also come the changing of how business owners and high credit card spenders earn airline elite status.

Now, I still value status, but I earn it at least in part by spend and not just on my primary carrier but on secondary carriers too. Credit card spend and the associated benefits have become exceedingly important and I am certain I am not alone. This one is for the business owners.

Those who earn elite status by accruing elite qualifying miles via airline credit cards instead of the back of a tired A320 still get complimentary upgrades, access to first or business class lounges even on award tickets, free checked bags, and priority boarding whether you fly the carrier or not. Business owners can still be free agents as many of us have moved to and become an American Airlines Aadvantage Executive Platinum status holder. Maybe that’s good, maybe it’s not, but it’s the world we live in.

As Matthew covered earlier this week, United Airlines just rewrote the rules for Premier qualification. Starting January 1, 2027, Premier 1K requires 32,000 PQPs, up from 28,000. The United Club Card earns one PQP per $15 spent, and United is raising that card’s annual PQP cap to 32,000 to match. Do the math and the till reaches $480,000 in credit card spend for 1K, or $457,500 once the Club card’s 1,500 annual bonus PQP is counted. Even then, you still have to fly four United-operated flights.

Compare that with American, where spending $200,000 on a cobranded Citi card earns Executive Platinum with no flying at all. Same top tier of a legacy carrier, less than half the spend. That gap got me wondering what it actually costs to buy the top of every US loyalty program (plus Air Canada, which issues a US card, and the four big hotel chains) using nothing but credit card spend.

Setting the table, this assumes a traveler starts at zero status, flies or stays zero times (with the exception of United’s four-flight minimum), and use the single best card path available to a US resident. To compare apples to apples, I assigned each path an “annual cost” equal to the card’s annual fee plus the rewards you give up. Most cobranded cards earn one mile per dollar on everyday spend, which I value at roughly 1.2 cents, against a 2% cash back card you could be using instead. That’s a drag of about 0.8% on every dollar. If your benchmark is a 2x transferable points card, roughly double the drag figures below.

American looks like $200,000, but the Citi AAdvantage Executive card now carries a $695 fee and awards up to 40,000 bonus Loyalty Points per year, with 10,000-point bumps at 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points. On the road to Executive Platinum, that’s 30,000 Loyalty Points you don’t have to spend for, which drops the real requirement to $170,000. You also collect Loyalty Point Rewards along the way, including a 175,000-point milestone where systemwide upgrades are among the choices. However, much like Hyatt’s Globalist-light at 55 nights in a re-qualifying year, it comes up just short of the biggest prize (at Hyatt it’s a category 1-7 free night award certificate). Executive Platinum-light is at exactly at 200,000 which, for clarity, is the status itself and the milestones at every stop to 175,000, but at 250,000 Loyalty Points the larger tranche of systemwide upgrades (four more) become available.

Delta gives every Reserve and Platinum card a $2,500 MQD Headstart, and the Headstart is awarded per card type. The Reserve earns one MQD per $10, so a single Reserve gets you to Diamond at $255,000 in spend. However, if you stack all four eligible cards and you start with 10,000 MQDs, which cuts the spend to $180,000 on a Reserve. Delta has confirmed MQD thresholds are unchanged for 2027 Medallion status, which is earned during 2026, so Diamond sits at 28,000 today. Delta hasn’t published thresholds for status earned during 2027 (the year United’s new rules cover), so treat 28,000 as a placeholder until it does. The cost of carrying those annual fees is higher, and there are more initial hoops to jump through, but it’s still a mostly simple path and optimal for those that are on the edge of that spend level.

United has lost the plot. The Quest card earns at the same one PQP per $20 rate as the Explorer and caps out at 18,000 PQPs, so the Club card is the only real path. The Starter PQP deposit now requires a United card too, but it only helps members who already hold status. The Club card does deposit 1,500 bonus PQP each year outside the spending cap, which trims the from-zero figure to $457,500, and since those bonuses stack across the personal and business Club cards, holding both gets it to $435,000. But $457,500 in a calendar year, while achievable for many small business owners is so divorced from reality it gets its own section below.

Atmos Rewards (Alaska and Hawaiian) earns one status point per $2 on the Summit card, plus a 10,000-point anniversary boost. That puts Atmos Platinum, which carries oneworld Emerald, at $140,000, while Titanium at 135,000 status points runs $250,000. Spend $60,000 in a card year and you also unlock a 100,000-point Global Companion Award. I mention the Atmos Platinum level here because it does qualify for top tier one world status (as does American’s Platinum Pro at 125,000 Loyalty Points, which I’ve now added to the chart) but doesn’t achieve the true highest achievable status level. Atmos also awards status points on award flights, so any award travel shortens the path, and because the Summit earns 3x redeemable points on foreign purchases (status points stay at one per $2), routing overseas spend here cuts the real drag well below my table.

Southwest rewrote Rapid Rewards for 2027, and status got easier to buy. Every Southwest card, even the $99 Plus, now earns one tier qualifying point per dollar with no cap. Platinum, the new top tier, takes 140,000 points, and cardholders get a one-time 10,000-point boost after hitting 130,000. That’s $130,000 in spend. The sleeper: Platinum now includes an unlimited Companion Pass, so one card gets you both. Sign-up bonuses, bonus categories and partner points no longer count toward any of it.

JetBlue requires 250 tiles for Mosaic 4 – a status I tried this year on a challenge. The Premier card earns one tile per $1,000 in spend and 25 tiles just for holding it, so that’s $225,000. Spending $75,000 also unlocks companion pass credits worth up to $2,000 a year combined, which takes a real bite out of the cost.

Frontier has become the cheapest top tier in the country when it cut Elite Diamond to 75,000 points. The card earns one elite status point per dollar, and Diamond comes with unlimited companion travel. It is still Frontier and other than those with very limited ability to pay with a credit card for business expenses (I know a lot of business owners in this position) and based in Denver, it’s mostly a non-starter.

Air Canada doesn’t allow its top tier to be acquired solely through spend. Super Elite requires 125,000 SQC, and the Chase Aeroplan card tops out at 25,000 SQC from spending plus 35K status at $75,000. The card did get a $195 fee and automatic 25K status in its September refresh, which is nice, but 35K is a hard ceiling and a long way off from top tier. As for the rest of the field, Allegiant, Breeze and Sun Country don’t offer comparable spend-to-status paths.

Hotels are a different game because two of the four chains just hand you a top or near-top tier for the annual fee. The Hilton Aspire grants Diamond for as long as you hold it, though Hilton’s new Diamond Reserve tier still requires 80 nights plus $18,000 in spend. The new IHG Premier Select, launched October 1, grants Diamond Elite after $25,000 in a calendar year, still the cheapest true top tier on either chart.

Marriott won’t sell you Titanium. The Brilliant and Business cards together provide 40 elite night credits, so you still need 35 real nights to reach 75. Hyatt is the only chain where top status is truly for sale. The World of Hyatt card gives five tier-qualifying nights a year plus two more for every $5,000 spent, which reaches 60 nights at $140,000. The business card earns five nights per $10,000, so pairing the personal card’s free five nights with $110,000 on the business card should get you there for less. Hyatt points are also worth more than most airline miles, so the real drag on that spend is smaller than my table shows but I wanted the rules consistent.

Lowest *absolute* cost: Frontier Elite Diamond. At $75,000 and under $700 all-in, nothing is cheaper on paper. If you fly Frontier from a focus city and travel with family, unlimited companion travel is valuable. For everyone else, cheap status on an airline you don’t want to fly is still worthless. I will add, however, that if I was based in Denver, I might actually add this to the stack simply for the added availability on non-stop flights. But as Gary Leff often says about the Greyhound loyalty program is that the reward of the program is more travel on Greyhound, a valid point here.

Lowest cost with real substance: Southwest Platinum. One card, $130,000, and you walk away with top-tier status and a Companion Pass. For a domestic family traveler, this is the best bundle in the country, and with lounges, first class, and international partners (…in the future, with no date for partner redemptions.)

Best overall value: American Executive Platinum. For $170,000 you get the top published tier of a legacy carrier, oneworld Emerald lounge access worldwide, no flight minimum, and milestone rewards along the way. Delta Diamond costs $85,000 more in spend, and United 1K costs $287,500 more and still makes you fly. Objectively, this is the airline status to buy.

Cheapest oneworld Emerald: American Platinum Pro. At 125,000 Loyalty Points, the Citi Executive card’s 50,000 and 90,000 bonuses drop the spend to $105,000, the cheapest path to Emerald lounge access on the chart. Atmos Platinum gets there at $140,000 on a cheaper card, so on my math the two land within $20 a year of each other. Atmos fits West Coast travelers who will use the Global Companion Award and earn status points on award flights. Platinum Pro fits anyone already on the road to Executive Platinum.

Delta: one card beats four. The four-card stack saves $75,000 in spend, but at my drag assumption that’s worth about $600 against $1,350 in extra annual fees. Unless you’re using the Platinum cards’ credits, carry one Reserve. Diamond also unlocks a Choice Benefit option of a $500 statement credit (cut from $700 this year) on a Reserve card, which covers most of the $650 fee. The Reserve’s annual companion certificate, which has real availability, can cover the rest. Still, $255,000 only makes sense if you live in Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis or Salt Lake City and have nowhere else to go. While Delta’s product is excellent, it should also be noted that redemptions are far less valuable with SkyMiles than with any of the others, possibly including Frontier.

Worst value: United Premier 1K. It takes $457,500, four flights, and roughly $4,350 a year in fees and forgone rewards. A business that can push nearly $500,000 through one card has better things to do with the rewards on that spend, like buying the Polaris seat outright. Unless you’re captive in Newark, Houston or San Francisco, I’d pass. Further, the PlusPoint upgrades are worth less than systemwide upgrades on American because of the variability of the price point required to redeem them.

Best hotel value: Hyatt Globalist. Hilton Diamond is the easiest status in travel, and it’s worth having for $550 a year. But Globalist is the only hotel status I’d spend six figures to earn. Daily breakfast, suite upgrades that confirm at booking, waived resort fees and guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout are best in breed but more importantly, Hyatt’s are notoriously good at delivering those benefits. I was Hilton Diamond for half a decade and can count on one (maybe two) hand(s) the amount of times where I received a substantial upgrade at a property; Hyatt is the inverse, I can count less than ten times where the room I booked was the one I received (excluding Hyatt Place.)

Best stack: Hilton Aspire plus one airline. The Aspire requires no spend, so it pairs with any airline play. A household spending $200,000 a year can run $170,000 through the Citi Executive card, hold the Aspire, and own Executive Platinum and Hilton Diamond at the same time. At $310,000 in annual credit card spend, swap Hilton for Hyatt Globalist instead.

I always say, points are personal; it’s not the best absolute value but the best value for you and how you travel. The cheapest status is the wrong status if it’s on the wrong airline. Before you move any spend, consider the following:

One important note, while the purpose of this has post is earning solely from credit card spend, the reality for most readers will, in fact, also travel. If a business owner is going to spend just $10,000 on United, the credit card spend drops to $307,500 – still higher than ANY comparable peer, but it helps to shorten the gap. In practice, most will find that they require less than the “from-zero” amount of spend.

United is absolutely insane to expect anyone to spend nearly $460,000 on a credit card to gain access to some domestic upgrades, occasional lounge access (though Polaris is fantastic), and some PlusPoint possible upgrades. Granted, that may not be the carrier’s goal and it’s more about moving the goal posts for an increase on top tier flyers who already spend more because of the increases in the cost of airfare over the last couple of years. But I also think it demonstrates just how out of touch the management team in Chicago is with the competitive landscape. When Delta looks like a reasonable choice, you’ve lost connection with reality.
