#98. Chase Sapphire Reserve Authorized User Cost & Benefits: Worth It?

The Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) has a $795 annual fee, and it’s possible to add authorized users for a $195 fee. There are often questions about whether adding authorized users is worth it, and that largely comes down to how much you value airport lounge access, as is the case with several premium credit cards.

Let’s discuss that in a bit more detail, as the Chase Sapphire Reserve offers a lot of valuable perks, plus a generous welcome bonus, so for many people it’s worthwhile.

Let me emphasize that the below analysis applies specifically to the personal version of the Sapphire Reserve, and not the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (learn more). On the business version of the card, there’s no cost to add authorized users, but they also don’t receive extra perks, like lounge access, so it’s a more straightforward question that comes down to spending.

Link: Learn more about the Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card

You can add authorized users to the Chase Sapphire Reserve for an annual fee of $195 per person. This is in addition to the annual fee for the primary cardmember. There’s no hard limit on how many authorized users you can add, so you can potentially add quite a few people.

Adding an authorized user to the Chase Sapphire Reserve is easy. Just log into your Chase account, and then click on your Sapphire Reserve. Once on that page, click on the “More” tab, then go to the “Account services” section, and click on “Authorized users.”

There you’ll just have to enter the name, date of birth, and address of the person you want to add to your card. Once requested, the card will be mailed to the primary cardmember, and it will be up to them to get the card to the authorized user. It typically takes five to seven business days for the card to be shipped.

There are a few implications of being added on someone else’s Chase Sapphire Reserve, which are worth discussing.

First, if you’re an authorized user on the Chase Sapphire Reserve, the good news is that you’d still be eligible to apply for the card yourself, including earning the bonus. So you don’t have to be worried about that. Furthermore, there’s no credit pull (hard or soft) for the authorized user to get added.

However, the bad news is that being added as an authorized user on someone else’s personal card would count as another card toward the Chase 5/24 rule, in case that’s a concern for you.

It’s also important for the primary cardmember to understand that they’re liable for any purchases that authorized users make, so be sure you trust the people you’re adding as authorized users. I imagine most people are just adding family members in order to consolidate spending and track expenses (and maybe even get some help on completing spending for a welcome bonus), in which case that’s hopefully not a big deal.

The good news for authorized users is that being attached to someone else’s personal card can help you build your credit history, and can potentially help your credit score. That’s because the card typically reports to your personal credit report.

Before I share what card benefits Chase Sapphire Reserve cardmembers do and don’t receive, below is a brief chart with a summary.

Chase Sapphire Reserve authorized users do receive the following:

Chase Sapphire Reserve authorized users don’t receive the following:

As I see it, one of the primary reasons to add an authorized user is for the lounge access. Whether you value the Priority Pass™ membership, or Chase Sapphire Lounge or Air Canada Lounge access, paying $195 per year for that could be a good deal, especially if you would frequently visit these lounges.

The Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) has an annual fee of just $95 for the primary cardmember, and there’s no cost to add authorized users. Since many people try to decide between the Sapphire Preferred and Sapphire Reserve, this is something worth considering.

Being able to add authorized users on the Chase Sapphire Preferred at no extra cost is potentially a valuable advantage. The way I view it:

The Chase Sapphire Reserve is a well rounded premium travel rewards card that has a great bonus. Cardmembers can add authorized users to the card for $195 each, and that comes with perks like a Priority Pass™ membership, Chase Sapphire Lounge access, and Air Canada Lounge access. On top of that, there’s the same points earning structure, travel protection, and rental car coverage, as the primary cardmember.

Essentially the math should come down to whether you value the lounge access at $195 per year. For many, the Chase Sapphire Preferred may be a better fit — there’s no cost to add authorized users, and they rack up points at an accelerated rate, and also get useful travel and car rental coverage.

What do you make of the value proposition of adding Chase Sapphire Reserve authorized users?

#99. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#100. Disney Ships Reposition to the West Coast After Alaska Season

The Disney Magic and the Disney Wonder recently repositioned to the West Coast after wrapping up Disney Cruise Line’s two-ship season in Alaska.

Both ships arrived in Vancouver for the deployment in May, kicking off a series of weeklong cruises that also included visits to destinations in Canada’s British Columbia.

As part of Disney’s largest season in the region, each vessel offered 15 cruises to Alaska before concluding its season in late September.

Debuting in the region, the Disney Magic offered regular cruises to Icy Strait Point, Ketchikan and Skagway, while the Disney Wonder operated similar itineraries.

Sailing roundtrip from Vancouver, itineraries also had scenic cruising at Dawes Glacier and the Inside Passage.

The two vessels are now operating a fall season on the West Coast, with cruises departing from San Diego, California.

The Disney Magic is offering a series of three- to seven-night cruises to the Mexican Riviera and Baja California that sail to Catalina Island, Ensenada, Cabo San Lucas and Puerto Vallarta.

The 1998-built ship will continue to sail in the region through early November, when it is scheduled to offer a 14-night Panama Canal voyage that ends in Galveston.

Operating from the Pacific Coast on a year-round basis, the Disney Wonder is set to offer cruises from San Diego through late April 2027.

The vessel’s schedule includes both short cruises to Baja California and six- and seven-night itineraries to the Mexican Riviera, visiting Isla Catalina, Ensenada, Cabo San Lucas, Puerto Vallarta and Mazatlán.

Both ships are set to return to Alaska for the 2027 summer, offering additional itineraries from Vancouver between May and September.

In related news, the Disney Wonder underwent a drydock during its season in Alaska, pausing its operations in the region to undergo maintenance at the Esquimalt Graving Dock in Victoria.

#101. How To Reinstate Expired American AAdvantage Miles Without Paying A Fortune

I was super bummed yesterday when I realized that I let my dad down, and that he had a substantial sum of AAdvantage miles expire. I just couldn’t accept that mistake, though in the process, I made a positive discovery that might come in handy for some other people…

I’m sure I’m not the only one in the OMAAT community who is responsible for keeping track of the miles & points for my family. My dad has an upcoming trip on American, so I logged into his AAdvantage account to check the details and make sure there were no schedule changes, and my heart sank when I saw the below message, about how he had 141,977 miles expire.

I clicked the “Reactivate miles” button, and there was the opportunity to reinstate those miles for $1,000.

As a reminder, AAdvantage miles expire after 24 months of inactivity, which isn’t exactly an unreasonable policy. Any mileage earning or redemption activity resets the expiration, and the easiest way to extend that expiration is to just donate 1,000 miles to charity.

Obviously this frustrated me to no end, but let me just say that I actually don’t mind AAdvantage’s expiration policy, at least conceptually. Delta SkyMiles and United MileagePlus miles never expire, and while that’s great, ultimately I view that as coming at some cost.

After all, there’s a cost to not expiring miles, and I imagine it takes away from the programs being rewarding in other ways. I’m all for investing in those who are actually engaged in the program. But of course that doesn’t mean I’m going to be happy when miles do expire. 😉

My dad and I called AAdvantage customer service to ask if there are any ways to reinstate AAdvantage miles, and I was pleasantly surprised to learn that there is. Essentially, American offers a challenge for reinstating AAdvantage miles, with two options:

You have to choose which option you’d like to register for, because miles are then automatically reinstated after completing qualifying activity. And regarding the first option, it was explained to me that even if he got denied for the card, he’d still have his miles reinstated if he earned 1,000 Loyalty Points.

Let me emphasize that this is what was explained to us, and there’s of course no guarantee that this will be around forever, and I imagine there’s a time limit here for how long it’s available (my dad’s miles expired around three months ago, for what it’s worth).

It goes without saying that these are much better options than just outright spending $1,000:

Having miles expire is incredibly frustrating, especially when it’s a sizable balance of them. I’m disappointed in myself that I let my dad’s AAdvantage miles expire by mistake — I try to track all points currencies, but sometimes things slip through the cracks.

American wanted $1,000 to reinstate the roughly 142,000 AAdvantage miles, which would’ve been a good deal if that was the only option to get the miles back. However, as it turns out, American offers a challenge of sorts for those who had miles expire.

My dad was given the option of either earning 2,000 Loyalty Points within three months, or of earning 1,000 Loyalty Points plus opening an AAdvantage credit card.

Hopefully this is useful for someone else, though ideally you just won’t find yourself in this situation. 😉

#102. Old-school glamour, new-school luxury: Inside the reborn Delano Miami Beach

Dating back to 1947, Delano is a hotel synonymous with Miami glamour, South Florida celebrity culture and striking art deco architecture. A playground for the rich and famous throughout its years, the original hotel hosted presidents and dignitaries before being reborn in the 1990s under the groundbreaking guidance of Ian Schrager and Philippe Starck. At one point, Delano was home to a restaurant co-owned by Madonna and a nightclub from Lenny Kravitz.

But when the COVID-19 pandemic crippled the hospitality industry in 2020, the famed Delano closed its doors.

Now, the hotel is back, this time simply dubbed Delano Miami Beach, and it's as gorgeous and glamorous as ever after reopening this summer. Touted to "[honor] the legacy of its predecessor while redefining it for a new era," it was clear from the get-go that the newest iteration of the legendary hotel had big shoes to fill.

So I went down to South Florida to check in and check it out myself. Here's what it was like staying at Delano Miami Beach.

The vibe: Chic, airy and flat-out cool. The new Delano Miami Beach is both a living gallery and place to see and be seen.The location: Situated on the iconic Collins Avenue in Miami Beach, the hotel is located in the heart of all the action.Getting there: Delano Miami Beach is about 12 miles from Miami International Airport. Expect to pay between $25-45 for a cab or rideshare.Parking: Overnight valet parking costs $65 per night.Size: The hotel has 171 rooms and suites, multiple pools, beach access, a fitness center and a soon-to-open spa.Food and drink: There are two popular restaurants, plus a buzzy lobby-adjacent bar, pool and beach service, and a cafe.Pet policy: Dogs and cats up to 50 pounds are allowed to stay at Delano Miami Beach for a fee of $250.

Delano Miami Beach offers rooms, suites and two-story bungalows with direct access to the pool. During my stay, I was placed in a partial ocean-view king suite that had a living room area, a hallway with closet space and beautiful bathroom and a large bedroom.

The very chic living room had a massive TV (with streaming capabilities); a well-stocked minibar with snacks, top-shelf liquors and Noam Beer (a German beer in a truly gorgeous bottle); and a coffee maker. There was also a lounge-style couch, an armchair and a small table with two chairs. From one small sliver of the window in the living room, I could see the ocean, but the view put the emphasis on "partial" in my partial ocean view. If you're serious about having direct views of the water, be sure to book an ocean-view room.

The hallway served as both a corridor between rooms and a closet, thanks to a curtained-off area with plush robes, hangers, a luggage rack and other areas to organize clothes, luggage and everything else you might be carrying.

For a suite, the bathroom was compact, but the design was beautiful. Illuminated, abstract mirrors blended with a bold white dual vanity and a large soaking tub. The bathroom was stocked with Byredo Gypsy Water products and soft towels — and the shower's water pressure was great.

The head-to-toe white and beige bedroom felt like sleeping in a cloud. In the headboard, a built-in switch controlled the lights and blinds, though I enjoyed the views of Collins Avenue's iconic art deco building when the blinds were up. The room also had a large TV (once again, with streaming capabilities), reading lights built into the headboard and an armchair with a small table.

I really enjoyed the suite, especially the sleek design of the lamps and furniture. It was a great home-away-from-home for my two-night stay.

Delano Miami Beach's food and drink scene was buzzing before it opened, thanks to the first U.S. outposts of famed restaurants Gigi Rigolatto and Mimi Kakushi.

To put it bluntly: Gigi Rigolatto Miami is a scene in the best possible way. For my Friday night dinner, the restaurant was bustling and full of life. The famed Paris restaurant serving Italian dishes was also full of delicious flavors. For my meal, I started with fiori di zucchine, or fried zucchini flowers with ricotta and truffle ($38), which were lightly and beautifully fried, and could have served as meal itself. But, as multiple people told me, I couldn't go to Gigi without trying the spaghetti limone e caviale, spaghetti with a lemon sauce and 30 grams of Oscietra caviar ($135). The pasta was rich, citrusy-sweet and balanced well with the salty caviar. The dish was plentiful enough for a small group of people, but let's just say I was feeling selfish that night (and luckily, I was dining alone).

In Dubai, Mimi Kakushi has been a trendy staple of the restaurant scene since 2021. Now open in Miami, the restaurant serves a menu of Japanese dishes from fresh nigiri to gyoza, Wagyu steaks, miso black cod and everything in between. I could eat Japanese food for every meal, so I tried a nice sampling of my favorites: an earthy, bold miso soup with truffle ($12), perfectly crafted pieces of freshwater eel nigiri and tuna nigiri ($17 for two pieces, each) and black cod and tiger prawns gyoza with citrus miso ($28). The well-crafted, umami-packed miso set the bar high for the rest of the meal, and the nigiri was as light and fresh as I've had. In fact, I was tempted to order more nigiri, but after packing in all of the delicious gyoza, I decided to call it and appreciate the great meal I had.

But not without dessert! To end the meal, I tucked away a piece of Hokkaido cheesecake with strawberries and an earthy matcha sauce ($18). The subtle sweetness of the cheesecake was the perfect base for the rich matcha, and after I said I was done, I went back in for "just one more bite" multiple times.

As I told people I was heading to Mimi Kakushi, everyone I talked to insisted I order "the world's coldest martini." Well, I love martinis, so it was an obvious must. Dubbed the Nara Nara ($38), the martini consists of Botanist Gin being chiseled from a giant block of ice (kept at a freezing –4°F) tableside, making for a show as cool as the drink itself.

Adjacent to the lobby, Rose Bar is open nightly for drinks. The menu has an interesting cocktail menu with options like the Rose old fashioned with Macallan 12, banana, salted caramel and chocolate ($35) and the chamomile penicillin made with Johnnie Walker Black Label, chamomile, ginger, carrot, honey and Campari ($23).

Delano Miami Beach also has an Italian-style coffee shop with classic coffee drinks, upscale pours like an iced pistachio milk shakerato ($15), juices, pastries, breakfast items and fruit bowls. Various food menus from the different restaurants are also available for order at the pool and beach.

Service throughout the hotel was near exceptional, and it seemed like most of the people working at Delano Miami Beach were truly happy to be there — and happy to assist. Especially at Rose Bar, the outdoor bar at Gigi and the pool. The only mishap I experienced was a manager berating a bartender about one foot in front of me, while I was the only person at the bar trying to listen to the live music. Luckily, the pool staff over the course of my stay made up for it, and I can't thank Malou, Tania and Arian for their incredible hospitality.

Cash rates at Delano Miami Beach start around $600 per night. As an Accor property, members of its loyalty program can trade in multiples of 2,000 points for 40 euros (about $44) off a stay.

Delano Miami Beach also participates in The Edit by Chase Travel, allowing eligible cardholders to receive elite-like benefits like daily breakfast for two, property credits and more.

Delano Miami Beach has all the expected accessibility features travelers should anticipate in the United States, including dedicated accessible rooms and public spaces, and a pool with a lift.

As always, TPG recommends calling the hotel before booking to ensure they can meet your needs.

Miami Beach has no shortage of incredible luxury hotels, but few are as storied as Delano. All in all, I thoroughly enjoyed my two-night stay, and my only regret is that I couldn't stay longer. From mouthwatering nigiri at Mimi to salty caviar at Gigi, and the best pool attendants I've ever encountered, the all-new Delano Miami Beach really brought back to life a true Miami legend.

#103. Citi Strata Card Eligibility Rules: Elite, Premier, & Strata Bonus Requirements

Citi has a portfolio of cards earning ThankYou points, with the Citi Strata Card lineup being the core of that — this includes the Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (learn more), Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more), and Citi Strata℠ Card (learn more).

As is the case with any credit card lineup, it’s important to understand the approval and bonus eligibility rules, so that you can know how many cards you can apply for, how many welcome offers you can earn, etc. In this post, I’d like to take a look at the approval and bonus rules for the Citi Strata lineup, especially factoring in the recent changes that we saw.

Link: Learn more about the Citi Strata Elite℠ Card, Citi Strata Premier® Card, or Citi Strata℠ Card

Citi ThankYou has three “flagship” cards in its product lineup, at very different price points. Here are the basics of the welcome offers of these cards:

There are pros and cons to each of these cards, and for many people, there could be value in creating a portfolio of these cards. Broadly speaking:

At a minimum, you’re definitely going to want to have either the Citi Strata Elite Card or Citi Strata Premier Card, as these cards let you unleash the full potential of the ThankYou ecosystem, and transfer points to airline and hotel partners (including American AAdvantage) at the best ratio!

What does it take to get approved for the Citi Strata Elite Card, Citi Strata Premier Card, or Citi Strata Card? The good news is that eligibility for these three cards is considered independently, so in theory, you’re eligible for all three cards (including the welcome offers).

So let’s go over the things you should consider if applying for one of these cards, given that credit card issuers have all kinds of rules that we should be aware of.

Citi will generally approve cardmembers for at most one Citi card every eight days, and at most two Citi cards every 65 days. This is a rolling limit, so just make sure you observe that. This is specific to Citi cards — applying for cards with other issuers won’t count toward that limit.

The welcome bonuses on the Citi Strata Elite Card, Citi Strata Premier Card, and Citi Strata Card, aren’t available to those who have received a new cardmember bonus on those exact cards in the past. The cards each used to have a 48-month rule, meaning that you couldn’t earn the bonus on a particular card if you had received a new cardmember bonus on that particular card in the past 48 months. That has been changed, though, and now it’s a “once in a lifetime” rule.

Let me emphasize that those requirements are considered independently. That’s to say that if you already have the Citi Strata Premier Card, you’d be eligible for the Citi Strata Elite Card (including the welcome bonus), and vice versa.

One other thing worth noting is that for Citi Strata Card eligibility, that also factors in whether you’ve earned a bonus on the Citi Rewards+ Card in the past. That’s because the Citi Strata Card was formerly known as the Citi Rewards+ Card, before it was rebranded.

In the interest of being thorough, I should also mention that if you have the Citi Prestige Card (which is no longer open to new applicants), you’re still eligible for the welcome offers on any of these cards, as that’s considered a separate product.

There’s not a consistent rule as to what credit score you need in order to be approved for the Citi Strata Elite Card, Citi Strata Premier Card, or Citi Strata Card. Credit score is one of only many considerations when being approved for a card. In general, I’d recommend having a credit score in the “good” to “excellent” range if you’re going to apply for this card.

Personally, I probably wouldn’t apply if my credit score were under 700, and ideally, I’d hope to have a credit score of 740 or higher. That being said, people with scores lower than that have been approved, and conversely, people with scores higher than that have been rejected. There are lots of factors that go into approval — your income, your credit history, how much credit Citi has already extended you, etc.

To answer a few more of the frequently asked questions when it comes to Citi Strata Elite Card, Citi Strata Premier Card, or Citi Strata Card approval…

No card issuer is terribly consistent when it comes to approving people for cards, as there are so many factors that go into this decision. Personally, I find Citi cards to be reasonably easy to get approved for, assuming you have good credit, including a substantial amount of credit history, and meet the eligibility requirements.

Eligibility for each of the Citi Strata products is considered independently, so over time you absolutely could pick up the Citi Strata Elite Card, Citi Strata Premier Card, and Citi Strata Card. Just make sure you follow the Citi 8/65 rule, and that you haven’t received a new cardmember bonus on that exact card (or its predecessor) in the past.

I think it absolutely could make sense to create a portfolio of Citi ThankYou cards, in order to maximize your points. Broadly speaking:

Approvals on Citi credit cards can be instant, and you’ll often find that to be the case. However, in some situations a manual review may be needed, so don’t worry if you get a message stating that your application requires further processing time — it doesn’t mean you’ll be rejected. You can generally expect that you’ll get a final decision within a week or so of applying.

If you apply for one of the Citi Strata Card products, there’s not a single credit bureau that Citi always pulls from. It could be Equifax, Experian, or Transunion, depending on a variety of factors.

What are the negative impacts of applying for a credit card and getting denied? The only downside is that there’s a new inquiry on your credit file, which could temporarily ding your score by a few points. While everyone’s situation is different, personally, I wouldn’t consider that to be a big issue, as losing a few points temporarily shouldn’t have major implications.

Meanwhile getting approved for the card and using it responsibly could have a very positive impact on your credit score, by improving your total available credit, history of on-time payments, credit utilization, etc.

Yes, you can. If you’ve been denied for one of the versions of the Citi Strata Card, you could apply again. Just because you get denied once doesn’t mean you’ll be denied again, especially if aspects of your credit worthiness have improved (for example, if your credit score went up, the number of cards you opened in the past two years went down, etc.).

However, I’d wait six months (or so) between applications, and make sure that something has changed (for the better) about your credit situation.

You’re only eligible for the welcome bonus on a Citi card if you apply for it outright, and not if you product change to it. So while product changing or downgrading cards can often make sense, the lack of bonus eligibility is one major downside to not applying directly.

If you’re the authorized user on someone else’s Citi card, are you eligible for the welcome bonus on that card as well, if you apply outright? The answer is absolutely — being an authorized user on someone’s card never precludes you from being able to apply directly, and earn the bonus.

Citi has a robust portfolio of personal cards earning ThankYou points, particularly with the Citi Strata Elite Card, Citi Strata Premier Card, and Citi Strata Card. These cards all offer excellent welcome bonuses, and can be extremely rewarding, especially for those looking to earn American AAdvantage miles.

The good news is that these cards shouldn’t be too difficult to get approved for, and on top of that, you should be able to apply for all of these cards over time, including earning the welcome bonuses. Just make sure you have a good credit score and are familiar with Citi’s eligibility requirements.

If you’ve applied for the Citi Strata Elite Card, Citi Strata Premier Card, or Citi Strata Card, what was your experience like?

#104. I just saved $450 on a 2-night hotel stay by changing how I use this Amex Platinum benefit

I recently saved around $450 on a two-night hotel stay by booking it with the right card. And I did it in a way I honestly hadn't tried before, but absolutely will again.

The American Express Platinum Card®, which I have and love, comes with up to $600 in annual hotel statement credits, split into two up-to-$300 credits each calendar year — one from January through June and another from July through December.

These can be used on eligible prepaid stays booked through American Express Travel® at either Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection. The Hotel Collection requires a minimum two-night stay.

But as I recently discovered, how you use that credit can make a big difference in the value you get from it.

Related: How to maximize the $300 Amex Platinum hotel credit

To be transparent, I've mostly used our Amex Platinum hotel statement credits for stays at Fine Hotels + Resorts rather than The Hotel Collection.

That's partly because Fine Hotels + Resorts allows one-night bookings, but also because its properties come with more extensive benefits, including complimentary breakfast for two and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout.

The problem with that strategy is that Fine Hotels + Resorts properties are generally pretty pricey. As in, it's not uncommon for stays to cost $500 to $1,000 per night.

TPG Tip: You can use sites such as MaxMyFHR to quickly find some of the lower-cost hotels and dates where you can use these benefits.

While a up-to-$300 credit can make a one-night luxury stay more affordable, that isn't always the best fit when I'm traveling with my family.

The Hotel Collection includes a range of upscale properties, some of which can be more affordable than Fine Hotels + Resorts options.

On a recent long weekend trip to Disney World with my family, we used our $300 credit to book a two-night stay at the Walt Disney World Swan, which is part of The Hotel Collection.

For those not familiar with the Walt Disney World Swan, it's actually a Marriott property located on Disney property, within walking distance of both Epcot and Disney's Hollywood Studios. It's basically a perfect combination for someone who loves points, card perks and Disney.

The nearby Walt Disney World Dolphin and Walt Disney World Swan Reserve are also Marriott properties available through Amex's The Hotel Collection.

Related: Best hotels near Disney World you can book with points

Our two-night stay at the Swan over a busy holiday weekend cost $672 through Amex Travel, plus a resort fee that we paid directly to the hotel.

That charge triggered the $300 Amex Platinum statement credit, bringing our pre-resort-fee cost down to just $372 total, or $186 per night. For a nice hotel on Disney property during a holiday weekend, this was already a great deal.

But that wasn't the only reason this was such a great way to book the stay.

While The Hotel Collection's benefits aren't as extensive as those at Fine Hotels + Resorts, they still made a pretty big difference. In this case, booking through Amex Travel and The Hotel Collection came with a $150 property credit.

We used most of that credit on dinner and drinks for the whole family at Rosa Mexicano at the neighboring Dolphin, and the rest on some other incidentals. We charged the meal back to our room at the Swan, allowing us to use the credit on something we would have paid for anyway.

The Hotel Collection typically advertises a $100 property credit as part of its benefits, but some hotels offer more, as was the case here.

Factoring in the $150 property credit, which we used toward expenses we would have paid for anyway, we received $450 in combined value from the stay. That brought our effective cost to $222 total, or $111 per night, before the resort fee.

That's a pretty unbeatable deal for a hotel on Disney property during a busy holiday weekend.

We were also able to get a 2 p.m. late checkout, which was pretty generous considering how busy the weekend was. Late checkout is subject to availability with The Hotel Collection, unlike the guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout you'd get through Fine Hotels + Resorts.

My Marriott Platinum benefits were also honored on the stay, which tacked on a $20 daily breakfast voucher that we were able to redeem at one of the on-property grab-and-go shops.

By combining the Amex Platinum's $300 hotel statement credit with a $150 property credit through The Hotel Collection, we received about $450 in value on a two-night stay we were already planning.

That alone doesn't offset the card's $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), but making the most of benefits like this one throughout the year is exactly how you can come out ahead with premium rewards cards.

And after years of primarily using my Amex Platinum hotel credits on short Fine Hotels + Resorts properties, I'll absolutely be giving The Hotel Collection a closer look going forward.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Platinum Card.

#105. Royal Caribbean’s Oasis Swaps Bahamas for Canada

Royal Caribbean changed the itinerary of the current cruise onboard the Oasis of the Seas due to adverse weather conditions.

Sailing from Cape Liberty, the Oasis-class vessel was initially scheduled to offer a seven-night cruise to destinations in the Bahamas and Florida.

According to a statement sent to guests before departure, the planned itinerary will no longer go ahead. Instead, the ship will now sail North, docking in Halifax, Nova Scotia, for an overnight stay.

“Along with our meteorologist team, we’ve been closely monitoring inclement weather developing off the East Coast for our October 18, 2026, sailing,” Royal Caribbean said.

“The weather’s impact makes it hard to provide you with a safe and comfortable journey to Florida and the Bahamas,” the company continued.

Sailing from Royal Caribbean’s cruise terminal in Bayonne, the cruise was originally scheduled to visit Port Canaveral, Perfect Day CocoCay and Nassau before returning to the U.S. Northeast.

“After exploring all of our options, we’ve decided to sail to Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada, for an overnight stay instead,” Royal Caribbean explained.

In its statement, the company noted that the sailing required different documentation from guests, adding that some nationalities may need visas to visit Canada.

“We truly appreciate your understanding and flexibility regarding this unexpected change,” Royal Caribbean added.

To thank guests for their “continued loyalty and to help make up for the inconvenience,” the company offered refundable onboard credits.

According to the statement, the credit was applied for first and second guests, based on stateroom categories.

Inside and outside staterooms received $200, while balcony cabins received $300 and suites received $600. Royal Caribbean also offered an additional $100 per person for each third or more guest.

As a gesture of goodwill, the company also offered a 50 percent Future Cruise Credit to be used toward another sailing.

Any prepaid shore excursions for the cancelled ports were fully refunded as onboard credit. If unused, the amounts will be refunded to the credit card associated with passengers’ onboard accounts.

Launched in 2009 as the first ship in Royal Caribbean’s Oasis class series, the Oasis of the Seas is currently wrapping up a summer scheduled in the U.S. Northeast.

In November, the vessel returns to Fort Lauderdale for a series of three- and four-night cruises to the Bahamas.

#106. Patina Osaka Review: Beautiful Design, Excellent Dining, And A Highway Noise Problem

For the hotel portion my first class quest to Japan, I had the chance to spend a night at the 221-key Patina Osaka, which opened in May 2025. This followed a stay at the Bulgari Tokyo and Waldorf Astoria Osaka, and then I also stayed at the Osaka Station Hotel (Marriott Autograph Collection). Osaka’s hotel market has really been taken to the next level in recent years, and that’s very cool to see, because it’s an underrated city that doesn’t get enough love from foreigners.

For those not familiar with Patina, it’s the sister brand of Capella Hotels & Resorts, which is among my favorite hotel brands in the world. Patina so far has two hotels, in the Maldives and Osaka. The idea is that Patina has the same general DNA as Capella properties in terms of amazing design, an emphasis on food & beverage, and a focus on culture, but the properties have a higher room count, and lack some of the exclusive amenities of Capella, like a lounge all guests can visit.

It’s worth noting that Patina Osaka was also rated the best hotel in the world, according to the recent Travel + Leisure 2026 rankings (these kinds of rankings create their own issues).

Anyway, how was my stay at Patina Osaka? All-in-all, it was very good. The hotel’s design is beautiful, the staff were friendly, and the food & beverage outlets were excellent. However, I had one major issue with this hotel, which is that it’s basically located on top of a highway, and if you’re staying on one side of the hotel, expect a lot of noise.

Furthermore, since Patina Osaka is a standalone building, you don’t quite get the same views as at some of the other hotels that are located at the top of skyscrapers. These are minor points in the scheme of things, but worth mentioning. Anyway, that’s enough of an intro, let’s get into the review…

Relatively speaking, Osaka is a good value luxury hotel market, given the quality of properties. Rates at Patina Osaka vary throughout the year, but typically start at around $550 per night, including taxes and service charges.

That’s exactly how much my stay cost, which I booked through Virtuoso. For booking through Virtuoso, I received a complimentary upgrade subject to availability, free breakfast, and a $100 property credit.

I should also mention that Patina participates in GHA Discovery, a loyalty program that often flies under the radar. I had recently taken advantage of a GHA Titanium status match, so I was curious to see what the experience would be like.

Patina Osaka is located in a standalone 20-story building, which in and of itself is unique, since so many hotels in Japan take up a small number of floors at the top of a skyscraper.

In terms of the hotel’s location, it’s next to Osaka Castle and Osaka Castle Park. On the surface that’s appealing, since that’s a popular attraction, and it makes for nice views. However, it is a bit removed from much of the action, so you’re not really otherwise in the heart of things. Furthermore, as I’ll discuss in more detail in the rooms section, the hotel is located off a major highway. So either you’re looking at Osaka Castle (beautiful) or you’re looking at the highway (bleh!).

Anyway, as you arrive at Patina Osaka, you definitely get an urban resort vibe, which I quite like. There’s lots of greenery, and the hotel’s driveway and entrance area is quite large.

My arrival experience at Patina Osaka was smooth. I was welcomed by the bellmen, my bag was taken, and I was escorted to the elevators, to take me up to the lobby. While the hotel is in a standalone building, the lobby is still on 20th floor, presumably since that makes for the best views.

There’s still a nice ground floor area, and it’s also where one of the restaurants is located. I like the way that wood is used, as it has a very Japanese feel to it.

The 20th floor lobby setup at Patina Osaka is interesting. The space is gorgeous and has a great sense of place, with floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking Osaka Castle, and I love the slanted ceiling. One quirky thing is that the reception desk is basically one side of the bar.

I don’t have an issue with that, but when I see that kind of a setup, I immediately think of limited service hotels in the US. Of course the service standard here was completely different. On the surface, a 221 room property having just two check-in “stations” isn’t sufficient, though they also invite you to have a seat during check-in formalities, so they do a good job with that.

Anyway, I received a very warm welcome, and was given a welcome drink and cold towel.

My room was soon ready, and the front desk associate offered to escort me to the room, but that wasn’t necessary, so I politely declined.

I also quickly had a look at the rest of the lobby. There’s a ton of seating in the lobby area, which guests are free to just lounge around in, but food and drinks are also available, if you’d like. This area also has the best views of Osaka Castle.

Also on the lobby level is The Listening Room by OJAS, advertised as offering the ability to “meditate in the elegant envelopment of sound.” There are complimentary “morning soundscapes,” or guests can make private bookings for one-hour slots. I love this concept, I think, though I’m still not sure I actually understand it? You’re just supposed to sit here and listen to nice music, or…?

With keys in hand, I headed to my room at Patina Osaka. One quirk with the hotel is that there are two sets of elevators — one to guest rooms, and one to public spaces — and I kind of found it confusing to remember which elevator bank served which purpose.

I was assigned room 1412, located on the 14th floor. Guest rooms are located on floors six through 17. I loved the design of the elevator areas and hallways, as they all have a great sense of place.

I was in a premier city view room, which is marketed as being 678 square feet (63 square meters). So that’s an absolutely massive size for a non-suite, and it represented an upgrade of a couple of levels, presumably based on a combination of my Virtuoso booking plus GHA Discovery Titanium status.

The room featured a long entryway with a closet space right by the door, the bathroom off to the side, and the rest of the room down the hallway.

In the center of the room was a comfortable king size bed, with a chair and ottoman next to it. The bed was comfortable (though not as comfortable as at the Waldorf Astoria, based on my preferences). I liked the design behind the bed, but otherwise, that side of the room had pretty minimalist decor.

I also appreciated the very simple lighting controls next to the bed, along with USB-A and USB-C outlets.

The other side of the room had a much more interesting design, with a unique dining table that had two chairs (one “standard,” one more traditionally Japanese, in the sense that it was on the “floor,” but the floor was actually an elevated, hard, day bed, of sorts).

Waiting on that table was a welcome amenity, with some tea, grapes, matcha, and sweets.

The minibar was beautifully designed, and had a complimentary Nespresso machine and tea kettle, along with a variety of drinks and snacks for purchase.

The bathroom was then back toward the entrance, and I loved the design of this space, including double sinks, a huge shower “complex” with a walk-in shower and bathtub, and a bidet-style toilet. The shower pressure was phenomenal, as was the case at all hotels I stayed at in Japan.

Toiletries were from Bamford, as is standard across Capella and Patina, and I absolutely love that.

Now let me get to the part of the room that should’ve been a very nice amenity, but wasn’t. My room at Patina Osaka had a balcony, which is a rare amenity at a city hotel in Japan, so I thought that was cool. However, you may see the issue based on the below picture.

The issue is that Patina Osaka is basically located on top of a major highway. Obviously it’s incredibly noisy when you’re on your balcony, but you even hear a little bit of this when you’re in your room, with the door shut. And keep in mind that I was located on one of the higher floors, so I imagine the noise is even worse on lower floors.

For that matter, the view from these city-facing rooms just isn’t particularly inspiring. It’s not bad, it’s just not anything that has a “wow” factor.

This to me was a real detractor from the experience. I don’t want to be overly dramatic here, because I actually use a white noise machine, so noise doesn’t bother me. But a majority of the top city hotels in Japan are located at the top of skyscrapers, so they generally have amazing views, even if you get a non-premium room view.

The fact that roughly half of the rooms at the hotel not only face a loud highway, but don’t have terribly inspiring views in the distance, is something that I don’t love. So if I were to stay here again, I’d make sure that I’m in a room with a view of Osaka Castle instead.

Also, maybe this is a hot take, but I don’t actually love the Osaka Castle view that much. Don’t get me wrong, it’s a nice view, but it’s pretty static, and it’s just not something I’d specifically seek out, compared to views from other hotels. In Japan I love being on very high floors, and seeing life happening down below.

Patina Osaka has an impressive spa complex that takes up the entire fourth floor, and it measures around 15,000 square feet (1,400 square meters). The spa has six treatment rooms, and while I didn’t get any services, there were some interesting options — find the spa treatment menu here.

All the spa facilities are also accessible by guests daily from 7AM until 10PM, and there’s a very nice selection of options. For one, the hotel has a gorgeous 66-foot (20-meter) indoor lap pool. Seating around the pool is pretty limited, but it wasn’t at all busy when I visited.

The pool area also has a very nice whirlpool.

Additional spa facilities are located within the gender segregated locker and changing rooms.

There’s also a cold plunge and a whirlpool, along with a sauna and steam room.

However, there’s no onsen, if that’s something that’s important to you.

Patina Osaka has a gym on the fourth floor, located within the wellness complex. This is accessible by guests 24/7. The gym is a good size, and has modern equipment, for both strength training and cardio. There’s even a yoga and pilates area.

Capella and Patina properties are all about design, and all about having great food & beverage outlets, and Patina Osaka is no exception. To cover the basics:

Let’s start with Inaki, which is located on the 19th floor, and serves breakfast from 7AM until 10:30AM, lunch from 11:30AM until 3PM, and dinner from 5:30PM until 10PM. The restaurant can seat up to 120 people, and it’s where I had breakfast. While I didn’t have lunch or dinner here, the menu has a focus on basque cuisine, and you can find all the details here.

Before I even talk about the breakfast selection, let me say that I think the restaurant should open at 6:30AM rather than 7AM. I got there right at 7AM and was the first person in line, but before they opened, there were close to two dozen people waiting. To me that’s a sign that breakfast should open earlier.

Breakfast consisted of a combination of a buffet, plus an unlimited a la carte concept, so you could order as many dishes as you’d like. The buffet was high quality and a good size, but not massive.

The buffet had fresh juices, all kinds of pastries and sweets, cereal, fresh fruit, yogurt, cold cuts, cheese, salad, rice, soup, and other Asian specialties (both from Japan and other countries).

That could then be supplemented with items from the below menu.

I was super boring here, since I had noodles for breakfast the previous morning, so I had the avocado toast with a poached egg — go ahead and rib me, I deserve it!

Drinks at breakfast were excellent, and I had both a cappuccino and a matcha latte.

Next, let’s talk about P72, which is located on the ground floor, and it’s open for lunch and dinner, from 11:30AM until 10PM. The restaurant can seat up to 84 people (38 on the terrace, so that’s highly weather dependent), and I had lunch here — you can find all the details here.

This is a fun concept on a couple of levels. For one, the restaurant has a unique design — you wouldn’t think you’re at a restaurant on the ground floor of a city hotel, but instead, you’d think you’re out in nature, at some secluded resort. Very cool.

This restaurant’s concept is that it has mindful dishes made with produce that’s grown in-hotel, and served farm-to-table. For example, there’s a selection of lunch set menus, and I chose the below one.

This meal was exceptional, and such a great concept. The meal started with some delicious freshly baked bread.

The first course was a vegetable terrine with pickles, ricotta cheese, and fresh herbs.

The second course was a chilled pumpkin soup with saffron soy milk cream and pumpkin seed oil.

The main course was a grilled dry-aged beef rump with organic vegetables and onion jus.

Then the dessert was a hojicha blancmange, and I had a coffee to go along with that (which was included).

Next, Patina Osaka has Barin, which is located on the 19th floor, and it’s open for lunch 11:30AM until 3PM, and for dinner from 5:30PM until 10PM. It has the capacity for 32 guests, with 10 counter seats, 16 table seats, and a private dining room with six seats.

The cuisine here is a combination of teppanyaki, as well kaiseki, and you can find all the details here. Let me just apologize, I got absolutely screwed on this trip when it comes to the days of the weeks that the Japanese restaurants at the hotel were closed. At all three hotels up until this point, I stayed on exactly the nights where the venues were closed, so I wasn’t able to eat here. I mean, I don’t remember the last time I’ve seen a restaurant closed on a Thursday, but it is what it is…

Next, there’s Nijiri, also located on the 19th floor, and it’s open daily from 11:30AM until 6:30PM. This can seat up to 26 guests, and it’s a tea lounge serving afternoon tea. I didn’t dine here, because I can only consume so much food, but you can find all the details here.

Lastly, there’s Sonata Bar & Lounge, located on the 20th floor, as it’s essentially the lobby lounge and bar. This is open daily from 2PM until 11PM (it opens at 12PM on weekends), and can seat up to 126 people (90 indoors and 36 outdoors). You can find all the details here.

For a lobby bar, this is definitely a nicely elevated space, with plenty of fun seating options.

In particular, it transforms into something much more charming in the evenings, when lights are dimmed, there are candles, etc. The terrace is also a lovely space, weather permitting.

I stopped here in the evening for a drink, and had an excellent negroni, with some bar snacks.

I had intended to go out for dinner, but then I had some work to do, so I decided to just stay in, and ordered a club sandwich. I’ve gotta say, it was one of the best (and most unconventional) club sandwiches I’ve ever had.

For the most part, service at Patina Osaka was excellent. Staff were all friendly, though given the room count at the hotel, service wasn’t necessarily overly personalized, which isn’t surprising. I got the sense that this hotel had higher occupancy than the Waldorf Astoria.

One thing I want to mention is that the staff at the hotel were a combination of Japanese and foreign. In particular, a lot of the front office staff were from the Philippines. There’s nothing wrong with that, of course — Filipinos are known for their kindness and excellent service — but it definitely doesn’t give you that “authentic” Japanese service experience. I wasn’t expecting that Waldorf Astoria would have a higher percentage Japanese staff than Patina, for example.

I’m happy I had the chance to check out Patina Osaka, both based on what I heard about this hotel specifically, and also based on its affiliation with the Capella brand, which I love. All-in-all, Patina Osaka is a great hotel, with beautiful design, excellent dining, an expansive wellness complex, and friendly service.

My one real complaint about this hotel is that the city view rooms basically face a highway, and also have quite a bit of noise. Because this hotel is a standalone building, rather than being at the top of a skyscraper, it also doesn’t have quite the views you’ll find at other properties. Given the very high quality of hotels in Osaka, that’s a noticeable downside, at least based on my preferences.

Patina is also interesting in comparison to Capella — Patina properties are essentially more reasonably priced and larger, while maintaining the same general focus on design, as well as quality food & beverage outlets. However, it’s definitely not as special as Capella in terms of the level of attentiveness, as well as some of the exclusive features, like a lounge for all guests.

All-in-all, I’d recommend Patina Osaka, though I’d also say it didn’t blow me away. If you are going to stay here, make sure you get a room with a view of Osaka Castle. Personally, I’d be more likely to return to the Waldorf Astoria, or to check out the Four Seasons.

So, Patina is to Capella as Janu is to Aman?

Have you (or anyone else) tried Janu Tokyo yet, or should I submit that Reader Story for your consideration as well? Bah!

I stayed at Janu Tokyo and yes, that is the best comparison for Patina/Capella. I liked the hotel and the rooms are huge, it has a great spa, and the restaurants are really buzzy. One side has great views of Tokyo Tower. However, I had heard how great the location was because it's walkable to Roppongi. While that's true, and I prefer that area to Chuo since there's more to do/restaurants etc, it's set within...

I stayed at Janu Tokyo and yes, that is the best comparison for Patina/Capella. I liked the hotel and the rooms are huge, it has a great spa, and the restaurants are really buzzy. One side has great views of Tokyo Tower. However, I had heard how great the location was because it's walkable to Roppongi. While that's true, and I prefer that area to Chuo since there's more to do/restaurants etc, it's set within a huge luxury shopping complex and I really didn't like that. For one, you're surrounded by Hermes, Chanel, LV and so on and could be literally anywhere in the world. It's also such a maze and just leaving the hotel our first morning took us forever. Staff pointed us in different directions for walking out and both got us more confused (once we got it, this was no longer an issue, but still a long walk just to leave the complex). I found the location off putting enough that I wouldn't stay again. Also the spa is a membership club and can get really busy with their members.

It looks like an excellent city hotel. I don't know if it is the best in the world though. I will check it out sometime soon.

“I don’t want to be overly dramatic here.” LOL.

Ugh, avocado toast in Japan?! (Of all places) :'(

"I’d recommend Patina Osaka, though I’d also say it didn’t blow me."

Noise and views aside, a beautiful property.

Ben, for your Japanese hotel reviews do you mind noting how firm the bed is? They are notorious for preferring firm beds (Andaz Tokyo bed in particular was a marble slab more firm than the carpeted floor, ask me how I know) which can make or break a stay.

Nice hotels will throw a thin duvet over the mattress and put the bedding on top - makes the hard Japanese mattresses much nicer

@ Super -- Yep! I tend to prefer less firm, and found the Bulgari Tokyo and Waldorf Astoria Osaka had very soft beds, while the Patina Osaka had a fairly soft bed. None were hard.

What happened to the design of the home page of this website ? Now it wastes so much space on both sides.

really appreciate you tweaking your trip to fit this one in per my recommendation Ben, it's why you're the best.

Also really interesting seeing some of the flaws here. Definitely shattered the perfect idea I had in my head of this place based on pictures! Design is still gorgeous though

@ Funkyflapjak -- I appreciate the inspiration, and keep the requests coming!

Congratulations, You’ve been upgraded!!! from your quiet room to the slightly larger room next to the highway! Sounds familiar….

Great review and so glad to read. I've always thought it was such a strange location despite being next to the hotel, and seems you're in agreement. Can't imagine staying here unless rates are significantly better than the other choices in town, and I say that as someone who loves Capella.

Prime example how rankings are / can be bought or selectively influenced. If this is the REALLY the WORLD’S Best Hotel, then we all must also believe that the EARTH IS FLAT.

One of the best hotels in the world? Ok? It certainly looks decent. Like an Edition Hotel came to Osaka. But I would hardly imagine this as ranking anywhere near the top. Such a strange thing these rankings. I am certainly not rushing there anytime soon.

I stayed there last year when it just opened. So top notch!

Note that an onsen requires an actual source of heated mineral water. A skyscraper hotel isn’t going to have an onsen.

Also, ¥8000 for lunch? Have we traveled back to the late 1980s? Ouch.

Typically I like to book a one bedroom suite when I travel. This property’s one bedroom suites are basically a large jr suite as there is no separation between bedroom and living room unless you are booking their highest category suites. That and the noise from a highway means Four Seasons is a better choice for me despite smaller square footage.

#107. United adds new easternmost city in Canada in 6-route expansion with partner Air Canada

United Airlines and Air Canada have agreed to expand their partnership on routes between the U.S. and Canada.

And the two carriers are planning to launch a half-dozen new routes between the two countries for next summer.

As part of the cross-border expansion, United on Friday announced it would return to St. John's in Canada's easternmost province of Newfoundland and Labrador for the first time in more than a decade.

Plus, the airline on Friday announced service to two additional Canadian cities from its hub at Denver International Airport (DEN).

What to know: United ditches flight segments, raises bar for 1K in Premier status shakeup

Meanwhile, Air Canada is adding three additional U.S. routes: Louisville, Indianapolis and Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) will get new service to destinations north of the border.

However, the Canadian flag carrier also plans to cut several U.S. routes from its schedule as part of the shakeup, TPG has confirmed.

In all, United plans to add three new routes to Canada:

This expansion will mark the first time United has offered service from Newark to St. John's since 2016.

The EWR-YYT route will give the airline a new easternmost destination in Canada.

Today, that label belongs to Halifax, which United already serves from three U.S. cities.

WestJet is currently the only carrier flying between the U.S. and St. John's.

As part of its U.S. network shakeup, Air Canada announced three routes it'll launch for summer 2027.

Beyond these new routes, United and Air Canada also announced plans to add additional flights or larger planes on a handful of existing routes.

However, Air Canada will also cut five U.S. routes from its schedule, as first reported by Ishrion Aviaton.

In a statement to TPG, the carrier cited "commercial reasons," saying it "regularly reviews its schedule to ensure capacity is aligned with customer demand and travel patterns."

Friday's route announcement between Air Canada and United came as the carriers announced an agreement to expand their cooperation on service between the U.S. and Canada.

The proposal is currently under review by Canadian regulators.

On top of partnering through the Star Alliance, the two airlines share a joint venture that allows them to coordinate on schedule and pricing. That aspect of the tie-up dates back to 2022.

"The new routes and flights we're announcing today further underscore our commitment to investing in Canada and making travel between our two countries easier," United's chief network planner, Patrick Quayle, said in a statement shared by Air Canada Friday.

Travel demand between the U.S. and Canada has seen some volatility over the past couple years, and that's led to a host of airline route adjustments during that stretch.

Across all airlines in 2026, the total number of flights and seats between the two countries is down roughtly 6% versus two years ago, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

#108. Virgin Confirms New Itinerary Change on the West Coast

Virgin Voyages confirmed that the current cruise of the Brilliant Lady will follow a different itinerary than originally scheduled.

After departing from Los Angeles on October 17, 2026, the vessel was set to operate a seven-night cruise to the Mexican Riviera.

In a statement published last week, the company had warned guests before sailing that planned ports of call could change due to adverse weather conditions.

At the time, the company said that hurricanes in the region could require the Brilliant Lady to sail north instead of heading to the Mexican Riviera.

“We’ve been closely monitoring the projected path of Hurricane Trudy, and the forecasts have varied quite a bit. We aren’t too concerned about the remnants of Hurricane Simon, but Trudy is a more complicated situation,” Virgin explained in letter issued on October 16, 2026.

“Following the guidance of the National Hurricane Center, heading south could put the ship on the stronger, more dangerous side of the storm. That’s too much of a safety risk and a gamble we’re not willing to take,” it continued.

Virgin said that the safety of guests and crew “will always be its guiding light in making these tough calls,” noting that the ship will now head to California.

“Our teams have worked incredibly hard behind the scenes to put together the best possible alternative itinerary, one that keeps you safe and still gives you a great vacation.”

The Brilliant Lady will now visit San Francisco, San Diego and Ensenada before returning to Los Angeles as scheduled on October 24, 2026.

The company added that weather is out of its control and ports may be “understandably limited at such short notice.”

“We know this isn’t the itinerary you originally planned, and trust us, we were hoping to take you to the sunny shores of Cabo as well,” Virgin said.

“We also know we’re sharing these details close to embarkation, but we wanted to be as confident in the latest forecast as possible and confirm the alternative itinerary before reaching out.”

Shore excursions for cancelled ports booked through Virgin will be automatically refunded to guests’ onboard folio.
