#109. Chase Sapphire Lounges Locations, Hours, Access Rules, & Amenities: Complete Guide

Chase Sapphire Lounges by The Club is the lounge network that’s operated by Chase, intended primarily for those with the Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) and Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (learn more). The network currently has nine locations, including in Boston (BOS), Dallas (DFW), Las Vegas (LAS), New York (JFK & LGA), Philadelphia (PHL), Phoenix (PHX), San Diego (SAN), and Washington (IAD).

In this post, I’d like to take a close look at everything you need to know about Chase’s airport lounge network, which is operated in collaboration with Airport Dimensions. Chase Sapphire Lounges really offer an incredible experience, among the best you’ll find at any airports in the US, with both buffet and a la carte dining, excellent cocktails, and some special amenities at some locations.

In this post, I want to cover everything you need to know about the Chase Sapphire Lounge network, from the entry requirements, to locations and hours, to amenities.

Link: Learn more about the Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card or Sapphire Reserve for Business℠

The Chase Sapphire Lounge by The Club portfolio has unique entry requirements. These lounges are intended primarily as a perk for those with the Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) and Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (learn more).

All Chase Sapphire Lounges have the same entry requirements, as follows:

This is an excellent network of lounges, and it could be a good value to add authorized users to the Chase Sapphire Reserve, as they get the same lounge access privileges as the primary cardmember. Meanwhile authorized users on the Sapphire Reserve Business don’t receive any sort of lounge access (but they can also be added to the card with no additional annual fee).

Lastly, I should mention that while the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) is a great product, it doesn’t offer any sort of lounge access.

If you’d like all of the above about Chase Sapphire Lounge access requirements in an easier to read chart, see below. 😉

There are currently nine Chase Sapphire Lounge locations, and they’re all in the United States. On top of that, there are at least two more in the pipeline. I should also mention that there used to be a Chase Sapphire Lounge Hong Kong (HKG), but that closed in January 2026, as it was rebranded. Furthermore, there used to be a Chase Sapphire Terrace Austin (AUS), and that closed in March 2025, as the airport has other plans for the space.

I’ve been lucky enough to visit five of these lounges, so let’s go over the details of each location below, and I’ll post them in alphabetical order based on airport name. Before I do, below is a chart with the basics of the lounge network, including the airports, locations, hours, and approximate size.

Here are the basics of the Chase Sapphire Lounge Boston Logan (BOS):

The BOS Chase Sapphire Lounge is gorgeous, easily the nicest lounge at the airport. In terms of food & drinks, the lounge has seasonal menus featuring dishes from Sarma, local roasts from Atomic Coffee Roasters, a curated wine list from Parcelle, and craft cocktails, with both a buffet and QR code ordering for food.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge BOS amenities include a taproom with local beers on tap, shower suites, a relaxation area, massage chairs, a family and kids room, and a nursing room.

Read my review of the Chase Sapphire Lounge Boston Logan.

Here are the basics of the Chase Sapphire Lounge Dallas Fort Worth (DFW):

The DFW Chase Sapphire Lounge is the latest addition to the network, and it appears to be among the best. In terms of food & drinks, the lounge has seasonal menus featuring dishes from Encina, local roasts from Cherry Coffee, a curated wine list from Parcelle, and craft cocktails, with both a buffet and QR code ordering for food. This is also the first and only Chase Sapphire Lounge location to have a grab & go food selection, so that’s really fun.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge DFW amenities include a dedicated whiskey lounge with guided pairings and a custom barrel selection. There’s also a dedicated wellness zone with Face Haus facials, shower rooms, and resting pods. The lounge also has a family and kids room, a nursing room, and areas for working.

Here are the basics of the Chase Sapphire Lounge New York Kennedy (JFK):

The JFK Chase Sapphire Lounge is actually operated in partnership with Etihad Airways, as the former Etihad Airways Lounge has been taken over and renovated. Because the lounge is operated in partnership with Etihad, first and business class passengers, as well as Etihad Guest Platinum and Gold members, also get access to the lounge.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge JFK is a bit smaller than most of the others, but still has beautiful decor and an excellent selection of food, with ready to eat and a la carte options (including halal options). There’s also a bar with cocktails, as well as cold brew on tap, with Joe Coffee partnership for coffee.

The lounge doesn’t have much in the way of other amenities, though. The only other major features would be the shower rooms and prayer rooms.

Read my review of the Chase Sapphire Lounge New York Kennedy.

Here are the basics of the Chase Sapphire Lounge Las Vegas (LAS):

The LAS Chase Sapphire Lounge is the second smallest in the network, and it has 87 seats, spread across two floors. In terms of food & drinks, the lounge has seasonal menus featuring dishes from Momofuku, local roasts from Dark Moon Coffee Roasters, a curated wine list from Parcelle, and craft cocktails, with both a buffet and QR code ordering for food.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge LAS amenities are fairly limited due to the lounge’s small size. The lounge does have a champagne parlor, where travelers can enjoy sparkling drink selections by bar cart service, including glasses of champagne, mimosas, and seasonal spritz cocktails, as well as passed bites, to their seat.

Here are the basics of the Chase Sapphire Lounge New York LaGuardia (LGA):

The LGA Chase Sapphire Lounge is a two-story stunner that will make you feel like you’re not at an airport. The lounge features seasonal menus featuring dishes from Sailor, craft cocktails by Apotheke, curated wines by Parcelle, Joe Coffee self-serve and barista made options, and a tea selection.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge LGA amenities include a play room for kids, a nursing room, an arcade, two relaxation chairs, and a Face Haus spa, offering complimentary 30-minute treatments on a first come, first served basis.

This lounge also has the Reserve Suites by Chase, consisting of three private rooms that can be reserved in blocks of three hours. If you book this, you’ll receive a dedicated suite attendant, a special menu from Jeffrey’s Grocery, a personal bathroom with a shower, a signature caviar service upon arrival, a special wine list curated by Parcelle, a fully-stocked snack and refreshments center, and a gift prior to departing. The cost? $2,200-3,000, depending on which room you select.

Read my review of the Chase Sapphire Lounge New York LaGuardia.

Here are the basics of the Chase Sapphire Lounge Philadelphia (PHL):

The PHL Chase Sapphire Lounge is the second biggest lounge in the network, and sets a new standard for lounges at the airport. In terms of food & drinks, the lounge has seasonal menus featuring dishes from Middle Child Clubhouse, local roasts from Elixr Coffee, a curated wine list from Parcelle, and craft cocktails, with both a buffet and QR code ordering for food.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge PHL amenities include a beer garden with craft beer, a game room with retro arcade machines, private rest pods, facial treatments from Face Haus, a family and kids room, a nursing room, and private phone booths.

Read my review of the Chase Sapphire Lounge Philadelphia.

Here are the basics of the Chase Sapphire Lounge Phoenix (PHX):

The PHX Chase Sapphire Lounge is the smallest lounge in the network. In terms of food & drinks, the lounge has seasonal menus featuring dishes from Gallo Blanco (available at the Airstream), local roasts from Press Coffee, a curated wine list from Parcelle, and craft cocktails, with both a buffet and QR code ordering for food.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge PHX amenities are limited due to its small size, but include private bathrooms. However, there are no showers, spa facilities, or family or kids rooms. I should also mention that this used to be the one lounge in the network that would accept reservations in advance, but that’s no longer the case.

Here are the basics of the Chase Sapphire Lounge San Diego (SAN):

The SAN Chase Sapphire Lounge is without a doubt the best lounge at the airport. In terms of food & drinks, the lounge has seasonal menus featuring dishes from Oscars Mexican Seafood, local roasts from Groundwork Coffee, a curated wine list from Parcelle, and craft cocktails, with both a buffet and QR code ordering for food.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge SAN amenities include a wellness area with bookable private rest pods, on-demand digital meditation from Devi Brown, and facial treatments from Face Haus, along with a family and kids room, as well as a nursing room.

Here are the basics of the Chase Sapphire Lounge Washington Dulles (IAD):

The IAD Chase Sapphire Lounge is operated in partnership with Etihad Airways, as the former Etihad Airways Lounge has been taken over and renovated. This is a similar arrangement to what you’ll find at the New York JFK location, so Etihad first and business class passengers, as well as Etihad Guest Platinum and Gold members, also get access to the lounge.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge IAD is a bit smaller than the others, but still has beautiful decor and an excellent selection of food, with ready to eat and a la carte options. There’s also a bar with cocktails, as well as cold brew on tap, though it doesn’t have the same culinary collaborations as the other locations.

The lounge doesn’t have much in the way of other amenities, though. The only other major feature would be the shower rooms and prayer rooms.

Read my review of the Chase Sapphire Lounge Washington Dulles.

In addition to the nine Chase Sapphire Lounges that are currently open, there are firm plans for at least two additional Chase Sapphire Lounge locations to open. Specifically, here are the planned Chase Sapphire Lounges we can expect, in the order that they’re expected to open:

Note that while there are also plans for a Chase Sapphire Lounge Seattle (SEA), that hasn’t received formal approval from airport authorities yet, so that’s not yet a given.

When details of Chase Sapphire Lounges were first announced, I was skeptical. After all, they’re run in partnership with The Club, and they were initially partially open to Priority Pass members (but not anymore, unless the Priority Pass membership is through Chase), so I figured the quality of the lounges would reflect that.

Well, I sure was wrong. Chase has done an amazing job with its lounges so far, and they just keep getting better. The food and drink selection in Chase Sapphire Lounges is top notch. Food options include both individually plated options that you can grab from a buffet, plus some a la carte options.

The drink selection is equally impressive, with signature cocktails, and some lounges having barista made coffee and cold brew on tap.

The entry requirements for these lounges have also been streamlined a bit, which makes things more straightforward. Now they’re just open to those with cards like the Chase Sapphire Reserve and Sapphire Reserve Business, while I think it was confusing when other Priority Pass members were entitled to one lounge visit per year.

Chase is only one of three card issuers in the United States to have a robust credit card lounge network. How do Amex Centurion Lounges and Capital One Lounges compare? Here’s how I see it:

I think one thing worth mentioning is that the premium credit cards from American Express and Capital One no longer offer complimentary guesting privileges at their lounge networks without reaching a certain spending requirement, while Chase Sapphire Lounges do, so that’s a major advantage. Below is a brief comparison of the lounge networks.

Chase is continuing to expand its airport lounge presence, with the Chase Sapphire Lounges by The Club concept. The network now has locations in Boston (BOS), Dallas Fort Worth (DFW), Las Vegas (LAS), New York Kennedy (JFK), New York LaGuardia (LGA), Philadelphia (PHL), Phoenix (PHX), San Diego (SAN), and Washington Dulles (IAD), with more lounges expected in the future. It’s exciting to see this network grow.

When it comes to accessing Chase Sapphire Lounges, the primary way to do so is by having the Chase Sapphire Reserve or Sapphire Reserve Business, in which case you can visit the lounges an unlimited number of times, with up to two guests. Other Priority Pass members no longer receive complimentary access to these lounges, though they can purchase access for $100 per person.

Fortunately the quality of these lounges is exceptional, and they’re among the best credit card lounges out there, in my opinion.

What do you make of Chase’s airport lounge concept?

#110. The Plaza is closing, Dallas will welcome a beautiful new hotel and other hospitality news from this week

As TPG's hotel reporter, I spend a lot of nights each year in hotel rooms. But this week I traded in the hotel for a stay at my friend's farm out in west Tennessee. It's been a good reminder that while satin sheets and made-to-order omelets are always great, hospitality comes in many shapes and forms.

But while I've been out taking it slow in the country, the world of hotel news has kept on spinning.

The most exciting news this week is that World of Hyatt has finally made it possible to transfer points between members online — and without having to fill out a PDF and email it in. The loyalty program also launched some new offers with Air Canada, like the chance to temporarily earn points between the two programs.

We also reported on a social-forward new hotel opening in Silicon Valley.

Here's the other hotel news you need to know about this week.

Earlier this year, I stayed in my first Hilton LXR property, Ka La'i Waikiki Beach, LXR Hotels & Resorts, in Hawaii. I really enjoyed how the brand gives independent, luxury hotels a proper place in the points-and-miles world. Now, in Bengaluru, India, LXR is planting a new flag with the opening of The Den Bengaluru, LXR Hotels & Resorts. The resort features 226 rooms and suites, a rooftop Mediterranean and Indian restaurant, The Sanctuary Spa, a pool and even a game room called The Playhouse.

How to book: Rates at The Den Bengaluru start around $176 per night or 66,000 Hilton Honors points per night.

Related: Best hotels and resorts in Hawaii

As a native Texan, I pass through Dallas quite a bit while visiting my family up in the Panhandle. Next year, I'll be sure to spend an extra night or two at the highly anticipated new Auberge Collection hotel, The Knox. Now accepting reservations from Jan. 29, 2026, the Martin Brudnizki hotel in the Knox Street district is a design-lover's dream. Set right off the Katy Trail, the hotel is close to nature, great shopping, popular restaurants and everything else Dallas has to offer. Once open, the hotel will feature bars and restaurants, a spa and a pool to help beat the fierce Texas heat.

How to book: Cash rates start around $800 per night.

When my corgi Splenda got invited to stay at The Plaza, NYC's most iconic hotel, a few years ago, we jumped at the chance. If a stay at The Plaza is on your bucket list, you'd better go soon; The Plaza will close for four years starting in January "for a restoration of the 18-story building's landmark facade," according to The New York Times. Luckily for folks heading to the city for holiday celebrations, there's one more chance to visit the hotel, which opened back in 1907, before the renovations start.

Related: The 24 best hotels in New York City

Hilary Duff inspired a whole generation of millennial travelers with the 2003 film "The Lizzie Mcguire Movie." Specifically, it had every tween with a television hoping to visit Rome (and maybe fall in love with an Italian superstar). In the Eternal City, Generator Rome is now offering the "What Dreams are Made of" package, which includes — on top a stay at the hotel — a day exploring Rome on a Vespa for two, a Lizzie McGuire-themed map of filming locations, a one euro coin to make a wish at the Trevi Fountain and two Lizzie McGuire-inspired cocktails at the end of the day.

#111. Commonly asked questions about Southwest's recent Rapid Rewards reboot and Companion Pass changes

Southwest announced significant changes to its Rapid Rewards loyalty program on Thursday. The airline will roll out new terminology soon while revising the perks and rules of various pieces of the program, all starting on January 1, 2027.

Change often creates confusion, and this change is no exception. Southwest has switched up so many things in the last few years. Even Southwest frequent flyers may feel their heads spinning.

Related: The new playbook for booking and flying with Southwest Airlines

There are a lot of ways that the airline is marketing the changes as offering "more opportunity" for customers, and there are a few new modest perks of note.

But points and miles enthusiasts who have largely been laser-focused on maximizing status perks or earning a Southwest Companion Pass are mostly losers in the new playbook.

We've been hearing some common questions from TPG readers about the latest round of Southwest Rapid Rewards changes and what it means for status on the airline. Is your status changing in meaningful ways relative to your travel habits? Is the Companion Pass really dead?

Here's what we know about the answers to these and other common questions. Plus, find out what action steps some Southwest travelers should take now to lock in a few perks before it's too late.

The new Rapid Rewards program goes into effect on January 1, 2027, meaning that program members with elite status will finish out the current year under a familiar program. For travelers who already have earned status on Southwest in 2026 (or who will before year's end), the transition to the new system in 2027 should be seamless.

Rapid Rewards members who earn A-List status in 2026 become Silver for all of 2027 as of January 1, 2027. Similarly, those who earn A-List Preferred status in 2026 will become Gold for all of 2027. The transition won't require any action on the part of customers.

The only truly new status that Southwest has created is Platinum, which now will include the coveted unlimited Companion Pass, and no one will start 2027 with that status. Instead, it must be earned under the new 2027 Rapid Rewards program rules.

If you want to keep the same Silver or Gold status perks beyond 2027 (or earn the new Platinum status), however, slightly modified earning rules go into effect in the new year. Those rules change the pathway to 2028 Gold and Silver status.

Once A-List members become Silver and A-List Preferred members become Gold, 2027 will look mostly the same for the vast majority of them. Status perks like free checked bags, early boarding groups, and free seat assignments will remain constant at comparable status tiers.

Silver (formerly A-List) members will even see improved earning bonuses on qualifying flight purchases in 2027 and beyond—40% extra instead of 25% that A-List received.

Gold (formerly A-List Preferred) members, however, will see their earning bonuses on flight purchases reduced, from 100% to just 60%. Thankfully, Southwest will provide a soft landing for A-List Preferred members who earn status this year. The airline's website states, "Members who earn A-List Preferred status for 2027 based on their 2026 activity will retain their 100% flight-point earning bonus through December 31, 2027. The 60% earning bonus applies to Gold status earned under the new program terms."

Southwest is also introducing a few intermediate thresholds (before Silver status and between Gold and Platinum) called "Milestone Rewards" that may result in a few extra perks for some members whose earnings fall between status levels.

Under the new rules, members who earn 95,000 TQPs or fly 75 qualifying one-way flights can unlock three Companion Pass trips. Each trip can cover a round-trip itinerary.

That's a significant distinction for those of you who won't qualify for Platinum. You can still earn limited Companion Pass benefits without reaching the highest tier.

But as with most program loyalty changes, Southwest gives with one hand and takes away with the other. Customers who purchase Southwest's two most expensive fare types, Choice Preferred and Choice Extra, will earn fewer Rapid Rewards points on those purchases starting in 2027. Choice Preferred fares will earn 8 points per dollar spent (previously 10x), and Choice Extra fares will earn 10 points per dollar spent (previously 14x).

The combination of these changes could make the program substantially less lucrative for some types of status holders. For example, a member with A-List Preferred status currently earns 28 Rapid Rewards points per dollar spent on Choice Extra fares (14x plus a 100% bonus). By 2028, an equivalent Gold member will only earn 16 points per dollar spent on that same fare (10x plus a 60% bonus)—a mere 57% of previous earnings.

In contrast, a Silver member who regularly purchases cheaper Basic or Choice fares will end up a bit better off.

Under Southwest's current program, there are three types of Rapid Rewards points: those redeemable for airfare, those that also count towards A-List and A-List Preferred status, and those that also count towards Companion Pass qualification.

The new system essentially merges the final two categories into a single one: Tier Qualifying Points (TQP). Tier Qualifying Points are the primary way to unlock status (in addition to flying a set number of one-way flights), including the Platinum tier, which now awards an unlimited Companion Pass.

There are a number of ways that members will continue to earn Rapid Rewards points that can be redeemed for airfare, but that don't award Tier Qualifying Points. Those include:

Many of these methods used to count towards Companion Pass qualification. They won't in 2027.

Starting in 2027, there will be a very limited number of ways to earn Tier Qualifying Points on Southwest. The most common will be 1) points from spending on a co-branded credit card (1 TQP per dollar spent) or 2) base points earned from spending on qualifying airfare. (Group bookings, booking Getaways by Southwest, and some qualifying debit card purchases also earn TQP.)

Members will earn differently on qualifying airfare based on the fare type they purchase:

Southwest may occasionally offer promotions for members to earn bonus Tier Qualifying Points. What's unclear is what those promotions will be and whether they will be sufficiently rewarding to make up even a fraction of the loss caused now that so many kinds of points no longer count towards Companion Pass.

Under the new Rapid Rewards program, going into effect on January 1, 2027, the only way to earn an unlimited Companion Pass is by achieving Platinum status. What happens to all the Rapid Rewards members who have already earned a Companion Pass through other methods?

If you have earned a Companion Pass that expires in 2026, regardless of the method you used to earn it, nothing changes. You still have the same ability to use it until the end of the year.

For travelers who earned a Companion Pass in 2026 with an expiration date of December 31, 2027, nothing changes for you either. You do not have to hit Platinum or worry about Tier Qualifying Points if you simply want to use the pass benefits until year-end 2027.

Sometimes when airlines make loyalty program changes, the new rules go into effect immediately. That means there are no opportunities to continue taking advantage of the previous program perks.

Mercifully, that's not the case with the upcoming Rapid Rewards changes. In fact, Southwest is giving customers a few more months to earn a Companion Pass the old-fashioned way. Anyone who applies and is approved for a co-branded credit card before December 2, 2026, will still be able to apply card welcome bonus points toward Companion Pass qualification.

Related: Current Chase Southwest credit card offers

Additionally, Southwest is giving customers a little more runway when it comes to using this method. Even if the customer completes the spending requirement on that card in early 2027, the welcome bonus points will continue to count towards Companion Pass qualification, as if they had been earned in 2026.

The catch is, however, that the Companion Pass awarded for new card signups in the next few weeks will only be valid until the end of 2027. If you had been planning to get one or two new credit cards this fall but were waiting to complete the minimum spend until January 2027 to earn a Companion Pass valid through 2028, that method will no longer work.

Of course, in order for any method to work at all, a Rapid Rewards member has to be able to earn the currently required 135,000 Companion Pass Qualifying Points in a very short period of time. Regular Southwest flyers or anyone who spends heavily on a Southwest credit card might be most of the way there. A single credit card welcome bonus might put them over the top.

But the road will be hard for many others. There simply isn't a lot of time left in the year to earn under the old system. Additionally, if you've received a bonus on any personal Southwest credit card in the last 24 months, you might not even be eligible for a new personal card. And anyone who plans to earn most of the points through a welcome bonus on two cards—one personal and one business—might have a hard time obtaining both approvals.

So consider carefully whether there is a reasonably clear pathway available to you, particularly given that the Companion Pass will only provide one year of use.

Welcome bonuses on Southwest co-branded credit cards will no longer count towards earning the Southwest Companion Pass after January 1, 2027 (with the minor exception already discussed). So is all hope lost for points and miles enthusiasts who strategically rely on credit cards after the next few months are up?

The answer to that question is still to be decided. The old method of getting the bulk of the points needed for a Companion Pass with welcome bonuses is dead.

But there is, of course, still the classic way to earn a Companion Pass by putting a massive amount of spending on a Southwest credit card—$130,000 to be exact. Earning Platinum status requires 140,000 TQPs (you get a 10,000 TQP bonus in 2027 after hitting 130,000 TQPs).

The new 1 TQP awarded for each $1 spent will actually make that method a little more straightforward. But that number will be impossibly daunting for many. And with so many other rewards credit cards offering better multipliers on most kinds of credit card spending, the opportunity costs of pursuing this method to earn a Companion Pass might be pretty enormous.

In the past, Southwest also offered limited-time promotional Companion Passes. Sometimes these were awarded as a welcome bonus for a new co-branded credit card. Other times, a promotional pass was tied to registering for a promotion and purchasing and flying on Southwest flights within a defined time period.

It seems highly likely that Southwest will continue to offer promotions of this nature. So there may be other Companion Pass pathways to come, some of which might involve credit cards.

In fact, Southwest has also been sharing bits and pieces about a new premium-level co-branded credit card planned very soon. That card is confirmed to include lounge access and other perks for top spenders willing to pay a presumably hefty annual fee. It's possible that this card might include a perk to help make it easier to earn the Companion Pass, like reduced Tier Qualifying Points or additional bonuses.

Status at Southwest is changing, most significantly with the Companion Pass that has been relatively easy for many points and miles fans to earn for more than a decade. There is a limited-time pathway to getting one more Companion Pass valid through the end of 2027 for some Southwest flyers, but many more are simply out of luck.

In 2027 and beyond, everyone except the highest spenders and most frequent flyers will have to look for new ways to fly Southwest for less. Here's to hoping the new year brings some new opportunities.

#112. Delta Flight Attendants Clash So Badly That Pilots Call Supervisor For Help

A Delta pilot made an unusual request with the operations team on the ground during a flight’s descent, whereby he asked for help due to some problematic people onboard. The issue? The problem people weren’t passengers, but instead, they were the only two flight attendants in the cabin.

AIRLIVE has the story of an incident that happened on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, involving Delta flight DL5090, operated by Delta Connection carrier Endeavor Air. The CRJ-900 was operating from Greenville-Spartanburg Airport (GSP) to Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW).

On the surface, the 508-mile flight was routine, in the sense that it departed on-time, and even landed well ahead of schedule. However, that’s not to say the flight was without drama.

During the approach, the pilots contacted ground operations to request that an inflight supervisor meet the aircraft at the gate. The reason?

“We are experiencing conflict issues among the flight attendants and will likely need to separate them to prevent further escalation or an incident.”

Let me emphasize that the CRJ-900s have two flight attendants, so that means the entire crew in the cabin was engaged in some sort of a conflict.

There are no further details about what exactly the conflict between flight attendants was, and the aircraft ultimately landed safely. There didn’t seem to be any operational impacts — I assume the crew was finishing their night in Detroit, and it’s also an airport where Endeavor Air would likely have reserve flight attendants. I’d imagine the flight attendants didn’t work another sector together after that!

It goes without saying that if you put two strangers in a space together and force them to work together, they’re not all going to get along equally well. After all, we all have different personalities and approaches to doing things.

Whether we’re talking about pilots or flight attendants, there are some flights where people make a new best friend, and other flights where people can’t stand the person they’re working with.

However, as professionals, you’d hope they could put aside their differences, because that’s what they’re paid to do. The whole point of crew resource management is to work together, and to eliminate the impact of different personalities on performing jobs.

While that works a vast majority of the time, sometimes it doesn’t. Heck, it’s not just flight attendants — just recently an Air New Zealand flight was canceled after the pilots reportedly had a fight on a layover, as they just couldn’t get along.

Unless one person was just acting completely erratically and endangering others, it generally takes two people to cause a mess like this. After all, the more reasonable person could just mind their business and give the other person some space, in the name of deescalation, and then file a report later. But if a situation becomes so bad — on an 80-minute flight, no less — that the pilots have to be called, and a supervisor has to literally meet the plane… well, yikes!

While we don’t know the exact details of what went down, a Delta Connection flight approaching Detroit had “conflict issues” among the two flight attendants in the cabin, to the point that they would likely need to be separated “to prevent further escalation or an incident.”

Stuff like this shouldn’t happen, but it does happen with some frequency. Unless one flight attendant was acting completely out of line and endangering others, I’m just amazed by the lack of basic deescalation skills that it must take to get to this point.

What do you make of this Delta Connection flight attendant conflict incident?

#113. Norwegian to Reveal Details of Last Prima-Class Ship

Norwegian Cruise Line will announce details of the last vessel in its Prima-class series on Tuesday, October 20, 2026.

In a teaser published on its social media profiles, the company said the new ship will be revealed at 9:15 a.m. eastern standard time.

Norwegian noted the newbuild will be the “grand finale” of the Prima class, noting that it was “beautifully imagined” with passengers in mind.

According to the latest update of Cruise Industry News’s global cruise ship orderbook, the sixth and final Prima-class ship will be delivered by the Fincantieri shipyard in 2028.

Similar to the 2027-built Norwegian Aura, the 170,000-ton ship is expected to carry 3,880 guests at double occupancy.

The Prima class currently includes the newest vessels in Norwegian Cruise Line’s fleet, having started with the Norwegian Prima in 2022.

With all vessels built in Italy by Fincantieri, the series also includes the 2023-built Norwegian Viva and the 2025-built Norwegian Aqua.

Earlier this year, the line also welcomed the Norwegian Luna, which kicked off its maiden season from PortMiami in late March.

Set to enter service in the Mediterranean in 2027, the next vessel in the series will be the Norwegian Aura.

Approximately ten percent larger than its predecessors, the 170,000-ton ship will become the largest in Norwegian Cruise Line’s fleet.

The ship is currently under construction at Fincantieri’s Marghera shipyard, with a delivery scheduled for the second quarter.

After offering itineraries in Europe and the Mediterranean, the Aura is set to reposition to PortMiami in late May.

As part of its inaugural season, the ship will offer a series of seven-night cruises to the Caribbean departing from its South Florida homeport.

In addition to the two final Prima-class vessels, Norwegian is also preparing a new ship design in partnership with Fincantieri.

At 227,000 tons, the first of the new vessels will debut in 2030 and will be among the largest in the world.

#114. American Flight Attendants Furious Over Mandatory Credit Card Training

American Airlines’ flight attendants are being forced to undergo a training course on how to sell credit cards, and the union isn’t happy about this, claiming that the company is trying to redefine their jobs. Does the union have a point, or are they overreacting?

The Association of Professional Flight Attendants (APFA), which represents American’s more than 30,000 flight attendants, has issued an interesting memo, as reported by PYOK. As anyone who has been following the airline industry know, the major US carriers earn a large percentage of their profits (or at least reduce their losses) through their loyalty programs, which are extremely lucrative.

On American, we’ve long seen flight attendants have the opportunity to promote credit cards onboard, and they can earn a commission if their “sales” lead to successful applications. American is trying to improve its financial performance, and as part of that, the airline is trying to encourage flight attendants to be more consistent about onboard credit card pitches.

As part of this, the airline is now making it mandatory for flight attendants to complete an online training module about credit card sales. Failure to complete this module could lead to dismissal. So the issue here is that being trained on credit cards is no longer voluntary, but instead, is required. Still, actually promoting credit cards onboard isn’t required, but is up to the individual flight attendants.

The union is claiming this new training module violates the collective bargaining agreement with management, claiming “our Scope is one of our most important protections,” and “it is what prevents management from redefining what a Flight Attendant is and what they can be required to do on a whim.”

American is also rolling out a new flight attendant scoring system, which will be known as Me@Work. One of the factors intended to be displayed here will be the number of successful credit card applications attributed to each flight attendant.

The union is of course within its rights to try to challenge anything that’s beyond the scope of the collective bargaining agreement. However, does this really fit into that category? Here’s how I see it:

Based on my understanding of the situation, I think the union is overreacting here. I would understand the frustration if flight attendants were being forced to promote credit cards, but simply requiring training on something that many flight attendants do choose to participate in doesn’t strike me as being unreasonable. But that’s just me.

I get the argument of “if they require this, then what else could they require in the future?” But let’s be honest, this is literally a massive part of the airline business model nowadays, and if it weren’t for AAdvantage, odds are that American would’ve lost money in recent years.

American flight attendants are being required to undergo training for promoting credit cards. This training is mandatory, regardless of whether or not flight attendants intend to actually promote credit cards (which they earn a commission for).

The union argues that this is beyond the scope of the collective bargaining agreement, and that management is crossing a line. Meanwhile I’d imagine the argument from management would be that flight attendants aren’t being forced to promote credit cards, they just have to be trained on it, so that in the event they do choose to promote credit cards, they understand the rules.

What do you make of this complaint from the American flight attendant union?

Delta Air Lines is beefing up its transatlantic plans for next year.

The Atlanta-based carrier announced a new route on Friday for its 2027 peak summer travel season.

Delta will fly between Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) and Iceland's Keflavík International Airport (KEF) near Reykjavík with daily nonstop seasonal service starting on April 12 and running through Oct. 30, 2027.

KEF will represent Delta's 14th long-haul destination from BOS, where the airline has fought for passenger share since the return of travel following the COVID-19 pandemic.

The new route will join three other newcomers for the 2027 travel season:

Delta will fly the new BOS-KEF route with a Boeing 757-200 featuring a Premium Select cabin with recliner seats rather than the carrier's Delta One cabin that reatures lie-flat seats. Boston to Reykjavík typically takes about 5 hours, though, so it's a short hop, at least.

Delta first flew to Iceland in June 2011, the airline said, when it began service from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

But this is not Delta's first time flying to Iceland from Boston. The airline first launched the route in May of 2021, as post-lockdown travel was just starting up again.

That service was also flown on the 757-200, and was discontinued in September of that year, according to data from Cirium. Delta has not flown the route since then.

While the new iteration of the service covers the busy summer travel season, it notably spills over to cover "shoulder season" before and after peak summer, when travelers who are not locked to the academic calendar can often find smaller crowds and shorter queues at top summer destinations — not to mention better deals.

A growing number of travelers have been drawn to shoulder season in recent years, enough so that airlines are increasingly starting their summer schedules earlier, and running them later. All of Delta's new flights start earlier or end later than the traditional summer flight schedule.

For Boston, meanwhile, the Iceland route serves to underscore Delta's emphasis on the Bay State capital, where it competes fiercely with JetBlue to be the New England city's top airline. Delta's two biggest overall competitors — American Airlines and United Airlines — both have a fraction of Delta's presence in Boston.

For the summer 2026 travel season, Delta added flights to Madrid and Nice from BOS, and increased frequencies to Barcelona. JetBlue, meanwhile, has focused its small but growing transatlantic operation on Boston, as well as JFK, further underscoring the competition.

In 2019, Delta operated a total of 80,513 flights into and out of Boston, according to data from Cirium, while JetBlue dominated that year with 114,936 flights.

While the pandemic interrupted the airlines' growth, Delta managed to squeak past JetBlue in terms of total number of flights in 2023, and has remained on top since then.

#117. Why you should still care about Bilt Rewards even if you don’t want one of its credit cards

I don't currently have a Bilt credit card, and I don't have plans to open one any time soon. Despite that, I earn Bilt Points every month on my rent and every time I take a Lyft ride.

If you're like me, you may be ignoring Bilt altogether or assuming you can't earn Bilt points on your rent.

Here's how you can earn Bilt points without a Bilt credit card and what to consider before paying rent with one.

If you rent an apartment and your complex participates in Bilt, you may be able to earn Bilt Points on your rent with any credit card you link to your account.

Of course, you'll need to set up a Bilt account if you don't have one already. I recommend checking with your leasing office before assuming you can pay your rent with a credit card through Bilt. Even if a complex participates in Bilt, they have the option to only accept Bilt credit cards rather than any credit card.

Alternatively, you can log into your Bilt account and check what payment options are available to you for your rent. If you're able to pay your rent with any credit card, you'll have the option to link your card to your account and use it to pay your rent via autopay.

Provided your leasing office accepts any credit card through Bilt, you'll earn 1 point for every $2 spent on your rent. This will be on top of whatever points you earn with the credit card you use, though keep in mind you'll need to pay a 3% transaction fee on every rent payment.

I often use my rent to help meet the spending requirements for welcome bonuses, so I consider this transaction fee a small price to pay for heaps of rewards. Just keep in mind that you'll likely need to use both Bilt and your card issuer's transfer partners to get enough value to offset that transaction fee.

For example, a $2,000 rent payment would incur a $60 processing fee. Whether that's worth paying depends on the rewards you'll earn and whether the payment helps you reach a valuable welcome bonus or spending threshold.

At this time, you can only pay your mortgage through Bilt if you have a Bilt credit card.

If you take rides regularly with Lyft, I recommend linking your Bilt and Lyft accounts to earn extra points. You'll earn 2 points per dollar spent on Lyft, which will stack with the rewards you earn on your credit card. I enjoy using my Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) with Lyft, since I earn 5 Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent (through Sept. 30, 2027).

You can also earn Bilt points at the following rates with your linked credit cards:

Thankfully, Bilt doesn't currently lock its transfer partners behind its credit cards. This is a big advantage for me, since Bilt is the only program I have access to that transfers to Atmos Rewards.

Aside from Atmos, Bilt has quite a few other valuable transfer partners, including Air Canada Aeroplan, Southwest Airlines Rapid Rewards and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. It has also recently added Amtrak Guest Rewards as a partner; that's a highlight for me, since I take a few Amtrak rides to and from Seattle every year.

Keep in mind that if you have base Blue Status (which you probably will if you don't have a Bilt card), you must transfer at least 2,000 points each time. Silver, Gold and Platinum Bilt members have a 1,000-point minimum. As with all transferable rewards, transfers are irreversible.

Recently, I transferred 4,000 points to Atmos Rewards from Bilt to top off my account for a one-way redemption between Portland International Airport (PDX) and Spokane International Airport on Alaska Airlines.

Since Atmos Rewards points are difficult to earn, I likely would not have been able to make this redemption without Bilt points. The cash price for this 5,000-point redemption was $184. After factoring in the $5.60 I paid in taxes and fees, I received around 3.6 cents per point in value, a sizable amount.

You shouldn't expect to accrue tons of Bilt points without a Bilt card, but regularly paying your rent and a handful of other expenses through the program will net you a decent stash over time. I earn a little over 800 points per month from my rent, which, after several months, adds up to enough points for most short-haul domestic flights through Atmos Rewards.

First and foremost, if you're currently working toward a welcome bonus with a credit card, using your card for rent payments could help you meet the spending requirement.

Many of the best welcome offers require spending in the thousands to earn them, so your rent can go a long way toward reaching that goal. Just remember that the 3% transaction fee you need to pay will eat a little into the overall value of your welcome bonus.

If you're not currently spending toward a welcome bonus, consider whether any of your cards offer extra perks for a certain amount of spending. For example, with my United℠ Explorer Card (see rates and fees), I can earn a $100 United travel credit after spending $10,000 on my card in a calendar year. Rent payments could help me reach that threshold through spending I already planned to make.

Since you'll earn regular credit card rewards on top of Bilt points when you pay your rent through Bilt, it may be worth choosing a card that earns more than 1 point per dollar spent or 1% cash back on nonbonus spending. Cards like the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card and Citi Double Cash® Card (see rates and fees) earn at least 2 miles per dollar spent or 2% cash back on every purchase.*

If you're a Air France KLM Visa Signature® credit card cardholder, you can currently earn 3 miles per dollar spent on rent payments through Bilt, on up to $50,000 annually (then 1.5 miles per dollar spent) and 75,000 miles earned maximum.

*With the Citi Double Cash, you'll earn 1% cash back when you buy and 1% cash back when you pay your bill.

While you don't need a Bilt credit card to make use of Bilt points, it may be worth considering one if any of the following apply to you:

If you want to earn rewards on rent or mortgage payments without paying a transaction fee, or your property only accepts Bilt credit cards, opening one may be worth considering. Currently, Bilt offers the following credit cards:

You don't necessarily need a Bilt credit card to earn transferable Bilt points. If your apartment complex participates in Bilt and accepts outside credit cards, you may be able to earn points on rent, along with additional rewards through partners like Lyft.

Bilt cards are a great option for certain travelers, but they don't make sense for everyone. As someone who frequently flies with Alaska Airlines, I'm very glad that I can still earn Bilt points that I can then transfer to Atmos Rewards.

Maximizing every dollar you spend is key to getting the most out of travel rewards, and your rent certainly isn't an exception to that. However, before paying rent with a credit card, make sure the rewards you'll earn justify the 3% transaction fee.

#118. Port of Seattle Celebrates Record Cruise Season

The Port of Seattle marked the completion of its 2026 cruise season on Sunday, October 18, 2026, according to a press release.

Topping last year’s record, the cruise schedule delivered an estimated $1.2 billion in regional economic benefit while providing more than 5,120 individuals direct and indirect jobs throughout the season.

The Port of Seattle said that the season also saw a record number of passengers and sailings with 330 calls and nearly 2 million guests, plus an uptick in shore power use by ships in berth.

“Seattle’s cruise industry continues to be a powerful economic engine for our region, supporting businesses and strengthening the communities that make this place special,” said Port of Seattle Commissioner Sam Cho.

“Each season, cruise supports thousands of direct and indirect jobs, generates more than $1.2 billion in annual economic impact, and remains the Port’s fastest-growing maritime sector. We’re honored that visitors from around the world choose Seattle as their gateway to connect with the natural beauty of the Pacific Northwest and our neighbors in Alaska,” he added.

Highlights of the season included the arrival of two new cruise lines, MSC Cruises and Virgin Voyages, for their maiden seasons at the port.

In a new record, over 65 percent of the cruise ships visiting Seattle utilized shore power at berth, the port authority said.

The milestone comes as Seattle approaches the 2028 date for 100 percent utilization by homeported ships, it added.

The port also saw its first LNG bunker operation in 2026, with the Star Princess safely and successfully bunkering liquified natural gas in Elliott Bay.

“As we celebrate another record-breaking season, we’re equally proud of our progress towards a more sustainable maritime future through expanded shore power use and investments in cleaner maritime operations. Together with our cruise line partners, we’re demonstrating that economic growth and environmental stewardship can go hand in hand,” said Cho.

#119. The World’s Best Hotel Awards Are Great For Rates, But Hard On Expectations

I recently completed a trip to Japan, where I stayed at Patina Osaka, which was recently rated the world’s best hotel by Travel + Leisure. It got a perfect score of 100 (and for the record, these ratings use decimals, so it wasn’t 99.XX, but literally 100.00). I’ll be reviewing this property shortly, but before I do, I’d like to discuss the topic of hotel awards and guest expectations more broadly.

Obviously we live in peak recommendation culture era, especially in travel. There’s a big circle jerk (pardon my English) between hotels and publications — hotels love to get awards, and publications and other sources like to have their name marketed for free, for issuing certain rankings. And when you consider the way many people get information nowadays (through short form video, where “world’s best hotel” certainly gets some attention), it’s a great marketing technique.

While “The World’s 50 Best” hotel rankings are perhaps the most anticipated by the industry, Travel + Leisure also has quite some pull (for the record, “The World’s 50 Best Hotels” list ranked Patina Osaka as number 33). So I’d like to talk about that briefly, including the psychology of how these rankings impacts consumers… or at least me!

Hotels of course love to win awards that rank them as being among the best hotels in the world. It doesn’t take an economist to figure out why:

So yeah, these awards are the best thing that can happen to a hotel’s business (the above reference to “great” of course refers to how hotels should feel, rather than how guests should feel).

Let me be perfectly honest, without giving away too much. I’ve already reviewed the Waldorf Astoria Osaka, and had an excellent stay. After that, I immediately went to the Patina Osaka.

I was expecting I would come away with an even better impression, given that this is the world’s best hotel according to Travel + Leisure, while it’s the 33rd best hotel in the world according to “The World’s 50 Best” hotel rankings. The Waldorf Astoria Osaka otherwise doesn’t make either of those lists.

The Patina Osaka was excellent, don’t get me wrong. I really enjoyed my stay. However, it had a couple of minor downsides, and I couldn’t help but walk away a bit disappointed. Ford (who wasn’t with me) was curious to hear about my stay at Patina Osaka, and when he asked me via text how it was, I said it was “pretty good.”

Now, that’s probably not fair, because it’s a great hotel. But I also think it’s a good reminder of how perception of a hotel (or any experience, more broadly) comes down to the experience we actually had, compared to the experience we thought we were going to have.

So when a hotel rating would have you believe that you’re about to have the most amazing hospitality experience of your life, and then it’s “just” very good, you can’t help but almost feel a little disappointed.

Over the years, I’ve spoken to some hoteliers who work at properties that have won these same types of high ratings, and they have also expressed this same sentiment — it’s great for business, but it makes it hard for staff. As you’d expect, people think everything will be perfect, and that the hotel won’t say “no” to anything, because after all, this is the best in the world.

The irony, of course, is that most of the hotels winning these awards have a high room count and those definitely aren’t my favorite kinds of hotels. But that gets at how these ratings are often handed out — whether it’s an expert panel or just the public voting, hotels with higher room counts are much more likely to actually have people staying who can contribute to these ratings, rather than a small hotel with just a dozen rooms.

Of course I should know this as well as anyone, and not have my expectations impacted in this way. You really have to view these rankings more as a list of solid luxury hotels, rather than viewing them as some sort of holy scripture that needs to be followed.

I mean, on the airline front, it’s kind of like Hainan Airlines, Korean Air, and Asiana Airlines, being Skytrax 5-star airlines, while some other world class airlines don’t make the list. But yeah, I think we all know what’s really going on there…

We’re seeing an increasing number of publications claiming to have some sort of authoritative list of the world’s best hotels. I always enjoy seeing which hotels rank, though it’s really important to not to read too much into the lists.

From the perspective of hotels, getting a very high ranking absolutely allows them to raise rates, given the increase in demand. The problem is that with that increase in demand also comes an increase in expectations. If you stay at a hotel that markets how it won an award for being the world’s best, you’re expecting a life changing hospitality experience, rather than just another good hotel stay.

What do you make of all of these hotel rankings, and the psychology of it?

In all seriousness, regardless of who’s doing the rating, I remain skeptical on hotels and airlines; feels very ‘pay to play’… the only standout remains Michelin for restaurants; they’re on it.

About five years ago, the French government launched a criminal probe into Michelin. Michelin had approached the tourist board/chamber of commerce at destinations. The proposition was simple: a payment for X number of stars in the area, more for Y stars, and even more for Z stars. A number protested and it went public. Hence the probe. The fact is that Michelin has become a pay-to-play racket.

The Michelin guide is a debased shadow of it's former self and has been since they started selling plaques (originally, even mentioning that you were in the Michelin guide was grounds for delisting) and when they started trying to cover every cuisine at every type of establishment.

Now they're just like any other "best of" list trading on their former reputation.

@ Ltl -- To answer your question, no, I don't at all think I'm doing the same thing. Let's take my rankings of first class, for example. I've flown every single first class product (except Air Cote d'Ivoire), so I can share from firsthand experience exactly how they compare. Nobody has stayed at every single luxury hotel in the world. And for that matter, they only stay at a tiny percentage of them. So the rankings aren't in any way comparative, they're just people saying "hey, I had a nice stay here, therefore it must be the best hotel in the world."

You'll notice that for my lists of the best business class lounges and best business class products, I don't create a ranked list, I just share the products that I think are among the best. I could probably claim to create an authoritative ranking, but I choose not to, because I recognize there are a lot of products out there I haven't flown (even if I'm confident they won't make the list).

To me there's a big distinction there. Someone experiencing every product and then creating a ranked list has some legitimacy to me. Meanwhile someone trying a few hotels and then proclaiming which is the best in the world, with an exact ranking, is less legitimate to me. Is that unreasonable?

You are absolutely right that there are other sites that create all kinds of awards, and to me, the motive there is pretty clear. It's not something I do.

For example, hotel concierge services are something I use regularly and is an important factor in my evaluation of...

Ben, despite the honesty of your reviews, experiencing every airline and hotel once is not sufficient to make authoritative rankings. There is variability in service between crews and a variability in hard products in the same class on the same airline. Ranking hotels would require staying in various room types and using all of the services. For example, hotel concierge services are something I use regularly and is an important factor in my evaluation of a hotel. I might be wrong but you don't strike me as someone who uses those services. The experience in a premium suite won't match the experience in the least expensive room. Also, airlines and hotels probably recognize you as an influencer. Your experiences may be atypical. I think one-time experiences by one atypical individual are not as reliable as aggregated reports from a large group of individuals. While your reviews are very helpful, I put more value in a 4.5 rating and comments from 100 people versus a 5.0 or 4.0 rating and comments from one person.

@ Sushicat -- When I rank first class products, I always acknowledge that experiences can vary, and I never claim that my preferences should line up with those of others. Have you really become so jaded (and pampered) that the only thing that excites you anymore is expecting a "life changing hospitality experience", be it in a hotel or on a plane?

Maybe you need to seriously consider moving the focus of your blog upward in terms of exclusivity and cost for the places you go and write about. Move your focus to private jets and flights--what is the best private jet for US domestic vs international travel, or how to rent or lease private jets. Limit your hotels and resorts stays and reviews to only places that someone like Bill Gates, Soros, or other billionaires would go to escape the mere multimillionaires that can pollute even higher end resorts.

There is also room to move up in terms of ocean voyages beyond merely very expensive cruises that are still open to the general public. Move into reviewing private yachts--how much can you afford and get if you are only a single digit billionaire vs. what you can get if you are someone like Larry Ellison, and where to go in your private yacht, either for gorgeous private views or to be seen by the paparazzi.

After all, by your own figuring you wave already flown every first class airline experience that exists. Maybe this new focus can provide the hospitality experiences you are seeking.

For 99% of my travel, an hotel or an airline is a means to an end, and then I only see how the end is going to be fulfilled, and don’t pay any attention to rankings. To put it bluntly, a direct 2 hour flight in Ryan beats every day an 8 hour flight with one or two scales to enjoy a 5 star airline. Hotels are the same, for business or pleasure I wil set what are my requirements and see how to fulfill them at a reasonable cost. Don’t get me wrong, I have travelled in most of the premium airlines and stayed in very fancy hotels. But most times I am paying top dollars for location more than for a flawless service and wow amenities that are the issues theoretically captured by the rankings.

I enjoy finer things in life as much as anyone. However, I don't give a rat's ass to ratings of airlines, hotels and restaurants from any of these ratings firms or for that matter individuals like Ben. Chasing the ratings is a fool's errand.

When it comes to air travel, whether I get a comfortable seat (lie-flat for long haul) and a decent meal are the only factors I consider after price.

One of the things I've noticed when staying at a really nice hotel in a vacation destination is there's very often one person who felt this trip could fix whatever they didn't like about their life, and when it inevitably doesn't, they somehow blame the hotel for coming up short. I've seen someone dress down the hotel restaurant manager at a five star resort in a way that made me friends with the guy at the other table who mouthed to me "what a douchebag". I've seen someone flip out because a hotel didn't have sufficiently "romantic" stationary to write a note to his wife on. A restaurant my wife and I really like suddenly started getting bad reviews after they got a Bib Gourmand award because random out-of-towners had wild expectations for a pizza place. Getting that high profile status leads to the worst broken, unreasonable expectations falling on the heads of the staff that work there.

Think the best should be on what based on what memorable impression a property can leave on most patrons.

One example, stayed at Capella Bangkok once upon a time. Soon after it was voted the best on the planet. I told somebody I stayed at that property and instantly they asked me what made it the best in the world. I really could not recall my trip there. It was fine. Great service. Some pretty good restaurants. But nothing that really stood out. Nothing that could separate it from a host of other ultra luxe properties on the planet. But i have stayed at palace hotels in India. Some beyond perfect experiences, some slightly less than perfect. But the grandeur of those palaces, made it the most memorable stays of my life. And i don't think any of those hotels made it to the list of the "Top 50" hotels in the world list i saw recently.

So i don't think these lists are worth the paper they are printed on.

When it comes to air travel, whether I get a comfortable seat (lie-flat for long haul) and a decent meal are the only factors I consider after price. When it comes to hotels, a clean room with a comfortable bed in a convenient location are the only factors I consider after price. With regards to hotels, the cuisine I am in the mood for and the hygiene (hard to measure, but I know what I don't like when I see it) of the place are the things that matter most to me.

#120. Waldorf Astoria Osaka Review: Hilton Gem With Amazing Design, Service, & Facilities!

Want to take advantage of Hilton for Luxury benefits at no extra cost (when paying for your stay with cash), including a room upgrade, free breakfast, a hotel credit, and more? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. He doesn’t charge booking fees, and may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

For the hotel portion my first class quest to Japan, I had the chance to spend a night at the 252-key Waldorf Astoria Osaka, which opened in April 2025. This followed a stay at the Bulgari Tokyo, and then in Osaka I also checked out the Patina Osaka and Osaka Station Hotel (Marriott Autograph Collection). I must say, Osaka is having quite the glow-up when it comes to the number of new luxury hotel openings, as each hotel is special in its own way.

I adored the Waldorf Astoria Osaka, and think it’s a spectacular hotel. It has flawless service, impressive amenities, excellent dining outlets, and more. It also has gorgeous André Fu design, the same person behind so many other great hotels, ranging from Capella Taipei to Upper House Hong Kong.

Honestly, all three hotels I stayed at in Osaka were excellent, though I think this might actually be my favorite. I’d say the only slight downside is that I didn’t find the breakfast to be that over-the-top impressive, but it was still very good.

Compared to Tokyo and Kyoto, Osaka is a relatively affordable luxury hotel market. Rates at the Waldorf Astoria Osaka vary throughout the year, with peak dates being around Cherry Blossom (since Osaka is a popular jumping off point for Kyoto), as well as any time there’s a major convention in town.

Generally you’ll find Waldorf Astoria Osaka rates of $500-700 per night, before taxes and fees. Generally the best way to book a Waldorf Astoria property is through the Hilton for Luxury program, which offers complimentary breakfast, a property credit, top priority for upgrades, double points at many properties, and more. Ford and his team are happy to help with these requests, and can be reached at [email protected].

In this case, I booked using Fine Hotels + Resorts®, as I was redeeming an American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) up to $300 hotel credit for my stay. So the rate was around $550 for my one-night stay, but then after the $300 credit, I really paid $250 out of pocket. I then received a property credit and more.

Note that if I had redeemed Hilton Honors points, the cost of my one-night stay would’ve been 120,000 points. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, those points are worth 0.5 cents each. So in this case, paying cash was the better value, especially after factoring in the extra perks I could receive on a stay of one night.

The Waldorf Astoria is located in Osaka’s Umekita District, which is one of the city’s financial and shopping hubs. I’ve been to Osaka several times, and I can’t say that I have a strong preference on the best area to stay in, though I found this to be quite central, and enjoyed going on walks from the hotel.

More specifically, the Waldorf Astoria is located on the top floors of the Grand Green Osaka South Building, taking up floors 28 to 38.

In terms of getting to and from the hotel, the property is located just a very short walk from Osaka Station, giving easy access to public transit. However, it’s located across the river from the Shin-Osaka Station (which is where bullet trains operate from), so unless you want to walk for an hour, you’ll want to take the subway or a car.

As I pulled up to the Waldorf Astoria Osaka, I was immediately greeted by name by a bellmen, which caught me totally off guard, given that this is a 250+ room hotel. For the record, I booked just a few days before arrival, and had zero contact with the hotel before my stay, but clearly they figured out “who” I am (not that I’m anyone special, but I do review hotels, so…), and that was confirmed based on the welcome amenity.

So while I always prefer to fly under the radar when possible, I do give hotels credit when they look into their guests, because it shows that they’re paying attention more broadly (and for the record, I don’t usually get any sort of special treatment at Hilton properties).

Anyway, on the ground floor the Waldorf Astoria essentially has a welcome area and bellman station. This is already a gorgeous space, but isn’t even one of the primary facilities of the hotel.

I was immediately escorted to the elevator, which would take me up to the 29th floor, where the lobby is located. Note that there are separate elevators between the ground floor and lobby, and between the lobby and guest rooms, so you need to take two sets of elevator rides to get from your room to the ground floor.

The 29th floor of the Waldorf Astoria Osaka is where you’ll find many of the public areas, and it’s a gorgeous, sprawling space. The reception area was always very well staffed, and the lobby also had plenty of seating.

The reception area is downright mesmerizing, and the double-height space is supposed to look like a lantern, of sorts.

My check-in process was quick. I was thanked for my Hilton Honors™ Diamond Status and for booking through a consortia, and I was then escorted up to my room. For context, below are the welcome letters I received, reflecting the perks on account of my elite status and booking.

I was assigned room 3724, located on the 37th floor. The elevators between the lobby and guest rooms are quick, and I loved the design of the hallways.

I was assigned a king corner suite with a river view. That’s obviously a great upgrade — I’ve heard of some Diamond members getting similar upgrades, so I can’t say with certainty whether that upgrade was just due to my status, the fact that they figured out “who” I am, or what. Anyway, I’m just adding that disclaimer.

These corner suites are very spacious, and are 1,000 square feet (93 square meters). The suite featured a long entryway, leading into the living room.

The living room was gorgeous, with a sitting area containing a couch and a chair, as well as a dining table with two chairs. I loved the design, between the wood, the pops of color, the texture of the coffee table, etc.

Waiting on the coffee table was a lovely welcome amenity, with some tea and sweets. As you can see, this is how I figured out that they knew of my blog.

The minibar was located in the living room, and had a complimentary selection of Nespresso coffee and tea, plus drinks and snacks for purchase.

There was a half bath off the living room, with a bidet-style toilet, naturally.

The bedroom was separated from the living room by a door, and was spacious, with 180 degree views. The bed was very comfortable, and there was also a chair with a small table in the corner of the room.

The bedroom had the best views. The views in one direction were incredible, facing the city on both sides of the river.

The view in the other direction was a little less impressive, as there’s a huge high rise being built immediately next to the Waldorf Astoria.

Then next to that was the primary bathroom, with double sinks, a soaking tub, a walk-in shower, and a toilet in a separate area. Shower water pressure was excellent, with two shower heads.

Toiletries were from Aesop, which nowadays seems to be brand standard for Waldorf Astoria — I’m a huge fan of that! There was also an excellent selection of dry amenities.

I found room cleanliness to be very good, I appreciated that turndown service was offered, and the Wi-Fi in the room was fast and free. The one thing I’ll say (and this might just reflect my lack of tech savviness) is that I found the room controls to be a little unnecessarily complicated to use. Like, please just give me one master switch I can push, rather than a combination of several buttons, a tablet, etc. But maybe that’s just me.

All-in-all, though, what an incredible suite!

The Waldorf Astoria Osaka spa is located on the 30th floor. The spa is open daily from 10AM until 9PM, there are four treatment rooms, and you can find the treatment menu here, with services in partnership with Burgener Switzerland.

Also in the spa complex you’ll find the 66-foot (20-meter) indoor pool, with lovely views. It’s open daily from 6:30AM until 10PM.

Guests can also use all the spa facilities, including the changing rooms and lockers, the whirlpool, the sauna, the steam room, and the relaxation area. I thought all the facilities were great, except the relaxation area felt a bit basic for a hotel of this caliber.

The Waldorf Astoria Osaka also has a gym located next to the spa, which is open 24/7. The gym is one big rectangular room, with Technogym equipment. It’s not the biggest gym ever, but the equipment was high quality, and I appreciated the heavy weights.

Here’s a unique amenity — the Waldorf Astoria Osaka has a “library” on the 30th floor, the same floor as the spa. It’s open daily from 9AM until 10PM, and it’s essentially just a quiet place to sit that’s not in your room.

There’s even a complimentary Nespresso machine you can help yourself to, including drinks with milk, like cappuccinos.

I very much appreciate this concept, since I’m always looking for coffee and a quiet place from which to work when traveling (ideally not in my room, so I don’t get tempted to get into bed, and then fall asleep). So I love this concept, I just wish it would open a little earlier. Like, why not make it 24/7, as it would be awesome to grab a first cup of coffee here at 5AM?

The Waldorf Astoria Osaka is very much a food & beverage destination, including for locals, and it has quite the array of outlets, all located on the 28th and 29th floor:

Let’s start with Jolie Brasserie, described as a French-inspired brasserie, serving breakfast from 6:30AM until 11AM, lunch from 11:30AM until 2:30PM, and dinner from 5:30PM until 10PM. It’s a very nice restaurant with great views of the city, though it’s also large. That’s not surprising, given that it’s the primary breakfast venue, and this hotel has a lot of rooms.

This is where I had breakfast. The idea is that breakfast includes a buffet, as well as a selection of a la carte dishes. Let’s start with the buffet. I found the selection to be high quality, but not particularly big. A section of the buffet was located in the main dining area, and this included all kinds of pastries, cereal, and juice.

Then the other area of the buffet was back by the kitchen. Given the size of the hotel, I found the actual buffet area to be a little too condensed, in the sense that it would get crowded. This area of the buffet had fresh fruit, yogurt, salads, veggies, cold cuts, french toast, waffles, cheese, smoked salmon, guacamole, hummus, rice porridge, sausage, hash browns, grilled tomatoes, etc.

Again, it was a good selection, it just wasn’t the most memorable buffet I’ve seen (I was surprised by which hotel had — by far — the best breakfast on this trip).

The buffet could be supplemented with a dish from the a la carte selection. It’s interesting how menus are customized to different guests. For example, since I’m a Hilton Diamond member, I was given a menu with a special “chef’s selection,” with two dishes and a latte that other guests don’t get (maybe non-Diamond members get the “short order cook’s selection,” I dunno?).

To drink, I first had a cappuccino, which was just perfectly smooth, and had nice art as well.

I then later decided I had to order the exclusive Hilton Diamond latte of the day, which was a ginger peach iced latte. It was obviously very tasty, though I don’t typically like sweet drinks, and it was definitely a bit on the sweet side (though not terribly so).

I then had the wagyu beef braised udon with onsen style egg, another Hilton Diamond specialty, which was very good.

All-in-all, it was a good breakfast, though not one of the most memorable I’ve had. I didn’t have lunch or dinner at Jolie Brasserie, but you can find the menus here.

Next, Peacock Alley is a venue you’ll find at every Waldorf Astoria in the world, and it’s essentially the lobby lounge concept. I must say, this might be my favorite Peacock Alley venue in the world (perhaps along with the one at the Waldorf Astoria New York).

This one is just stunning, and if you’ve seen pictures of the Waldorf Astoria Osaka, odds are that this is one of the photos you’ve seen. With the super high ceilings, plus this being oriented in the direction with the best views, it really is a one-of-a-kind venue. There’s also often live music.

Peacock Alley has drinks and food available all day, and you can find the menu and drink list here. I came here in the evening for a negroni, to enjoy the views. The negroni was excellent, and I loved the design of the large cube.

Next, there’s Canes & Tales, the hotel’s speakeasy, open nightly from 5PM until 12AM (until 1AM on weekends). This has both indoor and outdoor seating, and it’s also a very nice, themed space, with a totally different vibe than Peacock Alley.

The hotel has a variety of themed cocktails, and the staff here really have a passion for mixology, and you can find the drink list here. I had the “May Day” cocktail, with gin, vermouth, strawberry and shiso shrub, and fresh matcha foam. It was as tasty as it was beautifully presented, and I appreciated that it wasn’t overly sweet.

Back in the day, the Waldorf Astoria Osaka would offer an additional food & beverage credit for Hilton Diamond members. In the meantime, that has been replaced by a paid happy hour at Canes & Tales exclusively for Diamond members, available nightly from 5PM until 6:30PM. The idea is that for 5,500 JPY (~35 USD), you receive unlimited cocktails, beer, and wine, along with a selection of canapés, for 60 minutes.

I don’t want to look a (paid?) gift horse in the mouth, but I don’t love this concept. I guess it’s one thing if you value the small canapés, but essentially creating a system where you need to have a few of the boring drinks to come out ahead just strikes me as not very fitting of a luxury hotel. But maybe that’s just me.

Lastly, the hotel has Tsukimi Sushi and Tsukimi Teppanyaki, which are the signature Japanese venues. They serve lunch and dinner select days of the week — you can find the Tsukimi Sushi menu here, and the Tsukimi Teppanyaki menu here. The catch is that neither venue was open on the day of my stay, so I couldn’t actually dine there.

I’m sure both are great, though honestly, Osaka is an amazing food city, and odds are that you’ll find much better value and equally good restaurants if you go out. Then again, that’s true for most international luxury hotels. 😉

I found service at the Waldorf Astoria Osaka to be stellar across the board. Japan in general has a very high service standard, but the Waldorf Astoria Osaka was excellent, even with the very high expectations I had.

I’d note that the staff were overwhelmingly Japanese, which I appreciate. Many international hotels in Japan are largely staffed by foreigners, and that takes some of the fun out of the experience, in my opinion. Just more generally, the service felt very authentic, and to a very high standard, given the number of keys at this hotel. I’ll take it a step further — I actually thought service here was a little better than at Patina Osaka, which I wasn’t anticipating.

From the front office staff, to all the restaurant workers, I have nothing but good things to say about the service here.

I had heard great things about the Waldorf Astoria Osaka before my stay, and it sure didn’t disappoint. From the André Fu design, to the excellent service, to the extensive food & beverage outlets, to the amazing views, this really is a very good hotel, and I’d return in a heartbeat. I’m just sad that I didn’t have more than one night to enjoy this property. Osaka really has become an incredible hotel market, and it’s now operating in a completely different league than several years back.

What’s your take on the Waldorf Astoria Osaka?
