#121. Riviera Reports Surge in Bookings, Solo Departures and Group Sales

Riviera Travel River Cruises announced today that it continues to see strong interest in its North American product and is on track to exceed 100 percent year-over-year (YOY) growth for the second consecutive year.

As of September 2026, Riviera’s North American business was up 92 percent year-over-year, positioning the brand to exceed 100 percent by the year’s end.

“When we rebranded in 2025, we had the vision of making Riviera Travel River Cruises a household name, one that would be known for delivering a truly exceptional product and experience,” said Stuart Milan, president of North America for Riviera Travel River Cruises.

“We are overjoyed to be celebrating another banner year in 2026 and excited to continue the mission in 2027, welcoming more North Americans onboard our ships than ever before and expanding our offerings in some very special ways,” added Milan.

In a press release, the company said that as Riviera prepares to launch the world’s first dedicated solo cruise ship, it has more than doubled its YOY solo bookings and demand for solo departures is up 80 percent from 2025.

Group bookings have emerged as Riviera’s fastest-growing segment, largely thanks to its generous eighth-guest-sails-free promotion.

A detailed breakdown shows that Riviera Travel River Cruises’ Rhine and Moselle bookings are up 200 percent year over year. Bookings for the brand’s Mekong River itinerary, which was introduced last year, are up 300 percent.

A key driver behind Riviera Travel River Cruises’ North American growth is the relationships the company has built with its travel partners.

As of September 2026, more than 3,000 travel advisors have registered for the company’s training program, Riviera Explorer, which recently celebrated its first anniversary.

Over the last year, more than 55,000 training modules have been completed, with more than 600 graduates.

Milan credited its dedicated team and travel advisor partners with the success.

Looking ahead to 2027, Riviera Travel River Cruises has several new initiatives on the horizon, including transforming the George Elliot into the world’s first dedicated solo ship and expanding into Southeast Asia with its Vietnam, Cambodia and Mekong River Cruise itinerary.

The brand also recently announced its 2028 sales and new Riviera Moment collection, featuring even more immersive, unique river cruise experiences tailored to North American travelers.

#123. IHG Credit Card Free Night Awards: How To Earn & Redeem Them, Maximize Value

Chase & IHG One Rewards have a portfolio of co-branded credit cards. Three of the four cards — The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more) — offer the opportunity to earn free night award certificates, which can be extremely valuable.

I’d argue that these cards are absolutely worth having, primarily for the free night certificates, as they help with justifying the annual fee. In this post, I’d like to take a close look at everything you need to know about earning and redeeming IHG One Rewards free night certificates.

Three of IHG One Rewards’ co-branded Chase credit cards offer free night awards as an anniversary benefit, with no spending required:

On top of that, two of the cards offer a second free night award annually based on spending:

Below is a chart showing all five opportunities across three cards to earn free night awards with IHG cards currently open to new cardmembers.

Let me emphasize that the IHG card portfolio recently underwent a refresh, and free night awards on previously issued cards are still worth 40,000 points. That will continue to be the case through the end of 2026, and then as of 2027, the newly issued certificates will get the higher value of 50,000 points. The same applies to those who have the legacy IHG Select Card, which is no longer open to new applicants — as of 2027, those certificates will also be worth up to 50,000 points, and will be eligible for top-offs.

Sometimes IHG also has promotions offering free night awards through non-credit card means, but that’s not a consistent aspect of the program.

The IHG Premier Select Card, IHG Premier Card, and IHG Business Card, all offer anniversary free night certificates, meaning you get your first certificate roughly 12 months after you open your card (you don’t get a certificate the first year, since most people don’t celebrate their zero year anniversary). 😉

You can expect the free night certificate to post automatically, and it will be available for redemption in your account online. They typically post very shortly after your anniversary date.

When it comes to the spend based certificates (based on spending a certain amount within a calendar year), those will post within eight weeks of when you reach the spending threshold (and often sooner), rather than only posting on the account anniversary.

IHG credit card free night certificates are generally valid for 12 months from the date of issue. You not only have to book by the expiration date, but you have to also stay by the expiration date as well. This means that if you’re issued the certificate on October 20, 2026, you would have to book and stay by October 20, 2027.

Generally speaking, these certificates can’t be extended, so if you don’t use them by the expiration date, expect that you’ll lose them.

The IHG Premier Select Card, IHG Premier Card, and IHG Business Card free night awards are valid at properties costing up to a certain number of points. The great thing is that you can supplement these certificates with points in order to redeem at more expensive properties.

In other words, you could now book a hotel costing 70,000 IHG points by redeeming one free night certificate worth 60,000 points, plus redeeming 10,000 points. This makes it much easier to get full value out of the certificate. This is some incredible flexibility to have, and makes these certificates much more valuable.

Note that a majority of IHG properties are bookable for under the amounts that these certificates are for, though admittedly many of the luxury and aspirational properties around the globe cost more. So it’s nice to be able to redeem for stays at those properties with these certificates.

Even without exceeding the cap, I’ve been able to redeem at some fantastic hotels, ranging from the InterContinental Ljubljana, to the InterContinental Johannesburg, to the Kimpton Miami. All of these properties would have cost $200-350 per night if paying cash.

IHG credit card anniversary free night certificates come from the same inventory as points stays, so if you can redeem points for a stay, you can also redeem this certificate.

IHG One Rewards advertises “no blackout dates,” though this is different than the “no blackout dates” policies from Hilton Honors and World of Hyatt. Let me explain:

If planning in advance this shouldn’t be an issue, with very few exceptions.

On the account anniversary of the IHG Premier Select Card, IHG Premier Card, and IHG Business Card, the free night certificate will automatically be deposited in your IHG One Rewards account.

To access these certificates, log into your IHG One Rewards account, and navigate to the “See Rewards Wallet” section.

That will bring you to a section that shows “Redeem your rewards,” and then “Free Nights and booking rewards.”

If you click on the “Details” button, you can see the expiration date of your certificate. The “View Details” button on the next page will also show you the terms associated with the certificate, including how many points it’s potentially worth, confirmation that the certificate can be topped off with points, etc.

If you click the “Book Free Night” button, you’ll be brought to the main IHG booking page, where you’ll see the free night certificate listed as one of the rate preferences.

Once you enter a destination, you’ll see all the options for redeeming your certificate. You’ll see that properties show a “Chase Anniversary Night” rate.

In some situations, the price is listed as “FREE,” which means that the free night award covers the stay. Meanwhile other properties will show a certain number of points, which is the supplement needed on top of the certificate. If a property has a resort or destination fee, that should also display on the search result page.

If a property only shows a cash rate, that means there’s no availability using points or free night awards. However, you can click “View available dates,” and then it will show you a calendar with availability.

The final confirmation page will show the cancelation policy for the booking, which should be identical to what it would be if you were outright redeeming points. This is typically going to be a pretty flexible policy, but varies by property.

Let me emphasize that if you want to book a longer stay and not all nights are being booked with free night awards, you’ll need to book those reservations separately. In other words, if you’re staying at a hotel and are using a free night award for one night and points for three nights, you’d need to reserve this as two separate reservations.

Furthermore, IHG credit cards offer a fourth night free perk on award redemptions, but that only applies when redeeming points, and not when redeeming free night awards. So that’s something worth being strategic about, if you are planning a stay of four nights.

It’s absolutely possible to earn more than one IHG free night award per year. As you can see, with the three IHG cards currently open to new cardmembers that issue free night awards, you could potentially earn up to five free night awards, including three as anniversary perks, and two for spending. If you’re strategic, it’s possible to get approved (and earn the welcome bonuses) on all three cards.

If you’re looking to book a longer stay but don’t have enough free night certificates, you can always supplement a free night award by redeeming points for another night. And if you don’t have many IHG points, note that IHG One Rewards often sells points at a discount, which can represent a great deal.

The free night certificates issued with the IHG Premier Select Card, IHG Premier Card, and IHG Business Card, have to be used for a reservation in the name of the primary cardmember. Some have had luck making a reservation for two guests, then adding the second guest’s name, and then having them check in, but that’s not a published policy.

When redeeming an IHG free night certificate, you generally don’t have to pay any percentage-based taxes or service charges, since for those purposes the rate is zero. That being said, if there’s a fixed per-night tax or tourism fee, or if there’s a resort or destination fee at the property, you are on the hook for that. The destination fee will typically be listed on the page that displays rates.

The IHG Premier Select Card, IHG Premier Card, and IHG Business Card, offer a variety of valuable perks, which in my opinion more than justify the annual fee. But I’ll take it a step further — with each card I think the free night certificate alone nearly justifies the annual fee, in and of itself.

But of course you don’t just have to view it this way, as there are so many other perks to the cards. For example, each offers IHG food & beverage rewards, which can save you on the cost of on property spending at IHG properties quarterly. That very nicely compliments the free night awards, since it lets you get even more value from those stays.

There are lots of great perks to the IHG Premier Select Card, IHG Premier Card, and IHG Business Card. However, I’d argue the single best perk is the anniversary free night certificate offered with each card. These can be redeemed at properties costing up to 50,000 to 60,000 points per night. You can even top off these certificates with points, to be able to redeem at more expensive hotels, which greatly minimizes breakage.

If you travel with any frequency and stay at IHG properties, then having multiple IHG cards should be a no-brainer.

What do you make of the value of IHG’s free night awards?

#124. Fun: FAA Will Let Air Traffic Controllers Ride In Airline Cockpit Jumpseats

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is bringing back a program that hasn’t been active since before the pandemic, whereby air traffic controllers can fly in the jumpseat on commercial flights. What a cool concept!

Air traffic controllers and pilots of course both perform vital roles that keep our aviation system moving. While they ultimately work together with the same goal, that’s not to say that they always see eye-to-eye, given their very different functions.

So along those lines, the FAA is bringing back a program that’s intended to help air traffic controllers see things from the perspective of pilots. Specifically, the FAA is bringing back the Flight Deck Training program, giving air traffic controllers the opportunity to gain firsthand experience aboard commercial, general aviation, and military aircraft.

The idea is that the program allows air traffic controllers to apply for jumpseat access on eligible flights, to gain firsthand experience with flight deck operations, including pilot workload, cockpit procedures, and how air traffic control instructions impact flight crews. The FAA has worked with the National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA) to reinstate this program, as it was paused at the start of the pandemic.

The expectation is that this will launch after Thanksgiving. All major US airlines have agreed to participate in this program. Controllers can fly on two flights per year under this program, and a controller’s air traffic manager will consider the facility’s available staffing and needs in evaluating a request.

The way this works, controllers will apply electronically to fly on specific flights, including identifying a training objective. Once approved internally, the FAA will transmit the request to the airlines. Controllers will go through multiple steps of vetting at the airport and when they reach the airplane. After the flight, controllers will submit a report explaining what they learned.

As the FAA explains, this program has already been tested, and benefits have been identified, including helping controllers understand when they should refrain from issuing complex instructions, and the impact that instructions, such as changes in the landing runway, can have on pilot workload.

Here’s how FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford describes this:

“After listening to our frontline controllers, we’re excited to bring back the Flight Deck Training program. Our controllers are the backbone of the National Airspace System and giving them opportunities to build their knowledge and gain firsthand experience makes them better at what they do. Communication is key and this program will give controllers and pilots an up-close view of each other’s responsibilities and challenges.”

Meanwhile here’s how NATCA President Nick Daniels describes this:

“NATCA is pleased to see this vital component of air traffic controller training reinstated. There is no substitute for firsthand experience in the cockpit. The Flight Deck Training program gives participants a unique perspective on the challenges pilots face and how their decisions and actions interact with the air traffic control system, ultimately strengthening their understanding of the National Airspace System.”

In general, it’s of course fantastic for people who are essentially working together to get a firsthand look at how their actions impact those performing other functions. So this is a learning experience, and it’s of course also really fun — as an avgeek, there’s nothing like flying in the cockpit of a large jet!

Now, I have to imagine that those who actually take advantage of this opportunity are the great controllers who already do their best, and who are genuinely looking to learn through firsthand experience. What would crack me up is if one of those notorious JFK controllers took a ride in the jumpseat. Specifically, that one guy who is the “star” of roughly half of the memorable ATC interactions we hear at JFK.

Gosh, I would love to be a fly on the wall if he were in a jumpseat. Admittedly the person in the jumpseat has to be silent during critical phases of flight, but goodness, I’m sure he’d have quite some “coaching” for pilots, as to how they should do their job.

The FAA is bringing back a program that has been suspended for well over six years, whereby air traffic controllers can fly in the jumpseat on aircraft. The idea is to give air traffic controllers a sense of what it’s like to be a pilot, and how instructions can impact the workload in the flight deck.

This is of course an awesome concept, and it makes perfect sense. I’m just visualizing all kinds of hilarious interactions in my head involving that JFK controller.

What do you make of this jumpseat opportunity for air traffic controllers?

To answer at least one of your questions: if a pilot decides they don't want ATC in flight deck, then the controller must leave the plane (before door closes) or find a seat in the back (after door closes). Controllers are required to plan alternate flights as a backup.

Having worked for a major both before and after 9/11 I don’t remember very many controllers riding in the cockpit, but I’ll take your word on it. The program actually goes back to the 70’s when they were referred to as “Fam Trips”. Load factors are a lot higher today which creates more demand for the jumpseats than in earlier days and these days a lot of eligible employees would prefer to ride in a jumpseat rather than a center seat in coach. Maybe a better idea would be a program that allows controllers to sit with a Dispatcher or ATC Coordinator in the airline’s operations center or, better yet, let them observe a Sim ride. That would show them a lot and be a lot more fun.

#125. United Business Card Review: Is The Card Worth The $150 Annual Fee?

The United℠ Business Card is a popular business credit card that’s issued by Chase, and it’s an excellent value for many small businesses, especially for users who are loyal to United MileagePlus. The card has a big welcome bonus, offers some helpful bonus categories, and comes with perks that can more than offset the annual fee.

This post is my in-depth United Business Card review. Let’s dive in with a look at the details of this United Airlines business card, and then I’ll give you my overall thoughts on its benefits and how it compares to other options.

Link: Learn more about the United℠ Business Card

Before I get into my United Business Card review, here’s a high-level look at the card details, including its sign-up bonus and other key points:

These are what I consider to be the main pros and cons of the United Business Card:

Before I even talk specifically about the United Business Card, I’d like to briefly discuss why having a co-branded MileagePlus credit card is more important than ever before. As we know, US airlines make a lot of their profits from their loyalty programs, so getting people engaged there has really become a priority.

However, no airline has taken it as far as United when it comes to giving people an incentive to pick up a co-branded credit card, both on the earning and redemption front.

When it comes to earning MileagePlus miles, the number of miles you earn per dollar spent is based on your elite status, and whether or not you have an eligible co-branded MileagePlus credit card. Regardless of your elite tier, you earn an extra 3x miles per dollar spent on United spending. At my valuation of 1.3 cents per MileagePlus mile, that’s an incremental 3.9% return on spending, so that’s worth something.

When it comes to redeeming MileagePlus miles, you’ll nowadays find that award pricing is heavily dependent on whether you have MileagePlus elite status and/or a co-branded credit card. United makes a vast majority of its Polaris business class award seats available exclusively to MileagePlus members (rather than members of partner programs), and the pricing is way better if you have a co-branded credit card.

So if you’re at all engaged in MileagePlus, you’ll want to have a premium co-branded credit card, whether it’s the United Business Card, or another product.

Understandably, when people apply for credit cards, one major motivating factor is the welcome bonus. Of course in order to understand the welcome bonus, it’s also important to know the eligibility rules, and to understand any fees you’ll be paying. So let’s start with those details for the United Business Card.

The United Business Card is currently offering a welcome bonus of 90,000 MileagePlus bonus miles plus 2,000 Premier Qualifying Points (PQPs) after spending $5,000 within the first three months. You can earn a further 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first three months your account is open.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, MileagePlus miles are worth 1.3 cents each, making the bonus miles potentially worth $1,300. That doesn’t factor in the PQPs, which can help you earn status. The value of that will obviously vary considerably depending on whether you’re pursuing elite status, and where you’d otherwise end the year.

The welcome bonus on the United Business Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months. In addition to that, there are the typical restrictions when applying for Chase cards, including Chase’s well-known 5/24 rule: you’ll likely be denied if you’ve opened five or more credit cards in the past 24 months, though some cards (including many business cards) are excluded from that total.

Chase doesn’t publish a minimum credit score you need to get approved for the United Business Card, but you’ll have the best approval odds with good to excellent credit.

The United Business Card has a $150 annual fee. You can also add employee cards at no extra cost, and you can set individual spending limits for each one. This is a reasonable ongoing annual fee for a perks-rich card.

The United Business Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this is a good card for purchases abroad. Visa has excellent global acceptance, and you may earn bonus miles for purchases abroad, including at restaurants.

The United Business Card has a handful of bonus categories worth knowing about. Plus, spending on the card can earn PQP toward United MileagePlus status. Here’s how that all works.

While I wouldn’t say the bonus categories are industry-leading, the United Business Card does offer bonus miles on some purchases. With the card, you can earn 2x MileagePlus miles on:

You can earn 1x miles on all other purchases. Based on my valuation of ~1.3 cents per United mile, that’s a 2.6% return on United purchases and the bonus categories, and a 1.3% return on everything else.

While there are lots of cards offering bonus categories, I’d say that’s a pretty well-rounded rewards structure for an airline credit card.

Spending money on the United Business Card can help you earn MileagePlus status, though not in as lucrative a way as the more premium version of the card. The card offers one Premier Qualifying Point (PQP) for every $20 spent on purchases, up to a maximum of 4,000 PQPs per year.

For context, below are the MileagePlus elite requirements for 2027 (for the purposes of qualifying for elite status in 2028). As you can see, spending on the card won’t put that much of a dent into earning higher elite tiers, given the cap of 4,000 PQPs.

The United Business Card has a big welcome bonus and a fairly solid rewards structure for an airline small business credit card. The good news is that beyond that, the card has great perks as well.

This is true whether you’re an occasional United flyer, or you’re an elite member who is looking for extra perks. Here’s what you need to know about all the benefits offered by the United Business Card.

The primary cardmember on the United Business Card and one companion traveling on the same reservation receive a standard free first checked bag when flying United or United Express. In order to be eligible for this, you have to pay for your ticket with your United Airlines credit card.

Given that United ordinarily charges $45-50 per checked bag, this is potentially a value of up $100 per person on a roundtrip, or a value of up to $200 if two people are traveling.

For having the United Business Card, you receive two United Club passes annually. This includes the year where you open your card, and in any subsequent years. These will automatically be deposited into your MileagePlus account within four weeks.

When it comes to United Club access, United Club passes ordinarily cost $59 each, so that’s a value of up to $118.

For having the United Business Card, you and your companions receive priority boarding on United and United Express flights. You can board before general boarding, after customers with Premier Access, and those requiring special assistance. This would be in Group 2.

For having the United Business Card, you receive 25% back in the form of statement credits on purchases of food, beverages, and Wi-Fi, on United-operated flights when you pay with your card. The statement credit should post within six to eight weeks of your eligible purchase posting to your statement.

Every calendar year, you can receive a $125 United TravelBank cash if you make at least five United flight travel-related purchases on your United Business Card, each totaling at least $100.

This includes purchases like seat upgrades, Economy Plus, inflight food, beverages, and Wi-Fi, baggage service charges, or other United fees. The statement credit will post to your account within 24 hours of your fifth qualifying purchase of $100 or more.

Every year on your account anniversary, you receive 5,000 bonus miles if you have the United Business Card in conjunction with a personal United credit card, like the United℠ Explorer Card (learn more).

That’s a pretty awesome incentive to keep both a personal and business card, and frankly, it’s a really smart incentive for United to offer, given that many personal and business cards have overlapping benefits.

The United Business Card offers a $10 Instacart credit monthly, up to $120 total each calendar year. This applies for purchases made through Instacart with your United Business Card, and currently the benefit is valid through December 31, 2027.

If you use Instacart anyway, then this could be worth close to face value. For others, the small increments of the credits will make it hard to get much value.

If you spend $25,000 on the United Business Card in a calendar year, you earn two Economy Plus seat upgrades for flights within the continental United States. You need to buy the ticket with your card, and the upgrades must be used within 12 months.

The United Business Card offers up to $8 back per month on rideshare purchases (and $12 in December), in the form of a statement credit, when paying with your card. This allows you to earn up to $100 in statement credits every calendar year, and an annual opt-in is required.

On the one hand, these statement credits are easy enough to use. The catch is that there are probably better cards for rideshare spending in terms of maximizing rewards.

United Hotels is United’s hotel booking platform. The United Business Card offers up to $100 back on United Hotels purchases each anniversary year. Specifically, you can get a $50 statement credit on both your first and second prepaid hotel stays purchased through United Hotels with your United Business Card.

This could prove valuable for some, though keep in mind there’s typically an opportunity cost to booking through a hotel portal (in terms of earning loyalty points, there being lower rates elsewhere, etc.).

The United Business Card offers up to $100 back on JSX flight purchases per anniversary year. This comes in the form of a statement credit, and you must use your United Business Card to make the purchase. JSX is a hop-on jet service, which United owns a stake in. If you fly JSX with any frequency, then this is a great perk.

The United Business Card offers up to a $25 statement credit each anniversary year when you use the card to buy FareLock on a United or United Express operated flight. FareLock lets you hold a fare for three, seven, or 14 days.

The United Business Card offers a variety of protection benefits when traveling, assuming you pay for purchases with your card. These features include the following:

Make sure you check your cardmember agreement for all of the details since there are terms & conditions.

The United Business Card offers a primary collision damage waiver (CDW) benefit. Just decline the rental company’s collision insurance and charge the entire rental cost to your card.

Coverage is primary when renting for business purposes and provides reimbursement up to $60,000 for theft and collision damage for most rental vehicles with an MSRP of $125,000 or less worldwide.

When you pay with the United Business Card, eligible new purchases are covered against damage or theft for 120 days, up to $10,000 per item. The card also adds an extra year to eligible United States manufacturer warranties of three years or less.

In general, I don’t recommend using airline credit cards for everyday spending, unless you have a specific reason to do so. That being said, if you are a United flyer, then at least having some MileagePlus credit card is very important, given that it offers increased mileage earning rates, and reduced mileage redemption rates. It’ll make a huge difference.

In the case of the United Business Card, I think this is a card that’s worth getting for the upside with MileagePlus, the reasonable annual fee, the welcome bonus, and the long term perks. That being said, I don’t think this card is worth spending much money on:

What perks make the United Business Card worthwhile? Beyond the improved mileage earning rates and reduced mileage redemption rates, non-elite members will benefit from the priority boarding, first checked bag free, two United Club passes, and 25% savings on inflight purchases.

Furthermore, the card offers hundreds of dollars in credits. While there are some hoops to jump through to maximize those credits, most cardmembers should be able to get at least some value from them.

The one thing I’d note is that while this is a great card for the perks, if you actually want to earn MileagePlus miles through spending, remember that MileagePlus is a Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer partner, so you can convert Ultimate Rewards points into United miles at a 1:1 ratio.

There are so many great Ultimate Rewards cards that earn points at a potentially faster rate than you’d earn directly through United, so that’s something worth considering.

See this post for the best credit cards for earning United miles.

Obviously you can’t view a credit card in isolation, so it’s important to compare the United Business Card to some other cards on the markets, both other MileagePlus credit cards, as well as other potentially lucrative business cards.

If you’re looking for a personal United Airlines credit card, consider the United Quest℠ Card (learn more), which has a pretty compelling value proposition and is my personal favorite United card.

While the card has a $350 annual fee, the perks are potentially more than worth it. These include:

For many, those first few perks alone will more than offset the annual fee. The United Quest Card also earns 10x total miles on United flights (compared to 8x total with the United Business Card), 5x miles on prepaid hotel stays booked through Renowned Hotels and Resorts, and 2x miles on dining, select streaming services, and all other travel (and 1x miles on everything else).

If you’re open to a non-business United credit card, there’s also the United℠ Explorer Card (learn more) with a $150 annual fee.

Like the United Business Card, it gets you a first checked bag free on United, two United Club passes annually, and several statement credits. The United Explorer Card also offers:

If you’re not set on a United card but you want a dedicated business credit card, there are some other great options that earn flexible points. Consider these if you want options for redeeming your rewards for more than just United and Star Alliance partner flights:

If you have a small business and fly United Airlines with any frequency, then the United Business Card is definitely a card to consider. The card has a generous welcome bonus, and on top of that offers several perks that make this card worth holding onto. However, this isn’t a card I’d recommend using for your everyday spending.

The thing to remember is that whether you go with the United Business Card, it is important to get a co-branded MileagePlus credit card, given that it gives you access to improved mileage earning rates, plus improved mileage redemption rates. If you’re looking for a personal card instead, consider the United Explorer Card or United Quest Card.

If you want to learn more about the United Business Card, follow this link.

#126. MSC Opens Sales for 119-Night 2029 World Cruise

MSC Cruises has opened bookings for its 2029 world cruise, a 119-night voyage aboard the MSC Magnifica that visits 45 destinations in 21 countries, the company said in a press release.

The itinerary has nine overnight calls and 15 included shore excursions, and features a rare circumnavigation of Australia with new calls at Kangaroo Island, Broome and Darwin, plus a new overnight stay in Fremantle/Perth.

The ship then sails on to Indonesia for extended stays in Bali, Lombok and Java, including a new call at Celukan Bawang in north Bali.

Other new ports are Lautoka in Fiji and Timaru in New Zealand, while Milford Sound returns. Overnight stops are also planned in Rio de Janeiro, Ushuaia, Sydney and Singapore.

Guests can join the cruise in early January 2029 from four ports, Civitavecchia (Rome) on Jan. 4, Genoa, Marseille or Barcelona.

The fare includes the 15 excursions and the Dine & Drink beverage package, along with a 30 percent discount on laundry services.

MSC Voyagers Club members at Classic level and above get 5 percent off the booking price, and members also earn triple points on world cruise bookings made until Nov. 19 as part of a sales opening offer.

Airline credit cards offer a variety of value-added perks, including companion tickets worth hundreds or even thousands of dollars, access to airport lounges and free checked bags.  But one oft-advertised benefit is about convenience rather than savings: priority boarding.

This benefit, included with many airline credit cards, can get you to at least the middle of those long gate lines in time to find overhead space for your carry-on bag before the rest of the passengers trundle aboard.

Here's a look at what boarding privileges come with cobranded airline credit cards, followed by details on each airline to help you understand the nuances.

*For the purposes of boarding group order, we are not including preboarding as its own specially designated grouping.

Unfortunately, several airlines do not make priority boarding part of their credit card benefits. These generally include no-annual-fee cards and a select few mid-tier cards. Make sure to check your card's guide to benefits for more information.

**The information for these cards has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

For the vast majority of cobranded airline credit cards, you don’t need to use your card to purchase your flight — whether you’re paying cash or just covering taxes and fees on an award ticket — to receive priority boarding. Instead, the benefit is tied to your frequent flyer account.

As long as your loyalty number is attached to your reservation (and to any eligible companions on the same booking), you should receive the appropriate boarding group automatically.

Alaska Airlines offers preboarding for folks needing a little more time, plus seven additional distinct boarding groups.

As you can see, Atmos cardholders who do not hold elite status board with group C, the fourth out of seven formal groups. The other thing to note is that they must purchase their flight with their card to receive priority boarding, so just holding an Atmos credit card is not enough to enjoy priority boarding privileges.

Related: Why the Atmos Rewards Summit was our favorite new personal credit card last year

American Airlines' boarding procedure includes nine boarding groups plus special preboarding options. The good news is that if you have one of the major American AAdvantage credit cards, it should get you onto the plane early.

Here's a breakdown of American Airlines' boarding order and groupings:

The information for the AAdvantage MileUp card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The best you can hope for as just an AAdvantage cardholder without elite status is to be in the eighth boarding group out of all 13 groups. As for those who get onto the plane with Group 5 (the ninth boarding group in reality), they include members with the following credit cards:

While most AAdvantage credit cards are created equal when it comes to boarding, the AAdvantage Executive Mastercard will give you a one-group advantage over the others.

Note that you only have to hold one of these travel cards for the benefit to apply — you don't have to purchase your ticket with it.

Related: American Airlines elite status: What it is and how to earn it

Delta has eight official boarding groups, excluding preboarding, but actually nine if you count a non-numbered group for families with strollers. Delta cobranded credit card can help you move into Zone 5.

Assuming you don't have SkyPriority or other elite status and you're just flying economy, the best you can hope for as a Delta cardmember is to board before the first group in the main cabin.

While overhead space will likely be available at that point, it's not a sure bet, considering all the passengers who can board before you.

Related: The best credit cards for Delta flyers

This budget carrier has a cobranded credit card with Barclays that will get you onto the aircraft relatively early.

Here's how Frontier's boarding process goes.

Carrying the Frontier Airlines World Mastercard from Barclays will squeeze you in at the start of general boarding — or the fourth group out of seven. This lines up with most other airlines' cards, but might be slightly better or worse, depending on how many other passengers purchase carry-ons or one of the fare-bundling options.

Related: Why now is the perfect time to get the Frontier Airlines World Mastercard

With the JetBlue Business and JetBlue Premier Card, you'll receive Group 3 boarding on all JetBlue-operated flights.

If you hit Mosaic status through flying or credit card spending, you move up to the second overall boarding group and have overhead space basically guaranteed.

Note that JetBlue Plus Card and JetBlue Card holders do not receive priority boarding.

Holding a Southwest credit card will help you board the plane earlier.

Here's how Southwest boarding priority works:

All of the Southwest cards guarantee at least Group 5 boarding, though if you receive an earlier boarding position based on elite status, fare or seat type, you will move up in the boarding order (to Groups 1-4).

Related: Comparing Southwest card benefits: The Southwest Plus, Premier and Priority go head-to-head

United's boarding procedures involve seven groups (we're counting preboarding for this airline since it involves so many different types of passengers).

Each group includes many possible passengers and takes a unique approach to boarding.

The information for the United Presidential Plus, Presidential Plus Business and MileagePlus Awards cards has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

If there are multiple passengers on the same reservation seated in economy, each traveler will get the highest applicable boarding group given to any of the travelers within the reservation (except basic economy, which will always be Group 6 unless you're a Premier elite member, Star Alliance Gold member or select United cardholder).

Those with the basic United Gateway℠ Card (see rates and fees) don't receive any boarding or baggage privileges.

Related: The best credit cards for United Airlines flyers

Carrying an airline's midrange or premium credit card will get you on the plane earlier than most economy passengers, helping you secure overhead space for your bag.

While this perk alone is probably not worth carrying a credit card, particularly if you have elite status with an airline, by combining it with other benefits like free checked bags and discounts on inflight purchases, you can maximize your airline credit card to make the flying experience that much better.

#128. VIVA Cruises Reveals 2028 River Season with 325 Sailings Across 7 Ships

VIVA Cruises has unveiled its 2028 river cruise season, featuring an expanded program of 325 sailings across seven ships to mark the company’s 10th anniversary.

The anniversary season will include new itineraries, increased departures and a collection of themed cruises, offering more opportunities to explore Europe’s waterways, including the Rhine, Main, Moselle, Danube and Douro rivers, as well as itineraries through the canals of Germany and the Baltic coast.

It follows the announcement of the 2028 program for its VIVA Boutique line in France and Italy.

“As we celebrate 10 years of VIVA Cruises, we’re proud of how far we’ve come and excited for what lies ahead,” said Nasim Ghannadian, vice president sales & marketing North America of VIVA Cruises.

“Our 2028 season reflects that momentum, with more itineraries, expanded departures and unique onboard experiences that give travelers even more ways to discover Europe. We look forward to marking this milestone with our guests and continuing to deliver the exceptional river cruising experiences that define VIVA Cruises.”

The cruise line said that Vienna will play an even greater role in the 2028 cruise program, paired with an extended offer of roundtrip cruises on the Rhine, Moselle and Danube.

After undergoing extensive renovation in 2027, the Viva Moments will join the company’s Danube fleet, offering new seven-night itineraries between Passau, Vienna and Budapest.

The Viva Enjoy will offer even more seven-night cruises roundtrip from Vienna with 22 departures, with Regensburg introduced as an additional turnaround port.

The Viva Two introduces new five-night Danube cruises connecting Passau, Vienna, Budapest and Bratislava.

The Viva One increases its seven-night Moselle roundtrips from Düsseldorf from 10 to 15 departures, while introducing new four-night Rhine cruises in November and December, visiting destinations including Bonn, Mainz and Koblenz.

The ship will also operate an Ambassador Cruise, a special journey for loyal guests of the company.

Another highlight is a new 10-night cruises aboard the Viva Ruby, offering the opportunity to discover three countries in one journey: from Basel in Switzerland, via Nancy in France,  to Düsseldorf in Germany.

The 2028 season will also introduce more themed departures, centered around music, culinary exploration, wine and entertainment, including:

Complementing the offer are 320 shore excursions across 13 river regions, offering everything from cultural discoveries and regional flavors to exclusive experiences in smaller groups.

Cruises booked between October 15 and November 15, 2026, get a complimentary upgrade to the next higher cabin category.

#129. Royal Caribbean Places China at Center of Asia Strategy

Royal Caribbean is deepening its commitment to China while broadening its strategy across Asia, as the cruise company seeks to capitalize on changing travel preferences and growing demand for experience-led vacations.

Benjamin Bouldin, president of Greater China and managing director of Asia at Royal Caribbean, said China remains a critical market for the company after 17 years of continuous investment. But the strategy is evolving beyond a China-focused approach toward a more integrated Asia platform connecting Greater China, Southeast Asia and other regional markets.

For the 2026-27 season, the Spectrum of the Seas will continue operating from Shanghai and Hong Kong, which Bouldin described as complementary homeports. Shanghai provides access to mainland Chinese travelers and the country’s expanding outbound market, while Hong Kong serves as an international gateway to Southeast Asia and longer-haul markets.

The Spectrum is scheduled to operate more than 70 cruises ranging from two to nine nights, visiting about 20 destinations in Japan, South Korea and Vietnam. Royal Caribbean expects the ships to attract not only Chinese travelers but also international guests, particularly on longer Hong Kong departures. The company is responding with multilingual services, varied dining options, entertainment and guest communications aimed at an increasingly diverse customer base.

Royal Caribbean plans to expand the range and flexibility of its Asian offerings for 2027-28. That season will feature 56 sailings of three to 11 nights covering 22 Asian destinations. Among the new initiatives will be open-jaw cruises, including itineraries using Yokohama as both an arrival and departure point.

Bouldin said Chinese travelers are increasingly seeking novelty, deeper destination experiences and flexibility rather than conventional shopping-focused trips. That shift is influencing Royal Caribbean’s product development as the company attempts to position cruising as a broader vacation experience centered on discovery, entertainment and time with family and friends.

The broader fleet deployment reflects the regional strategy. The Navigator of the Seas will operate year-round from Singapore beginning in October 2026, while the Quantum of the Seas is scheduled to sail from Singapore from October 2027 through March 2028. The Voyager of the Seas will operate from Singapore and Hong Kong from January through April 2028, including new Hong Kong round trips and a Singapore-to-Hong Kong itinerary.

Royal Caribbean is also adapting to changes in China’s travel distribution system, which Bouldin said is becoming increasingly focused on independent travelers and digital sales. The company’s Royal Partner+ platform provides travel agents with live inventory, booking confirmations, sales tools, training and event support. By the end of the second quarter, more than 200 travel partners had joined the platform, with nearly 6,000 registered users across more than 40 Chinese cities.

Bouldin characterized China’s cruise industry as entering a “second golden decade,” with greater brand diversity and product variety helping expand the overall market. Royal Caribbean’s strategy, he said, is less about competing directly with individual brands and more about developing modern cruise products and strengthening connections among Asian markets.

The company sees China and the wider Asia-Pacific region as long-term growth opportunities, with its strategy focused on increasing cruise adoption through differentiated products, immersive itineraries, international sourcing and stronger regional connectivity.

Excerpted from the Fall 2026 Cruise Industry News Quarterly Magazine.
